items.title: JavaScript Strings
items.excerpt: Create and combine strings, read characters, and use the essential string methods to search, slice, change case, trim, split and replace text.
items.content:
Strings hold text: names, messages, URLs, whole articles. Because so much of web development is about text, JavaScript gives strings many built-in methods, ready-made functions that work on them.

Creating strings

const a = "double quotes";
const b = 'single quotes';
const c = `backticks: ${a.length} characters in a`;
console.log(a, b, c);

If your text contains one kind of quote, wrap it in the other, or escape it with a backslash:

const s1 = "It's easy";
const s2 = 'She said "hi"';
const s3 = 'It\'s also fine';
const s4 = "Line one\nLine two"; // \n is a new line
console.log(s1, s2, s3);
console.log(s4);

Template literals can span several lines directly:

const card = `Name: Asha
Course: JavaScript
Lesson: 7`;
console.log(card);

Length and characters

const word = "VitalStack";
console.log(word.length);        // 10
console.log(word[0]);            // "V": the first character is at index 0
console.log(word[word.length - 1]); // "k": the last character
console.log(word.at(-1));        // "k": at() accepts negative positions

Positions (indexes) start at 0, not 1. This is true for strings and arrays throughout JavaScript.

Strings are immutable: you can't change one character in place. Methods always return a new string.

Changing case and trimming

const email = "  Asha@Example.COM  ";
console.log(email.trim());               // "Asha@Example.COM"
console.log(email.trim().toLowerCase()); // "asha@example.com"
console.log("hello".toUpperCase());      // "HELLO"

trim() removes spaces from both ends, essential for cleaning form input. trimStart() and trimEnd() remove from one side.

Notice you can chain methods: each returns a new string, and the next method works on that.

Searching

const sentence = "Learn JavaScript at VitalStack";

console.log(sentence.includes("Java"));    // true
console.log(sentence.startsWith("Learn")); // true
console.log(sentence.endsWith("Stack"));   // true
console.log(sentence.indexOf("at"));       // 17: position of the first match
console.log(sentence.indexOf("Python"));   // -1: not found

Searches are case-sensitive. To search without caring about case, lower-case both sides:

const search = "javascript";
console.log(sentence.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase())); // true

Extracting parts with slice

const text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.slice(0, 4));  // "Java": from index 0 up to (not including) 4
console.log(text.slice(4));     // "Script": from 4 to the end
console.log(text.slice(-6));    // "Script": the last 6 characters

slice(start, end) is the main method for cutting strings. (substring is similar; you'll see it in older code.)

Replacing

const msg = "I like cats. cats are great.";
console.log(msg.replace("cats", "dogs"));    // replaces the first match only
console.log(msg.replaceAll("cats", "dogs")); // replaces every match

Splitting and joining

const csv = "HTML,CSS,JavaScript";
const parts = csv.split(",");
console.log(parts);              // ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"]
console.log(parts.join(" | "));  // "HTML | CSS | JavaScript"

const letters = "hello".split("");
console.log(letters);            // ["h", "e", "l", "l", "o"]
console.log(letters.reverse().join("")); // "olleh"

split turns a string into an array; join turns an array back into a string. Together they solve many text problems.

Padding and repeating

console.log("7".padStart(3, "0"));  // "007"
console.log("5".padStart(2, "0") + ":" + "3".padStart(2, "0")); // "05:03"
console.log("=".repeat(20));

padStart is perfect for formatting times, dates and invoice numbers.

A practical example: making a URL slug

function slugify(title) {
  return title
    .trim()
    .toLowerCase()
    .replaceAll(" ", "-");
}

console.log(slugify("  JavaScript Strings Explained ")); // "javascript-strings-explained"

(You'll learn functions properly in lesson 15. For now, notice how chaining makes each step clear.)

Comparing strings

console.log("abc" === "abc");     // true
console.log("abc" === "ABC");     // false
console.log("ä".localeCompare("z", "de")); // -1: sorts correctly for languages

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting indexes start at 0: the first character is str[0].
  • Expecting methods to change the original: name.toUpperCase() returns a new string; save it: name = name.toUpperCase().
  • Case-sensitive searches that miss matches.
  • **Using replace when you meant replaceAll.**

Exercise

  1. Take " hello WORLD " and turn it into "Hello world" (trim, lower-case, then capitalise the first letter with slice).
  2. Check if an email address contains @ and ends with .com.
  3. Count the words in a sentence with split(" ") and .length.
  4. Reverse any word and check whether it's a palindrome (like "level").
  5. Format the time 9:5 as "09:05" with padStart.

Summary

  • Create strings with quotes or backticks; escape quotes with \.
  • length and [index] read strings; indexes start at 0; strings never change in place.
  • Key methods: trim, toLowerCase, includes, indexOf, slice, replaceAll, split, padStart.
  • Chain methods to do several steps in one readable expression.

Next, you'll work with numbers and the Math object.

items.title: JavaScript Numbers
items.excerpt: Work with numbers: rounding, fixed decimals, converting from strings, NaN checks, the Math object, random numbers and formatting prices.
items.content:
Numbers are everywhere in programs: prices, scores, sizes, timers. JavaScript has a single number type for both whole numbers and decimals, plus a built-in Math object full of useful functions.

Integers and decimals

const items = 3;          // integer
const price = 249.99;     // decimal (floating point)
const big = 1_000_000;    // underscores make big numbers readable
console.log(items * price, big);

The decimal precision problem

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);    // false

Computers store decimals in binary, and some decimals (like 0.1) can't be stored exactly. It's the same in Python, Java and most languages. Two solutions:

// 1. Round when displaying
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2));  // "0.30"

// 2. For money, calculate in the smallest unit (paise, cents)
const pricePaise = 24999;     // ₹249.99
const totalPaise = pricePaise * 3;
console.log(totalPaise / 100); // 749.97

Rounding

const n = 4.567;
console.log(Math.round(n));  // 5: nearest whole number
console.log(Math.floor(n));  // 4: always down
console.log(Math.ceil(n));   // 5: always up
console.log(Math.trunc(-4.7)); // -4: just removes the decimals
console.log(n.toFixed(1));   // "4.6": a string with 1 decimal

toFixed() returns a string, which is perfect for display. Convert back with Number() if you need to calculate further.

Math.ceil is handy for page counts: 23 items at 10 per page needs Math.ceil(23 / 10) = 3 pages.

Converting strings to numbers

Values from form fields and URLs are always strings:

console.log(Number("42"));       // 42
console.log(Number("42.5"));     // 42.5
console.log(Number(""));         // 0 (careful!)
console.log(Number("42px"));     // NaN
console.log(parseInt("42px"));   // 42: reads digits until it hits something else
console.log(parseFloat("3.75 kg")); // 3.75
console.log(+"7");               // 7: the unary plus also converts
  • Number() is strict: the whole string must be a number.
  • parseInt() and parseFloat() read from the start and stop at the first invalid character.

NaN and checking for valid numbers

const result = Number("abc");
console.log(result);                 // NaN
console.log(result === NaN);         // false: NaN is not equal to anything, even itself!
console.log(Number.isNaN(result));   // true: the correct check
console.log(Number.isFinite(42));    // true
console.log(Number.isInteger(4.0));  // true
console.log(Number.isInteger(4.5));  // false

When validating user input, Number.isFinite(Number(value)) checks that it's a real, usable number.

The Math object

console.log(Math.max(4, 19, 7));   // 19
console.log(Math.min(4, 19, 7));   // 4
console.log(Math.abs(-12));        // 12: distance from zero
console.log(Math.sqrt(81));        // 9
console.log(Math.pow(2, 8));       // 256 (same as 2 ** 8)
console.log(Math.PI);              // 3.141592653589793

Math.max(...array) finds the largest value in an array (the ... "spread" operator is explained in the Arrays lessons):

const scores = [72, 95, 88];
console.log(Math.max(...scores)); // 95

Random numbers

Math.random() returns a decimal from 0 (included) up to 1 (not included):

console.log(Math.random());

// A whole number from 1 to 6, like a dice roll:
const dice = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
console.log("You rolled", dice);

// Pick a random item from an array:
const tips = ["Drink water", "Take a break", "Stretch"];
console.log(tips[Math.floor(Math.random() * tips.length)]);

The pattern Math.floor(Math.random() * N) gives a whole number from 0 to N − 1. (Don't use Math.random() for passwords or security codes; browsers have crypto.getRandomValues() for that.)

Formatting numbers for people

const amount = 1234567.891;
console.log(amount.toLocaleString("en-IN"));  // "12,34,567.891"
console.log(amount.toLocaleString("en-US"));  // "1,234,567.891"

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });
console.log(inr.format(249.5));    // "₹249.50"

const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });
console.log(usd.format(249.5));    // "$249.50"

const pct = new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { style: "percent" });
console.log(pct.format(0.42));     // "42%"

Intl.NumberFormat formats numbers correctly for any country, including currency symbols and digit grouping (Indian lakhs and crores, or Western thousands).

Common mistakes

  • Comparing decimals exactly: round first or work in whole units.
  • **Checking x === NaN**: always false. Use Number.isNaN(x).
  • **Forgetting toFixed returns a string**: price.toFixed(2) + 1 joins text.
  • **Math.random() * 6 without Math.floor**, giving decimals.
  • **Number("") being 0**: check for empty input separately.

Exercise

  1. Calculate the total of 3 items at ₹199.90 and show it with exactly 2 decimals.
  2. Write code that rolls two dice and prints both values and their sum.
  3. Convert "1500.75" to a number, add 18% tax, and format it as Indian rupees.
  4. Calculate how many pages are needed to show 47 search results at 10 per page.
  5. Check whether the input "12abc" is a valid number with Number() and Number.isNaN().

Summary

  • JavaScript has one number type; decimals can be slightly imprecise, so round or use whole units.
  • Math.round, floor, ceil and toFixed handle rounding.
  • Number(), parseInt() and parseFloat() convert strings; check results with Number.isNaN.
  • Math.random() makes random numbers; Intl.NumberFormat formats them for people.

Next, you'll make decisions in your code with if and else.

items.title: JavaScript If/Else
items.excerpt: Make decisions with if, else if and else, combine conditions, use truthy checks, write guard clauses and avoid deeply nested code.
items.content:
Programs need to make decisions: show a "Log in" button or the user's name, charge shipping or not, pass or fail a test. The if statement runs code only when a condition is true.

if

const temperature = 34;

if (temperature > 30) {
  console.log("It's hot. Drink water!");
}

console.log("This line always runs.");

The condition goes in brackets ( ). If it's true, the code inside the braces { } runs; if not, it's skipped.

else

const age = 16;

if (age >= 18) {
  console.log("You can vote.");
} else {
  console.log(`You can vote in ${18 - age} years.`);
}

Exactly one of the two blocks runs.

else if: more than two options

const score = 76;
let grade;

if (score >= 90) {
  grade = "A";
} else if (score >= 75) {
  grade = "B";
} else if (score >= 60) {
  grade = "C";
} else if (score >= 40) {
  grade = "D";
} else {
  grade = "F";
}

console.log(`Score ${score} → grade ${grade}`);

JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is true, then skips the rest. That's why the order matters here: a score of 95 is also >= 75, but it never reaches that check because the first condition already matched.

Combining conditions

const age = 25;
const hasLicence = true;
const isWeekend = false;

if (age >= 18 && hasLicence) {
  console.log("You can rent a car.");
}

if (isWeekend || age < 12) {
  console.log("Discounted ticket.");
} else {
  console.log("Regular ticket.");
}

if (!hasLicence) {
  console.log("Apply for a licence first.");
}

Use brackets to make complex conditions clear: if ((a && b) || c).

Truthy checks

Because every value is truthy or falsy, you can check whether something "exists":

const username = "";

if (username) {
  console.log(`Welcome back, ${username}!`);
} else {
  console.log("Welcome, guest!");
}

const cart = [];
if (cart.length) {
  console.log("You have items in your cart.");
} else {
  console.log("Your cart is empty.");
}

Remember: an empty array [] is truthy, so check cart.length, not cart. And 0 is falsy, so if (count) is false when count is 0.

A real example: form validation

<form id="signup">
  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" type="password">
  <button>Sign up</button>
  <p id="msg"></p>
</form>

<script>
  document.getElementById("signup").addEventListener("submit", function (event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    const pw = document.getElementById("pw").value;
    const msg = document.getElementById("msg");

    if (pw.length === 0) {
      msg.textContent = "Please enter a password.";
    } else if (pw.length < 8) {
      msg.textContent = "Use at least 8 characters.";
    } else if (!/[0-9]/.test(pw)) {
      msg.textContent = "Add at least one number.";
    } else {
      msg.textContent = "Looks good!";
    }
  });
</script>

Type different passwords and submit. (/[0-9]/.test(pw) checks for a digit using a regular expression; you don't need to understand it yet.)

Guard clauses: avoid deep nesting

Nested ifs quickly become hard to read:

function checkout(user, cart) {
  if (user) {
    if (cart.length > 0) {
      if (user.address) {
        return "Order placed!";
      } else {
        return "Add an address.";
      }
    } else {
      return "Cart is empty.";
    }
  } else {
    return "Please log in.";
  }
}
console.log(checkout({ address: "Pune" }, ["book"]));

The same logic with guard clauses handles the problem cases first and exits early:

function checkout(user, cart) {
  if (!user) return "Please log in.";
  if (cart.length === 0) return "Cart is empty.";
  if (!user.address) return "Add an address.";
  return "Order placed!";
}
console.log(checkout({ address: "Pune" }, []));

Flat, readable, and easy to extend. (You'll learn function and return in lesson 15.)

Ternary for simple choices

const isMember = true;
const price = isMember ? 199 : 299;
console.log(`Price: ₹${price}`);

Use the ternary for a quick choice between two values. Use if for anything that runs several statements.

Braces: always use them

JavaScript allows an if without braces for a single line:

const x = 5;
if (x > 3) console.log("big");

This is fine for very short guard clauses, but adding a second line later without adding braces is a classic bug. When in doubt, use braces.

Common mistakes

  • **= instead of ===** in the condition: if (x = 5) is always true.
  • **Wrong order of else if checks**, so a broad condition catches values meant for a later branch.
  • **Checking an empty array with if (arr)**, which is always true.
  • Semicolon after the condition: if (x > 3); { … } runs the block every time.

Exercise

  1. Given a number, print "positive", "negative" or "zero".
  2. Write a shipping calculator: free over ₹500, ₹40 under ₹500, and ₹0 for members whatever the total.
  3. Given an hour from 0–23, print "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening".
  4. Rewrite a three-level nested if from your own code with guard clauses.

Summary

  • if (condition) { … } runs code only when the condition is true; else handles the rest.
  • else if chains are checked top to bottom; the first match wins.
  • Combine conditions with &&, || and !; use truthy checks carefully.
  • Guard clauses keep logic flat and readable.

Next, you'll learn the switch statement for choosing between many fixed values.

items.title: How to Use AI to Learn Programming Faster
items.excerpt: A step-by-step study system for learning to code with an AI tutor: explanations at your level, practice questions, debugging help, project feedback and spaced review.
items.content:
Short answer: treat AI as a patient personal tutor, not an answer machine. Use it to explain concepts at your level, quiz you, give hints when you're stuck, and review your code, while you still write the code yourself.

Learning to code used to mean getting stuck alone for hours. Now you can get an explanation, a hint or a review in seconds. That's a huge advantage, if you use it in a way that builds skills instead of replacing them. Here's a study system that works.

The core rule: you write the code

Research on learning consistently shows that we remember what we actively produce, not what we passively read. An AI that writes all your code feels productive, but your brain does none of the work. So:

  • AI explains, quizzes, hints and reviews.
  • You design, type, run, debug and fix.

Keep that split and AI will roughly double your learning speed.

Step 1: Follow a structured course

AI is great at answering questions, but bad at deciding what you should learn next. Follow a course with a clear order, such as the VitalStack paths: HTML → CSS → JavaScript, or straight to Python for data and AI. Use the AI alongside each lesson, not instead of it.

Step 2: Get explanations at your level

When a lesson doesn't click, ask for a different explanation. Tell the AI what you already know:

I'm on lesson 13 of a JavaScript course. I understand arrays and loops
but not array methods like map and filter. Explain map using a real-life
analogy, then one tiny example, then compare it to the for loop I'd
normally write.

Useful variations:

  • "Explain it like I'm 12."
  • "Explain it with a cooking analogy."
  • "Show me the most common mistake beginners make with this."
  • "What's the difference between X and Y, in a table?"

Step 3: Practise with generated exercises

Courses have a limited number of exercises. AI can make unlimited ones, matched to your level:

Give me 5 practice exercises on Python dictionaries, from easy to
medium. Don't include the answers. After I send my solutions, review
them one by one.

Do them in your own editor, run them, then paste your solutions for feedback. This "practise → feedback" loop is the fastest way to improve.

Step 4: Debug with hints, not fixes

When your code breaks, resist asking for the fix. Ask for a hint:

My code should print the even numbers from a list but prints nothing.
Don't give me the corrected code. Give me one hint about where to look.

[your code]
[what you expected vs what happened]

If one hint isn't enough, ask for a second, more specific hint. Finding the bug yourself, even with help, teaches you the debugging skill you'll use for the rest of your career.

Also learn to read errors yourself first: copy the last line of the error, try to understand it, and only then ask: "I think this error means X. Am I right?"

Step 5: Get code reviews

Once your code works, ask how to make it better:

Here's my solution to an exercise. It works. Review it like a friendly
senior developer: is anything wrong, unclear or non-idiomatic? Suggest
improvements but explain why, and keep my overall approach.

You'll learn idioms (the "natural" way to write things in a language) much faster than from reading alone.

Step 6: Build small projects with AI as a mentor

Projects are where knowledge becomes skill. Use AI to plan, not to build:

I've finished HTML and CSS and 10 JavaScript lessons. Suggest 3 small
project ideas I could finish in a weekend. For the one I choose, break
it into 5 milestones, but don't write the code.

Then build milestone by milestone, asking for hints and reviews along the way. Good beginner projects: a tip calculator, a quiz, a to-do list (like our JavaScript project), a personal portfolio, an expense tracker (like our Python project).

Step 7: Review with spaced repetition

You forget quickly unless you review. Once a week:

Quiz me with 10 short questions on what I've learned this week: Python
lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. Ask one question at a time and
wait for my answer before giving feedback.

Questions you get wrong tell you exactly what to revise.

A weekly routine that works

Consistency matters far more than long sessions. One focused hour a day beats a seven-hour weekend binge.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Copy-pasting solutions you don't understand.
  • Asking before trying. Give yourself 15–20 minutes of honest effort first.
  • Endless tutorial mode. Reading and asking without building projects.
  • Trusting everything. AI can be wrong; run the code and check official docs when something seems off.
  • Skipping fundamentals because "AI can write it". You need fundamentals to judge what AI writes.

Frequently asked questions

Can I learn programming only with AI?

You can, but a structured course plus AI is faster and leaves fewer gaps. The course gives the path; the AI gives personal help along it.

How long does it take to learn to code with AI help?

For the basics of one language (variables to functions and small projects), about 2–3 months at an hour a day is realistic. Becoming job-ready usually takes 6–12 months of steady practice and projects.

Which language should I start with?

For websites, start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. For data, automation and AI, start with Python. Both are excellent first languages.

Is it okay to use AI in exercises?

Try every exercise yourself first. Then use AI to check, explain mistakes and suggest improvements.

Summary

  • Use AI as a tutor: explanations, exercises, hints, reviews and quizzes.
  • Keep the core rule: you write and debug the code.
  • Follow a structured course and build small projects from early on.
  • Review weekly with AI quizzes, and stay consistent with daily practice.

items.title: JavaScript Switch
items.excerpt: Choose between many exact values with switch, understand break and fall-through, use default, and know when an object lookup is cleaner.
items.content:
When you compare one value against many possible exact values, a long else if chain gets repetitive. The switch statement is designed for exactly this case.

Basic switch

const day = "tue";
let message;

switch (day) {
  case "mon":
    message = "Start of the week. Plan your lessons.";
    break;
  case "tue":
    message = "Tuesday: practise JavaScript.";
    break;
  case "wed":
    message = "Midweek review.";
    break;
  default:
    message = "Keep going!";
}

console.log(message);

How it works:

  1. The value in switch ( ) is compared with each case using strict equality (===).
  2. When a case matches, the code after it runs.
  3. break exits the switch.
  4. default runs if no case matches (like a final else).

The same logic with if/else

const day = "tue";
let message;

if (day === "mon") {
  message = "Start of the week. Plan your lessons.";
} else if (day === "tue") {
  message = "Tuesday: practise JavaScript.";
} else if (day === "wed") {
  message = "Midweek review.";
} else {
  message = "Keep going!";
}
console.log(message);

Both are correct. switch reads more clearly when there are many cases comparing the same value with fixed options.

Don't forget break: fall-through

Without break, execution "falls through" into the next case:

const level = 2;

switch (level) {
  case 1:
    console.log("Level 1 unlocked");
  case 2:
    console.log("Level 2 unlocked");
  case 3:
    console.log("Level 3 unlocked");
}
// Prints "Level 2 unlocked" and "Level 3 unlocked"

Once case 2 matches, every following case runs too, until a break or the end. Forgetting break is the most common switch bug.

Grouping cases on purpose

Fall-through is useful when several values should share the same code:

const month = 2;
let days;

switch (month) {
  case 2:
    days = 28;
    break;
  case 4:
  case 6:
  case 9:
  case 11:
    days = 30;
    break;
  default:
    days = 31;
}

console.log(`Month ${month} has ${days} days (ignoring leap years).`);

Empty cases stacked on top of each other all run the same block.

Switch uses strict comparison

const input = "1";

switch (input) {
  case 1:
    console.log("number one");
    break;
  case "1":
    console.log("string one");
    break;
}
// "string one": "1" !== 1

Values from forms are strings, so convert them (Number(input)) or use string cases.

Ranges with switch (true)

switch compares exact values, so ranges like "score above 90" are better written with if/else. You'll sometimes see this trick:

const score = 82;

switch (true) {
  case score >= 90:
    console.log("A");
    break;
  case score >= 75:
    console.log("B");
    break;
  default:
    console.log("C or below");
}

It works (each case expression is compared with true), but most developers find an if/else chain clearer for ranges.

Returning from switch inside a function

Inside a function, return exits immediately, so no break is needed:

function statusLabel(code) {
  switch (code) {
    case 200: return "OK";
    case 404: return "Not Found";
    case 500: return "Server Error";
    default:  return "Unknown status";
  }
}

console.log(statusLabel(404));
console.log(statusLabel(418));

An alternative: object lookup

For mapping values to values, an object is often shortest:

const labels = {
  200: "OK",
  404: "Not Found",
  500: "Server Error"
};

const code = 500;
console.log(labels[code] ?? "Unknown status");

You'll learn objects in lesson 14. Rule of thumb:

  • Object lookup: simple value → value mappings.
  • switch: each case needs to run different statements.
  • if/else: ranges and complex conditions.

Common mistakes

  • **Missing break**, causing accidental fall-through.
  • Type mismatch: case 1 won't match the string "1".
  • Using switch for ranges where if/else is clearer.
  • **Forgetting default** for unexpected values.

Exercise

  1. Write a switch that converts a number 1–7 into a day name, with a default "Invalid day".
  2. Group cases so that "sat" and "sun" print "Weekend" and other days print "Weekday".
  3. Write a simple calculator: given two numbers and an operator ("+", "-", "*", "/"), print the result.
  4. Rewrite your day-name switch as an object lookup.

Summary

  • switch compares one value against many case values with ===.
  • break stops execution; without it, code falls through to the next case.
  • Stack empty cases to share code; default handles everything else.
  • Use object lookups for simple mappings and if/else for ranges.

Next, you'll repeat code with for and while loops.

items.title: JavaScript Loops (for, while)
items.excerpt: Repeat code with for, while, do...while, for...of and for...in loops, control them with break and continue, and avoid infinite loops.
items.content:
Computers are great at repetition. A loop runs the same code many times: printing every item in a list, counting down a timer, trying a password until it's right. JavaScript has several loops; each suits a different situation.

The for loop

for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log(`Lap ${i}`);
}

The brackets have three parts, separated by semicolons:

  1. Start: let i = 1 runs once, before the loop begins.
  2. Condition: i <= 5 is checked before each round. If false, the loop stops.
  3. Update: i++ runs after each round.

So the loop runs with i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then stops when i becomes 6.

Counting in other ways

for (let i = 10; i > 0; i -= 2) {
  console.log(i); // 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
}

// Times table
const n = 7;
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  console.log(`${n} × ${i} = ${n * i}`);
}

Looping over an array by index

const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];

for (let i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) {
  console.log(`${i + 1}. ${fruits[i]}`);
}

Indexes start at 0, so the condition is i < fruits.length (not <=).

for...of: the easy way to loop over values

const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];

for (const fruit of fruits) {
  console.log(fruit);
}

for (const letter of "Hi!") {
  console.log(letter);
}

for...of gives you each value directly: no index, no off-by-one errors. Use it whenever you don't need the index. It works on arrays, strings and other "iterable" collections.

while

A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many rounds you'll need:

let balance = 1000;
let months = 0;

while (balance < 2000) {
  balance = balance * 1.1; // 10% growth per month
  months++;
}

console.log(`It takes ${months} months to double: ${balance.toFixed(2)}`);

do...while

do...while checks the condition after each round, so the code always runs at least once:

let roll;
let attempts = 0;

do {
  roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
  attempts++;
  console.log(`Rolled ${roll}`);
} while (roll !== 6);

console.log(`Got a 6 after ${attempts} attempts.`);

break and continue

  • break exits the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this round and moves on to the next.
const numbers = [4, 9, -1, 16, 25];

for (const n of numbers) {
  if (n < 0) {
    console.log("Negative number found, stopping.");
    break;
  }
  console.log(`√${n} = ${Math.sqrt(n)}`);
}

for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  if (i % 3 === 0) continue; // skip multiples of 3
  console.log(i);
}

Looping over objects with for...in

const course = { title: "JavaScript", lessons: 25, level: "beginner" };

for (const key in course) {
  console.log(`${key}: ${course[key]}`);
}

for...in loops over an object's keys (property names). Don't use it on arrays; use for...of there. You'll also see Object.entries() in the Objects lesson, which is often nicer.

Nested loops

A loop inside a loop runs the inner loop completely for every round of the outer one:

for (let row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {
  let line = "";
  for (let col = 1; col <= 4; col++) {
    line += "* ";
  }
  console.log(line);
}

Nested loops are useful for grids and tables, but can get slow on large data: 1,000 × 1,000 is a million rounds.

Building results in a loop

A very common pattern: start with an empty value and add to it in each round.

const prices = [199, 349, 99, 520];
let total = 0;
let expensive = [];

for (const price of prices) {
  total += price;
  if (price > 300) {
    expensive.push(price);
  }
}

console.log(`Total: ₹${total}`);
console.log("Items over ₹300:", expensive);

In the Array Methods lesson you'll learn shortcuts like reduce and filter that do this in one line.

Infinite loops

If the condition never becomes false, the loop never stops and the page freezes:

// DON'T RUN THIS
// let i = 0;
// while (i < 5) {
//   console.log(i);   // i never changes, so i < 5 is always true
// }

Always make sure something inside the loop moves it towards its end. If a page freezes, close the tab.

Which loop to use

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one errors: i <= arr.length goes one past the end.
  • Forgetting to update the counter in a while loop → infinite loop.
  • **Using for...in on arrays**, which gives string indexes and can include extra properties.
  • Changing an array's length while looping over it.

Exercise

  1. Print all even numbers from 2 to 20.
  2. Sum the numbers from 1 to 100 (the answer is 5050).
  3. Given an array of names, print only names longer than 4 characters with for...of.
  4. Print a 5-row triangle of stars (*, **, ***…) with nested loops.
  5. Use a while loop to find how many times you can halve 1000 before it drops below 1.

Summary

  • for counts; for...of loops over values; for...in loops over object keys.
  • while repeats while a condition is true; do...while runs at least once.
  • break exits a loop; continue skips to the next round.
  • Make sure every loop can end.

Next, you'll learn arrays, the main way to store lists in JavaScript.

items.title: JavaScript Arrays
items.excerpt: Store ordered lists in arrays: create them, read and change items by index, add and remove with push, pop, shift, unshift and splice, and copy with spread.
items.content:
An array is an ordered list of values: a shopping list, the lessons in a course, the scores in a game. Arrays are one of the two data structures you'll use constantly in JavaScript (the other is objects).

Creating arrays

const languages = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];
const scores = [92, 87, 95, 78];
const mixed = ["Asha", 21, true, null];
const empty = [];

console.log(languages);
console.log(scores.length); // 4

Square brackets, values separated by commas. An array can hold any mix of types, though in practice each array usually holds one kind of thing.

Reading items by index

const colours = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(colours[0]);                  // "red": the first item
console.log(colours[2]);                  // "blue"
console.log(colours[colours.length - 1]); // "blue": the last item
console.log(colours.at(-1));              // "blue": at() supports negative indexes
console.log(colours[10]);                 // undefined: there's no item 10

The first item is at index 0, the last at length - 1.

Changing items

const week = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
week[1] = "Tuesday";
console.log(week); // ["Mon", "Tuesday", "Wed"]

Even with const, you can change what's inside an array; you just can't replace the whole array with a new one.

Adding and removing at the ends

const queue = ["Asha", "Rohan"];

queue.push("Meera");       // add to the end
console.log(queue);        // ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]

queue.unshift("Kabir");    // add to the start
console.log(queue);        // ["Kabir", "Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]

const last = queue.pop();  // remove from the end
console.log(last, queue);  // "Meera" ["Kabir", "Asha", "Rohan"]

const first = queue.shift(); // remove from the start
console.log(first, queue);   // "Kabir" ["Asha", "Rohan"]

Adding and removing in the middle: splice

const tasks = ["wake up", "exercise", "breakfast", "study"];

tasks.splice(1, 1);                    // at index 1, remove 1 item
console.log(tasks);                    // ["wake up", "breakfast", "study"]

tasks.splice(2, 0, "shower");          // at index 2, remove 0, insert "shower"
console.log(tasks);                    // ["wake up", "breakfast", "shower", "study"]

tasks.splice(0, 1, "wake up early");   // replace the first item
console.log(tasks);

splice(start, deleteCount, ...itemsToInsert) changes the array in place.

Finding items

const tags = ["html", "css", "js", "css"];

console.log(tags.includes("js"));     // true
console.log(tags.indexOf("css"));     // 1: first position
console.log(tags.lastIndexOf("css")); // 3
console.log(tags.indexOf("python"));  // -1: not found

Slicing and joining arrays

const letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"];

console.log(letters.slice(1, 3)); // ["b", "c"]: copy from 1 up to (not including) 3
console.log(letters.slice(-2));   // ["d", "e"]
console.log(letters);             // unchanged

const more = letters.concat(["f", "g"]);
console.log(more);

console.log(letters.join("-"));   // "a-b-c-d-e"

slice makes a copy and doesn't change the original; splice changes the original. Their names are confusingly similar, so double-check which one you mean.

The spread operator

... "spreads" an array's items out. It's the modern way to copy and combine arrays:

const frontend = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];
const backend = ["Python", "SQL"];

const fullStack = [...frontend, ...backend];
console.log(fullStack);

const copy = [...frontend];
copy.push("React");
console.log(frontend); // unchanged
console.log(copy);

Why copying matters

Arrays are stored by reference: assigning an array to another variable doesn't copy it.

const original = [1, 2, 3];
const sameArray = original;  // not a copy!
sameArray.push(4);
console.log(original);       // [1, 2, 3, 4]: changed too

Both names point to the same array. Use [...original] when you need an independent copy.

Destructuring

Pull values out of an array into variables:

const point = [10, 25];
const [x, y] = point;
console.log(x, y);

const [winner, runnerUp, ...others] = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera", "Kabir"];
console.log(winner, runnerUp, others);

Arrays of arrays

const board = [
  ["X", "O", "X"],
  ["O", "X", "O"],
  ["O", "X", "X"]
];
console.log(board[1][2]); // "O": row 1, column 2

Sorting

const names = ["Rohan", "asha", "Meera"];
names.sort();
console.log(names); // ["Meera", "Rohan", "asha"]: uppercase sorts first!

const nums = [10, 1, 5, 100];
nums.sort();
console.log(nums);  // [1, 10, 100, 5]: sorted as text!

nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);
console.log(nums);  // [1, 5, 10, 100]: numeric sort

By default, sort compares items as strings. For numbers, always pass a compare function (a, b) => a - b (you'll understand the arrow syntax in lesson 16). sort and reverse change the original array.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one: the last item is arr[arr.length - 1], not arr[arr.length].
  • Sorting numbers without a compare function.
  • **Thinking = copies an array**: use spread.
  • **Mixing up slice (copy) and splice (change).**

Exercise

  1. Create an array of five favourite films. Print the first, the last and the total count.
  2. Add one film to the start and one to the end; remove the third one with splice.
  3. Combine two arrays of friends with the spread operator.
  4. Sort [45, 3, 120, 7, 64] from smallest to largest.
  5. Use destructuring to get the first two items of an array and the rest separately.

Summary

  • Arrays are ordered lists; indexes start at 0; length gives the count.
  • push, pop, shift, unshift and splice add and remove items.
  • includes, indexOf, slice, concat and join search and copy.
  • Use spread [...arr] to copy or combine; sort numbers with (a, b) => a - b.

Next, you'll learn powerful array methods like map, filter and reduce.

items.title: JavaScript Array Methods
items.excerpt: Transform and search data with forEach, map, filter, find, some, every and reduce, and chain them together to process lists in a few readable lines.
items.content:
Most real programs work with lists of data: products, users, messages, lessons. JavaScript arrays have built-in methods that let you loop, transform, search and summarise lists in one line each. Learning these well will change how you write code.

All the methods in this lesson take a function as an argument, which is called once for each item. We'll write those functions with the short arrow syntax, item => something. You'll learn functions in detail in lessons 15 and 16; for now, read n => n * 2 as "take n, give back n times 2".

The sample data

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, category: "electronics", inStock: false },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, category: "electronics", inStock: true },
  { name: "Backpack", price: 1899, category: "bags", inStock: true }
];
console.log(products.length, "products");

The examples below each start with a copy of this data so they run on their own.

forEach: do something with each item

const names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"];

names.forEach((name, index) => {
  console.log(`${index + 1}. ${name}`);
});

forEach simply runs the function for every item. It returns nothing. (for...of does the same job, and many developers prefer it.)

map: transform every item

map creates a new array of the same length, with each item transformed:

const prices = [120, 1499, 250];

const withTax = prices.map(p => Math.round(p * 1.18));
console.log(withTax); // [142, 1769, 295]

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120 },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250 }
];
const labels = products.map(p => `${p.name}: ₹${p.price}`);
console.log(labels);

Use map whenever you think "I want a list of X from this list of Y". It's how lists of data become lists of HTML elements on a page.

filter: keep only matching items

filter creates a new array with only the items for which the function returns true:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, inStock: false },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, inStock: true }
];

const available = products.filter(p => p.inStock);
console.log(available.map(p => p.name)); // ["Notebook", "USB cable"]

const cheap = products.filter(p => p.price < 300);
console.log(cheap.length); // 2

const numbers = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3];
console.log(numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)); // [12, 8]

find and findIndex: the first match

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Asha" },
  { id: 2, name: "Rohan" },
  { id: 3, name: "Meera" }
];

const user = users.find(u => u.id === 2);
console.log(user);           // { id: 2, name: "Rohan" }

const missing = users.find(u => u.id === 99);
console.log(missing);        // undefined

console.log(users.findIndex(u => u.name === "Meera")); // 2

find returns the first matching item (or undefined); filter returns an array of all matches.

some and every: yes/no questions

const scores = [72, 88, 45, 91];

console.log(scores.some(s => s < 50));   // true: at least one failed
console.log(scores.every(s => s >= 40)); // true: everyone passed

reduce: boil a list down to one value

reduce combines all items into a single result: a total, a maximum, a count, even an object.

const cart = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, qty: 3 },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, qty: 1 },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, qty: 2 }
];

const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0);
console.log(`Total: ₹${total}`); // ₹1208

How it works:

  • The function receives an accumulator (sum, the result so far) and the current item.
  • Whatever it returns becomes the accumulator for the next item.
  • The 0 at the end is the starting value.

Round by round: 0 → 360 → 610 → 1208.

Counting things by category:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", category: "stationery" },
  { name: "Headphones", category: "electronics" },
  { name: "Pen set", category: "stationery" }
];

const counts = products.reduce((acc, p) => {
  acc[p.category] = (acc[p.category] || 0) + 1;
  return acc;
}, {});

console.log(counts); // { stationery: 2, electronics: 1 }

Chaining methods

Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain them into a clear data pipeline:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, category: "electronics", inStock: false },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, category: "electronics", inStock: true },
  { name: "Backpack", price: 1899, category: "bags", inStock: true }
];

const result = products
  .filter(p => p.inStock)
  .filter(p => p.price < 1000)
  .sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)
  .map(p => `${p.name} (₹${p.price})`);

console.log(result);

Read it top to bottom: in stock → under ₹1000 → cheapest first → formatted labels. (Careful: sort changes the array it's called on. Here that's fine, because filter already made a new array.)

Other handy methods

const nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]];
console.log(nested.flat());                   // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

const words = ["hello", "world"];
console.log(words.flatMap(w => w.split(""))); // all letters in one array

const nums = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = nums.toSorted((a, b) => a - b); // sorted copy (modern browsers)
console.log(nums, sorted);

console.log(Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i * 10)); // [0, 10, 20, 30, 40]

Which method do I need?

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to return in an arrow function with braces: p => { p.price * 2 } returns undefined. Write p => p.price * 2 or add return.
  • **Using map just to loop** and ignoring its result; use forEach.
  • **Forgetting the starting value in reduce**.
  • **Expecting filter to return one item**; it always returns an array.

Exercise

Using the products array from the chaining example:

  1. Get an array of just the product names with map.
  2. Get all electronics with filter.
  3. Find the product called "Backpack" with find.
  4. Check if any product costs more than ₹1500 with some.
  5. Calculate the total price of all in-stock products with filter + reduce.
  6. Produce a list of "NAME – ₹PRICE" strings for stationery, sorted by price.

Summary

  • map transforms, filter selects, find gets the first match, reduce combines.
  • some and every answer yes/no questions about a list.
  • These methods return new arrays (except forEach, sort and reverse), so they chain well.
  • Chained methods turn complex data processing into readable pipelines.

Next, you'll learn objects, the way to group related data with names.

items.title: JavaScript Objects
items.excerpt: Group related data with objects: create them, read and update properties with dot and bracket notation, loop over them, copy them, destructure them and add methods.
items.content:
Arrays store ordered lists. Objects store related information under names, like a user's name, email and age, or a product's title, price and stock. Almost all data on the web, from API responses to settings, is made of objects.

Creating an object

const user = {
  name: "Asha Verma",
  age: 21,
  email: "asha@example.com",
  isMember: true,
  skills: ["HTML", "CSS"]
};

console.log(user);

An object is written with braces { } and contains properties: key: value pairs separated by commas. Values can be any type, including arrays and other objects.

Reading properties

const user = { name: "Asha", age: 21, "favourite colour": "teal" };

console.log(user.name);                 // dot notation
console.log(user["age"]);               // bracket notation
console.log(user["favourite colour"]);  // brackets for keys with spaces

const field = "name";
console.log(user[field]);               // brackets with a variable

console.log(user.phone);                // undefined: no such property
  • Dot notation (user.name) is the usual way.
  • Bracket notation is needed when the key is stored in a variable or contains spaces or hyphens.

Adding, changing and deleting

const book = { title: "Atomic Habits", pages: 320 };

book.pages = 322;            // change
book.author = "James Clear"; // add a new property
delete book.pages;           // remove

console.log(book);

Like arrays, a const object can have its properties changed; you just can't replace the whole object.

Nested objects

const order = {
  id: 1042,
  customer: {
    name: "Rohan",
    address: { city: "Pune", pin: "411001" }
  },
  items: [
    { name: "Notebook", qty: 2 },
    { name: "Pen", qty: 5 }
  ]
};

console.log(order.customer.address.city); // "Pune"
console.log(order.items[1].name);         // "Pen"
console.log(order.items.length);          // 2

Read nested paths from left to right: order → customer → address → city.

Optional chaining

If a part of the path might be missing, ?. stops safely instead of throwing an error:

const user = { name: "Meera" };

// console.log(user.address.city);  // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
console.log(user.address?.city);     // undefined, no error
console.log(user.address?.city ?? "City not set");

Methods: functions inside objects

const counter = {
  count: 0,
  increment() {
    this.count++;
    return this.count;
  },
  reset() {
    this.count = 0;
  }
};

counter.increment();
counter.increment();
console.log(counter.count); // 2
counter.reset();
console.log(counter.count); // 0

A function stored in an object is called a method. Inside it, this refers to the object the method was called on. You've used built-in methods all along: console.log, "text".toUpperCase().

Shorthand properties

When a variable has the same name as the key, you can write it once:

const name = "Kabir";
const age = 30;

const person = { name, age };   // same as { name: name, age: age }
console.log(person);

Looping over objects

const stock = { pens: 40, notebooks: 12, erasers: 0 };

console.log(Object.keys(stock));    // ["pens", "notebooks", "erasers"]
console.log(Object.values(stock));  // [40, 12, 0]
console.log(Object.entries(stock)); // [["pens", 40], ["notebooks", 12], ["erasers", 0]]

for (const [item, qty] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(`${item}: ${qty > 0 ? qty : "out of stock"}`);
}

Object.entries plus for...of is the cleanest way to loop over an object.

Checking whether a property exists

const settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 0 };

console.log("theme" in settings);           // true
console.log(Object.hasOwn(settings, "lang")); // false
console.log(settings.fontSize ? "set" : "not set"); // "not set": wrong, 0 is falsy!
console.log("fontSize" in settings ? "set" : "not set"); // "set": correct

Destructuring objects

const product = { title: "Backpack", price: 1899, stock: 7 };

const { title, price } = product;
console.log(title, price);

const { stock: available, colour = "black" } = product; // rename and default value
console.log(available, colour);

Destructuring is used everywhere in modern JavaScript, especially for function parameters.

Copying and merging

Objects, like arrays, are stored by reference:

const a = { x: 1 };
const b = a;      // same object, not a copy
b.x = 99;
console.log(a.x); // 99

const original = { theme: "light", size: 16 };
const copy = { ...original };                 // shallow copy
const updated = { ...original, theme: "dark" }; // copy + override
console.log(original, copy, updated);

The spread ... copies the top-level properties. Nested objects inside are still shared; for a full deep copy, use structuredClone(obj).

Arrays of objects

The most common data shape on the web:

const students = [
  { name: "Asha", score: 92 },
  { name: "Rohan", score: 78 },
  { name: "Meera", score: 85 }
];

const top = students.filter(s => s.score > 80).map(s => s.name);
console.log(top); // ["Asha", "Meera"]

Common mistakes

  • Missing commas between properties.
  • Dot notation with a variable: user.field looks for a property literally called "field". Use user[field].
  • Reading deep paths that might not exist: use ?..
  • **Thinking = copies an object**: use { ...obj } or structuredClone.

Exercise

  1. Create an object for a film with title, year, rating and an array of actors. Print a sentence about it.
  2. Add a director property, change the rating, and delete the year.
  3. Loop over the object with Object.entries and print each key and value.
  4. Create a bankAccount object with balance, deposit(amount) and withdraw(amount) methods. Don't allow withdrawing more than the balance.
  5. Use destructuring to pull out the title and rating.

Summary

  • Objects store key: value properties; read them with obj.key or obj["key"].
  • Use ?. for paths that may not exist and ?? for defaults.
  • Object.keys, values and entries let you loop over objects.
  • Destructuring and spread make reading, copying and merging objects easy.

Next, you'll learn functions, the reusable building blocks of every program.

items.title: JavaScript Functions
items.excerpt: Write reusable code with functions: declarations, parameters and arguments, return values, default and rest parameters, and functions as values.
items.content:
A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. Instead of repeating the same lines in ten places, you write them once as a function and call it ten times. Functions make code shorter, easier to read and easier to fix.

Declaring and calling a function

function greet() {
  console.log("Hello! Welcome to VitalStack.");
}

greet();
greet();
  • function starts the declaration, followed by the function's name and brackets.
  • The code inside { } is the function's body.
  • Writing greet() calls (runs) it. Without the brackets, nothing happens.

Parameters and arguments

Functions become powerful when they accept input:

function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
}

greet("Asha");
greet("Rohan");
  • name is a parameter: a variable that exists inside the function.
  • "Asha" is an argument: the actual value passed in when calling.

Several parameters are separated by commas:

function introduce(name, city, age) {
  console.log(`${name}, ${age}, lives in ${city}.`);
}

introduce("Meera", "Jaipur", 24);
introduce("Kabir", "Kochi");  // age is undefined

A missing argument becomes undefined.

Returning values

Most functions calculate something and give it back with return:

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

const sum = add(4, 6);
console.log(sum);              // 10
console.log(add(add(1, 2), 3)); // 6: use the result directly

return does two things:

  1. Sends a value back to wherever the function was called.
  2. Stops the function immediately. Code after return never runs.
function checkAge(age) {
  if (age < 0) {
    return "Invalid age";
  }
  if (age >= 18) {
    return "Adult";
  }
  return "Minor";
}

console.log(checkAge(25), checkAge(12), checkAge(-3));

A function without return gives back undefined.

console.log vs return

A very common beginner confusion:

function doubleLog(n) {
  console.log(n * 2);   // shows the value, but gives nothing back
}

function doubleReturn(n) {
  return n * 2;         // gives the value back to use later
}

const a = doubleLog(5);     // prints 10
const b = doubleReturn(5);  // prints nothing
console.log(a, b);          // undefined 10

Use return when the result is needed by other code; console.log is only for looking.

Default parameters

function createUser(name, role = "student", active = true) {
  return { name, role, active };
}

console.log(createUser("Asha"));
console.log(createUser("Rohan", "teacher"));

If an argument is missing (or undefined), the default is used.

Rest parameters

... collects any number of arguments into an array:

function total(...prices) {
  return prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
}

console.log(total(100, 250));          // 350
console.log(total(99, 199, 299, 49));  // 646

Object parameters

When a function needs many options, pass one object and destructure it. The order of arguments then no longer matters, and calls are self-explaining:

function formatPrice({ amount, currency = "INR", decimals = 2 }) {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", {
    style: "currency",
    currency,
    minimumFractionDigits: decimals
  }).format(amount);
}

console.log(formatPrice({ amount: 1499 }));
console.log(formatPrice({ amount: 20, currency: "USD", decimals: 0 }));

Function expressions

A function can also be stored in a variable:

const square = function (n) {
  return n * n;
};

console.log(square(9));

Functions are values in JavaScript: you can store them, put them in arrays and objects, and pass them to other functions. That's exactly what you did with map and filter:

function isEven(n) {
  return n % 2 === 0;
}

console.log([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].filter(isEven)); // pass the function itself, no brackets

A function passed to another function is called a callback.

Hoisting

Function declarations can be called before they appear in the code; JavaScript moves ("hoists") them to the top:

console.log(cube(3)); // 27: works

function cube(n) {
  return n ** 3;
}

Function expressions stored in const can't be used before their line.

Writing good functions

  • One job per function. calculateTotal shouldn't also update the page and send an email.
  • Name it with a verb that says what it does: getUser, formatDate, isValidEmail.
  • Keep it short. If it doesn't fit on your screen, split it.
  • Prefer returning values over changing variables outside the function.
function isValidEmail(email) {
  return email.includes("@") && email.includes(".") && email.length >= 6;
}

console.log(isValidEmail("asha@example.com")); // true
console.log(isValidEmail("asha.example"));     // false

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the brackets when calling: greet instead of greet().
  • **Forgetting return**, then wondering why the result is undefined.
  • **Code after return**, which never runs.
  • Calling a callback instead of passing it: arr.filter(isEven()) calls it immediately; write arr.filter(isEven).

Exercise

  1. Write celsiusToFahrenheit(c) that returns c * 9/5 + 32. Test it with 0, 37 and 100.
  2. Write isAdult(age) that returns true or false.
  3. Write average(...numbers) that returns the average of any number of values.
  4. Write createProfile({ name, city = "Unknown" }) that returns a sentence.
  5. Write capitalize(word) and use it with map on an array of lower-case names.

Summary

  • Declare functions with function name(params) { … } and call them with name(args).
  • return sends a value back and ends the function.
  • Default parameters, rest parameters and object parameters make functions flexible.
  • Functions are values: store them, and pass them as callbacks.

Next, you'll learn the short arrow function syntax used throughout modern JavaScript.

items.title: JavaScript Arrow Functions
items.excerpt: Write short functions with the arrow syntax, learn implicit returns and returning objects, and understand how arrow functions treat this differently.
items.content:
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write functions, added to JavaScript in 2015. You've already used them with map and filter. They're everywhere in modern code, so it's worth understanding them properly, including the one important way they behave differently.

From function to arrow

The same function, written three ways:

// 1. Function declaration
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}

// 2. Arrow function with a body
const double2 = (n) => {
  return n * 2;
};

// 3. Arrow function with an implicit return
const double3 = n => n * 2;

console.log(double(5), double2(5), double3(5)); // 10 10 10

To turn a function into an arrow function:

  1. Remove the word function.
  2. Put => between the parameters and the body.
  3. If the body is a single expression, remove the braces and return: the value is returned automatically (implicit return).

Parameter rules

const sayHi = () => "Hi!";               // no parameters: empty brackets required
const square = x => x * x;               // one parameter: brackets optional
const add = (a, b) => a + b;             // two or more: brackets required
const greet = (name = "friend") => `Hello, ${name}`; // defaults need brackets

console.log(sayHi(), square(4), add(2, 3), greet());

Many teams always use brackets, (x) => x * x, for consistency. Code formatters like Prettier do this by default.

When you need braces

If the function needs more than one statement, use braces and an explicit return:

const priceWithTax = (price, rate = 0.18) => {
  const tax = price * rate;
  const total = price + tax;
  return Math.round(total);
};

console.log(priceWithTax(1000)); // 1180

Watch out: with braces, nothing is returned unless you write return:

const broken = n => { n * 2 };
console.log(broken(5)); // undefined

Returning an object

Braces after => are read as a function body, not an object. Wrap an object in brackets:

const makeUserWrong = name => { name: name };    // body with a label, returns undefined
const makeUser = name => ({ name, joined: Date.now() > 0 });

console.log(makeUserWrong("Asha")); // undefined
console.log(makeUser("Asha"));      // { name: "Asha", joined: true }

Arrow functions as callbacks

Arrow functions shine when passing small functions to other functions:

const scores = [72, 95, 41, 88, 60];

const passed = scores.filter(s => s >= 50);
const curved = scores.map(s => Math.min(s + 5, 100));
const best = scores.reduce((max, s) => (s > max ? s : max), 0);
const sorted = [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a);

console.log(passed, curved, best, sorted);

Compare scores.filter(function (s) { return s >= 50; }): the arrow version is easier to read at a glance.

They're also common with timers and events:

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("One second later…");
}, 1000);

The big difference: this

Regular functions get their own this, which depends on how they're called. Arrow functions **don't have their own this**; they use the this of the code around them.

This makes arrow functions perfect inside methods:

const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  start() {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      this.seconds++;                 // "this" is still timer: correct
      console.log(`${this.seconds}s`);
      if (this.seconds === 3) clearInterval(id);
    }, 300);
  }
};

timer.start();

If you used function () { this.seconds++ } inside setInterval, this would not be the timer object and the code would break.

But it makes arrow functions a bad choice for methods themselves:

const user = {
  name: "Rohan",
  greetArrow: () => `Hi, I'm ${this?.name}`,       // this is NOT user
  greetMethod() { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; } // this IS user
};

console.log(user.greetArrow());  // "Hi, I'm undefined"
console.log(user.greetMethod()); // "Hi, I'm Rohan"

Rule of thumb:

  • Object methods → method shorthand name() { … }.
  • Callbacks, small helpers, functions inside methods → arrow functions.

Other differences (less common)

  • Arrow functions can't be used with new to create objects.
  • They don't have the old arguments object; use rest parameters (...args) instead.
  • They aren't hoisted: define them before you use them.
const logAll = (...args) => args.forEach(a => console.log(a));
logAll("one", "two", "three");

Readable arrow functions

Short isn't always clear. Name complex callbacks:

const orders = [
  { total: 1200, status: "paid" },
  { total: 300, status: "pending" },
  { total: 850, status: "paid" }
];

const isPaid = order => order.status === "paid";
const toTotal = order => order.total;
const sum = (a, b) => a + b;

const revenue = orders.filter(isPaid).map(toTotal).reduce(sum, 0);
console.log(revenue); // 2050

The last line now reads almost like a sentence.

Common mistakes

  • **Braces without return** → the function returns undefined.
  • Returning an object without wrapping brackets.
  • Arrow functions as object methods, losing this.
  • Overly clever one-liners that are hard to read.

Exercise

  1. Rewrite function triple(x) { return x * 3; } as an arrow function with an implicit return.
  2. Write an arrow function fullName(first, last) that returns a template string.
  3. Write toUser = name => ({ … }) that returns an object with name and createdAt: new Date().toISOString().
  4. Given an array of words, use filter and map with arrow functions to get the upper-case versions of words longer than 3 letters.
  5. Create a counter object whose start() method uses setInterval with an arrow function to count to 5.

Summary

  • (params) => expression returns the expression automatically.
  • Use braces and return for multi-line bodies; wrap returned objects in ( ).
  • Arrow functions use the surrounding this, which is ideal for callbacks inside methods.
  • Use method shorthand, not arrows, for object methods.

Next, you'll learn about scope: where variables can be seen and used.

items.title: Skills Every Developer Needs in the Age of AI
items.excerpt: Which developer skills matter more now that AI writes code: fundamentals, problem framing, reading code, debugging, testing, system design, security, communication and domain knowledge.
items.content:
Short answer: as AI makes writing code faster, the valuable skills shift toward everything around writing code: understanding the problem, reading and judging code, debugging, testing, designing systems, security, communication and knowledge of the business. Fundamentals become more important, not less, because they're how you judge AI output.

Here are the skills worth investing in, why they matter now, and how to build each one.

1. Strong fundamentals

AI can produce a sorting function in seconds. Knowing whether it's correct, efficient and appropriate requires understanding the basics:

  • Data types, control flow, functions and scope.
  • Data structures: lists/arrays, dictionaries/maps, sets, and when each is the right tool.
  • How the web works: HTTP, requests and responses, HTML/CSS/JavaScript in the browser.
  • Databases and SQL.
  • Basic performance ideas: why a loop inside a loop over large data is slow.

How to build it: finish a structured course in one language (our JavaScript or Python course), doing the exercises yourself before using AI.

2. Framing problems clearly

The quality of AI output depends on the quality of the request. Developers who can turn a vague idea into a precise specification (inputs, outputs, edge cases, constraints) get far better results from AI tools and from teammates.

How to build it: before coding anything, write three things: what it should do, an example input and output, and two edge cases. Practise writing precise prompts (our prompting guide).

3. Reading and reviewing code

As more code is generated, developers spend more time reading than writing. Reviewing well means spotting:

  • Logic errors and unhandled edge cases.
  • Security problems: unvalidated input, injection, exposed secrets.
  • Code that works but is hard to maintain.
  • "Hallucinated" functions or outdated APIs.

How to build it: read open-source code in projects you use. Review AI-generated code line by line and list everything you'd change. Ask to review classmates' or colleagues' pull requests.

4. Debugging

Every program breaks. Debugging is systematic thinking: reproduce the problem, form a hypothesis, test it, narrow it down. AI can suggest causes, but you need to verify them and understand the system well enough to know where to look.

How to build it: when you hit a bug, write down your hypothesis before changing anything. Learn your debugger (breakpoints, stepping, watching variables) and read error messages fully, starting from the last line.

5. Testing

Tests are how you know code works, especially code you didn't write yourself. They also make AI agents much more useful, because "make the tests pass" is a clear, checkable goal.

  • Unit tests for functions, with normal, edge and invalid inputs.
  • Integration tests for parts working together.
  • For AI features: evaluation sets that measure answer quality.

How to build it: add tests to every project from now on. When AI generates code, write (or at least review) the tests yourself.

6. System design

Choosing how pieces fit together (what goes in the database, which service calls which, how to handle failures, what happens with ten times more users) is judgement that AI can't fully provide, because it depends on your context, team and constraints.

How to build it: for each project, draw a simple diagram of the parts and data flow. Read about common designs: caching, queues, background jobs, authentication. Ask "what if this fails?" for every component.

7. Security and privacy awareness

AI-generated code repeats insecure patterns it learned from the internet, and AI features bring new risks like prompt injection and data leakage. Developers who think about security by default are increasingly valuable.

  • Validate input; use parameterised SQL queries.
  • Keep secrets out of code and repositories.
  • Apply least privilege, especially to AI agents with tools.
  • Know what data may and may not be sent to external services.

How to build it: read the OWASP Top 10 (a list of common web security risks) and check your own projects against it.

8. Working effectively with AI tools

Using AI well is itself a skill: giving context, asking for small pieces, iterating, verifying, and knowing when not to use it. See How to Use AI Coding Assistants Without Losing Your Skills.

How to build it: use an assistant on real projects with a strict rule: never commit code you can't explain.

9. Communication

Explaining trade-offs to a manager, writing clear documentation, describing a bug precisely, discussing requirements with non-technical people: these skills matter more as routine coding gets automated. Clear writing also directly improves your AI prompts.

How to build it: write a README for every project, and short posts about problems you solved. Explain a technical topic to a non-technical friend.

10. Domain knowledge

A developer who understands healthcare, finance, logistics or education, and can code, is far more valuable than one who only codes. Domain knowledge tells you which problems matter, what "correct" means and which edge cases are dangerous.

How to build it: pick an industry you find interesting (or already work in) and build projects for its real problems.

11. Learning how to learn

Tools and frameworks change every year. The lasting skill is learning new ones quickly: reading documentation, building a small test project, and connecting new ideas to what you already know.

How to build it: each month, learn one new tool by building something tiny with it from the official docs. Use AI as a tutor, not a replacement (our guide).

What matters less than before

  • Memorising syntax and library function names: tools help with recall.
  • Writing large amounts of boilerplate by hand.
  • Knowing one framework deeply but nothing else.

They still help, but they're no longer what sets a developer apart.

A simple self-check

Rate yourself from 1 to 5 on each skill:

Pick your two lowest scores and focus on them for the next month.

Frequently asked questions

Is it still worth learning to code?

Yes. Code is how ideas become working software, and understanding it is what lets you direct and check AI tools. The job is changing, not disappearing.

Should I specialise or be a generalist?

Build broad fundamentals first, then go deep in one area (front-end, back-end, data, AI engineering) while staying curious about the others. "T-shaped" developers are in demand.

What's one habit that improves most of these skills?

Building real projects end to end: planning, coding, testing, deploying and writing about them. Each project exercises almost every skill on this list.

Summary

  • AI speeds up writing code; the value shifts to judging, designing, testing and communicating.
  • Fundamentals matter more, because they're how you evaluate AI output.
  • Invest in problem framing, code review, debugging, testing, system design and security.
  • Communication, domain knowledge and learning how to learn keep you valuable as tools change.

items.title: JavaScript Scope
items.excerpt: Global, function and block scope explained, why let and const beat var, how shadowing works, and a first look at closures.
items.content:
Scope decides where a variable can be seen and used. A variable created inside a function isn't visible outside it; a variable created at the top of a file is visible everywhere. Understanding scope prevents bugs where variables clash, disappear or change unexpectedly.

Global scope

A variable declared outside any function or block is global: every part of the script can use it.

const siteName = "VitalStack";

function showName() {
  console.log(siteName); // can read the global
}

showName();
console.log(siteName);

Globals are convenient, but in a big program any code can change them, which makes bugs hard to trace. Keep globals to a minimum.

Function scope

Variables declared inside a function exist only inside that function:

function calculate() {
  const result = 6 * 7;
  console.log("Inside:", result);
}

calculate();
// console.log(result); // ReferenceError: result is not defined

Each call gets its own fresh variables, which disappear when the function ends. Two functions can use the same variable names without interfering:

function a() { const x = 1; console.log("a:", x); }
function b() { const x = 2; console.log("b:", x); }
a();
b();

Block scope

A block is any code inside { }: an if, a loop, or just braces. Variables declared with let and const inside a block exist only in that block:

const age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
  const message = "Adult";
  console.log(message);
}

// console.log(message); // ReferenceError

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  // i exists only inside the loop
}
// console.log(i); // ReferenceError

This is good: variables live only as long as they're needed.

Why var is confusing

var ignores blocks and only respects functions:

if (true) {
  var leaky = "I escaped the block!";
  let contained = "I stay inside";
}

console.log(leaky);        // works: var leaks out
// console.log(contained); // ReferenceError

And var can be used before its declaration without an error (it's "hoisted" with the value undefined):

console.log(early); // undefined, no error
var early = 5;

// console.log(later); // ReferenceError with let/const
// let later = 5;

The classic var loop bug:

for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("var:", i), 100);
}
// prints 4, 4, 4: all three share one i

for (let j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("let:", j), 200);
}
// prints 1, 2, 3: each round gets its own j

These surprises are why modern code uses only let and const.

The scope chain

When you use a variable, JavaScript looks for it in the current scope, then the scope outside it, and so on up to the global scope:

const level = "global";

function outer() {
  const level2 = "outer";

  function inner() {
    const level3 = "inner";
    console.log(level, level2, level3); // can see all three
  }

  inner();
  // console.log(level3); // ReferenceError: can't look inwards
}

outer();

Inner scopes can see outward; outer scopes can't see inward.

Shadowing

If an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, the inner one shadows (hides) the outer one inside that scope:

const colour = "blue";

function paint() {
  const colour = "red";   // a different variable
  console.log("inside:", colour);
}

paint();
console.log("outside:", colour); // still blue

This is allowed, but can be confusing. Use different names when you can.

Accidental globals

Assigning to a variable that was never declared creates a global by accident (in non-strict code):

function setScore() {
  score = 100;  // forgot let/const!
}
setScore();
console.log(score); // 100: a global was created

In strict mode, this throws an error instead. Modules and classes are strict automatically; in older scripts, add "use strict"; at the top of the file. And always declare variables with let or const.

Closures: functions remember their scope

A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. This is called a closure:

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;            // private to this counter
  return function () {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counterA = makeCounter();
const counterB = makeCounter();

console.log(counterA()); // 1
console.log(counterA()); // 2
console.log(counterB()); // 1: B has its own count
console.log(counterA()); // 3

count can't be reached from outside except through the returned function: it's private. Closures are used for private data, event handlers that remember settings, and many library patterns.

Another example: a function factory.

const makeGreeting = greeting => name => `${greeting}, ${name}!`;

const hello = makeGreeting("Hello");
const namaste = makeGreeting("Namaste");

console.log(hello("Asha"));
console.log(namaste("Rohan"));

Common mistakes

  • Using a variable outside the block where it was declared.
  • Accidental globals from missing let/const.
  • **Using var** and getting leaky or shared variables.
  • Shadowing by accident, then changing the wrong variable.

Exercise

  1. Write a function that declares a variable, then try to log it outside. Read the error.
  2. Create a global theme and a function that shadows it; log both.
  3. Run the var vs let loop example and explain the output in your own words.
  4. Write makeMultiplier(n) that returns a function multiplying its input by n. Create double and triple.
  5. Build a createWallet(start) closure with add(amount) and balance() functions, keeping the balance private.

Summary

  • Global variables are visible everywhere; function and block variables only inside.
  • let and const are block-scoped; var ignores blocks, so avoid it.
  • JavaScript looks outward through the scope chain, never inward.
  • Closures let functions remember variables from where they were created.

Next, you'll start working with the web page itself: selecting elements in the DOM.
