items.title: SOLID Principles and Design Patterns in Java
items.excerpt: Write maintainable Java with the five SOLID principles explained through simple before/after examples, plus the most asked design patterns - Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Builder and Observer.
items.content:
Knowing classes and inheritance isn't enough. Big codebases need structure so that a change in one place doesn't break five others. SOLID is a set of five principles for that, and design patterns are proven solutions to common design problems. Both are standard questions in Java interviews from 2 years of experience onwards.

S: Single Responsibility Principle

> A class should have one reason to change.

// ❌ One class doing everything
class Invoice {
    double total() { ... }
    void printPdf() { ... }        // presentation
    void saveToDatabase() { ... }  // persistence
    void emailCustomer() { ... }   // notification
}

// ✅ Each class has one job
class Invoice { double total() { ... } }
class InvoicePdfPrinter { void print(Invoice i) { ... } }
class InvoiceRepository { void save(Invoice i) { ... } }
class InvoiceMailer { void send(Invoice i) { ... } }

When the PDF layout changes, only InvoicePdfPrinter changes.

O: Open/Closed Principle

> Open for extension, closed for modification.

// ❌ Every new payment type means editing this method
double fee(String type, double amount) {
    if (type.equals("UPI")) return 0;
    else if (type.equals("CARD")) return amount * 0.02;
    // add another else-if for each new type...
}

// ✅ Add a new class instead of editing old code
interface Payment { double fee(double amount); }
class Upi implements Payment { public double fee(double a) { return 0; } }
class Card implements Payment { public double fee(double a) { return a * 0.02; } }
class Wallet implements Payment { public double fee(double a) { return a * 0.01; } }   // new: nothing else changes

This is polymorphism used as a design principle.

L: Liskov Substitution Principle

> A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is expected, without surprises.

The classic violation: Square extends Rectangle. Setting a square's width also changes its height, so code that does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); expects area 20 but gets 16. If a subclass has to break the parent's promises (throwing "not supported", ignoring calls), the inheritance is wrong. Use separate classes or a common interface.

I: Interface Segregation Principle

> Don't force classes to implement methods they don't use.

// ❌ A fat interface
interface Worker { void code(); void test(); void cookLunch(); }

// ✅ Small, focused interfaces
interface Coder { void code(); }
interface Tester { void test(); }
class Developer implements Coder, Tester { ... }

D: Dependency Inversion Principle

> Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes.

// ❌ OrderService is glued to one SMS provider
class OrderService {
    private final Msg91Sms sms = new Msg91Sms();
}

// ✅ Depend on an interface, receive the implementation from outside
interface Notifier { void send(String to, String msg); }

class OrderService {
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(Notifier notifier) { this.notifier = notifier; }   // constructor injection
    void place(String phone) { notifier.send(phone, "Order placed!"); }
}

Now you can swap SMS for email or WhatsApp, or pass a fake in tests. This is exactly what Spring's dependency injection automates: you'll see it animated in the Spring course.

Design patterns you must know

Singleton: exactly one instance

public final class AppConfig {
    private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig();   // created once, thread-safe
    private AppConfig() { }                                      // nobody else can call new
    public static AppConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}

Use sparingly: singletons are global state and make testing harder. (In Spring, beans are singletons by default, managed by the container instead.)

Factory: hide object creation

class NotifierFactory {
    static Notifier create(String channel) {
        return switch (channel) {
            case "sms" -> new SmsNotifier();
            case "email" -> new EmailNotifier();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown channel: " + channel);
        };
    }
}

Callers ask for "sms" and don't need to know the class names.

Strategy: swap algorithms at runtime

import java.util.function.DoubleUnaryOperator;

public class StrategyDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DoubleUnaryOperator noDiscount = p -> p;
        DoubleUnaryOperator festive = p -> p * 0.8;
        DoubleUnaryOperator flat200 = p -> Math.max(0, p - 200);

        for (DoubleUnaryOperator strategy : new DoubleUnaryOperator[] { noDiscount, festive, flat200 }) {
            System.out.println(strategy.applyAsDouble(1500));
        }
    }
}
1500.0
1200.0
1300.0

Each discount rule is a strategy object (here a lambda). The checkout code just calls applyAsDouble.

Builder: readable construction of complex objects

public class BuilderDemo {
    static class Pizza {
        private final String size; private final boolean cheese; private final boolean olives;
        private Pizza(Builder b) { size = b.size; cheese = b.cheese; olives = b.olives; }
        public String toString() { return size + " pizza, cheese=" + cheese + ", olives=" + olives; }

        static class Builder {
            private String size = "Medium"; private boolean cheese; private boolean olives;
            Builder size(String s) { size = s; return this; }
            Builder cheese() { cheese = true; return this; }
            Builder olives() { olives = true; return this; }
            Pizza build() { return new Pizza(this); }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Pizza p = new Pizza.Builder().size("Large").cheese().build();
        System.out.println(p);    // Large pizza, cheese=true, olives=false
    }
}

Much clearer than new Pizza("Large", true, false, false, true…). Lombok's @Builder generates this for you in Spring projects.

Observer: notify many listeners

interface OrderListener { void onPlaced(String orderId); }

class OrderEvents {
    private final List<OrderListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(OrderListener l) { listeners.add(l); }
    void placed(String id) { listeners.forEach(l -> l.onPlaced(id)); }
}

events.subscribe(id -> System.out.println("Email sent for " + id));
events.subscribe(id -> System.out.println("Stock updated for " + id));
events.placed("ORD-1001");

Spring's ApplicationEvents, JavaScript's addEventListener and RxJS all build on this idea.

Don't force patterns into code. Learn to recognise the problem first ("I keep adding else-ifs for types" → Strategy/polymorphism; "constructor with 8 parameters" → Builder). Patterns are vocabulary for discussing designs, not goals.

Exercise

  1. Find an SRP violation in code you wrote earlier and split the class.
  2. Refactor an if/else on a "type" String into polymorphic classes (OCP).
  3. Write a ShippingCostStrategy interface with Standard, Express and FreeAbove999 implementations.
  4. Implement a Notifier interface with Sms and Email versions and inject one into OrderService through the constructor.
Hint for 3

FreeAbove999 returns 0 when the cart total is above 999, otherwise delegates to Standard.

Interview corner

  • Explain SOLID. Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion (be ready with one example each).
  • How do you make a thread-safe singleton? Eager static final instance, the holder idiom, or an enum.
  • Factory vs Builder? Factory decides which class to create; Builder handles how to assemble a complex object step by step.
  • Which patterns does Spring use? Singleton (beans), Factory (BeanFactory), Proxy (AOP, @Transactional), Template (JdbcTemplate), Observer (events), Strategy, Dependency Injection.

Summary

  • SOLID keeps classes focused, extensible and loosely coupled.
  • Dependency inversion + constructor injection is the heart of Spring.
  • Know Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Builder and Observer, and when each fits.

items.title: Java OOP Project: Library Management System
items.excerpt: Design and build a Library Management System in Java using classes, encapsulation, inheritance, interfaces, enums, records, custom exceptions and polymorphic fine rules.
items.content:
"Design a library management system" is one of the most common Low-Level Design (LLD) interview questions. Let's build a working version that uses everything from this course.

Requirements

  • The library has books (with copies) and members.
  • Members can borrow and return books.
  • Students can borrow up to 3 books for 14 days; faculty up to 10 books for 30 days.
  • Late returns are fined: ₹5/day for students, ₹2/day for faculty.
  • You can search books by title or author.

Step 1: Find the classes

Step 2: The full program

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.*;

public class LibraryApp {

    // ---------- domain ----------
    record Book(String isbn, String title, String author) { }

    static class LibraryException extends RuntimeException {
        LibraryException(String message) { super(message); }
    }

    abstract static class Member {
        private final String id;
        private final String name;

        Member(String id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; }

        String id() { return id; }
        String name() { return name; }

        abstract int maxBooks();
        abstract int loanDays();
        abstract int finePerDay();

        @Override public String toString() { return name + " (" + getClass().getSimpleName() + ")"; }
    }

    static class Student extends Member {
        Student(String id, String name) { super(id, name); }
        int maxBooks() { return 3; }
        int loanDays() { return 14; }
        int finePerDay() { return 5; }
    }

    static class Faculty extends Member {
        Faculty(String id, String name) { super(id, name); }
        int maxBooks() { return 10; }
        int loanDays() { return 30; }
        int finePerDay() { return 2; }
    }

    static class Loan {
        final Member member;
        final Book book;
        final LocalDate due;

        Loan(Member member, Book book, LocalDate borrowedOn) {
            this.member = member;
            this.book = book;
            this.due = borrowedOn.plusDays(member.loanDays());     // polymorphic rule
        }

        int fine(LocalDate returnedOn) {
            long late = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(due, returnedOn);
            return late > 0 ? (int) late * member.finePerDay() : 0; // polymorphic rule
        }
    }

    // ---------- service ----------
    static class Library {
        private final Map<String, Book> books = new HashMap<>();
        private final Map<String, Integer> copies = new HashMap<>();
        private final List<Loan> loans = new ArrayList<>();

        void addBook(Book b, int count) {
            books.put(b.isbn(), b);
            copies.merge(b.isbn(), count, Integer::sum);
        }

        int available(String isbn) { return copies.getOrDefault(isbn, 0); }

        List<Book> search(String text) {
            String q = text.toLowerCase();
            return books.values().stream()
                    .filter(b -> b.title().toLowerCase().contains(q) || b.author().toLowerCase().contains(q))
                    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Book::title))
                    .toList();
        }

        Loan borrow(Member m, String isbn, LocalDate today) {
            Book book = Optional.ofNullable(books.get(isbn))
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new LibraryException("No book with ISBN " + isbn));
            if (available(isbn) == 0) throw new LibraryException("'" + book.title() + "' is not available");
            long current = loans.stream().filter(l -> l.member == m).count();
            if (current >= m.maxBooks()) throw new LibraryException(m.name() + " has reached the limit of " + m.maxBooks());
            copies.merge(isbn, -1, Integer::sum);
            Loan loan = new Loan(m, book, today);
            loans.add(loan);
            return loan;
        }

        int giveBack(Member m, String isbn, LocalDate today) {
            Loan loan = loans.stream()
                    .filter(l -> l.member == m && l.book.isbn().equals(isbn))
                    .findFirst()
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new LibraryException(m.name() + " didn't borrow " + isbn));
            loans.remove(loan);
            copies.merge(isbn, 1, Integer::sum);
            return loan.fine(today);
        }
    }

    // ---------- demo ----------
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Library lib = new Library();
        lib.addBook(new Book("111", "Wings of Fire", "A. P. J. Abdul Kalam"), 2);
        lib.addBook(new Book("222", "Clean Code", "Robert C. Martin"), 1);
        lib.addBook(new Book("333", "Head First Java", "Kathy Sierra"), 1);

        Member asha = new Student("S1", "Asha");
        Member prof = new Faculty("F1", "Dr. Rao");
        LocalDate day1 = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1);

        System.out.println(lib.search("java"));
        Loan l1 = lib.borrow(asha, "222", day1);
        System.out.println(asha + " borrowed " + l1.book.title() + ", due " + l1.due);

        try {
            lib.borrow(prof, "222", day1);
        } catch (LibraryException e) {
            System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
        }

        Loan l2 = lib.borrow(prof, "111", day1);
        System.out.println(prof + " borrowed " + l2.book.title() + ", due " + l2.due);

        int fineAsha = lib.giveBack(asha, "222", day1.plusDays(20));   // 6 days late
        int fineProf = lib.giveBack(prof, "111", day1.plusDays(20));   // on time
        System.out.println("Fines: Asha ₹" + fineAsha + ", Dr. Rao ₹" + fineProf);
        System.out.println("Clean Code copies now: " + lib.available("222"));
    }
}

Output:

[Book[isbn=333, title=Head First Java, author=Kathy Sierra]]
Asha (Student) borrowed Clean Code, due 2026-01-15
Error: 'Clean Code' is not available
Dr. Rao (Faculty) borrowed Wings of Fire, due 2026-01-31
Fines: Asha ₹30, Dr. Rao ₹0
Clean Code copies now: 1

Where each OOP idea appears

  • Encapsulation: Library keeps its maps private; you can only change them through addBook, borrow, giveBack, which enforce the rules.
  • Inheritance + abstraction: Member is abstract; Student and Faculty fill in the rules.
  • Polymorphism: Loan calls member.loanDays() and member.finePerDay() without knowing the member type. Adding Guest members means adding one class.
  • Records: Book is immutable data with free equals/hashCode/toString.
  • Custom exception: LibraryException carries clear error messages.
  • Collections and streams: maps for stock, a list of loans, streams for search.

Extend it (great for your portfolio)

  1. Reservations: if a book is unavailable, let a member join a queue (use ArrayDeque); notify the next member when it's returned (Observer pattern).
  2. Membership expiry: add an expiry date; expired members can't borrow.
  3. Persistence: save books and loans to CSV files (Java course lesson 15), or later to a database with JPA.
  4. Menu: add a Scanner-driven console menu.
  5. REST API: after the Spring Boot course, expose /books and /loans endpoints.
Hint for 1

Keep Map<String, Deque<Member>> waitlist. In giveBack, if the waitlist for that ISBN isn't empty, poll() the next member and print a notification.

In an LLD interview, talk before you code: list requirements, identify classes and relationships, then discuss how your design handles a new requirement ("what if we add e-books?"). That conversation is what's being judged.

What's next?

  • Servlet & JSP: put Java on the web.
  • JPA & Hibernate: store these objects in a real database.
  • Spring & Spring Boot: build production-ready back-ends using all these OOP ideas.

Summary

  • You designed classes from requirements and built a working system.
  • Polymorphic rules (maxBooks, loanDays, finePerDay) make new member types easy to add.
  • Encapsulated services enforce business rules in one place.

items.title: How Java Web Apps Work (HTTP and Servlets)
items.excerpt: Understand HTTP requests and responses, what a web server and servlet container do, where servlets fit under Spring Boot, and why every Java web developer should learn them.
items.content:
When you open a website, your browser sends a request and a server sends back a response. In Java, the code that answers those requests is a servlet. Even if you later use Spring Boot, every request still passes through a servlet under the hood (Spring's DispatcherServlet). Understanding servlets makes everything else make sense.

The restaurant analogy

  • You (the browser) place an order: "GET me the menu page".
  • The waiter (the web server / servlet container, e.g. Tomcat) takes the order to the right cook.
  • The cook (your servlet) prepares the dish (HTML or JSON).
  • The waiter brings back the response with a status: 200 "here you go", 404 "we don't have that", 500 "the kitchen had a problem".

HTTP in 2 minutes

A request has a method, a path, headers and sometimes a body:

GET /courses?level=beginner HTTP/1.1
Host: vitalstack.co.in
Accept: text/html
Cookie: JSESSIONID=A1B2C3

A response has a status code, headers and a body:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

<html><body><h1>Beginner courses</h1>...</body></html>

Methods

Status codes

HTTP is stateless: each request is independent, and the server doesn't remember you between requests. Sessions and cookies (lesson 5) add memory.

What is a servlet?

A servlet is a Java class that extends HttpServlet and handles requests for certain URLs:

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet("/hello")
public class HelloServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().println("<h1>Hello from a Java servlet!</h1>");
    }
}

When a browser visits /hello, Tomcat calls doGet and sends back whatever you write to the response.

The servlet container

You don't run servlets with main. A servlet container does it:

  • Apache Tomcat: the most popular (Spring Boot embeds it by default).
  • Jetty, Undertow: lighter alternatives.
  • Full Jakarta EE servers: WildFly, Payara, Open Liberty.

The container listens on a port (8080), parses HTTP, creates HttpServletRequest/HttpServletResponse objects, picks the servlet by URL, manages threads (one request = one thread from a pool), sessions and security.

javax vs jakarta

Java EE was handed to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE. From Jakarta EE 9, packages changed from javax.servlet.* to jakarta.servlet.*.

This course uses **Tomcat 10.1+ and jakarta.servlet**. If you copy old tutorials that use javax, change the imports.

Where servlets fit today

Browser ──HTTP──▶ Tomcat ──▶ Filters ──▶ Servlet ──▶ your code ──▶ Database
                                         ▲
                     Spring Boot: DispatcherServlet routes to @Controller methods

Modern teams rarely write raw servlets for big apps; they use Spring Boot. But interviews ask about the servlet lifecycle, filters, sessions and the request flow, and debugging Spring often means understanding this layer.

Open your browser's DevTools (F12) → Network tab, then reload any page. Click a request to see its method, status, headers and response. Do this on a few sites: it's the fastest way to understand HTTP.

Exercise

  1. In DevTools, find one request with status 200, one 304 and (if you can) a 404. What's in their headers?
  2. Write the HTTP request line your browser sends for https://example.com/search?q=java.
  3. Which HTTP method fits each action: view a product, add to cart, change quantity, remove an item?
Hint for 3

GET, POST, PUT (or PATCH), DELETE.

Interview corner

  • What is a servlet? A Java class that handles HTTP requests inside a servlet container, typically by extending HttpServlet.
  • What is a servlet container? Software (like Tomcat) that manages servlet lifecycle, maps URLs, handles threads, sessions and the HTTP protocol.
  • Is HTTP stateful? No, it's stateless; sessions/cookies add state.
  • GET vs POST? GET reads data, parameters go in the URL, and it should be safe and idempotent; POST sends data in the body to create/change something.

Summary

  • HTTP = request (method, path, headers, body) and response (status, headers, body).
  • A servlet handles requests for URLs; a container like Tomcat runs it.
  • New projects use jakarta.servlet with Tomcat 10.1+.
  • Spring Boot's DispatcherServlet is itself a servlet.

Next: set up Tomcat and Maven and run your first servlet.

items.title: Setting Up Tomcat, Maven and Your First Servlet
items.excerpt: Create a Maven web project, add the Jakarta Servlet API, write a servlet with @WebServlet, package a WAR, deploy it to Tomcat 10 and read request parameters.
items.content:
Let's build and run a real servlet application. You'll use Maven (Java's build tool) and Apache Tomcat 10.1.

Step 1: Install the tools

  • JDK 17 or 21 (from the Java course).
  • Maven: download from maven.apache.org or brew install maven / sudo apt install maven. Check with mvn -v.
  • Tomcat 10.1: download the zip from tomcat.apache.org and unzip it anywhere. Start it with bin/startup.sh (Mac/Linux) or bin\startup.bat (Windows), then open http://localhost:8080.

IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate and Eclipse can create and deploy web projects for you, but understanding the manual way helps when things break.

Step 2: Project structure

hello-web/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/
    ├── java/com/vitalstack/web/HelloServlet.java
    └── webapp/
        ├── index.html
        └── WEB-INF/          (private: not directly accessible by browsers)

Step 3: pom.xml

<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.vitalstack</groupId>
  <artifactId>hello-web</artifactId>
  <version>1.0</version>
  <packaging>war</packaging>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
    <failOnMissingWebXml>false</failOnMissingWebXml>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
      <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
      <version>6.0.0</version>
      <scope>provided</scope>   <!-- Tomcat already has it at runtime -->
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <finalName>hello</finalName>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-war-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.4.0</version>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
  • packaging war: a Web ARchive, the format Tomcat deploys.
  • scope provided: compile against the API, but don't bundle it (Tomcat provides it).

Step 4: The servlet

package com.vitalstack.web;

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.time.LocalTime;

@WebServlet("/hello")
public class HelloServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String name = req.getParameter("name");            // from ?name=Asha
        if (name == null || name.isBlank()) name = "friend";

        resp.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8");
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("<!doctype html><html><body>");
        out.println("<h1>Namaste, " + escape(name) + "!</h1>");
        out.println("<p>Server time: " + LocalTime.now().withNano(0) + "</p>");
        out.println("</body></html>");
    }

    private static String escape(String s) {               // never print user input raw (XSS!)
        return s.replace("&", "&").replace("<", "<").replace(">", ">").replace("\"", """);
    }
}

@WebServlet("/hello") maps the URL. (The old way was a <servlet-mapping> in WEB-INF/web.xml; both still work.)

Step 5: Build and deploy

mvn clean package                  # creates target/hello.war
cp target/hello.war /path/to/tomcat/webapps/

Tomcat unpacks it automatically. Open:

http://localhost:8080/hello/hello?name=Asha
  • The first /hello is the context path (from hello.war).
  • The second /hello is the servlet mapping.

To deploy at the root (http://localhost:8080/hello?name=Asha), name the file ROOT.war.

Reading request data

String q = req.getParameter("q");                 // one value
String[] tags = req.getParameterValues("tag");     // ?tag=java&tag=web
String agent = req.getHeader("User-Agent");        // a header
String method = req.getMethod();                   // GET, POST…
String path = req.getRequestURI();                 // /hello/hello
String ip = req.getRemoteAddr();

getParameter returns null when the parameter is missing. Always check.

Logs and errors

  • Tomcat logs are in tomcat/logs/ (catalina.out or catalina.<date>.log). Look there first when something fails.
  • An uncaught exception in a servlet gives the user a 500 page and a stack trace in the log.
  • A 404 usually means a wrong context path or mapping.

Faster development: the Cargo or Jetty Maven plugin can run your app with mvn jetty:run without copying WAR files, and IntelliJ Ultimate can redeploy on save. Spring Boot later removes this step entirely with an embedded server.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing javax.servlet code with Tomcat 10 (or jakarta with Tomcat 9): you get 404s or ClassNotFound errors.
  • Forgetting scope provided and bundling a servlet API jar into the WAR.
  • Visiting /hello instead of /<context>/hello.
  • Printing user input without escaping it: a security hole called XSS.

Exercise

  1. Create the project and get Namaste, Asha! in your browser.
  2. Add a /time servlet that returns the current date and time as plain text (text/plain).
  3. Add a /square?n=12 servlet that returns 144, and a 400 error (resp.sendError(400, "...")) when n is missing or not a number.
Hint for 3

Wrap Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("n")) in try/catch for NumberFormatException (null also throws it) and call resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "n must be a number").

Interview corner

  • What is a WAR file? A zip of a web application (classes, libraries, web resources, WEB-INF) deployable to a servlet container.
  • What is WEB-INF? A protected folder; browsers can't request files in it directly. It holds web.xml, classes and libs, and private JSPs.
  • @WebServlet vs web.xml? Both map servlets to URLs; annotations are simpler, web.xml centralises configuration.
  • What is the context path? The URL prefix of a web app inside the container, usually the WAR name.

Summary

  • A Maven project with packaging war and the jakarta.servlet-api (provided) builds a deployable WAR.
  • @WebServlet("/path") maps URLs; doGet writes the response.
  • Read input with getParameter, escape it before printing.
  • Deploy by copying the WAR into Tomcat's webapps folder.

Next: the servlet lifecycle, animated.

items.title: The Servlet Lifecycle
items.excerpt: Watch init, service, doGet/doPost and destroy in an animation, learn why one servlet object serves many threads, load-on-startup, init parameters and thread-safety rules.
items.content:
A servlet is created by the container, used for many requests, and finally destroyed. This lifecycle is a classic interview question, and understanding it prevents serious bugs.

The lifecycle, animated

Change the list of requests (try GET, POST, GET, GET) and watch which methods run:

  1. Load and instantiate: the container loads the class and creates one object (on the first request, or at startup).
  2. **init(): called once**. Open resources, read configuration.
  3. **service(): called for every** request. HttpServlet.service looks at the HTTP method and calls doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete…
  4. **destroy(): called once** when the app stops or is redeployed. Release resources.
import jakarta.servlet.ServletConfig;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebInitParam;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

@WebServlet(urlPatterns = "/counter", loadOnStartup = 1,
            initParams = @WebInitParam(name = "greeting", value = "Welcome"))
public class CounterServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private String greeting;
    private final AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();   // thread-safe counter

    @Override
    public void init(ServletConfig config) throws ServletException {
        super.init(config);                                    // keep the config available
        greeting = config.getInitParameter("greeting");
        log("CounterServlet initialised");
    }

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().println(greeting + "! You are visitor #" + hits.incrementAndGet());
    }

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        hits.set(0);
        resp.getWriter().println("Counter reset");
    }

    @Override
    public void destroy() {
        log("CounterServlet destroyed after " + hits.get() + " hits");
    }
}
  • loadOnStartup = 1 creates the servlet when the app starts instead of on the first request (no slow first hit). Lower numbers load first.
  • Init parameters configure a servlet without changing code.

One object, many threads

This is the most important point: the container creates one instance of your servlet and calls service() from many threads at the same time, one per concurrent request.

Request A ──thread-1──┐
Request B ──thread-2──┼──▶ the SAME CounterServlet object
Request C ──thread-3──┘

So instance fields are shared by all users. This is a bug:

@WebServlet("/profile")
public class ProfileServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private String currentUser;     // ❌ shared by everyone!

    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        currentUser = req.getParameter("user");
        // ... another request may overwrite currentUser right here ...
        resp.getWriter().println("Profile of " + currentUser);   // may show someone else's name!
    }
}

Rules:

  • Keep per-request data in local variables (each thread has its own stack).
  • Per-user data goes in the session (lesson 5).
  • Shared data must be thread-safe (AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap) or immutable.

The same rule applies to Spring: controllers and services are singletons too. Never store request or user data in their fields.

The ServletContext: app-wide data

Every web app has one ServletContext, shared by all servlets:

getServletContext().setAttribute("appName", "VitalStack");
String name = (String) getServletContext().getAttribute("appName");
String version = getServletContext().getInitParameter("version");   // from web.xml <context-param>

Use it for app-wide settings and shared resources (like a connection pool).

Lifecycle order with filters and listeners

When the app starts: ServletContextListener.contextInitialized → filters' init → servlets with loadOnStartup. When it stops, the reverse: servlets' destroy → filters' destroy → contextDestroyed. You'll meet filters and listeners in lesson 6.

Common mistakes

  • Overriding init(ServletConfig) without calling super.init(config), then getServletConfig() returns null. (Or override the no-argument init() instead.)
  • Mutable instance fields used per request.
  • Heavy work in doGet that should be done once in init.
  • Overriding service() and forgetting the doXxx dispatch.

Exercise

  1. Add log() calls to init, doGet and destroy, deploy, make some requests, then stop Tomcat. Check the order in the logs.
  2. Fix ProfileServlet above by using a local variable.
  3. Create a servlet that counts hits per page using a ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicInteger> keyed by req.getParameter("page").
Hint for 3

hits.computeIfAbsent(page, k -> new AtomicInteger()).incrementAndGet() is atomic and thread-safe.

Interview corner

  • Explain the servlet lifecycle. Load → instantiate → init() once → service() per request (dispatching to doGet/doPost…) → destroy() once.
  • How many servlet instances are created? One per servlet declaration (per container), shared by all threads.
  • Is a servlet thread-safe? Not automatically. Avoid mutable instance state or synchronise access.
  • What is load-on-startup? It makes the container initialise the servlet at application startup, in the given order.
  • ServletConfig vs ServletContext? Config is per servlet (init params); context is per web app (shared attributes).

Summary

  • init once, service/doXxx per request, destroy once.
  • One servlet object handles many concurrent threads: no per-request data in fields.
  • ServletConfig holds per-servlet settings; ServletContext is app-wide.

Next: requests, responses, forms, redirects and forwards.

items.title: Servlet Requests, Responses and Forms
items.excerpt: Handle HTML forms with doPost, validate input, set status codes and headers, return JSON, and understand forward vs redirect and the Post/Redirect/Get pattern.
items.content:
Real web apps take input: sign-up forms, search boxes, checkout pages. In this lesson you'll process forms safely and control exactly what goes back to the browser.

A form and its servlet

src/main/webapp/register.html:

<form action="register" method="post">
  <label>Name <input name="name" required></label>
  <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" required></label>
  <label>Course
    <select name="course">
      <option>Java</option><option>Spring Boot</option><option>React</option>
    </select>
  </label>
  <button>Register</button>
</form>

The servlet:

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.*;

@WebServlet("/register")
public class RegisterServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        req.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8");                       // before reading parameters
        String name = trim(req.getParameter("name"));
        String email = trim(req.getParameter("email"));
        String course = trim(req.getParameter("course"));

        List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        if (name.isEmpty()) errors.add("Name is required");
        if (!email.matches("^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+$")) errors.add("Email looks invalid");
        if (!Set.of("Java", "Spring Boot", "React").contains(course)) errors.add("Unknown course");

        if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
            resp.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST);   // 400
            resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
            resp.getWriter().println(String.join("\n", errors));
            return;
        }

        // ... save the registration (JDBC/JPA later) ...
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/thanks.html");  // Post/Redirect/Get
    }

    private static String trim(String s) { return s == null ? "" : s.trim(); }
}

Never trust the browser. HTML required and type="email" are only for convenience: anyone can send a request with curl or Postman. Always validate on the server.

Post/Redirect/Get (PRG)

If a POST returns a page directly and the user presses Refresh, the browser re-submits the form: duplicate registrations or double payments! The fix:

  1. POST the form.
  2. Server processes it and responds with a redirect (302/303) to a result page.
  3. Browser makes a fresh GET to that page. Refreshing just repeats the harmless GET.

Redirect vs forward

req.setAttribute("courses", List.of("Java", "Spring Boot"));
req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/courses.jsp").forward(req, resp);

Status codes and headers

resp.setStatus(201);                                      // Created
resp.sendError(404, "Course not found");                  // container error page
resp.setHeader("Cache-Control", "no-store");
resp.addHeader("X-App", "VitalStack");
resp.setContentType("application/json;charset=UTF-8");

Set the status and headers before writing the body. Once the response is "committed" (data sent), you can't change them.

Returning JSON (a mini REST API)

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet("/api/courses")
public class CourseApiServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("application/json;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().write("""
            [{"id":1,"title":"Java","lessons":16},
             {"id":2,"title":"Spring Boot","lessons":10}]
            """);
    }
}

In real apps, use a library like Jackson (new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(list)) to convert objects to JSON. Spring Boot does this automatically.

Reading a JSON request body

String body = new String(req.getInputStream().readAllBytes(), java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
// then parse with Jackson: mapper.readValue(body, Course.class)

File uploads

import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.MultipartConfig;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet("/upload")
@MultipartConfig(maxFileSize = 2 * 1024 * 1024)          // 2 MB
public class UploadServlet extends HttpServlet {
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException, ServletException {
        Part file = req.getPart("photo");                 // <input type="file" name="photo">
        String name = java.nio.file.Path.of(file.getSubmittedFileName()).getFileName().toString();
        file.write("/data/uploads/" + System.currentTimeMillis() + "-" + name);
        resp.getWriter().println("Uploaded " + name);
    }
}

The form needs enctype="multipart/form-data". Never trust the file name or type: check extensions and sizes, and store uploads outside the web root.

Common mistakes

  • Reading parameters before setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") → garbled Hindi or emoji.
  • Writing the body, then calling sendRedirect → IllegalStateException: response already committed.
  • Forgetting return after sending an error, so the code continues.
  • Returning a page directly after POST (duplicate submissions on refresh).

Exercise

  1. Build a contact form (name, email, message) with server-side validation and PRG to a thank-you page.
  2. Make /api/courses?id=2 return only that course, or a 404 JSON error {"error":"Not found"}.
  3. Make a BMI calculator form that shows the result on the same page using forward and request attributes.
Hint for 2

Set resp.setStatus(404) and write the JSON error body yourself; sendError would show the container's HTML error page.

Interview corner

  • forward vs sendRedirect? Forward is server-side within the same request (URL unchanged); redirect tells the browser to make a new request (URL changes).
  • What is the PRG pattern? Post/Redirect/Get: redirect after a successful POST to prevent duplicate submissions on refresh.
  • GET vs POST for forms? GET for searches/filters (bookmarkable, in URL); POST for actions that change data or contain sensitive data.
  • What does "response committed" mean? Headers/body have been sent to the client; status and headers can no longer change.

Summary

  • Read form data with getParameter (after setting UTF-8), validate on the server.
  • Use PRG after POST; forward to JSPs for views; redirect to change URL.
  • Set status/headers before the body; return JSON with the right content type.

Next: sessions and cookies, giving stateless HTTP a memory.
items.subject: servlet

items.title: Sessions and Cookies in Servlets
items.excerpt: Remember users across requests with HttpSession and cookies, build a login and logout flow, a shopping cart, and secure sessions with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and session-fixation protection.
items.content:
HTTP forgets you after every request. Yet websites keep you signed in and remember your cart. They do it with cookies and sessions.

The cloakroom analogy

At a wedding hall cloakroom, you hand over your bag and get a token number. The bag stays inside; you only carry the token. Next time you show the token, they find your bag.

  • The session is your bag, stored on the server.
  • The cookie JSESSIONID=8F2A… is the token, stored in your browser and sent with every request.

Cookies

A cookie is a small name=value pair the server asks the browser to store and send back:

// set a cookie
Cookie theme = new Cookie("theme", "dark");
theme.setMaxAge(60 * 60 * 24 * 365);     // seconds: 1 year (0 deletes it, -1 = until browser closes)
theme.setPath("/");
theme.setHttpOnly(true);                 // JavaScript can't read it
resp.addCookie(theme);

// read cookies
String current = "light";
if (req.getCookies() != null) {
    for (Cookie c : req.getCookies()) {
        if ("theme".equals(c.getName())) current = c.getValue();
    }
}

Cookies are limited (~4 KB each) and visible and editable by users. Never store passwords, roles or prices in cookies. Use them for preferences and the session id.

HttpSession

The container creates a session on demand and handles the JSESSIONID cookie for you:

HttpSession session = req.getSession();          // get, or create if none
session.setAttribute("user", "asha@example.com");
String user = (String) session.getAttribute("user");
session.removeAttribute("user");
session.invalidate();                            // destroy the whole session (logout)

HttpSession existing = req.getSession(false);    // get only; null if there is none

Session data lives in server memory, so it can hold objects (a cart, a user object), and users can't tamper with it.

A login and logout flow

import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebServlet("/login")
public class LoginServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String email = req.getParameter("email");
        String password = req.getParameter("password");

        if (!checkPassword(email, password)) {                 // look up the user, compare a password HASH
            resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/login.html?error=1");
            return;
        }
        HttpSession old = req.getSession(false);
        if (old != null) old.invalidate();                     // fresh session after login
        HttpSession session = req.getSession(true);
        session.setAttribute("user", email);
        session.setMaxInactiveInterval(30 * 60);               // 30 minutes idle timeout
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/dashboard");
    }

    private boolean checkPassword(String email, String password) {
        // demo only: real apps load the user and verify a BCrypt hash
        return "asha@example.com".equals(email) && "secret123".equals(password);
    }
}

@WebServlet("/logout")
class LogoutServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        HttpSession s = req.getSession(false);
        if (s != null) s.invalidate();
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/login.html");
    }
}

Every protected servlet can now check:

HttpSession s = req.getSession(false);
if (s == null || s.getAttribute("user") == null) {
    resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/login.html");
    return;
}

Repeating that check in every servlet is messy. Next lesson, a filter does it once for all pages.

A session shopping cart

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
List<String> cart = (List<String>) session.getAttribute("cart");
if (cart == null) {
    cart = new ArrayList<>();
    session.setAttribute("cart", cart);
}
cart.add(req.getParameter("product"));

Session security checklist

  • New session on login (invalidate then create, or req.changeSessionId()): prevents session fixation, where an attacker plants a known session id before you log in.
  • HttpOnly cookies: JavaScript (and XSS attacks) can't steal them. Tomcat sets HttpOnly on JSESSIONID by default.
  • Secure cookies: only sent over HTTPS. Always use HTTPS in production.
  • SameSite=Lax/Strict: reduces CSRF attacks (other sites making requests with your cookies).
  • Timeouts: expire idle sessions (setMaxInactiveInterval, or <session-timeout> in web.xml).
  • Logout with POST and invalidate().
  • Hash passwords with BCrypt or Argon2. Never store plain text.
<!-- WEB-INF/web.xml -->
<session-config>
  <session-timeout>30</session-timeout>
  <cookie-config>
    <http-only>true</http-only>
    <secure>true</secure>
  </cookie-config>
  <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>   <!-- never put the session id in URLs -->
</session-config>

Sessions at scale

Sessions live in one server's memory. With several servers behind a load balancer, you need sticky sessions, a shared session store (Redis via Spring Session), or stateless tokens like JWT (Spring Boot course). Many modern APIs are stateless for this reason.

Keep sessions small: store a user id, not the whole user with their order history. Every session costs server memory.

Common mistakes

  • req.getSession() on every request (creates sessions even for anonymous visitors). Use getSession(false) to only check.
  • Storing non-serialisable or huge objects in the session.
  • Logout via a GET link (can be triggered by other sites).
  • Keeping the same session id before and after login.

Exercise

  1. Build login, dashboard and logout servlets with the session check.
  2. Remember the user's preferred language in a cookie for 30 days and greet them in it.
  3. Build a session cart: /cart/add?product=Pen, /cart (list), /cart/clear.
  4. Show "You've visited this page N times in this session" using a session attribute.
Hint for 4

Integer n = (Integer) session.getAttribute("visits"); n = (n == null) ? 1 : n + 1; session.setAttribute("visits", n);

Interview corner

  • Session vs cookie? Cookies live in the browser and are sent with requests; sessions live on the server, identified by a cookie (JSESSIONID).
  • How does the server identify a session? By the session id in the JSESSIONID cookie (or URL rewriting if cookies are off).
  • What is session fixation and how do you prevent it? An attacker forces a known session id on a victim; prevent it by issuing a new session id at login.
  • How do you end a session? session.invalidate(), or let it time out.

Summary

  • Cookies are small browser-side values; sessions are server-side storage keyed by the JSESSIONID cookie.
  • getSession() creates; getSession(false) only checks; invalidate() logs out.
  • Secure sessions: new id on login, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, timeouts, HTTPS.

Next: filters and listeners, code that runs around every request.
items.subject: servlet

items.title: Servlet Filters and Listeners
items.excerpt: Run code before and after every request with filters (authentication, logging, encoding), watch a filter chain block a request in an animation, and react to app and session events with listeners.
items.content:
Some logic applies to many pages: checking login, logging requests, setting UTF-8, adding security headers. Copying it into every servlet is a maintenance nightmare. Filters wrap requests in one place, and listeners react to events like the app starting.

The airport security analogy

Before boarding, every passenger passes the same checkpoints: ticket check, security scan, passport control. Any checkpoint can stop you; otherwise you move on to the next. Filters are those checkpoints, and the servlet is the plane.

A filter chain, animated

Switch between "signed in" and "not signed in" and watch AuthFilter either pass the request on or stop it:

Writing a filter

import jakarta.servlet.*;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebFilter;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;

@WebFilter(urlPatterns = { "/dashboard/*", "/cart/*", "/api/*" })
public class AuthFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest req = (HttpServletRequest) request;
        HttpServletResponse resp = (HttpServletResponse) response;

        HttpSession session = req.getSession(false);
        boolean loggedIn = session != null && session.getAttribute("user") != null;

        if (!loggedIn) {
            if (req.getRequestURI().startsWith(req.getContextPath() + "/api/")) {
                resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED);        // 401 for APIs
            } else {
                resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/login.html");    // redirect for pages
            }
            return;                                // stop: the servlet never runs
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);         // continue to the next filter or the servlet
    }
}

The key line is chain.doFilter(...). Call it to continue; skip it to block.

Code before AND after the servlet

Everything after chain.doFilter runs on the way back, after the servlet has finished. Perfect for timing:

@WebFilter("/*")
public class TimingFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse resp, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, resp);                       // the request goes in…
        } finally {
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;   // …and comes back out
            HttpServletRequest r = (HttpServletRequest) req;
            r.getServletContext().log(r.getMethod() + " " + r.getRequestURI() + " took " + ms + " ms");
        }
    }
}

Common uses of filters

Spring Security is essentially a long, well-tested chain of servlet filters.

Filter order

With annotations, the order between filters is not guaranteed. When order matters (encoding before auth, logging first), declare them in web.xml, where the order of <filter-mapping> entries is the order of execution:

<filter><filter-name>timing</filter-name><filter-class>com.vitalstack.web.TimingFilter</filter-class></filter>
<filter><filter-name>auth</filter-name><filter-class>com.vitalstack.web.AuthFilter</filter-class></filter>
<filter-mapping><filter-name>timing</filter-name><url-pattern>/*</url-pattern></filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping><filter-name>auth</filter-name><url-pattern>/dashboard/*</url-pattern></filter-mapping>

Listeners: react to events

Listeners are notified when something happens in the app's life:

import jakarta.servlet.*;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebListener;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

@WebListener
public class AppListener implements ServletContextListener, HttpSessionListener {
    private static final AtomicInteger online = new AtomicInteger();

    @Override
    public void contextInitialized(ServletContextEvent e) {
        e.getServletContext().log("App started: create the DB connection pool here");
        e.getServletContext().setAttribute("online", online);
    }

    @Override
    public void contextDestroyed(ServletContextEvent e) {
        e.getServletContext().log("App stopping: close the pool here");
    }

    @Override public void sessionCreated(HttpSessionEvent e) { online.incrementAndGet(); }
    @Override public void sessionDestroyed(HttpSessionEvent e) { online.decrementAndGet(); }
}

Spring's ContextLoaderListener used exactly this hook to start the Spring container in classic web apps.

Filter vs servlet vs listener

  • Servlet: produces the response for specific URLs.
  • Filter: wraps requests for many URLs; can modify, log or block.
  • Listener: reacts to lifecycle events; doesn't handle requests directly.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting chain.doFilter: every request hangs or returns an empty page.
  • Calling chain.doFilter and then sending a redirect (response already committed).
  • A login filter that also protects /login.html, CSS and JS files → infinite redirect loop. Exclude public paths.
  • Relying on annotation order between filters.

Exercise

  1. Write an EncodingFilter for /* that sets UTF-8 on requests and responses.
  2. Write a SecurityHeadersFilter that adds X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: same-origin.
  3. Add an admin-only filter for /admin/* that checks a role session attribute and returns 403 otherwise.
  4. Show the number of online users (from the listener) on the dashboard.
Hint for 3

if (!"ADMIN".equals(session.getAttribute("role"))) { resp.sendError(403); return; }

Interview corner

  • What is a filter? An object that intercepts requests/responses for URL patterns to perform cross-cutting work (auth, logging, encoding) via doFilter and FilterChain.
  • How do you stop a request in a filter? Don't call chain.doFilter; send an error or redirect instead.
  • Filter vs interceptor? Filters are servlet-level (before DispatcherServlet); Spring HandlerInterceptors run inside Spring MVC around controller methods.
  • Name some listeners. ServletContextListener, HttpSessionListener, ServletRequestListener, attribute listeners.

Summary

  • Filters run before and after servlets; chain.doFilter passes control on, skipping it blocks.
  • Use filters for authentication, logging, encoding, headers and CORS.
  • Listeners react to app, session and request events.

Next: JSP and the MVC pattern for building HTML views.
items.subject: servlet

items.title: JSP, JSTL and the MVC Pattern
items.excerpt: Build HTML views with JSP, Expression Language and JSTL instead of println, structure apps with Model-View-Controller (servlet + JSP), and learn how this evolved into Spring MVC and Thymeleaf.
items.content:
Writing HTML with out.println("<tr><td>" + name + "</td></tr>") gets ugly fast. JSP (Jakarta Server Pages) flips it around: you write HTML and insert dynamic values where needed. Combined with servlets, you get the MVC pattern, the foundation of Spring MVC.

MVC: three jobs, three places

Browser ──request──▶ Controller (Servlet) ──uses──▶ Model (Java classes, DB)
                          │
                          └─forward with data──▶ View (JSP) ──HTML──▶ Browser
  • Model: data and business logic (Course, CourseService).
  • View: presentation only (JSP, HTML).
  • Controller: receives the request, calls the model, picks the view.

Each part can change without breaking the others: designers edit JSPs, developers edit Java.

The controller servlet

import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.List;

@WebServlet("/courses")
public class CourseController extends HttpServlet {

    public record Course(int id, String title, String level, int lessons) { }

    private static final List<Course> COURSES = List.of(
        new Course(1, "Java", "Beginner", 16),
        new Course(2, "Spring Boot", "Intermediate", 10),
        new Course(3, "Hibernate", "Advanced", 7));

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        String level = req.getParameter("level");
        List<Course> list = (level == null || level.isBlank()) ? COURSES
                : COURSES.stream().filter(c -> c.level().equalsIgnoreCase(level)).toList();

        req.setAttribute("courses", list);          // the model for the view
        req.setAttribute("level", level);
        req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/courses.jsp").forward(req, resp);
    }
}

JSPs inside WEB-INF can't be opened directly by the browser: users must go through the controller. That's good MVC hygiene.

The view: JSP with EL and JSTL

Add JSTL to pom.xml (Tomcat doesn't include it):

<dependency>
  <groupId>jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl</groupId>
  <artifactId>jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl-api</artifactId>
  <version>3.0.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.glassfish.web</groupId>
  <artifactId>jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl</artifactId>
  <version>3.0.1</version>
</dependency>

/WEB-INF/views/courses.jsp:

<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="fn" uri="jakarta.tags.functions" %>
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head><title>Courses</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Courses <c:if test="${not empty level}">(${fn:escapeXml(level)})</c:if></h1>

  <c:choose>
    <c:when test="${empty courses}">
      <p>No courses found.</p>
    </c:when>
    <c:otherwise>
      <table>
        <tr><th>#</th><th>Title</th><th>Level</th><th>Lessons</th></tr>
        <c:forEach var="course" items="${courses}" varStatus="s">
          <tr>
            <td>${s.count}</td>
            <td><c:out value="${course.title}"/></td>
            <td>${course.level}</td>
            <td>${course.lessons}</td>
          </tr>
        </c:forEach>
      </table>
    </c:otherwise>
  </c:choose>
</body>
</html>

The fn taglib provides helpers like fn:escapeXml, fn:length and fn:toUpperCase.

Expression Language (EL)

${...} reads values from request, session and application attributes:

JSTL core tags

Use <c:out> (or fn:escapeXml) for any value that came from a user. Plain ${...} in JSP does not escape HTML, so it can open XSS holes.

Avoid scriptlets

Old JSPs mixed Java code into HTML with <% ... %> scriptlets. It's hard to read, test and secure. Modern rule: no Java code in JSPs. Prepare everything in the servlet; the JSP only displays it with EL and JSTL.

How a JSP runs

The first time a JSP is requested, the container translates it into a servlet (Java code), compiles it, and runs it. A JSP is a servlet behind the scenes. That's why the first request to a new JSP is slower.

From here to Spring MVC

Same MVC idea, far less boilerplate. Many companies still maintain JSP apps, so knowing both is valuable.

Exercise

  1. Build the courses page with filtering links: All, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced.
  2. Add a /courses/detail?id=2 controller and JSP; show a 404 if the id doesn't exist.
  3. Create a reusable header with <%@ include file="/WEB-INF/views/header.jspf" %> and use it on both pages.
  4. Show "Welcome, ${sessionScope.user}" in the header when logged in, and a Login link otherwise.
Hint for 1

Use <c:url value="/courses"><c:param name="level" value="Beginner"/></c:url> to build links that include the context path.

Interview corner

  • What is MVC? Model-View-Controller: separates data/logic, presentation and request handling.
  • JSP vs servlet? A JSP is HTML with dynamic parts, compiled into a servlet; servlets are Java classes better suited to control logic.
  • What is EL and JSTL? EL (${}) accesses data in JSPs; JSTL is a tag library for loops, conditions, URLs and formatting.
  • Why put JSPs under WEB-INF? To force access through controllers so views always get prepared data.

Summary

  • MVC: servlet = controller, Java classes = model, JSP = view.
  • JSPs use EL and JSTL (no scriptlets); <c:out> escapes output.
  • JSPs compile into servlets; Spring MVC is the same pattern with less code.

Next: build a complete to-do app with servlets, JSP and JDBC.
items.subject: servlet

items.title: Servlet Project: To-Do App with JDBC
items.excerpt: Build a complete MVC to-do web app with servlets, JSP, sessions, a login filter and a MySQL or H2 database through JDBC with PreparedStatement, a DAO and a connection pool.
items.content:
Let's combine everything: servlets, JSP, sessions, filters and a real database. You'll build a to-do app where each user manages their own tasks.

Architecture

Browser
  │
  ▼
AuthFilter (/tasks/*)  ──not logged in──▶ /login
  │
  ▼
TaskServlet (controller)  ──▶ TaskDao (JDBC) ──▶ MySQL / H2
  │
  ▼
tasks.jsp (view)

Step 1: Database table

CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  title      VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  done       BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

Add the driver to pom.xml (MySQL shown; for quick practice use com.h2database:h2 instead):

<dependency>
  <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
  <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
  <version>8.4.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.zaxxer</groupId>
  <artifactId>HikariCP</artifactId>
  <version>5.1.0</version>
</dependency>

Step 2: A connection pool on startup

Opening a database connection is slow (~50-100 ms). A connection pool opens a few connections once and lends them out. HikariCP is the fastest (Spring Boot uses it by default).

package com.vitalstack.todo;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig;
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import jakarta.servlet.*;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebListener;

@WebListener
public class DbSetup implements ServletContextListener {
    private HikariDataSource ds;

    @Override
    public void contextInitialized(ServletContextEvent e) {
        HikariConfig cfg = new HikariConfig();
        cfg.setJdbcUrl(System.getenv().getOrDefault("DB_URL", "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/todo"));
        cfg.setUsername(System.getenv().getOrDefault("DB_USER", "todo"));
        cfg.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));      // never hard-code passwords
        cfg.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
        ds = new HikariDataSource(cfg);
        e.getServletContext().setAttribute("taskDao", new TaskDao(ds));
    }

    @Override
    public void contextDestroyed(ServletContextEvent e) {
        if (ds != null) ds.close();
    }
}

Step 3: The model and DAO

A DAO (Data Access Object) keeps all SQL in one class:

package com.vitalstack.todo;

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import java.sql.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class TaskDao {
    public record Task(int id, String title, boolean done) { }

    private final DataSource ds;
    public TaskDao(DataSource ds) { this.ds = ds; }

    public List<Task> findByOwner(String owner) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT id, title, done FROM tasks WHERE owner = ? ORDER BY done, created_at DESC";
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setString(1, owner);
            try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                List<Task> list = new ArrayList<>();
                while (rs.next()) {
                    list.add(new Task(rs.getInt("id"), rs.getString("title"), rs.getBoolean("done")));
                }
                return list;
            }
        }
    }

    public void add(String owner, String title) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO tasks(owner, title) VALUES (?, ?)")) {
            ps.setString(1, owner);
            ps.setString(2, title);
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }

    public void toggle(String owner, int id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("UPDATE tasks SET done = NOT done WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?")) {
            ps.setInt(1, id);
            ps.setString(2, owner);       // users can only change their OWN tasks
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }

    public void delete(String owner, int id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?")) {
            ps.setInt(1, id);
            ps.setString(2, owner);
            ps.executeUpdate();
        }
    }
}

**Always use PreparedStatement with ? placeholders.** Building SQL with "... WHERE owner = '" + owner + "'" allows SQL injection: a user typing ' OR '1'='1 could read or delete everyone's data.

Notice try-with-resources returns every connection to the pool, even when an exception happens.

Step 4: The controller

package com.vitalstack.todo;

import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.annotation.WebServlet;
import jakarta.servlet.http.*;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.sql.SQLException;

@WebServlet("/tasks")
public class TaskServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private TaskDao dao;

    @Override
    public void init() {
        dao = (TaskDao) getServletContext().getAttribute("taskDao");
    }

    private String owner(HttpServletRequest req) {
        return (String) req.getSession(false).getAttribute("user");    // the filter guarantees a session
    }

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        try {
            req.setAttribute("tasks", dao.findByOwner(owner(req)));
            req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/tasks.jsp").forward(req, resp);
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            throw new ServletException("Could not load tasks", e);
        }
    }

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        req.setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8");
        String action = String.valueOf(req.getParameter("action"));
        try {
            switch (action) {
                case "add" -> {
                    String title = req.getParameter("title");
                    if (title != null && !title.isBlank() && title.length() <= 200) dao.add(owner(req), title.trim());
                }
                case "toggle" -> dao.toggle(owner(req), Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("id")));
                case "delete" -> dao.delete(owner(req), Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("id")));
                default -> { resp.sendError(400, "Unknown action"); return; }
            }
        } catch (SQLException | NumberFormatException e) {
            throw new ServletException(e);
        }
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/tasks");         // Post/Redirect/Get
    }
}

Use the AuthFilter and LoginServlet from the previous lessons to protect /tasks.

Step 5: The view

/WEB-INF/views/tasks.jsp:

<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<!doctype html>
<html><body>
<h1>My tasks</h1>
<form method="post" action="<c:url value='/tasks'/>">
  <input type="hidden" name="action" value="add">
  <input name="title" placeholder="What needs doing?" maxlength="200" required>
  <button>Add</button>
</form>
<ul>
  <c:forEach var="t" items="${tasks}">
    <li>
      <form method="post" action="<c:url value='/tasks'/>" style="display:inline">
        <input type="hidden" name="id" value="${t.id}">
        <button name="action" value="toggle">${t.done ? '✅' : '⬜'}</button>
        <c:choose>
          <c:when test="${t.done}"><s><c:out value="${t.title}"/></s></c:when>
          <c:otherwise><c:out value="${t.title}"/></c:otherwise>
        </c:choose>
        <button name="action" value="delete">🗑</button>
      </form>
    </li>
  </c:forEach>
</ul>
<form method="post" action="<c:url value='/logout'/>"><button>Log out</button></form>
</body></html>

What you used

Extend it

  1. Add due dates and highlight overdue tasks.
  2. Add a filter: All / Active / Done.
  3. Replace the hard-coded login with a users table and BCrypt password hashes.
  4. Add CSRF protection: store a random token in the session and require it as a hidden field in every POST form.
  5. Rewrite the DAO with JPA (next course), then the whole app with Spring Boot, and compare the amount of code.
Hint for 4

Generate the token with SecureRandom + Base64 at login, put it in the session and in every form; in a filter for POST requests, compare req.getParameter("csrf") with the session value and return 403 if they differ.

Summary

  • A real web app = filter (security) + servlet (controller) + DAO (data) + JSP (view).
  • Use a connection pool, PreparedStatement and try-with-resources for JDBC.
  • Always scope queries by the current user and escape output.

Next course: JPA, to stop writing SQL and mapping code by hand.

items.title: JPA Introduction - What is ORM?
items.excerpt: Why writing JDBC by hand gets painful, what Object-Relational Mapping solves, how JPA, Hibernate and Spring Data JPA relate, and what the code looks like before and after.
items.content:
Java works with objects: a Course with a title and a list of lessons. Databases work with tables: rows and columns linked by foreign keys. Moving data between the two by hand is repetitive and error-prone. JPA (Jakarta Persistence API) does it for you.

The pain of plain JDBC

Saving and loading one simple object with JDBC:

// Save
String sql = "INSERT INTO course (title, price, level) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {
    ps.setString(1, course.getTitle());
    ps.setInt(2, course.getPrice());
    ps.setString(3, course.getLevel().name());
    ps.executeUpdate();
    try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) {
        if (keys.next()) course.setId(keys.getLong(1));
    }
}

// Load
try (Connection c = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM course WHERE id = ?")) {
    ps.setLong(1, id);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        if (rs.next()) {
            Course course = new Course();
            course.setId(rs.getLong("id"));
            course.setTitle(rs.getString("title"));
            course.setPrice(rs.getInt("price"));
            course.setLevel(Level.valueOf(rs.getString("level")));
            return course;
        }
    }
}

Now multiply that by 40 tables, add relationships (a course has lessons, lessons have quizzes), updates of only changed columns, caching, and different SQL dialects for MySQL vs PostgreSQL vs Oracle. That's a lot of boring, bug-prone code.

The same with JPA

em.persist(course);                          // INSERT, id filled in automatically
Course c = em.find(Course.class, 1L);        // SELECT and map to an object
c.setPrice(399);                             // UPDATE happens automatically at commit

You describe the mapping once with annotations, and JPA writes the SQL:

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int price;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private Level level;
    // getters and setters
}

What is ORM?

Object-Relational Mapping bridges the two worlds:

JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA

These names confuse everyone at first:

Spring Data JPA   ← writes repository classes for you (findByTitle…)
      │ uses
JPA (jakarta.persistence)   ← the STANDARD: annotations + EntityManager API (a specification)
      │ implemented by
Hibernate  (or EclipseLink, OpenJPA)   ← the ENGINE that actually generates SQL
      │ uses
JDBC   ← talks to the database driver
  • JPA is a specification: interfaces and annotations (@Entity, EntityManager).
  • Hibernate is the most popular implementation. It also has extra features beyond JPA (next course).
  • Spring Data JPA sits on top and removes even more boilerplate (Spring Boot course).

Write against JPA annotations and APIs; you'll be using Hibernate underneath in 90% of projects.

Package names: modern JPA (3.x, used by Spring Boot 3 and Hibernate 6) uses jakarta.persistence.*. Old tutorials use javax.persistence.*. Don't mix them.

What JPA gives you

  • Mapping classes to tables with annotations.
  • CRUD without SQL: persist, find, merge, remove.
  • Automatic change tracking ("dirty checking"): modify an object, and the UPDATE is generated.
  • Relationships: one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many.
  • JPQL: queries written against classes and fields, portable across databases.
  • Caching, lazy loading, optimistic locking, schema generation.

When ORM isn't the right tool

  • Heavy reporting with complex SQL: native SQL or a query library (jOOQ) can be clearer.
  • Bulk operations on millions of rows: use batch SQL.
  • Very simple apps: JdbcTemplate might be enough.

Most business apps, though, benefit hugely from JPA. It's in nearly every Java back-end job description.

Exercise

  1. Write the CREATE TABLE you'd expect for the Course entity above.
  2. Name three things JDBC code makes you do by hand that JPA automates.
  3. Explain in one sentence each: JPA, Hibernate, Spring Data JPA.
Hint for 1

CREATE TABLE course (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(255), price INT NOT NULL, level VARCHAR(255)). int maps to NOT NULL because a primitive can't be null.

Interview corner

  • What is ORM? A technique to map objects to relational tables so code works with objects instead of SQL and result sets.
  • JPA vs Hibernate? JPA is a specification (API); Hibernate is an implementation of it with extra features.
  • What is an entity? A lightweight persistent class annotated with @Entity, whose instances map to table rows.
  • Advantages of JPA over JDBC? Less boilerplate, database independence, automatic dirty checking, caching, relationship mapping, portable queries.

Summary

  • JDBC requires manual SQL and mapping; JPA automates it with annotations.
  • JPA = standard; Hibernate = implementation; Spring Data JPA = repositories on top.
  • Entities map to tables, fields to columns, references to foreign keys.

Next: set up JPA and save your first entity.
