items.title: Setting Up JPA and Your First Entity
items.excerpt: Add Hibernate and H2 with Maven, configure persistence.xml, write your first @Entity, save and load it with EntityManager, and read the SQL Hibernate generates.
items.content:
Let's run JPA for real. You'll use Hibernate 6 as the JPA provider and H2, an in-memory database that needs no installation. Later you can switch to MySQL or PostgreSQL by changing two lines.

Step 1: Maven dependencies

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
    <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
    <version>6.5.2.Final</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <version>2.2.224</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

hibernate-core brings in the jakarta.persistence API too.

Step 2: persistence.xml

Create src/main/resources/META-INF/persistence.xml:

<persistence xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence" version="3.0">
  <persistence-unit name="school">
    <class>com.vitalstack.Course</class>
    <properties>
      <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url" value="jdbc:h2:mem:school;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1"/>
      <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.user" value="sa"/>
      <property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.password" value=""/>
      <!-- create tables from entities (development only) -->
      <property name="jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action" value="drop-and-create"/>
      <!-- print the SQL so you can learn from it -->
      <property name="hibernate.show_sql" value="true"/>
      <property name="hibernate.format_sql" value="true"/>
    </properties>
  </persistence-unit>
</persistence>

A persistence unit is a named configuration: which database, which entity classes, which settings.

Step 3: The entity

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity                                   // this class maps to a table
public class Course {

    @Id                                   // primary key
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)   // auto-increment column
    private Long id;

    private String title;
    private int price;

    protected Course() { }                // JPA needs a no-argument constructor

    public Course(String title, int price) {
        this.title = title;
        this.price = price;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public void setTitle(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public void setPrice(int price) { this.price = price; }

    @Override public String toString() { return "Course{id=" + id + ", title='" + title + "', price=" + price + "}"; }
}

Entity rules:

  • Annotated with @Entity and has an @Id.
  • Has a public or protected no-argument constructor (JPA creates objects through it).
  • Not final, and persistent fields not final (Hibernate may create proxy subclasses).
  • Use wrapper types like Long for ids, so "not saved yet" is null.

Step 4: Save and load

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");   // heavy: create once per app

        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();     // light: one per unit of work
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Course java = new Course("Java", 499);
        em.persist(java);                                  // schedule INSERT
        em.persist(new Course("Spring Boot", 799));
        em.getTransaction().commit();                      // SQL is sent here
        System.out.println("Saved with id " + java.getId());
        em.close();

        EntityManager em2 = emf.createEntityManager();
        Course found = em2.find(Course.class, java.getId());   // SELECT by primary key
        System.out.println(found);
        em2.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Console output (formatted SQL shortened):

create table Course (price integer not null, id bigint generated by default as identity, title varchar(255), primary key (id))
insert into Course (price,title,id) values (?,?,default)
insert into Course (price,title,id) values (?,?,default)
Saved with id 1
select c1_0.id,c1_0.price,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
Course{id=1, title='Java', price=499}

Hibernate created the table, inserted the rows and mapped the result back into an object. You wrote zero SQL.

The main JPA objects

Changes (persist, update, remove) must happen inside a transaction. In Spring you'll simply annotate a method with @Transactional instead of calling begin/commit yourself.

Switching to MySQL

Add the driver dependency and change the properties:

<property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url" value="jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school"/>
<property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.user" value="school"/>
<property name="jakarta.persistence.jdbc.password" value="change-me"/>

Hibernate detects the database and generates MySQL-flavoured SQL. Your Java code doesn't change.

Use drop-and-create (or update) only while learning. In real projects, the schema is managed with migration tools like Flyway or Liquibase, and Hibernate is set to validate or none. Otherwise a deployment could drop your production tables!

Common mistakes

  • No Persistence provider for EntityManager named school: persistence.xml isn't in META-INF on the classpath, or the unit name doesn't match.
  • No default constructor for entity: add a protected no-arg constructor.
  • Persisting outside a transaction: nothing is saved, or TransactionRequiredException.
  • Creating a new EntityManagerFactory for every request (slow and leaks resources).

Exercise

  1. Run the example and find the generated CREATE TABLE and INSERT in the console.
  2. Add a level field (String) and a published boolean. Check the new columns.
  3. Save five courses, then load one by id and print it.
  4. Change a course's price inside a transaction without calling any save method. Is an UPDATE printed?
Hint for 4

Yes. A managed entity is tracked; at commit, Hibernate compares it with its snapshot and sends an UPDATE for changed fields. This is called dirty checking (lesson 4).

Interview corner

  • What is persistence.xml? The JPA configuration file defining persistence units (data source, entities, provider properties).
  • EntityManagerFactory vs EntityManager? EMF is heavyweight, thread-safe, one per app; EM is lightweight, not thread-safe, one per unit of work.
  • Why does an entity need a no-arg constructor? The provider instantiates entities by reflection when loading rows.
  • **What does hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto / schema-generation do?** Generates or updates the schema from entities; use only in development.

Summary

  • Add hibernate-core + a JDBC driver, configure a persistence unit in META-INF/persistence.xml.
  • @Entity + @Id + a no-arg constructor makes a class persistent.
  • EntityManagerFactory once; EntityManager per unit of work; changes inside transactions.

Next: control exactly how fields map to columns.

items.title: JPA Entity Mapping - Tables, Columns and Ids
items.excerpt: Control table and column names, lengths, nullability and uniqueness, choose an id generation strategy, map enums, dates, large text, embedded value objects and transient fields.
items.content:
By default JPA maps a class Course to a table Course and every field to a column of the same name. Real databases have naming conventions, constraints and special types. Annotations let you control all of it.

A fully mapped entity

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@Entity
@Table(name = "students",
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_student_email", columnNames = "email"))
public class Student {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String email;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)              // store "ACTIVE", not 0
    @Column(length = 20)
    private Status status = Status.ACTIVE;

    private LocalDate birthDate;              // DATE column
    private LocalDateTime joinedAt;           // TIMESTAMP column

    @Lob                                       // large text (CLOB)
    private String bio;

    @Embedded                                  // columns of Address live in this table
    private Address address;

    @Transient                                 // NOT stored in the database
    private int unreadNotifications;

    protected Student() { }

    public Student(String name, String email, Address address) {
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
        this.address = address;
        this.joinedAt = LocalDateTime.now();
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public Status getStatus() { return status; }
    public Address getAddress() { return address; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

public enum Status { ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, GRADUATED }
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.Embeddable;

@Embeddable                                    // a value object: no table, no id of its own
public class Address {
    private String city;
    private String pin;

    protected Address() { }
    public Address(String city, String pin) { this.city = city; this.pin = pin; }
    public String getCity() { return city; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        em.persist(new Student("Asha Kumar", "asha@example.com", new Address("Pune", "411001")));
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        Student s = em.createQuery("select s from Student s", Student.class).getSingleResult();
        System.out.println(s.getName() + " | " + s.getStatus() + " | " + s.getAddress().getCity());
        em.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Generated table (H2, reformatted for reading):

create table students (
    birthDate date,
    id bigint generated by default as identity,
    joinedAt timestamp(6),
    full_name varchar(100) not null,
    city varchar(255),
    email varchar(255) not null,
    pin varchar(255),
    bio clob,
    status enum ('ACTIVE','GRADUATED','SUSPENDED'),
    primary key (id),
    constraint uk_student_email unique (email))

The column type for status depends on the database: H2 and MySQL get an enum type, others a varchar.

Output: Asha Kumar | ACTIVE | Pune

@Table and @Column

These constraints matter only for schema generation; they don't validate data in Java. Use Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @Email, @Size) for that. You'll use it in the Spring Boot course.

Id generation strategies

@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "student_seq")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "student_seq", sequenceName = "student_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;

allocationSize = 50 lets Hibernate reserve 50 ids per database round trip: much faster inserts.

Enums: always STRING

@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
private Status status;

The default ORDINAL stores 0, 1, 2. If someone later inserts a new constant in the middle of the enum, every existing row silently changes meaning. STRING stores readable names and is safe.

Dates and times

Use java.time types: they map automatically.

Avoid old java.util.Date and @Temporal in new code.

Embeddables: value objects

Address has no identity of its own: it belongs to a student. @Embeddable + @Embedded store its fields as columns of the owner's table. Reuse it in Teacher and Company too. Rename columns per use with @AttributeOverride.

@Transient

Fields marked @Transient (or Java transient) aren't persisted: perfect for computed or temporary values.

Field vs property access

Where you put @Id decides the access type: on a field → JPA reads/writes fields directly (recommended); on a getter → JPA uses getters/setters. Don't mix them in one entity.

Keep entities focused on data and simple rules. Don't put HTTP or UI logic in them, and don't return entities directly from public APIs; map them to DTOs/records (Spring Boot course).

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING).
  • Using double for money: use BigDecimal with precision/scale, or store paise in a long.
  • Column names that are SQL reserved words (order, user, group) → rename with @Table/@Column.
  • Expecting nullable = false to validate before saving (it only affects DDL; the database throws an exception).

Exercise

  1. Map a Product entity: sku (unique, 20 chars), name (not null), price as BigDecimal(10,2), category enum, createdAt.
  2. Create an @Embeddable Money(amount, currency) and use it in Order twice (subtotal, tax) with @AttributeOverrides.
  3. Switch Student to a UUID id and check the generated DDL.
Hint for 2

@AttributeOverrides({ @AttributeOverride(name = "amount", column = @Column(name = "tax_amount")), @AttributeOverride(name = "currency", column = @Column(name = "tax_currency")) }) on the second field.

Interview corner

  • @Column(nullable=false) vs @NotNull? The first only shapes the DDL; the second is Bean Validation that checks before persisting.
  • IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE? IDENTITY uses auto-increment (no batching); SEQUENCE fetches ids from a sequence (batch-friendly with allocationSize).
  • Why EnumType.STRING? ORDINAL breaks when enum constants are reordered.
  • What is @Embeddable? A value type whose fields are stored in the owning entity's table.

Summary

  • @Table, @Column control names and constraints; @Id + @GeneratedValue choose ids.
  • Map enums as STRING, dates with java.time, big text with @Lob.
  • @Embeddable value objects group columns; @Transient skips fields.

Next: the EntityManager and the four states of an entity, animated.

items.title: EntityManager and Entity States
items.excerpt: Learn the four entity states (transient, managed, detached, removed) with an animation, use persist, find, merge, remove and detach correctly, and see automatic dirty checking generate UPDATEs.
items.content:
The most important idea in JPA is that every entity object is in one of four states. Once you understand the states, the "magic" (automatic updates, LazyInitializationException, merge surprises) becomes predictable.

The four states, animated

Step through a course's whole life: created, saved, edited, closed, merged back and deleted. Watch which SQL runs at each step:

            new                persist()                close()/detach()/clear()
 (none) ───────▶ TRANSIENT ─────────────▶ MANAGED ─────────────────────────▶ DETACHED
                                ▲  │  ▲                                          │
                    find()/query│  │  └──────────────── merge() ─────────────────┘
                                   │ remove()
                                   ▼
                                REMOVED ──commit──▶ deleted

Running it for real

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int price;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public void setTitle(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public void setPrice(int price) { this.price = price; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");

        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Course c = new Course("Java", 499);                 // TRANSIENT
        em.persist(c);                                       // MANAGED
        System.out.println("contains? " + em.contains(c));   // true
        em.getTransaction().commit();                        // INSERT

        em.getTransaction().begin();
        c.setTitle("Java Basics");                           // no method call needed...
        em.getTransaction().commit();                        // ...UPDATE (dirty checking)
        em.close();                                          // c is now DETACHED

        c.setTitle("Java 101");                              // nobody is watching this change

        EntityManager em2 = emf.createEntityManager();
        em2.getTransaction().begin();
        Course managed = em2.merge(c);                       // SELECT, copy state onto a MANAGED copy
        System.out.println("same object? " + (managed == c));   // false!
        em2.getTransaction().commit();                       // UPDATE

        em2.getTransaction().begin();
        em2.remove(managed);                                 // REMOVED
        em2.getTransaction().commit();                       // DELETE
        System.out.println("found after delete: " + em2.find(Course.class, c.getId()));
        em2.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output:

insert into Course (price,title,id) values (?,?,default)
contains? true
update Course set price=?,title=? where id=?
select c1_0.id,c1_0.price,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
same object? false
update Course set price=?,title=? where id=?
delete from Course where id=?
select c1_0.id,c1_0.price,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
found after delete: null

Dirty checking: updates without save()

When an entity becomes managed, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its values. At flush/commit, it compares the current values with the snapshot and generates UPDATEs for anything that changed. There is no update() method in JPA, and you don't need one.

This is why calling save() after modifying a managed entity in Spring Data is unnecessary inside a @Transactional method. And it's why accidentally modifying an entity (e.g. formatting a name for display) inside a transaction can silently change your database!

The EntityManager methods

The merge trap

merge returns a managed copy; the object you passed stays detached:

Course managed = em.merge(detached);
detached.setPrice(1);   // ❌ ignored: not tracked
managed.setPrice(1);    // ✅ tracked

Also, persist on a detached entity (one with an id from the database) throws EntityExistsException/PersistentObjectException. New → persist; existing and detached → merge.

remove needs a managed entity

em.remove(em.find(Course.class, 5L));              // ✅
em.remove(detachedCourse);                          // ❌ IllegalArgumentException: Removing a detached instance
em.remove(em.merge(detachedCourse));                // ✅ (but a find is clearer)

Where detached entities come from

  • The EntityManager closed (end of a web request).
  • Entities were serialised (sent to a client, stored in a session).
  • clear() or detach() was called.

Accessing a lazy relationship on a detached entity throws the famous LazyInitializationException (Hibernate course).

Common mistakes

  • Using the argument of merge instead of its return value.
  • Calling persist for updates.
  • Removing a detached entity.
  • Long-lived EntityManagers holding thousands of managed entities (memory + slow flushes). Keep units of work short.

Exercise

  1. Run the example. Then comment out em.getTransaction().commit() after setTitle("Java Basics") and see what changes.
  2. Load a course with find, call em.detach(course), change the price and commit. Is there an UPDATE?
  3. Use getReference for a non-existing id and print the title. What exception do you get, and when?
Hint for 2

No UPDATE: after detach the entity isn't tracked, so dirty checking ignores it.

Interview corner

  • Entity states? Transient, managed (persistent), detached, removed.
  • persist vs merge? persist makes a new entity managed (same instance); merge copies a detached entity's state onto a managed instance and returns that instance.
  • What is dirty checking? At flush, the provider compares managed entities with their snapshots and issues UPDATEs for changes.
  • find vs getReference? find hits the database (or cache) and returns null if missing; getReference returns a proxy without a query and fails later if the row doesn't exist.

Summary

  • Entities are transient, managed, detached or removed.
  • Managed entities are tracked: changes become UPDATEs automatically.
  • Use persist for new objects, merge's return value for detached ones, remove on managed ones.

Next: the persistence context, the cache behind all this.

items.title: The Persistence Context and First-Level Cache
items.excerpt: Discover why calling find() twice runs only one query, how the identity guarantee works, when Hibernate flushes, write-behind, and how to process large data without running out of memory.
items.content:
Every EntityManager has a persistence context: a map of all the managed entities it has loaded, keyed by type and id. It's also called the first-level cache. It explains why JPA sometimes runs fewer queries than you expect, and sometimes more memory than you'd like.

Watch the cache work

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int price;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public void setPrice(int price) { this.price = price; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager setup = emf.createEntityManager();
        setup.getTransaction().begin();
        setup.persist(new Course("Java", 499));
        setup.getTransaction().commit();
        setup.close();

        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        System.out.println("-- first find");
        Course a = em.find(Course.class, 1L);          // SELECT
        System.out.println("-- second find");
        Course b = em.find(Course.class, 1L);          // no SQL: from the persistence context
        System.out.println("same object? " + (a == b));

        em.getTransaction().begin();
        a.setPrice(399);
        System.out.println("-- commit");
        em.getTransaction().commit();                  // UPDATE
        em.close();

        EntityManager em2 = emf.createEntityManager();
        System.out.println("-- new EntityManager");
        Course c = em2.find(Course.class, 1L);         // new context: SELECT again
        System.out.println(c.getTitle() + " now costs " + c.getPrice());
        em2.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output:

-- first find
select c1_0.id,c1_0.price,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
-- second find
same object? true
-- commit
update Course set price=?,title=? where id=?
-- new EntityManager
select c1_0.id,c1_0.price,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
Java now costs 399

The identity guarantee

Within one persistence context, one database row = one Java object. a == b is true. This prevents two different copies of the same course with conflicting changes. Queries respect it too: if a JPQL query returns a row that's already managed, you get the existing object (the query still runs; the cache only short-circuits find by id).

Scope

The persistence context lives as long as its EntityManager:

  • Plain JPA: until you call em.close().
  • Spring: usually one per transaction (@Transactional method). Each web request gets a fresh one.

So the first-level cache is short-lived and private. It's not a shared application cache: that's the optional second-level cache (Hibernate course).

Flushing: when SQL is actually sent

JPA uses write-behind: persist, changes and remove are collected and sent later, at flush. Flush happens:

  1. When the transaction commits.
  2. Before a JPQL/native query whose results could be affected (flush mode AUTO), so the query sees your pending changes.
  3. When you call em.flush() explicitly.

Flushing sends SQL but doesn't commit: a later rollback still undoes everything.

Why delay? Hibernate can order statements to avoid constraint problems, skip updates for values changed back, and batch many inserts into one round trip (with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size).

Memory: the hidden cost

Every managed entity, plus its snapshot for dirty checking, stays in memory until the context ends. Loading 1,000,000 rows in one transaction can crash your app with OutOfMemoryError and makes each flush slower.

For big jobs, process in chunks and clear the context:

int batch = 50;
em.getTransaction().begin();
for (int i = 1; i <= 100_000; i++) {
    em.persist(new Course("Course " + i, 99));
    if (i % batch == 0) {
        em.flush();       // send the pending inserts
        em.clear();       // detach everything: free memory
    }
}
em.getTransaction().commit();

For read-only reports, use DTO projections or read-only queries (lesson 7) so entities aren't tracked at all.

"Why does my change not show up?" and "Why is the old value still there?" often come down to the persistence context: a value you changed is pending (not flushed yet), or the entity was loaded before someone else changed the row. Use em.refresh(entity) to reload it.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the first-level cache shares data across users or requests (it doesn't).
  • Running JDBC/native SQL updates and expecting already-loaded entities to change (they don't; refresh or clear).
  • Huge transactions that load or insert everything at once.
  • Calling flush() everywhere "to be safe": it removes batching benefits.

Exercise

  1. Run the example and confirm the second find prints no SQL.
  2. Inside one EntityManager, persist a course, then run select c from Course c before committing. Is the new course in the results? Why?
  3. Insert 1,000 courses with and without flush/clear every 50 and compare the time.
Hint for 2

Yes: with flush mode AUTO, Hibernate flushes pending inserts before running a query that touches the Course table.

Interview corner

  • What is the persistence context? The set of managed entity instances for an EntityManager, guaranteeing one instance per row and tracking changes.
  • What is the first-level cache? The persistence context acting as a cache for find by id; enabled always, scoped to the EntityManager/transaction.
  • When does flush happen? At commit, before relevant queries (AUTO), or on explicit flush().
  • flush vs commit? Flush sends SQL; commit ends the transaction and makes changes permanent.

Summary

  • The persistence context keeps one managed object per row and remembers snapshots.
  • Repeated find by id is served from it; queries still hit the database.
  • SQL is written at flush (commit, before queries, or explicit).
  • Clear the context in big batch jobs to save memory.

Next: relationships between entities.

items.title: JPA Relationships - OneToMany, ManyToOne, ManyToMany
items.excerpt: Map relationships between entities - @ManyToOne, bidirectional @OneToMany with mappedBy, the owning side, cascade, orphanRemoval, @ManyToMany with a join table, @OneToOne and default fetch types.
items.content:
Real data is connected: a course has many lessons, a student enrolls in many courses, a user has one profile. JPA maps these links between objects to foreign keys and join tables.

The four relationship types

ManyToOne: the simplest and most important

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Lesson {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)   // the OWNING side: has the FK column
    @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")
    private Course course;

    protected Lesson() { }
    public Lesson(String title) { this.title = title; }

    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public Course getCourse() { return course; }
    void setCourse(Course course) { this.course = course; }
}

The side with the foreign key column is the owning side. Only changes on the owning side are written to the database.

OneToMany: the inverse side, with mappedBy

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "course", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    @OrderColumn(name = "position")
    private List<Lesson> lessons = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title) { this.title = title; }

    // helper methods keep BOTH sides in sync
    public void addLesson(Lesson lesson) {
        lessons.add(lesson);
        lesson.setCourse(this);
    }

    public void removeLesson(Lesson lesson) {
        lessons.remove(lesson);
        lesson.setCourse(null);
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public List<Lesson> getLessons() { return lessons; }
}
  • mappedBy = "course" says "the course field in Lesson owns this relationship; I'm just a mirror". Without it, JPA creates an extra join table you didn't want.
  • Helper methods (addLesson) set both sides. If you only add to the list, the FK is never set (owning side unchanged)!

Cascade and orphan removal

  • cascade = CascadeType.ALL: operations on the course (persist, merge, remove…) cascade to its lessons. Persist a course → its new lessons are inserted too.
  • orphanRemoval = true: a lesson removed from the list is deleted (it can't exist without a course).

Use cascade only from a parent to children that it owns (Course → Lessons, Order → OrderItems). Never cascade REMOVE from @ManyToOne (deleting a lesson must not delete the course!).

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();

        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Course java = new Course("Java");
        java.addLesson(new Lesson("Variables"));
        java.addLesson(new Lesson("Loops"));
        java.addLesson(new Lesson("Methods"));
        em.persist(java);                                   // cascades to the 3 lessons
        em.getTransaction().commit();

        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Lesson loops = java.getLessons().get(1);
        java.removeLesson(loops);                           // orphanRemoval → DELETE
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.clear();

        Course loaded = em.find(Course.class, java.getId());
        System.out.println(loaded.getTitle() + " has " + loaded.getLessons().size() + " lessons:");
        loaded.getLessons().forEach(l -> System.out.println("- " + l.getTitle()));
        em.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}
Java has 2 lessons:
- Variables
- Methods

Fetch types: LAZY vs EAGER

Best practice: make everything LAZY (fetch = FetchType.LAZY on @ManyToOne/@OneToOne) and load what each use case needs with a fetch join or entity graph (next lesson). EAGER relationships load data you often don't need and are a common cause of slow apps (see the N+1 problem in the Hibernate course).

ManyToMany

@Entity
public class Student {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;
    private String name;

    @ManyToMany
    @JoinTable(name = "enrollment",
               joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
               inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id"))
    private Set<Course> courses = new HashSet<>();
}

// in Course (inverse side):
@ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")
private Set<Student> students = new HashSet<>();

Use a Set for many-to-many (Hibernate handles removals more efficiently than with a List).

The moment a link needs its own data (enrolled on which date, progress %, grade), replace @ManyToMany with a real entity Enrollment that has two @ManyToOnes. In practice, most many-to-many relationships end up this way.

OneToOne

@Entity
public class UserAccount {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;

    @OneToOne(mappedBy = "user", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Profile profile;
}

@Entity
public class Profile {
    @Id private Long id;

    @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @MapsId                          // share the primary key with the user
    private UserAccount user;
    private String bio;
}

@MapsId makes the profile's id equal to the user's id: simple and efficient.

Avoid these traps

  • toString/equals/hashCode including relationships: printing a course prints lessons, which print the course… → StackOverflowError, or triggers lazy loading everywhere. Exclude relationships.
  • JSON serialisation of entities with bidirectional links → infinite recursion. Return DTOs.
  • Bidirectional everything: only add the inverse side (@OneToMany) if you navigate that way.

Exercise

  1. Map Order (1) → OrderItem (many) with cascade, orphan removal and helper methods. Create an order with 3 items in one persist.
  2. Add Author ↔ Book many-to-many with a join table.
  3. Replace student ↔ course many-to-many with an Enrollment entity that stores enrolledOn and progress.
  4. What happens if you call course.getLessons().add(lesson) without setting lesson.setCourse(course)?
Hint for 4

Lesson is the owning side. Its course field is null, so with optional = false you get an error, otherwise the FK is saved as NULL and the lesson isn't linked.

Interview corner

  • What is the owning side? The side holding the foreign key (usually @ManyToOne); only its changes update the FK.
  • What does mappedBy do? Marks the inverse side and points to the owning field, preventing a duplicate join table/FK.
  • Default fetch types? ToOne = EAGER, ToMany = LAZY. Best practice: LAZY everywhere.
  • cascade vs orphanRemoval? Cascade propagates operations from parent to children; orphanRemoval deletes children removed from the parent's collection.

Summary

  • @ManyToOne owns the FK; @OneToMany(mappedBy) mirrors it; keep both sides in sync with helper methods.
  • Cascade from parents to owned children; orphanRemoval deletes removed children.
  • Prefer LAZY fetching; turn rich many-to-many links into entities.

Next: querying with JPQL.

items.title: JPQL Queries, Joins, Projections and Pagination
items.excerpt: Query entities with JPQL using parameters, joins, JOIN FETCH, aggregates, GROUP BY, DTO projections with records, pagination, named queries, native SQL and the Criteria API.
items.content:
find() only loads by id. For everything else (search, filters, reports), JPA has JPQL: a query language that looks like SQL but works with entities and fields, not tables and columns.

The setup

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private String level;
    private int price;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private Teacher teacher;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, String level, int price, Teacher teacher) {
        this.title = title; this.level = level; this.price = price; this.teacher = teacher;
    }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public Teacher getTeacher() { return teacher; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Teacher {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;

    protected Teacher() { }
    public Teacher(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String getName() { return name; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

public record LevelStats(String level, long courses, double avgPrice) { }

Queries in action

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Teacher ravi = new Teacher("Ravi"), meera = new Teacher("Meera");
        em.persist(ravi); em.persist(meera);
        em.persist(new Course("Java", "Beginner", 499, ravi));
        em.persist(new Course("Spring Boot", "Intermediate", 799, ravi));
        em.persist(new Course("React", "Beginner", 599, meera));
        em.persist(new Course("Hibernate", "Advanced", 899, meera));
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.clear();

        // 1. Filter with a named parameter
        List<Course> cheap = em.createQuery(
                "select c from Course c where c.price < :max order by c.price", Course.class)
            .setParameter("max", 700)
            .getResultList();
        cheap.forEach(c -> System.out.println("cheap: " + c.getTitle() + " " + c.getPrice()));

        // 2. Join through a relationship
        List<String> ravisCourses = em.createQuery(
                "select c.title from Course c join c.teacher t where t.name = :name", String.class)
            .setParameter("name", "Ravi")
            .getResultList();
        System.out.println("Ravi teaches " + ravisCourses);

        // 3. JOIN FETCH: load courses AND their teachers in one query
        List<Course> all = em.createQuery(
                "select c from Course c join fetch c.teacher order by c.title", Course.class)
            .getResultList();
        all.forEach(c -> System.out.println(c.getTitle() + " by " + c.getTeacher().getName()));

        // 4. Aggregates + GROUP BY straight into a record (DTO projection)
        List<LevelStats> stats = em.createQuery(
                "select new com.vitalstack.LevelStats(c.level, count(c), avg(c.price)) " +
                "from Course c group by c.level order by c.level", LevelStats.class)
            .getResultList();
        stats.forEach(System.out::println);

        // 5. Pagination
        List<Course> page2 = em.createQuery("select c from Course c order by c.id", Course.class)
            .setFirstResult(2)          // skip 2 rows (page size 2 → page 2)
            .setMaxResults(2)
            .getResultList();
        System.out.println("page 2: " + page2.stream().map(Course::getTitle).toList());

        // 6. A single value
        Long total = em.createQuery("select sum(c.price) from Course c", Long.class).getSingleResult();
        System.out.println("total = " + total);
        em.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output:

cheap: Java 499
cheap: React 599
Ravi teaches [Java, Spring Boot]
Hibernate by Meera
Java by Ravi
React by Meera
Spring Boot by Ravi
LevelStats[level=Advanced, courses=1, avgPrice=899.0]
LevelStats[level=Beginner, courses=2, avgPrice=549.0]
LevelStats[level=Intermediate, courses=1, avgPrice=799.0]
page 2: [React, Hibernate]
total = 2796

JPQL vs SQL

JPQL can't do everything SQL can (e.g. some window functions), but Hibernate 6 supports a lot of modern SQL in HQL.

Always use parameters

// ❌ SQL injection risk, and no statement caching
em.createQuery("select c from Course c where c.title = '" + title + "'");
// ✅
em.createQuery("select c from Course c where c.title = :title").setParameter("title", title);

JOIN vs JOIN FETCH

  • join c.teacher t lets you filter on the teacher, but the teachers aren't loaded: accessing getTeacher().getName() later triggers extra queries.
  • join fetch c.teacher loads the teachers in the same query. This is the main cure for the N+1 problem (Hibernate course).

Don't use join fetch together with pagination on a collection (join fetch c.lessons + setMaxResults): Hibernate has to load everything and paginate in memory (it warns you). Paginate the parents first, then fetch their collections in a second query.

DTO projections

select new com.vitalstack.LevelStats(...) creates plain objects instead of managed entities. They're not tracked (no snapshots, no dirty checking), so they're faster and lighter for read-only screens and reports. Records are perfect for this.

Named queries

Define reusable queries on the entity (validated at startup!):

@Entity
@NamedQuery(name = "Course.byLevel", query = "select c from Course c where c.level = :level")
public class Course { ... }

em.createNamedQuery("Course.byLevel", Course.class).setParameter("level", "Beginner").getResultList();

Bulk updates and deletes

int updated = em.createQuery("update Course c set c.price = c.price * 9 / 10 where c.level = :lvl")
        .setParameter("lvl", "Beginner")
        .executeUpdate();

Bulk statements go straight to the database and bypass the persistence context: entities already loaded keep their old values. Run them in their own transaction or clear() afterwards.

Native SQL

When you need database-specific SQL:

List<Object[]> rows = em.createNativeQuery(
        "SELECT level, COUNT(*) FROM course GROUP BY level").getResultList();

Criteria API (dynamic queries)

For search screens where filters are optional, the type-safe Criteria API builds queries in code:

CriteriaBuilder cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Course> q = cb.createQuery(Course.class);
Root<Course> c = q.from(Course.class);
List<Predicate> where = new ArrayList<>();
if (level != null) where.add(cb.equal(c.get("level"), level));
if (maxPrice != null) where.add(cb.le(c.get("price"), maxPrice));
q.select(c).where(where.toArray(Predicate[]::new));
List<Course> result = em.createQuery(q).getResultList();

In Spring Data JPA you'll mostly use derived query methods and @Query instead, with Specifications for dynamic filters.

Common mistakes

  • Using table/column names instead of entity/field names in JPQL.
  • getSingleResult() with no or multiple rows → NoResultException / NonUniqueResultException.
  • Forgetting distinct when fetch-joining collections in old Hibernate versions (Hibernate 6 de-duplicates automatically).
  • Loading whole entities for a read-only list where a projection would do.

Exercise

  1. Find all courses whose title contains "a" (case-insensitive), sorted by price descending.
  2. Count courses per teacher using a record projection TeacherCount(name, count).
  3. Write a paginated query for page N with page size 10.
  4. Give every Advanced course a 20% discount with one bulk update.
Hint for 1

where lower(c.title) like :q with .setParameter("q", "%a%").

Interview corner

  • JPQL vs SQL? JPQL queries entities and fields, is portable, and returns objects; SQL queries tables/columns.
  • JOIN vs JOIN FETCH? JOIN for filtering/joining; JOIN FETCH also initialises the association in the same query.
  • How do you paginate in JPA? setFirstResult(offset) and setMaxResults(size).
  • Why use DTO projections? They avoid managed-entity overhead and fetch only needed columns.

Summary

  • JPQL works with entities, fields and relationships; always use parameters.
  • JOIN FETCH loads related data in one query; projections into records are fast and safe for reads.
  • Paginate with setFirstResult/setMaxResults; bulk updates bypass the persistence context.

Next: inheritance mapping and lifecycle callbacks.

items.title: JPA Inheritance Mapping and Lifecycle Callbacks
items.excerpt: Map class hierarchies with SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED and TABLE_PER_CLASS, share audit fields with @MappedSuperclass, and run code automatically with @PrePersist, @PreUpdate and entity listeners.
items.content:
Your Java model uses inheritance (a Payment can be a UpiPayment or CardPayment), but relational tables don't have inheritance. JPA offers several strategies to bridge the gap, plus callbacks to run code automatically when entities are saved or updated.

@MappedSuperclass: share fields, not a table

Most entities need id, createdAt and updatedAt. Put them in a base class:

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

@MappedSuperclass                          // not an entity: its fields are copied into each subclass table
public abstract class BaseEntity {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    protected Long id;
    protected LocalDateTime createdAt;
    protected LocalDateTime updatedAt;

    @PrePersist                             // runs just before INSERT
    void onCreate() { createdAt = updatedAt = LocalDateTime.now(); }

    @PreUpdate                              // runs just before UPDATE
    void onUpdate() { updatedAt = LocalDateTime.now(); }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public LocalDateTime getCreatedAt() { return createdAt; }
    public LocalDateTime getUpdatedAt() { return updatedAt; }
}

You can't query a @MappedSuperclass (select b from BaseEntity b fails). It's just a code-sharing tool.

Entity inheritance strategies

When you do want polymorphic queries (select p from Payment p returning UPI and card payments), make the parent an entity and choose a strategy:

1. SINGLE_TABLE (default): one table for the whole hierarchy

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
@DiscriminatorColumn(name = "method")                 // which subclass is this row?
public abstract class Payment extends BaseEntity {
    protected int amount;
    public int getAmount() { return amount; }
    public abstract String describe();
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
@DiscriminatorValue("UPI")
public class UpiPayment extends Payment {
    private String vpa;
    protected UpiPayment() { }
    public UpiPayment(int amount, String vpa) { this.amount = amount; this.vpa = vpa; }
    public String describe() { return "UPI ₹" + amount + " from " + vpa; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
@DiscriminatorValue("CARD")
public class CardPayment extends Payment {
    private String last4;
    protected CardPayment() { }
    public CardPayment(int amount, String last4) { this.amount = amount; this.last4 = last4; }
    public String describe() { return "Card ₹" + amount + " ****" + last4; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        em.persist(new UpiPayment(499, "asha@okaxis"));
        CardPayment card = new CardPayment(1299, "4242");
        em.persist(card);
        em.getTransaction().commit();

        Thread.sleep(20);
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        card.amount = 999;                                   // triggers @PreUpdate at flush
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        System.out.println("updated later than created? " + card.getUpdatedAt().isAfter(card.getCreatedAt()));
        em.clear();

        em.createQuery("select p from Payment p order by p.id", Payment.class)    // polymorphic query
          .getResultList()
          .forEach(p -> System.out.println(p.describe()));
        em.close();
        emf.close();
    }
}

Generated schema and output:

create table Payment (amount integer not null, createdAt timestamp(6), id bigint generated by default as identity,
                      updatedAt timestamp(6), method varchar(31) not null, last4 varchar(255), vpa varchar(255), primary key (id))
updated later than created? true
UPI ₹499 from asha@okaxis
Card ₹999 ****4242

One table, a method discriminator column, and nullable columns for subclass fields. Fastest for queries (no joins), but subclass columns can't be NOT NULL.

2. JOINED: one table per class, linked by primary key

@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.JOINED)

payment(id, amount…), upi_payment(id, vpa), card_payment(id, last4). Clean, normalised, subclass columns can be NOT NULL, but every query needs joins.

3. TABLE_PER_CLASS: one complete table per concrete class

Each subclass table repeats all parent columns. Polymorphic queries need UNIONs: slow. Rarely used.

Before reaching for entity inheritance, ask whether a single entity with an enum type field (or an @Embeddable) would do. Inheritance in the database is harder to change later than in Java.

Lifecycle callbacks

Typical uses: timestamps, normalising data (email = email.toLowerCase()), computing derived fields.

Entity listeners: reusable callbacks

public class AuditListener {
    @PrePersist
    public void beforeSave(Object entity) {
        System.out.println("Saving " + entity.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
}

@Entity
@EntityListeners(AuditListener.class)
public class Course { ... }

Spring Data JPA offers ready-made auditing (@CreatedDate, @LastModifiedBy) built on this mechanism.

Callback rules

  • Don't call the EntityManager or run queries inside callbacks (undefined behaviour).
  • Keep them fast and side-effect free (no emails, no HTTP calls). Use events or a service layer for that.
  • @PreUpdate runs only if Hibernate detects a change.

Exercise

  1. Create a BaseEntity with audit fields and make two entities extend it. Check both tables have the columns.
  2. Switch the Payment hierarchy to JOINED and compare the generated tables and the SQL of the polymorphic query.
  3. Add a @PrePersist that lowercases and trims emails on a Student entity.
  4. Add a NetBankingPayment subclass and query only card payments with select p from CardPayment p.
Hint for 2

You'll see three tables and a query that left-joins the subclass tables, with a case expression to work out each row's type.

Interview corner

  • Inheritance strategies in JPA? SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, TABLE_PER_CLASS (plus @MappedSuperclass for non-entity base classes).
  • @MappedSuperclass vs @Entity parent? MappedSuperclass only shares mappings (no table, not queryable); an entity parent allows polymorphic queries and associations.
  • What is a discriminator column? A column that stores which subclass a row belongs to (SINGLE_TABLE, optionally JOINED).
  • What are lifecycle callbacks? Methods annotated @PrePersist, @PostLoad etc. that JPA calls around entity operations.

Summary

  • @MappedSuperclass shares common fields like id and audit timestamps.
  • SINGLE_TABLE is fast and simple; JOINED is normalised; TABLE_PER_CLASS is rarely worth it.
  • Callbacks and entity listeners run code automatically around persistence events.

Next: transactions and locking for safe concurrent updates.

items.title: JPA Transactions and Locking
items.excerpt: Keep data correct when many users act at once. Learn ACID transactions, rollback, the lost update problem, optimistic locking with @Version, pessimistic locks and isolation levels.
items.content:
Two users buy the last seat at the same moment. A teacher and an admin edit the same course simultaneously. Without care, one change overwrites the other or your stock goes negative. Transactions and locking keep data correct under concurrency.

ACID in one table

Commit and rollback

EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
try {
    tx.begin();
    Account from = em.find(Account.class, 1L);
    Account to = em.find(Account.class, 2L);
    from.withdraw(500);          // throws if the balance is too low
    to.deposit(500);
    tx.commit();                 // both UPDATEs together
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    if (tx.isActive()) tx.rollback();   // undo everything
    throw e;
}

In Spring this whole pattern becomes one annotation, @Transactional, animated in the Spring course.

The lost update problem

time   Admin (tx 1)                    Teacher (tx 2)
 1     read course: price 499          read course: price 499
 2     set title "Java Pro"            set price 399
 3     commit → UPDATE title, price=499
 4                                     commit → UPDATE title="Java", price=399
                                       ❌ the admin's title change is lost

Both transactions read the same version, and the last commit silently wins. JPA's solution is optimistic locking.

Optimistic locking with @Version

Add a version field:

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private int price;

    @Version                      // incremented on every update
    private int version;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public void setTitle(String t) { title = t; }
    public void setPrice(int p) { price = p; }
    public int getVersion() { return version; }
}

Every UPDATE now includes the version in its WHERE clause:

update Course set price=?, title=?, version=? where id=? and version=?

If another transaction already changed the row, the version doesn't match, 0 rows are updated, and JPA throws OptimisticLockException. Let's prove it:

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager setup = emf.createEntityManager();
        setup.getTransaction().begin();
        Course c = new Course("Java", 499);
        setup.persist(c);
        setup.getTransaction().commit();
        setup.close();

        EntityManager admin = emf.createEntityManager();
        EntityManager teacher = emf.createEntityManager();
        admin.getTransaction().begin();
        teacher.getTransaction().begin();
        Course a = admin.find(Course.class, c.getId());     // both read version 0
        Course t = teacher.find(Course.class, c.getId());

        a.setTitle("Java Pro");
        admin.getTransaction().commit();                     // version 0 → 1
        System.out.println("admin saved, version " + a.getVersion());

        t.setPrice(399);
        try {
            teacher.getTransaction().commit();               // still thinks version 0
        } catch (RollbackException e) {
            System.out.println("teacher's save rejected: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        admin.close(); teacher.close(); emf.close();
    }
}
admin saved, version 1
teacher's save rejected: OptimisticLockException

Nothing was lost. The app can now tell the teacher "Someone else changed this course. Please reload and try again."

Optimistic = assume conflicts are rare, detect them at write time. No database locks are held while users think, so it scales very well. It's the default choice for web apps.

Pessimistic locking

When conflicts are frequent and retrying is expensive (seat booking, stock counters), lock the row while you work:

Seat seat = em.find(Seat.class, seatId, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
if (seat.isBooked()) throw new IllegalStateException("Already booked");
seat.book(userId);
// the lock is released at commit/rollback; other transactions wait at their find()

Keep pessimistic transactions very short, and set a lock timeout (jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout).

A simple and robust alternative for counters is a single atomic UPDATE: update Product p set p.stock = p.stock - 1 where p.id = :id and p.stock > 0. If it returns 0, the item is sold out. No race condition possible.

Isolation levels

Databases offer isolation levels that trade correctness for concurrency:

\*MySQL InnoDB prevents most phantoms at REPEATABLE READ.

  • Dirty read: seeing another transaction's uncommitted change.
  • Non-repeatable read: reading the same row twice and getting different values.
  • Phantom read: re-running a query and getting new rows.

Usually you keep the database default and use @Version or explicit locks where it matters.

Transaction tips

  • Keep transactions short: never wait for user input or call slow external APIs inside one.
  • Read-only operations can use read-only transactions (Spring: @Transactional(readOnly = true)) for small optimisations.
  • Handle OptimisticLockException with a friendly message or an automatic retry.

Exercise

  1. Add @Version to an entity and reproduce the conflict above.
  2. Write a "transfer" with rollback when the source balance is too low. Verify neither balance changed.
  3. Implement "book seat" using PESSIMISTIC_WRITE and explain what a second concurrent booking does.
  4. Rewrite a stock decrement as one atomic JPQL update.
Hint for 2

Throw an exception after the withdraw when the balance goes negative, catch it, roll back, then reload both accounts in a new EntityManager to check.

Interview corner

  • What is optimistic locking? Detecting concurrent modifications using a version column; the stale update fails with OptimisticLockException.
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic? Optimistic detects conflicts at commit without locks; pessimistic locks rows to prevent conflicts.
  • What is a lost update? Two transactions read the same data and the later write overwrites the earlier one unknowingly.
  • Default isolation in MySQL and PostgreSQL? MySQL InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL: READ COMMITTED.

Summary

  • Transactions make changes atomic; roll back on errors.
  • @Version gives optimistic locking: stale updates fail instead of overwriting.
  • Pessimistic locks (FOR UPDATE) suit short, hot-spot operations.
  • Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions can see.

Next course: Hibernate, the engine behind JPA, with fetching strategies, the N+1 problem and caching.

items.title: Hibernate Introduction and Architecture
items.excerpt: What Hibernate adds on top of JPA, its architecture (SessionFactory, Session, Transaction, dialects), how to use the native Session API, HQL, and the Hibernate-only features you'll meet in real projects.
items.content:
Hibernate is the engine that powers most Java applications' database access. It's the default JPA provider in Spring Boot, and has been around since 2001. In the JPA course you used Hibernate through the standard API. This course looks under the hood: how it works, its extra features, and how to make it fast.

JPA vs Hibernate (again, but deeper)

Your code ──▶ JPA API (EntityManager, @Entity, JPQL)      ← portable standard
                 │
                 ▼  implemented by
            Hibernate ORM (Session, HQL, extra annotations, caching, batching…)
                 │
                 ▼
            JDBC driver ──▶ MySQL / PostgreSQL / Oracle / H2

Everything in the JPA course works the same. Hibernate adds:

  • The native Session API (a superset of EntityManager).
  • HQL: a superset of JPQL.
  • Extra annotations: @NaturalId, @BatchSize, @Formula, @DynamicUpdate, @SQLRestriction, @Immutable, @CreationTimestamp…
  • Second-level and query caches.
  • Envers auditing, multi-tenancy, statistics, StatelessSession and more.

Architecture

In fact, in Hibernate 6 SessionFactory extends EntityManagerFactory and Session extends EntityManager. You can switch between them:

Session session = entityManager.unwrap(Session.class);                 // JPA → Hibernate
SessionFactory sf = entityManagerFactory.unwrap(SessionFactory.class);

Using Hibernate natively

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SessionFactory sf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school").unwrap(SessionFactory.class);

        sf.inTransaction(session -> {                          // begin + commit/rollback for you
            session.persist(new Course("Java", 499));
            session.persist(new Course("Hibernate", 899));
        });

        try (Session session = sf.openSession()) {
            Course c = session.get(Course.class, 1L);            // like em.find
            System.out.println("get: " + c.getTitle());

            Course byTitle = session.bySimpleNaturalId(Course.class).load("Hibernate");   // @NaturalId lookup
            System.out.println("natural id: " + byTitle.getPrice());

            long count = session.createSelectionQuery("select count(*) from Course", Long.class)   // HQL
                                .getSingleResult();
            System.out.println("count: " + count);
        }
        sf.close();
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.annotations.NaturalId;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @NaturalId                       // a unique business key Hibernate can look up and cache
    private String title;
    private int price;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, int price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
}

Output:

get: Java
natural id: 899
count: 2

Notice HQL lets you skip select c in simple queries (from Course), and sessionFactory.inTransaction(...) handles commit and rollback.

Configuration options you'll see

save() vs persist(), load() vs get()

Old Hibernate code uses session.save(), saveOrUpdate(), update() and load(). These are deprecated in Hibernate 6. Use the JPA-style methods:

Interviewers still ask "save vs persist": save returns the generated id immediately and works outside transactions in old versions; persist returns void and follows JPA semantics.

In Spring Boot you almost never touch Session directly. But knowing the architecture helps you read Hibernate's logs and tune its properties, which is where real performance wins come from.

Exercise

  1. Unwrap a Session from an EntityManager and call session.getStatistics() after a few queries (enable hibernate.generate_statistics).
  2. Add @NaturalId to a Student.email field and load a student by email.
  3. Rewrite a JPQL query as HQL using the short from Course where price > 500 form.
Hint for 1

sf.getStatistics().getPrepareStatementCount() tells you how many SQL statements ran. It's great for catching N+1 problems in tests.

Interview corner

  • What is Hibernate? An ORM framework and the most popular JPA implementation.
  • SessionFactory vs Session? SessionFactory is heavyweight, thread-safe, created once; Session is a lightweight, non-thread-safe unit of work with its own persistence context.
  • What is a dialect? The component that adapts generated SQL to a specific database.
  • get vs load? get hits the database and returns null if missing; load (getReference) returns a proxy and throws ObjectNotFoundException when used if the row doesn't exist.

Summary

  • Hibernate implements JPA and adds Session, HQL, extra annotations, caching and tuning options.
  • SessionFactory once, Session per unit of work; both are JPA objects underneath.
  • Prefer persist/merge/getReference over deprecated save/update/load.

Next: lazy loading and proxies, the source of many Hibernate surprises.

items.title: Hibernate Lazy Loading, Proxies and LazyInitializationException
items.excerpt: How Hibernate loads related data only when you touch it, what proxies and persistent collections are, why LazyInitializationException happens, and four correct ways to fix it.
items.content:
Load a course and Hibernate doesn't immediately load its 50 lessons, its teacher and their profile. It loads them lazily: only when your code first touches them. This saves huge amounts of work, but it's also behind the most famous Hibernate error: LazyInitializationException.

Lazy vs eager

  • EAGER: load the related data immediately, always.
  • LAZY: load it on first access.

Defaults (from JPA): @ManyToOne/@OneToOne are EAGER; @OneToMany/@ManyToMany are LAZY. Best practice: LAZY everywhere, then load what each use case needs.

How lazy loading works

For a lazy @ManyToOne, Hibernate puts a proxy in the field: a generated subclass of your entity that holds only the id. For a lazy collection, it puts a PersistentBag/PersistentSet: a list that knows how to load itself.

Lesson ──course──▶ Course$HibernateProxy (id = 1, not initialised)
                         │ first call to getTitle()
                         ▼
                   SELECT ... FROM course WHERE id = 1  → now initialised

Calling getId() on a proxy doesn't trigger a query (the id is already known). Any other getter does, if the Session is still open.

See it happen

package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "course", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
    private List<Lesson> lessons = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public void add(Lesson l) { lessons.add(l); l.course = this; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public List<Lesson> getLessons() { return lessons; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Lesson {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String title;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    Course course;

    protected Lesson() { }
    public Lesson(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public Course getCourse() { return course; }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Hibernate;
import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("school");
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        Course java = new Course("Java");
        java.add(new Lesson("Variables"));
        java.add(new Lesson("Loops"));
        em.persist(java);
        em.getTransaction().commit();
        em.close();

        EntityManager em2 = emf.createEntityManager();
        System.out.println("-- load course");
        Course c = em2.find(Course.class, java.getId());
        System.out.println("lessons loaded? " + Hibernate.isInitialized(c.getLessons()));
        System.out.println("-- touch lessons");
        System.out.println("count: " + c.getLessons().size());          // SELECT lessons now
        System.out.println("-- load a lesson");
        Lesson l = em2.find(Lesson.class, 1L);
        System.out.println("course is a proxy: " + l.getCourse().getClass().getSimpleName().contains("Proxy")
                + ", id without query: " + l.getCourse().getId());
        em2.close();                                                       // Session closed

        EntityManager em3 = emf.createEntityManager();
        Course detached = em3.find(Course.class, java.getId());
        em3.close();
        try {
            detached.getLessons().size();                                  // too late!
        } catch (LazyInitializationException e) {
            System.out.println("ERROR: " + e.getMessage());
        }
        emf.close();
    }
}

Output:

-- load course
select c1_0.id,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
lessons loaded? false
-- touch lessons
select l1_0.course_id,l1_0.id,l1_0.title from Lesson l1_0 where l1_0.course_id=?
count: 2
-- load a lesson
course is a proxy: false, id without query: 1
select c1_0.id,c1_0.title from Course c1_0 where c1_0.id=?
ERROR: failed to lazily initialize a collection of role: com.vitalstack.Course.lessons: could not initialize proxy - no Session

(The lesson and its course are already in this Session's persistence context, so no SQL runs and getCourse() returns the real object here, not a proxy. In a fresh Session, you'd get a Course$HibernateProxy.)

Why LazyInitializationException happens

The entity was loaded in a Session that's now closed. Later code (often a view template, a JSON serializer, or a toString()) touches a lazy relationship, and there's no Session left to run the query.

Typical in Spring: a @Transactional service returns an entity, the transaction ends, and the controller or Jackson then accesses course.getLessons().

Four correct fixes

1. Fetch what you need in the query (JOIN FETCH):

Course c = em.createQuery(
    "select c from Course c join fetch c.lessons where c.id = :id", Course.class)
    .setParameter("id", id).getSingleResult();

2. Entity graphs: declare what to load without changing the JPQL:

EntityGraph<Course> graph = em.createEntityGraph(Course.class);
graph.addAttributeNodes("lessons");
Course c = em.find(Course.class, id, Map.of("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", graph));

In Spring Data: @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "lessons") on a repository method.

3. Map to a DTO inside the transaction: return exactly the data the screen needs, so nothing lazy escapes:

record CourseView(String title, List<String> lessonTitles) { }
// inside the @Transactional service method:
return new CourseView(c.getTitle(), c.getLessons().stream().map(Lesson::getTitle).toList());

4. Initialise explicitly inside the transaction: Hibernate.initialize(c.getLessons()).

Fixes to avoid

  • Switching to EAGER: now *every* query loads the lessons, even where unneeded, and it often causes N+1 queries (next lesson).
  • Open Session in View (Spring's spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, the default!): keeps the Session open until the view renders, so lazy loading "just works", but queries run from the web layer, connections are held longer, and N+1 problems hide. Spring Boot logs a warning for this. Set it to false and fetch properly.
  • hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans=true: opens a new connection for every lazy access. An anti-pattern.

Proxies are subclasses, so course.getClass() == Course.class can be false and instanceof checks on proxies of a hierarchy can surprise you. Use Hibernate.getClass(obj) or Hibernate.unproxy(obj) when the real class matters, and write equals with instanceof and getters, not direct field access.

Exercise

  1. Run the example, then add join fetch to load a course with lessons and access them after closing the EntityManager. No exception?
  2. Use an entity graph to load a lesson with its course.
  3. Write a CourseSummary record with title and lesson count using a JPQL projection (no lazy loading at all).
Hint for 3

select new com.vitalstack.CourseSummary(c.title, size(c.lessons)) from Course c or count(l) with a left join c.lessons l group by c.title.

Interview corner

  • What is lazy loading? Deferring the loading of associated data until it's first accessed, using proxies and persistent collections.
  • What causes LazyInitializationException? Accessing an uninitialised lazy association after the Session/persistence context is closed.
  • How do you fix it? JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, DTO projections, or initialising inside the transaction, not EAGER or open-session-in-view.
  • What is a Hibernate proxy? A runtime subclass of the entity holding the id, which loads the real data on first access.

Summary

  • LAZY loads on access via proxies and persistent collections; prefer it everywhere.
  • Accessing lazy data after the Session closes throws LazyInitializationException.
  • Fix with JOIN FETCH, entity graphs or DTOs; avoid EAGER and open-session-in-view.

Next: the N+1 query problem, animated.
