items.title: Spring MVC - Controllers, Requests and Responses
items.excerpt: Follow a request through DispatcherServlet in an animation, then build controllers with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody, return JSON or views, and handle errors with @RestControllerAdvice.
items.content:
Spring MVC is the web layer of Spring. Instead of one servlet per URL (Servlet course), Spring has one servlet, the DispatcherServlet, that routes every request to the right method in your @Controller classes.

The life of a request

Pick a request for an existing course (/1) and a missing one (/99):

  1. DispatcherServlet receives every request (front controller pattern).
  2. HandlerMapping finds the controller method whose mapping matches the URL and HTTP method.
  3. Argument resolvers convert path variables, query parameters and JSON bodies into Java parameters.
  4. Your controller calls services and returns a value.
  5. Message converters (Jackson) turn the returned object into JSON, or a ViewResolver renders an HTML template.
  6. Exceptions go to @ExceptionHandler / @RestControllerAdvice methods.

A REST controller

package com.vitalstack;

public record Course(Long id, String title, int price) { }
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record NewCourse(@NotBlank String title, @Min(0) int price) { }
package com.vitalstack;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

@RestController                                   // every method returns data (JSON), not views
@RequestMapping("/api/courses")
public class CourseController {
    private final Map<Long, Course> store = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicLong ids = new AtomicLong();

    public CourseController() {
        add("Java", 499);
        add("Spring", 799);
    }

    private Course add(String title, int price) {
        long id = ids.incrementAndGet();
        Course c = new Course(id, title, price);
        store.put(id, c);
        return c;
    }

    @GetMapping                                               // GET /api/courses?maxPrice=600
    public List<Course> list(@RequestParam(required = false) Integer maxPrice) {
        return store.values().stream()
                .filter(c -> maxPrice == null || c.price() <= maxPrice)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Course::id))
                .toList();
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")                                      // GET /api/courses/1
    public Course get(@PathVariable long id) {
        Course c = store.get(id);
        if (c == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("Course " + id + " not found");
        return c;
    }

    @PostMapping                                              // POST /api/courses  {"title":"React","price":599}
    public ResponseEntity<Course> create(@Valid @RequestBody NewCourse body) {
        Course c = add(body.title(), body.price());
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(c);   // 201 Created
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)                    // 204
    public void delete(@PathVariable long id) { store.remove(id); }
}

Central error handling

package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.*;

@RestControllerAdvice                              // applies to all controllers
public class ApiErrors {

    @ExceptionHandler(NoSuchElementException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
    public Map<String, String> notFound(NoSuchElementException e) {
        return Map.of("error", e.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
    public Map<String, String> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        Map<String, String> errors = new TreeMap<>();
        e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(f -> errors.put(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage()));
        return errors;
    }
}

Trying it

package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.boot.*;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.web.context.WebServerInitializedEvent;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClientResponseException;

@SpringBootApplication
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Main.class, "--server.port=0", "--spring.main.banner-mode=off",
                "--logging.level.root=warn").close();
    }

    @EventListener
    void call(WebServerInitializedEvent e) {
        RestClient http = RestClient.create("http://localhost:" + e.getWebServer().getPort());
        System.out.println(http.get().uri("/api/courses").retrieve().body(String.class));
        System.out.println(http.get().uri("/api/courses?maxPrice=600").retrieve().body(String.class));
        System.out.println(http.post().uri("/api/courses").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body("{\"title\":\"React\",\"price\":599}").retrieve().toEntity(String.class));
        for (String req : new String[] { "/api/courses/99" }) {
            try { http.get().uri(req).retrieve().body(String.class); }
            catch (RestClientResponseException ex) { System.out.println(ex.getStatusCode() + " " + ex.getResponseBodyAsString()); }
        }
        try {
            http.post().uri("/api/courses").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body("{\"title\":\"\",\"price\":-5}").retrieve().body(String.class);
        } catch (RestClientResponseException ex) { System.out.println(ex.getStatusCode() + " " + ex.getResponseBodyAsString()); }
    }
}

Output:

[{"id":1,"title":"Java","price":499},{"id":2,"title":"Spring","price":799}]
[{"id":1,"title":"Java","price":499}]
<201 CREATED Created,{"id":3,"title":"React","price":599},[...headers...]>
404 NOT_FOUND {"error":"Course 99 not found"}
400 BAD_REQUEST {"price":"must be greater than or equal to 0","title":"must not be blank"}

(In your own app, test endpoints with a browser, curl, Postman or IntelliJ's HTTP client instead.)

Request mapping cheat sheet

@Controller with HTML views

For server-rendered pages (often with Thymeleaf), use @Controller and return a view name:

@Controller
public class PageController {
    @GetMapping("/courses")
    public String courses(Model model) {
        model.addAttribute("courses", courseService.findAll());
        return "courses";                          // renders templates/courses.html
    }
}
<li th:each="c : ${courses}" th:text="${c.title}">Course title</li>

Same MVC pattern as servlets + JSP, with far less code.

Controllers should be thin: read the request, call a service, return a response. Business rules belong in @Service classes, where they're easy to test and reuse.

Exercise

  1. Add PUT /api/courses/{id} that replaces a course and returns 404 if it doesn't exist.
  2. Add GET /api/courses/search?q=ja (case-insensitive title search).
  3. Add a validation rule: title at most 60 characters (@Size(max = 60)), and check the 400 response.
  4. Return a Location header for created courses using ResponseEntity.created(URI).
Hint for 4

URI uri = URI.create("/api/courses/" + c.id()); return ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(c);

Interview corner

  • What is DispatcherServlet? Spring MVC's front controller that receives all requests and delegates to handlers, converters and view resolvers.
  • @Controller vs @RestController? @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody: return values are written to the response body (JSON).
  • @PathVariable vs @RequestParam? Path segment vs query string parameter.
  • How do you handle exceptions globally? @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods.

Summary

  • DispatcherServlet routes requests to controller methods by URL and HTTP method.
  • @RestController + @GetMapping/@PostMapping + @PathVariable/@RequestParam/@RequestBody.
  • Return records or ResponseEntity; validate with @Valid; handle errors centrally.

Next: Spring JDBC with JdbcTemplate.

items.title: Spring JdbcTemplate and Testing Spring Apps
items.excerpt: Run SQL without JDBC boilerplate using JdbcTemplate and NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, map rows to records, insert with generated keys, and write fast unit tests and Spring integration tests.
items.content:
JPA is great for rich domain models, but sometimes you just want to run SQL: reports, bulk updates, legacy schemas. JdbcTemplate gives you plain SQL without the JDBC boilerplate (connections, statements, result sets, exceptions). It's the Template Method pattern in action: Spring does the fixed steps, you supply the SQL and the mapping.

Plain JDBC vs JdbcTemplate

// Plain JDBC: ~15 lines, easy to leak connections
try (Connection c = ds.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT id, title, price FROM course WHERE price < ?")) {
    ps.setInt(1, 600);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        while (rs.next()) list.add(new Course(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("title"), rs.getInt("price")));
    }
} catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }

// JdbcTemplate: one statement
List<Course> list = jdbc.query("SELECT id, title, price FROM course WHERE price < ?",
        (rs, n) -> new Course(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("title"), rs.getInt("price")), 600);

JdbcTemplate also translates SQLException into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy (DuplicateKeyException, EmptyResultDataAccessException…), and joins Spring transactions automatically.

A complete repository

package com.vitalstack;

public record Course(long id, String title, int price) { }
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.RowMapper;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.MapSqlParameterSource;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.NamedParameterJdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.support.GeneratedKeyHolder;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

@Repository
public class CourseDao {
    private static final RowMapper<Course> MAPPER =
            (rs, rowNum) -> new Course(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("title"), rs.getInt("price"));

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final NamedParameterJdbcTemplate named;

    public CourseDao(JdbcTemplate jdbc, NamedParameterJdbcTemplate named) {   // auto-configured by Spring Boot
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.named = named;
    }

    public long insert(String title, int price) {
        var keys = new GeneratedKeyHolder();
        named.update("INSERT INTO course(title, price) VALUES (:title, :price)",
                new MapSqlParameterSource().addValue("title", title).addValue("price", price),
                keys, new String[] { "id" });
        return keys.getKey().longValue();
    }

    public Optional<Course> findById(long id) {
        return jdbc.query("SELECT * FROM course WHERE id = ?", MAPPER, id).stream().findFirst();
    }

    public List<Course> cheaperThan(int max) {
        return named.query("SELECT * FROM course WHERE price < :max ORDER BY price",
                new MapSqlParameterSource("max", max), MAPPER);
    }

    public int count() {
        return jdbc.queryForObject("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM course", Integer.class);
    }

    public int raisePrices(int percent) {
        return jdbc.update("UPDATE course SET price = price + price * ? / 100", percent);
    }
}
package com.vitalstack;

import org.springframework.boot.*;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

@SpringBootApplication
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(Main.class);
        app.setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE);
        app.run(args).close();
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner demo(CourseDao dao) {
        return args -> {
            long id = dao.insert("Java", 499);
            dao.insert("Spring", 799);
            dao.insert("SQL", 299);
            System.out.println("new id: " + id + ", total: " + dao.count());
            System.out.println("cheap: " + dao.cheaperThan(600));
            System.out.println("rows updated: " + dao.raisePrices(10));
            System.out.println("find 1: " + dao.findById(1).orElseThrow());
            System.out.println("find 42: " + dao.findById(42));
        };
    }
}

src/main/resources/schema.sql (Spring Boot runs it at startup for embedded databases):

CREATE TABLE course (
  id    BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  price INT NOT NULL
);
# application.properties
spring.main.banner-mode=off
logging.level.root=warn
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:jdbcdemo

Output:

new id: 1, total: 3
cheap: [Course[id=3, title=SQL, price=299], Course[id=1, title=Java, price=499]]
rows updated: 3
find 1: Course[id=1, title=Java, price=548]
find 42: Optional.empty

JdbcTemplate methods

Spring 6.1 also added **JdbcClient**, a fluent API: jdbcClient.sql("SELECT * FROM course WHERE id = :id").param("id", 1).query(Course.class).optional().

Use query(...).stream().findFirst() (or JdbcClient's .optional()) for "maybe one row". queryForObject throws EmptyResultDataAccessException when nothing matches, which surprises a lot of people.

When to use what

Testing Spring code

Unit tests need no Spring: construct the class with fakes (constructor injection pays off):

class PriceServiceTest {
    @Test
    void appliesGst() {
        PriceService service = new PriceService(new BigDecimal("0.18"));
        assertEquals(new BigDecimal("118.00"), service.withGst(new BigDecimal("100.00")));
    }
}

Integration tests start (part of) the Spring context:

@JdbcTest                                    // only JDBC beans + an embedded database
@Import(CourseDao.class)
class CourseDaoTest {
    @Autowired CourseDao dao;

    @Test
    void insertsAndFinds() {
        long id = dao.insert("Docker", 399);
        assertEquals("Docker", dao.findById(id).orElseThrow().title());
    }
}

Test slices (@JdbcTest, @DataJpaTest, @WebMvcTest) start only what's needed, so they're fast. @SpringBootTest starts everything. Each test runs in a transaction that's rolled back afterwards, so tests don't affect each other.

Exercise

  1. Add deleteById(long id) that returns true if a row was deleted.
  2. Write List<CategoryTotal> totalsByCategory() with a GROUP BY query mapped to a record.
  3. Insert 1,000 courses with batchUpdate and time it against a loop of update.
  4. Write a @JdbcTest for cheaperThan.
Hint for 1

return jdbc.update("DELETE FROM course WHERE id = ?", id) == 1;

Interview corner

  • What is JdbcTemplate? A Spring helper that handles JDBC resources, exceptions and transactions so you only write SQL and row mapping.
  • RowMapper? A function mapping one ResultSet row to an object.
  • JdbcTemplate vs JPA? SQL-centric and explicit vs object-centric with automatic mapping, caching and dirty checking.
  • @SpringBootTest vs test slices? Full context vs only the beans for one layer, which is faster.

Summary

  • JdbcTemplate removes JDBC boilerplate; NamedParameterJdbcTemplate and JdbcClient add named parameters and a fluent API.
  • RowMappers turn rows into records; exceptions become DataAccessExceptions.
  • Unit-test with plain constructors; integration-test with slices like @JdbcTest.

You've finished the Spring course! Next: Spring Boot, where you'll build a production-ready REST API with all of this auto-configured.

items.title: Spring Boot Introduction
items.excerpt: What Spring Boot adds to Spring - starters, auto-configuration and an embedded server - watch an app start up in an animation, create a project with Spring Initializr and understand its structure.
items.content:
Spring Boot is how almost every new Java back-end is built today. It takes the Spring Framework and removes the setup: no XML, no external Tomcat, no hunting for compatible library versions. You write business code; Boot configures the rest.

Spring Boot in three ideas

  1. Starters: one dependency pulls in a tested set of libraries. spring-boot-starter-web = Spring MVC + Jackson + embedded Tomcat + validation support.
  2. Auto-configuration: Boot looks at your classpath and properties and creates the beans you'd otherwise configure by hand. H2 on the classpath? You get a DataSource. Spring Data JPA? You get an EntityManagerFactory and transaction manager.
  3. Embedded server: the app is a plain java -jar app.jar with Tomcat inside. No WAR deployment.

Plus production features: health checks, metrics, externalised config and profiles.

Watch an app start

Switch between starters and see what auto-configuration creates:

The whole application

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class CourseApiApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CourseApiApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@SpringBootApplication combines three annotations:

That last point matters: keep the application class in the root package (com.vitalstack.courses) and put everything else below it (...courses.web, ...courses.service), or your beans won't be found.

Create a project with Spring Initializr

Go to start.spring.io (or IntelliJ: New Project → Spring Boot):

  • Project: Maven, Language: Java, Spring Boot: latest 3.x
  • Group: com.vitalstack, Artifact: course-api
  • Java: 21 (or 17)
  • Dependencies: Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, H2 Database, Validation, Spring Boot DevTools

Download, unzip, open in your IDE and run the main class. You'll see:

Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
Started CourseApiApplication in 1.9 seconds

Visit http://localhost:8080: a "Whitelabel Error Page" (404), because there are no endpoints yet. That's success!

Project structure

course-api/
├── pom.xml                         ← dependencies (starters) + spring-boot-maven-plugin
├── mvnw, mvnw.cmd                  ← Maven wrapper: no Maven install needed (./mvnw spring-boot:run)
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/vitalstack/courses/
    │   │   └── CourseApiApplication.java
    │   └── resources/
    │       ├── application.properties    ← configuration
    │       ├── static/                   ← static files (CSS, JS, images)
    │       └── templates/                ← Thymeleaf HTML templates
    └── test/java/...                     ← tests

The parent POM manages versions, so starters have no version numbers:

<parent>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
  <version>3.3.4</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Common starters

Running and building

./mvnw spring-boot:run          # run in development
./mvnw clean package            # build target/course-api-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
java -jar target/course-api-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --server.port=9090

DevTools restarts the app automatically when you recompile, and disables template caching in development.

To see what auto-configuration did and why, start the app with --debug. The "CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT" lists every auto-configuration that matched or didn't. It's the best way to understand Boot's "magic".

Exercise

  1. Generate a project on start.spring.io with Spring Web and run it.
  2. Change the port to 9090 in application.properties (server.port=9090) and restart.
  3. Run with --debug and find DataSourceAutoConfiguration in the report. Did it match? Why or why not?
Hint for 3

Without a database driver or Spring Data on the classpath, DataSourceAutoConfiguration doesn't match ("did not find required class"). Add H2 and it will.

Interview corner

  • What is Spring Boot? An opinionated extension of Spring offering starters, auto-configuration, an embedded server and production-ready features.
  • What does @SpringBootApplication do? Combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan.
  • How does auto-configuration work? Configuration classes guarded by conditions (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty) create beans when their conditions match.
  • What is a starter? A dependency descriptor that brings a consistent set of libraries for a feature.

Summary

  • Spring Boot = Spring + starters + auto-configuration + embedded server.
  • @SpringBootApplication in the root package scans everything below it.
  • Create projects at start.spring.io; run with ./mvnw spring-boot:run or java -jar.

items.title: Build Your First REST API with Spring Boot
items.excerpt: Design REST endpoints, build a full CRUD API for courses with @RestController, return correct status codes with ResponseEntity, and test it with curl or Postman.
items.content:
A REST API lets other programs (a React or Angular front end, a mobile app, another service) work with your data over HTTP using JSON. Let's build a complete CRUD API for courses, step by step.

REST design in one table

Resources are nouns in the URL; the HTTP method is the verb:

Use plural nouns (/courses), lowercase, hyphens for multiple words (/course-reviews), and nest for ownership (/courses/5/lessons).

The code

A record for the data:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

public record Course(Long id, String title, String level, int price) { }

A service that holds the data (in memory for now; the next lesson adds a database):

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

@Service
public class CourseService {
    private final Map<Long, Course> courses = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicLong nextId = new AtomicLong();

    public CourseService() {
        create(new Course(null, "Java Basics", "BEGINNER", 499));
        create(new Course(null, "Spring Boot", "INTERMEDIATE", 799));
    }

    public List<Course> findAll() {
        return courses.values().stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Course::id)).toList();
    }

    public Optional<Course> findById(long id) { return Optional.ofNullable(courses.get(id)); }

    public Course create(Course c) {
        long id = nextId.incrementAndGet();
        Course saved = new Course(id, c.title(), c.level(), c.price());
        courses.put(id, saved);
        return saved;
    }

    public Optional<Course> update(long id, Course c) {
        if (!courses.containsKey(id)) return Optional.empty();
        Course updated = new Course(id, c.title(), c.level(), c.price());
        courses.put(id, updated);
        return Optional.of(updated);
    }

    public boolean delete(long id) { return courses.remove(id) != null; }
}

The controller maps HTTP to the service:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.support.ServletUriComponentsBuilder;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/courses")
public class CourseController {
    private final CourseService service;

    public CourseController(CourseService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping
    public List<Course> all() { return service.findAll(); }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Course> one(@PathVariable long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.of(service.findById(id));              // 200 with body, or 404
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<Course> create(@RequestBody Course course) {
        Course saved = service.create(course);
        URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
                .path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(saved.id()).toUri();
        return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved);         // 201 + Location header
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Course> update(@PathVariable long id, @RequestBody Course course) {
        return ResponseEntity.of(service.update(id, course));
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable long id) {
        return service.delete(id) ? ResponseEntity.noContent().build() : ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }
}

And the application class:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class CourseApiApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CourseApiApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Try it with curl

curl localhost:8080/api/courses
curl localhost:8080/api/courses/1
curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/api/courses -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"title":"React","level":"BEGINNER","price":599}'
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/api/courses/3 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"title":"React 19","level":"BEGINNER","price":649}'
curl -i -X DELETE localhost:8080/api/courses/2
curl -i localhost:8080/api/courses/99

Responses:

GET    /api/courses     → 200 [{"id":1,"title":"Java Basics","level":"BEGINNER","price":499},{"id":2,"title":"Spring Boot","level":"INTERMEDIATE","price":799}]
GET    /api/courses/1   → 200 {"id":1,"title":"Java Basics","level":"BEGINNER","price":499}
POST   /api/courses     → 201 Location: http://localhost:8080/api/courses/3  {"id":3,"title":"React","level":"BEGINNER","price":599}
PUT    /api/courses/3   → 200 {"id":3,"title":"React 19","level":"BEGINNER","price":649}
DELETE /api/courses/2   → 204
GET    /api/courses/99  → 404

Jackson converted records to JSON and JSON back into records automatically. On Windows PowerShell, use curl.exe or Postman / Insomnia / IntelliJ's HTTP client, which are friendlier for JSON.

The layers

HTTP ──▶ Controller (web: parse request, pick status) ──▶ Service (business rules) ──▶ Repository (data)

Even in this small app, keeping the controller thin pays off: the service can be reused by a scheduled job or a message listener, and tested without HTTP.

ResponseEntity.of(optional) is a neat shortcut: 200 with the body if present, 404 if empty. And always return 201 + Location for creates: front-end developers will thank you.

Common mistakes

  • Verbs in URLs (/getCourses, /createCourse): let the HTTP method be the verb.
  • Returning 200 for everything (even errors) with {"success": false}.
  • Missing Content-Type: application/json on POST/PUT → 415 Unsupported Media Type.
  • Putting business logic in controllers.

Exercise

  1. Add GET /api/courses?level=BEGINNER filtering (use @RequestParam(required = false)).
  2. Add PATCH /api/courses/{id}/price that accepts {"price": 399} and changes only the price.
  3. Add a lessons count field and GET /api/courses/{id}/summary returning a smaller JSON object.
  4. Test every endpoint with Postman and save the requests as a collection.
Hint for 2

Accept @RequestBody Map<String, Integer> body (or a small record PriceChange(int price)) and build a new Course with the new price.

Interview corner

  • What makes an API RESTful? Resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP methods, stateless requests, representations (JSON), and proper status codes.
  • PUT vs PATCH? PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes part of it.
  • Which status for create? delete? 201 Created (with Location); 204 No Content.
  • Is GET idempotent? POST? GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

Summary

  • Nouns in URLs, HTTP methods as verbs, correct status codes.
  • @RestController + mappings + ResponseEntity give full control.
  • Controller → service → repository layering keeps code clean.

items.title: Spring Data JPA - Repositories Without Code
items.excerpt: Connect Spring Boot to H2 or MySQL, map entities, get CRUD for free with JpaRepository, write derived query methods and @Query, paginate and sort, and seed data at startup.
items.content:
In the JPA course you wrote EntityManager code and transactions by hand. Spring Data JPA goes further: you declare an interface, and Spring generates the implementation at startup, including queries derived from method names.

Dependencies and configuration

Starters: spring-boot-starter-data-jpa plus a driver (com.h2database:h2 for learning, com.mysql:mysql-connector-j or org.postgresql:postgresql for real databases).

# application.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:courses
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
spring.h2.console.enabled=true

For MySQL you'd change just the connection:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/courses
spring.datasource.username=courses
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

Boot auto-configures the DataSource (HikariCP pool), Hibernate, the EntityManagerFactory and the transaction manager from these few lines.

The entity

package com.vitalstack.courses;

public enum Level { BEGINNER, INTERMEDIATE, ADVANCED }
package com.vitalstack.courses;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String title;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private Level level;

    private int price;
    private boolean published;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, Level level, int price, boolean published) {
        this.title = title; this.level = level; this.price = price; this.published = published;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public Level getLevel() { return level; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
    public boolean isPublished() { return published; }
    public void setPrice(int price) { this.price = price; }
}

The repository: just an interface

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.*;
import org.springframework.data.repository.query.Param;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> {

    // derived queries: Spring reads the method name and writes the JPQL
    List<Course> findByLevel(Level level);
    List<Course> findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(String text);
    List<Course> findByPublishedTrueAndPriceLessThanOrderByPriceAsc(int max);
    Optional<Course> findFirstByOrderByPriceDesc();
    long countByLevel(Level level);
    boolean existsByTitleIgnoreCase(String title);

    // paging
    Page<Course> findByPublishedTrue(Pageable pageable);

    // explicit JPQL when names get too long
    @Query("select avg(c.price) from Course c where c.level = :level")
    Double averagePrice(@Param("level") Level level);

    // bulk update
    @Modifying
    @Query("update Course c set c.price = c.price - c.price * :pct / 100 where c.level = :level")
    int discount(@Param("level") Level level, @Param("pct") int pct);
}

JpaRepository already gives you: save, saveAll, findById, findAll (with Sort or Pageable), count, existsById, deleteById, delete, flush and more. No implementation class anywhere!

Derived query keywords

Typos in method names fail at startup, not at runtime. A nice safety net.

Using it in a service and controller

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.data.domain.*;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import java.util.List;

@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class CourseService {
    private final CourseRepository repo;

    public CourseService(CourseRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    public List<Course> search(String q) { return repo.findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(q); }
    public Page<Course> page(int page, int size) {
        return repo.findByPublishedTrue(PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("price").descending()));
    }
    public List<Course> cheap(int max) { return repo.findByPublishedTrueAndPriceLessThanOrderByPriceAsc(max); }
    public Double average(Level level) { return repo.averagePrice(level); }

    @Transactional                                  // writes need a read-write transaction
    public int discount(Level level, int pct) { return repo.discount(level, pct); }
}
package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.data.domain.Page;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/courses")
public class CourseController {
    private final CourseService service;

    public CourseController(CourseService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping("/search")
    public List<Course> search(@RequestParam String q) { return service.search(q); }

    @GetMapping("/cheap")
    public List<Course> cheap(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "700") int max) { return service.cheap(max); }

    public record CoursePage(List<String> items, int page, int totalPages, long total) { }
    public record LevelStats(Level level, Double averagePrice) { }

    @GetMapping
    public CoursePage page(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                           @RequestParam(defaultValue = "2") int size) {
        Page<Course> p = service.page(page, size);
        return new CoursePage(p.getContent().stream().map(Course::getTitle).toList(),
                p.getNumber(), p.getTotalPages(), p.getTotalElements());
    }

    @GetMapping("/stats/{level}")
    public LevelStats stats(@PathVariable Level level) {
        return new LevelStats(level, service.average(level));
    }

    @PostMapping("/discount/{level}")
    public Map<String, Integer> discount(@PathVariable Level level, @RequestParam int pct) {
        return Map.of("updated", service.discount(level, pct));
    }
}

Seeding data at startup

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import java.util.List;

@SpringBootApplication
public class CourseApiApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CourseApiApplication.class, args);
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner seed(CourseRepository repo) {
        return args -> repo.saveAll(List.of(
                new Course("Java Basics", Level.BEGINNER, 499, true),
                new Course("Spring Boot", Level.INTERMEDIATE, 799, true),
                new Course("Hibernate Deep Dive", Level.ADVANCED, 999, true),
                new Course("React", Level.BEGINNER, 599, true),
                new Course("JavaScript Draft", Level.BEGINNER, 199, false)));
    }
}

(Alternatively, put INSERTs in src/main/resources/data.sql.)

Results

GET  /api/courses/search?q=java       → [{"id":1,"title":"Java Basics",…}, {"id":5,"title":"JavaScript Draft",…}]
GET  /api/courses/cheap?max=700       → [Java Basics (499), React (599)]   (drafts excluded)
GET  /api/courses?page=0&size=2       → {"items":["Hibernate Deep Dive","Spring Boot"],"page":0,"totalPages":2,"total":4}
GET  /api/courses?page=1&size=2       → {"items":["React","Java Basics"],"page":1,"totalPages":2,"total":4}
GET  /api/courses/stats/BEGINNER      → {"level":"BEGINNER","averagePrice":432.3333333333333}
POST /api/courses/discount/BEGINNER?pct=10 → {"updated":3}

Pageable works straight from request parameters too: declare Pageable pageable as a controller parameter and call /api/courses?page=1&size=20&sort=price,desc. But return a DTO (not Page itself) to keep a stable JSON format.

Common mistakes

  • @Modifying queries without a write transaction → TransactionRequiredException.
  • Huge derived names: switch to @Query.
  • findAll() on big tables: always paginate lists.
  • Returning entities with lazy relationships from controllers (LazyInitializationException or JSON loops). Use DTOs: next lesson.

Exercise

  1. Add findByLevelOrderByTitle(Level level) and expose it as GET /api/courses/level/{level}.
  2. Add findTop3ByPublishedTrueOrderByPriceDesc() for "premium courses".
  3. Write a @Query that returns the total price of published courses per level as a record projection.
  4. Open the H2 console at /h2-console (JDBC URL jdbc:h2:mem:courses) and look at the table.
Hint for 3

@Query("select new com.vitalstack.courses.LevelTotal(c.level, sum(c.price)) from Course c where c.published = true group by c.level") List<LevelTotal> totals();

Interview corner

  • What is Spring Data JPA? A Spring module that generates repository implementations from interfaces, including derived queries.
  • CrudRepository vs JpaRepository? JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository/ListCrudRepository and adds JPA-specific methods like flush and batch deletes.
  • How do derived queries work? Spring parses the method name into a JPQL query at startup.
  • What does @Modifying do? Marks a @Query as an update/delete statement (needs a transaction).

Summary

  • Configure the datasource in properties; Boot sets up Hibernate and transactions.
  • interface X extends JpaRepository<Entity, Id> gives CRUD, paging and sorting.
  • Derived query methods and @Query cover most queries; @Modifying for bulk updates.

Next: DTOs, validation and clean error responses.

items.title: DTOs, Validation and Error Handling in Spring Boot
items.excerpt: Separate API models from entities with DTO records, validate input with Bean Validation, return clean RFC 7807 ProblemDetail errors with @RestControllerAdvice, and map 400, 404 and 409 correctly.
items.content:
A professional API rejects bad input with clear messages, never leaks internal details, and returns consistent error responses. This lesson adds three things to the course API: DTOs, validation and error handling.

Why DTOs?

A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a class shaped for the API, separate from the entity shaped for the database.

Records are perfect DTOs:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;

public record CourseRequest(
        @NotBlank(message = "Title is required")
        @Size(max = 100, message = "Title must be at most 100 characters")
        String title,

        @NotNull(message = "Level is required")
        Level level,

        @Min(value = 0, message = "Price can't be negative")
        @Max(value = 50000, message = "Price looks too high")
        int price) { }
package com.vitalstack.courses;

public record CourseResponse(Long id, String title, Level level, int price) {
    static CourseResponse from(Course c) {
        return new CourseResponse(c.getId(), c.getTitle(), c.getLevel(), c.getPrice());
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.courses;

public enum Level { BEGINNER, INTERMEDIATE, ADVANCED }
package com.vitalstack.courses;

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Course {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 100)
    private String title;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private Level level;
    private int price;

    protected Course() { }
    public Course(String title, Level level, int price) { this.title = title; this.level = level; this.price = price; }

    public void update(String title, Level level, int price) { this.title = title; this.level = level; this.price = price; }
    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public Level getLevel() { return level; }
    public int getPrice() { return price; }
}
package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> {
    boolean existsByTitleIgnoreCase(String title);
}

Domain exceptions

package com.vitalstack.courses;

public class CourseNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public CourseNotFoundException(long id) { super("Course " + id + " was not found"); }
}
package com.vitalstack.courses;

public class DuplicateCourseException extends RuntimeException {
    public DuplicateCourseException(String title) { super("A course titled '" + title + "' already exists"); }
}

The service speaks in DTOs and exceptions

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
@Transactional
public class CourseService {
    private final CourseRepository repo;

    public CourseService(CourseRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public CourseResponse get(long id) {
        return repo.findById(id).map(CourseResponse::from).orElseThrow(() -> new CourseNotFoundException(id));
    }

    public CourseResponse create(CourseRequest req) {
        String title = req.title().trim();                     // normalise first, then check duplicates
        if (repo.existsByTitleIgnoreCase(title)) throw new DuplicateCourseException(title);
        return CourseResponse.from(repo.save(new Course(title, req.level(), req.price())));
    }

    public CourseResponse update(long id, CourseRequest req) {
        Course c = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new CourseNotFoundException(id));
        c.update(req.title().trim(), req.level(), req.price());     // dirty checking saves it
        return CourseResponse.from(c);
    }
}

@Valid in the controller

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.net.URI;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/courses")
public class CourseController {
    private final CourseService service;

    public CourseController(CourseService service) { this.service = service; }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public CourseResponse get(@PathVariable long id) { return service.get(id); }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<CourseResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody CourseRequest req) {
        CourseResponse created = service.create(req);
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/courses/" + created.id())).body(created);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public CourseResponse update(@PathVariable long id, @Valid @RequestBody CourseRequest req) {
        return service.update(id, req);
    }
}

@Valid runs the annotations on CourseRequest before your method is called. If anything fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException and your method never runs.

Consistent errors with ProblemDetail

Spring Boot 3 supports RFC 7807 Problem Details, a standard JSON error format. One class handles errors for every controller:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.http.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(CourseNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail notFound(CourseNotFoundException e) {
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
        p.setTitle("Course not found");
        return p;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateCourseException.class)
    public ProblemDetail conflict(DuplicateCourseException e) {
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, e.getMessage());
        p.setTitle("Duplicate course");
        return p;
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException e) {
        Map<String, String> fields = new TreeMap<>();
        e.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(f -> fields.put(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage()));
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Some fields are invalid");
        p.setTitle("Validation failed");
        p.setProperty("errors", fields);
        return p;
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class CourseApiApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(CourseApiApplication.class, args);
    }
}

The responses

POST /api/courses {"title":"Java Basics","level":"BEGINNER","price":499}
← 201 {"id":1,"title":"Java Basics","level":"BEGINNER","price":499}

POST /api/courses {"title":"","level":null,"price":-5}
← 400 {"type":"about:blank","title":"Validation failed","status":400,"detail":"Some fields are invalid",
       "instance":"/api/courses","errors":{"level":"Level is required","price":"Price can't be negative","title":"Title is required"}}

POST /api/courses {"title":"java basics","level":"BEGINNER","price":10}
← 409 {"type":"about:blank","title":"Duplicate course","status":409,
       "detail":"A course titled 'java basics' already exists","instance":"/api/courses"}

GET /api/courses/99
← 404 {"type":"about:blank","title":"Course not found","status":404,
       "detail":"Course 99 was not found","instance":"/api/courses/99"}

Front-end developers can now show the errors map next to each form field.

Validation annotations

Create your own with a custom @Constraint annotation when needed (e.g. @IndianPinCode).

Validate twice, in different places: Bean Validation for format (required, length, range) at the API edge, and business rules (unique title, enough stock) in the service, throwing domain exceptions. The database constraints (unique, not null) are the last safety net.

Status codes for errors

Exercise

  1. Add @Size(min = 3) to title and check the 400 response for "Go".
  2. Add an email field to a StudentRequest with @Email and a custom message.
  3. Handle OptimisticLockingFailureException and return a 409 ProblemDetail.
  4. Add a catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) that logs the error and returns a generic 500 ProblemDetail without internal details.
Hint for 4

Log with log.error("Unexpected error", e) and return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Something went wrong. Please try again.").

Interview corner

  • Why use DTOs instead of entities in APIs? Stable contracts, no over-exposure, no lazy-loading/JSON recursion issues, control over input fields.
  • How does @Valid work? It triggers Bean Validation (Hibernate Validator) on the argument; failures raise MethodArgumentNotValidException.
  • @ControllerAdvice vs @RestControllerAdvice? The latter adds @ResponseBody so handler results become JSON.
  • What is ProblemDetail? Spring's implementation of RFC 7807, a standard JSON format for HTTP API errors.

Summary

  • Request/response DTO records decouple the API from entities.
  • @Valid + constraint annotations validate input automatically.
  • Domain exceptions + @RestControllerAdvice + ProblemDetail give consistent 400/404/409 errors.

items.title: Spring Boot Configuration, Profiles and Logging
items.excerpt: Configure Spring Boot with application.yml, typed @ConfigurationProperties, dev/test/prod profiles and environment variables, and log properly with SLF4J, log levels, log files and request logging.
items.content:
The same jar should run on your laptop, a test server and production, with different databases, secrets and log levels. Spring Boot's configuration system and logging make this easy.

application.yml

YAML is popular for its nesting. It's equivalent to application.properties:

# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: course-api
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:courses
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false

server:
  port: 8080
  servlet:
    context-path: /

app:
  catalog:
    max-page-size: 50
    featured-courses: [java-basics, spring-boot]
    signup-bonus-xp: 100

logging:
  level:
    root: info
    com.vitalstack: debug
    org.hibernate.SQL: debug           # log SQL statements

Use one format per project (YAML or properties) to avoid confusion. If both exist, properties wins for the same key.

Typed settings

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.*;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;
import java.util.List;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.catalog")
public record CatalogProperties(
        @Min(1) @Max(200) int maxPageSize,
        List<String> featuredCourses,
        @PositiveOrZero int signupBonusXp) { }

Register it with @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class (or @EnableConfigurationProperties(CatalogProperties.class)) and inject it anywhere:

@Service
public class CatalogService {
    private final CatalogProperties props;
    public CatalogService(CatalogProperties props) { this.props = props; }

    public int pageSize(int requested) { return Math.min(requested, props.maxPageSize()); }
}

If max-page-size is set to 0, the app refuses to start with a clear message. Bad configuration is caught at deploy time, not at 2 am.

Profiles in Spring Boot

src/main/resources/
├── application.yml          ← common defaults
├── application-dev.yml      ← local development
├── application-test.yml     ← automated tests
└── application-prod.yml     ← production
# application-prod.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST}:5432/courses
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
logging:
  level:
    root: warn
    com.vitalstack: info

Activate with --spring.profiles.active=prod or the SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod environment variable. In tests, @ActiveProfiles("test").

You can also keep several profiles in one YAML file separated by --- and spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod.

Environment variables everywhere

Any property can be overridden by an environment variable with relaxed binding:

This is how Docker, Kubernetes, Render, Railway and most hosts configure Spring Boot apps.

Logging with SLF4J

Spring Boot uses SLF4J with Logback by default. Get a logger per class:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class EnrollmentService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(EnrollmentService.class);

    public void enroll(long studentId, long courseId) {
        log.debug("Enrolling student {} in course {}", studentId, courseId);   // {} placeholders: no string building if disabled
        try {
            // ... business logic ...
            log.info("Student {} enrolled in course {}", studentId, courseId);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            log.error("Enrollment failed for student {} in course {}", studentId, courseId, e);   // exception last
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

(With Lombok, @Slf4j creates the log field for you.)

Log levels

Set levels per package in configuration, and change them at runtime with Actuator's /actuator/loggers endpoint (lesson 9).

Log files and format

logging:
  file:
    name: logs/course-api.log      # also write to a file (rotated automatically, 10 MB by default)
  logback:
    rollingpolicy:
      max-history: 14              # keep 14 days

For log platforms (ELK, Loki, Datadog), Spring Boot 3.4+ supports structured JSON logs with logging.structured.format.console=ecs.

Never log passwords, OTPs, full card numbers, tokens or personal data like Aadhaar numbers. Logs are copied to many places and kept for a long time. Log ids, not secrets.

Common mistakes

  • Indentation errors in YAML (use spaces, never tabs).
  • String concatenation in logs ("user " + id) instead of {} placeholders.
  • Logging an exception's message but not the exception itself (you lose the stack trace).
  • Committing application-prod.yml with real passwords.

Exercise

  1. Convert your application.properties to application.yml.
  2. Create CatalogProperties and print the featured courses at startup with a CommandLineRunner.
  3. Add dev and prod profiles with different log levels and a different server.port, and switch between them.
  4. Add DEBUG and INFO logs to your service, then run with logging.level.com.vitalstack=info and confirm the DEBUG lines disappear.
Hint for 2

@Bean CommandLineRunner show(CatalogProperties p) { return args -> log.info("Featured: {}", p.featuredCourses()); } plus @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class.

Interview corner

  • properties vs yml? Same features; YAML is hierarchical and more readable for nested config.
  • How do you configure different environments? Profiles (application-{profile}.yml) plus environment variables for secrets.
  • Which logging framework does Spring Boot use? SLF4J API with Logback by default (Log4j2 optional).
  • **Why use {} placeholders?** The message is only built if the level is enabled, and it's cleaner.

Summary

  • application.yml + profiles + environment variables configure every environment from one jar.
  • @ConfigurationProperties records give typed, validated settings.
  • Log with SLF4J at the right level, with placeholders, without secrets.

items.title: Spring Security with JWT in Spring Boot
items.excerpt: Secure a Spring Boot REST API - how the security filter chain works, password hashing with BCrypt, a login endpoint that issues JWT tokens, protecting routes by role, and testing with a Bearer token.
items.content:
Right now anyone can create or delete courses. Let's add authentication (who are you?) and authorisation (what are you allowed to do?) with Spring Security and JWT tokens, the standard approach for REST APIs used by React, Angular and mobile apps.

How Spring Security works

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters (remember the Servlet course) that runs before your controllers:

Request ──▶ [CORS] ──▶ [Bearer token filter] ──▶ [Authorization filter] ──▶ Controller
                              │                          │
                     reads "Authorization:        checks the URL's rules
                      Bearer eyJ…", verifies       (permitAll, hasRole…)
                      the signature, sets the      → 401 / 403 if not allowed
                      current user

Just adding spring-boot-starter-security locks every endpoint (with a generated password printed in the log). You then configure the rules you want.

What is a JWT?

A JSON Web Token is a signed string with three parts: header.payload.signature.

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhc2hhIiwicm9sZXMiOiJBRE1JTiIsImV4cCI6MTc2MDAwMDAwMH0.k3V…

The payload (base64, not encrypted, anyone can read it) holds claims: sub (username), roles, exp (expiry). The server signs it with a secret key; if anyone changes the payload, the signature no longer matches. The server doesn't store sessions: each request carries its token. That's stateless authentication, ideal for APIs and multiple servers.

Dependencies

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>   <!-- JWT encode/decode (Nimbus) -->
</dependency>

Security configuration

package com.vitalstack.secure;

import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.ImmutableSecret;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.*;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.dao.DaoAuthenticationProvider;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.*;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jose.jws.MacAlgorithm;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.*;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.*;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                                    // stateless API with tokens: no CSRF cookie risk
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/login").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/courses/**").permitAll()      // anyone can browse
                .requestMatchers("/api/courses/**").hasRole("ADMIN")                 // only admins change courses
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(jwt -> jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(rolesFromToken())))
            .build();
    }

    // Demo users. In a real app, load users from the database (a UserDetailsService backed by a repository).
    @Bean
    UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
        return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(
            User.withUsername("asha").password(encoder.encode("student123")).roles("STUDENT").build(),
            User.withUsername("admin").password(encoder.encode("admin123")).roles("ADMIN").build());
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }      // never store plain passwords

    @Bean
    AuthenticationManager authManager(UserDetailsService users, PasswordEncoder encoder) {
        DaoAuthenticationProvider provider = new DaoAuthenticationProvider();
        provider.setUserDetailsService(users);
        provider.setPasswordEncoder(encoder);
        return new ProviderManager(provider);
    }

    @Bean
    SecretKeySpec jwtKey(@Value("${app.jwt.secret}") String secret) {
        return new SecretKeySpec(secret.getBytes(), "HmacSHA256");
    }

    @Bean
    JwtEncoder jwtEncoder(SecretKeySpec key) { return new NimbusJwtEncoder(new ImmutableSecret<>(key)); }

    @Bean
    JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(SecretKeySpec key) {
        return NimbusJwtDecoder.withSecretKey(key).macAlgorithm(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build();
    }

    private JwtAuthenticationConverter rolesFromToken() {
        JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
        roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");          // read the "roles" claim…
        roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");               // …so hasRole("ADMIN") matches "ADMIN"
        JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
        converter.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
        return converter;
    }
}

The login endpoint

package com.vitalstack.secure;

import org.springframework.security.authentication.*;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.GrantedAuthority;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jose.jws.MacAlgorithm;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.*;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;
import java.util.Map;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/auth")
public class AuthController {
    public record LoginRequest(String username, String password) { }

    private final AuthenticationManager auth;
    private final JwtEncoder encoder;

    public AuthController(AuthenticationManager auth, JwtEncoder encoder) { this.auth = auth; this.encoder = encoder; }

    @PostMapping("/login")
    public Map<String, String> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
        Authentication user = auth.authenticate(
                new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(req.username(), req.password()));   // throws if wrong → 401
        String roles = user.getAuthorities().stream()
                .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority).map(a -> a.replace("ROLE_", ""))
                .reduce((a, b) -> a + " " + b).orElse("");
        JwtClaimsSet claims = JwtClaimsSet.builder()
                .subject(user.getName())
                .claim("roles", roles)
                .issuedAt(Instant.now())
                .expiresAt(Instant.now().plus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS))           // short-lived tokens
                .build();
        String token = encoder.encode(JwtEncoderParameters.from(
                JwsHeader.with(MacAlgorithm.HS256).build(), claims)).getTokenValue();
        return Map.of("token", token);
    }
}

Protected endpoints

package com.vitalstack.secure;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.security.core.annotation.AuthenticationPrincipal;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;
import java.util.List;

@RestController
public class SecureController {

    @GetMapping("/api/courses")
    public List<String> courses() { return List.of("Java Basics", "Spring Boot"); }          // public

    @DeleteMapping("/api/courses/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void delete(@PathVariable long id) { }                                           // ADMIN only

    public record Me(String username, String roles) { }

    @GetMapping("/api/me")
    public Me me(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {                                       // any logged-in user
        return new Me(jwt.getSubject(), jwt.getClaimAsString("roles"));
    }
}
package com.vitalstack.secure;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class SecureApiApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(SecureApiApplication.class, args); }
}
# application.properties
# at least 32 random characters; in production: app.jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET}
app.jwt.secret=change-me-to-a-long-random-secret-of-32-chars-or-more

Trying it

GET    /api/courses                                → 200 ["Java Basics","Spring Boot"]
GET    /api/me                                     → 401 (no token)
POST   /api/auth/login {"username":"asha","password":"wrong"}       → 401
POST   /api/auth/login {"username":"asha","password":"student123"}  → 200 {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9…"}
GET    /api/me   Authorization: Bearer <asha token>                → 200 {"username":"asha","roles":"STUDENT"}
DELETE /api/courses/1   Authorization: Bearer <asha token>         → 403 Forbidden (not an admin)
DELETE /api/courses/1   Authorization: Bearer <admin token>        → 204

The front end stores the token after login and sends Authorization: Bearer <token> with each request (you'll do this in the React and Angular courses).

Method-level security

Add @EnableMethodSecurity to a configuration class and protect service methods directly:

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void deleteCourse(long id) { ... }

@PreAuthorize("#studentId == authentication.name or hasRole('ADMIN')")
public Progress progressOf(String studentId) { ... }

Security checklist

  • ✅ BCrypt (or Argon2) for passwords; never store or log plain passwords.
  • ✅ Secret from an environment variable, at least 256 bits; rotate if leaked.
  • ✅ Short-lived access tokens (15-60 min) plus refresh tokens for long sessions.
  • ✅ HTTPS always: tokens in plain HTTP can be stolen.
  • ✅ Configure CORS for your front-end origin only (http.cors(...) with a CorsConfigurationSource).
  • ✅ Rate-limit the login endpoint.
  • ❌ Don't put sensitive data in the JWT payload: it's readable by anyone.

For bigger systems, don't build login yourself: use an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, Google). Your Spring Boot API then only validates their tokens with spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri, a few lines of configuration.

Exercise

  1. Add an INSTRUCTOR role that can create courses (POST) but not delete them.
  2. Change the token lifetime to 15 minutes and add the user's email as a claim.
  3. Store users in a database table with a UserDetailsService that loads them through a Spring Data repository.
  4. Configure CORS to allow http://localhost:5173 (a Vite React app).
Hint for 1

.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/courses/**").hasAnyRole("ADMIN", "INSTRUCTOR") placed before the general /api/courses/** admin rule (rules match top to bottom).

Interview corner

  • Authentication vs authorisation? Proving identity vs checking permissions.
  • How does Spring Security work? A chain of servlet filters (SecurityFilterChain) that authenticate requests and enforce access rules before controllers.
  • What is a JWT and why stateless? A signed token carrying claims; the server verifies the signature instead of storing sessions.
  • 401 vs 403? 401: not authenticated (missing/invalid token); 403: authenticated but not allowed.
  • Why disable CSRF for token APIs? CSRF exploits cookies sent automatically; Bearer tokens in headers aren't sent automatically by browsers.

Summary

  • Spring Security is a filter chain; configure it with a SecurityFilterChain bean.
  • Hash passwords with BCrypt; issue short-lived signed JWTs at login.
  • Protect URLs with permitAll/hasRole, and methods with @PreAuthorize.

Next: testing Spring Boot applications.

items.title: Testing Spring Boot Applications
items.excerpt: Write fast unit tests with JUnit 5 and Mockito, test controllers with @WebMvcTest and MockMvc, repositories with @DataJpaTest, full flows with @SpringBootTest, and real databases with Testcontainers.
items.content:
Tests let you change code without fear. Spring Boot gives you everything in one starter (spring-boot-starter-test: JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, MockMvc, JSONPath) and test slices that start only the part of the app you're testing, so tests stay fast.

The testing pyramid

        /\        few   @SpringBootTest: whole app, real HTTP (slow, broad)
       /  \             
      /----\      some  slices: @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest (medium)
     /      \           
    /--------\    many  plain unit tests: no Spring at all (milliseconds)

We'll test the course API from the DTO and validation lesson (CourseService, CourseController, CourseRepository, ApiExceptionHandler).

1. Unit tests with Mockito (no Spring)

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.InjectMocks;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;
import java.util.Optional;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.*;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.*;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class CourseServiceTest {

    @Mock CourseRepository repo;              // a fake repository
    @InjectMocks CourseService service;       // the real service, with the fake injected

    @Test
    void createsCourseWhenTitleIsNew() {
        when(repo.existsByTitleIgnoreCase("Docker")).thenReturn(false);
        when(repo.save(any(Course.class))).thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0));

        CourseResponse res = service.create(new CourseRequest(" Docker ", Level.BEGINNER, 399));

        assertThat(res.title()).isEqualTo("Docker");          // trimmed
        verify(repo).save(any(Course.class));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsDuplicateTitle() {
        when(repo.existsByTitleIgnoreCase("Java")).thenReturn(true);

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.create(new CourseRequest("Java", Level.BEGINNER, 1)))
                .isInstanceOf(DuplicateCourseException.class)
                .hasMessageContaining("already exists");
        verify(repo, never()).save(any());
    }

    @Test
    void missingCourseThrowsNotFound() {
        when(repo.findById(42L)).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.get(42)).isInstanceOf(CourseNotFoundException.class);
    }
}

These run in milliseconds. Constructor injection is what makes them so easy.

2. Controller tests with @WebMvcTest

@WebMvcTest starts only the web layer (controllers, advice, JSON conversion, validation). Services are replaced with mocks:

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.WebMvcTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.mock.mockito.MockBean;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;

import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.*;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.*;

@WebMvcTest(CourseController.class)
class CourseControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockBean CourseService service;      // Spring Boot 3.4+: @MockitoBean

    @Test
    void returnsCourseAsJson() throws Exception {
        when(service.get(1)).thenReturn(new CourseResponse(1L, "Java Basics", Level.BEGINNER, 499));

        mvc.perform(get("/api/courses/1"))
           .andExpect(status().isOk())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Java Basics"))
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.price").value(499));
    }

    @Test
    void returns404ProblemDetail() throws Exception {
        when(service.get(99)).thenThrow(new CourseNotFoundException(99));

        mvc.perform(get("/api/courses/99"))
           .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("Course 99 was not found"));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsInvalidBody() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/courses")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"title\":\"\",\"level\":\"BEGINNER\",\"price\":-1}"))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.title").value("Title is required"))
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.errors.price").value("Price can't be negative"));
    }

    @Test
    void createReturns201WithLocation() throws Exception {
        when(service.create(any())).thenReturn(new CourseResponse(7L, "Docker", Level.BEGINNER, 399));

        mvc.perform(post("/api/courses")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"title\":\"Docker\",\"level\":\"BEGINNER\",\"price\":399}"))
           .andExpect(status().isCreated())
           .andExpect(header().string("Location", "/api/courses/7"));
    }
}

No server, no database: MockMvc calls the DispatcherServlet directly. If your app uses Spring Security, these tests also run through the security filters: add @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN") on tests that need a logged-in user.

3. Repository tests with @DataJpaTest

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.orm.jpa.DataJpaTest;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@DataJpaTest                                       // JPA + embedded H2 + rollback after each test
class CourseRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired CourseRepository repo;

    @Test
    void findsTitlesIgnoringCase() {
        repo.save(new Course("Spring Boot", Level.INTERMEDIATE, 799));

        assertThat(repo.existsByTitleIgnoreCase("spring boot")).isTrue();
        assertThat(repo.existsByTitleIgnoreCase("react")).isFalse();
    }
}

Each test runs in a transaction that's rolled back, so tests don't affect each other.

4. Full integration tests with @SpringBootTest

package com.vitalstack.courses;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.boot.test.web.client.TestRestTemplate;
import org.springframework.http.*;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class CourseApiIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired TestRestTemplate http;

    @Test
    void createThenFetch() {
        var created = http.postForEntity("/api/courses",
                new CourseRequest("Kubernetes", Level.ADVANCED, 999), CourseResponse.class);
        assertThat(created.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);

        var fetched = http.getForEntity(created.getHeaders().getLocation(), CourseResponse.class);
        assertThat(fetched.getBody().title()).isEqualTo("Kubernetes");
    }
}

The whole app starts on a random port and the test talks to it over real HTTP.

Running the tests

./mvnw test
[INFO] Tests run: 9, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

Testcontainers: test against the real database

H2 behaves differently from MySQL/PostgreSQL in places. Testcontainers starts a real database in Docker for your tests:

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class PostgresIntegrationTest {
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                          // Boot 3.1+: configures the DataSource automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    // tests now run against PostgreSQL 16
}

Name tests after behaviour (rejectsDuplicateTitle), test one thing each, and follow Arrange → Act → Assert. When a bug is reported, first write a test that fails because of it, then fix the code: the bug can never silently return.

Exercise

  1. Add a unit test for CourseService.update that checks the entity's fields change.
  2. Add a @WebMvcTest for PUT /api/courses/{id} returning 404 for a missing course.
  3. Add a @DataJpaTest for a derived query like findByLevel.
  4. Measure: run ./mvnw test and compare the time of the unit tests vs @SpringBootTest in the report.
Hint for 2

when(service.update(eq(5L), any())).thenThrow(new CourseNotFoundException(5)); then perform a PUT with a valid JSON body and expect status().isNotFound().

Interview corner

  • @SpringBootTest vs @WebMvcTest vs @DataJpaTest? Whole application context vs web layer only vs JPA layer only (with an embedded DB and rollback).
  • @Mock vs @MockBean? @Mock is plain Mockito (unit tests); @MockBean (or @MockitoBean) replaces a bean inside the Spring test context.
  • What is MockMvc? A way to test Spring MVC controllers by simulating HTTP requests without a server.
  • Why Testcontainers? Tests run against the same database engine as production, catching dialect and migration issues.

Summary

  • Many fast unit tests with Mockito; fewer slice tests; a few full integration tests.
  • @WebMvcTest + MockMvc for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories, @SpringBootTest for end-to-end.
  • Testcontainers gives real databases in tests.

Next: relationships, pagination and performance in a real API.
