items.title: Jmix Project: Course Admin App and Deployment
items.excerpt: Put it all together - a course admin app with dashboards, reports, a REST API for a mobile or React front end, and production deployment as a jar or Docker container with PostgreSQL.
items.content:
Let's turn the pieces into a complete Course Admin application that a training institute could actually use, then deploy it.

Requirements

  1. Admins manage categories, instructors and courses with lessons.
  2. Instructors manage only their own courses.
  3. A dashboard shows course counts per level and the newest courses.
  4. Managers export a course catalogue report to Excel/PDF.
  5. A public website (React or Angular) reads published courses through a REST API.

1. Data model and views (lessons 3-4)

  • Entities: Category, Instructor (linked to a User), Course (with published flag, level, price), Lesson (composition).
  • Generate list and detail views for each; add a published filter condition and a Publish button.

2. Security (lesson 6)

3. A dashboard view

Create a blank view (*User Interface → New → View → Blank view*) and set it as the start page of the main view:

<view xmlns="http://jmix.io/schema/flowui/view" title="Dashboard">
    <layout>
        <h3 text="Courses by level"/>
        <hbox id="statsBox" spacing="true"/>
        <h3 text="Newest courses"/>
        <dataGrid id="newestGrid" width="100%" height="20em" dataContainer="newestDc">
            <columns>
                <column property="title"/>
                <column property="instructor"/>
                <column property="createdDate"/>
            </columns>
        </dataGrid>
    </layout>
    <data readOnly="true">
        <collection id="newestDc" class="com.vitalstack.courseadmin.entity.Course">
            <fetchPlan extends="_base">
                <property name="instructor" fetchPlan="_instance_name"/>
            </fetchPlan>
            <loader id="newestDl" maxResults="10">
                <query><![CDATA[select c from Course c order by c.createdDate desc]]></query>
            </loader>
        </collection>
    </data>
    <facets>
        <dataLoadCoordinator auto="true"/>
    </facets>
</view>
@Route(value = "dashboard", layout = MainView.class)
@ViewController("DashboardView")
@ViewDescriptor("dashboard-view.xml")
public class DashboardView extends StandardView {

    @Autowired private DataManager dataManager;
    @ViewComponent private HorizontalLayout statsBox;

    @Subscribe
    public void onBeforeShow(final BeforeShowEvent event) {
        List<KeyValueEntity> rows = dataManager.loadValues(
                        "select c.level, count(c) from Course c group by c.level")
                .properties("level", "count")
                .list();
        for (KeyValueEntity row : rows) {
            Span card = new Span(row.getValue("level") + ": " + row.getValue("count"));
            card.addClassName("stat-card");
            statsBox.add(card);
        }
    }
}

Because it uses DataManager, an instructor's dashboard automatically counts only their courses (row-level security).

4. Reports add-on

Install Reports from *Add-ons* in Studio. Admins then design reports in the running app: a band with a JPQL query (select c.title, c.level, c.price from Course c where c.published = true), and a template (XLSX, DOCX or HTML → PDF). Add a Run report button to the course list. No code needed for most business reports.

Other popular add-ons: BPM (approval workflows with BPMN, e.g. "new course → manager approval → publish"), Email (templated notifications), Charts, Audit (entity change history), Multitenancy.

5. REST API for the public site

Install the REST API add-on (and authorization server) to expose entities and services over HTTP with OAuth2 tokens, respecting the same roles. For a public, read-only catalogue, a plain Spring MVC controller is often simpler, because Jmix apps are Spring Boot apps:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/public/courses")
public class PublicCourseController {
    private final UnconstrainedDataManager dataManager;      // public data, filtered explicitly below

    public PublicCourseController(UnconstrainedDataManager dataManager) { this.dataManager = dataManager; }

    public record CourseCard(String title, String level, BigDecimal price) { }

    @GetMapping
    public List<CourseCard> published() {
        return dataManager.load(Course.class)
                .query("select c from Course c where c.published = true order by c.title")
                .list().stream()
                .map(c -> new CourseCard(c.getTitle(), String.valueOf(c.getLevel()), c.getPrice()))
                .toList();
    }
}

Permit /public/** without login in a security configuration bean, and enable CORS for your website's domain. Your React or Angular course projects can call this endpoint.

6. Deployment

Build a production jar

./gradlew -Pvaadin.productionMode=true bootJar
java -jar build/libs/course-admin-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

Production mode bundles and minifies the front end for fast loading.

Configure for production

main.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/courseadmin
main.datasource.username=courseadmin
main.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
jmix.ui.session-timeout=30m
logging.level.root=info

Pass secrets as environment variables, exactly like Spring Boot (lesson 9 of the Spring Boot course).

Docker

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY build/libs/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "app.jar"]

Or ./gradlew -Pvaadin.productionMode=true bootBuildImage. Run it next to PostgreSQL with Docker Compose on a VPS, behind Nginx with HTTPS. Vaadin UIs use a server-side session per user, so with several app instances enable sticky sessions on the load balancer.

Before going live

  • ✅ Change or disable the default admin account.
  • ✅ Real database with backups; Liquibase runs migrations on startup.
  • ✅ HTTPS; secrets in environment variables.
  • ✅ Test every role with a real non-admin user.
  • ✅ Production mode build.

A Jmix project like this (entities, role-based security, dashboard, report, REST endpoint, deployed with Docker) is a strong portfolio piece for enterprise Java jobs, and many Indian IT services companies build exactly these kinds of internal systems for clients.

Exercise

  1. Build the Course Admin app with all five requirements.
  2. Add a BPM approval: instructors submit a course; a manager approves it before it's published.
  3. Add an email notification to the instructor when their course is approved.
  4. Deploy it with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL on your machine or a VPS.
Hint for 2

Without the BPM add-on, a simple version is a status enum (DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED) plus buttons enabled by specific policies. Use BPM when processes have many steps, deadlines or branching.

Interview corner

  • How do you deploy a Jmix app? As a Spring Boot jar (production mode) or container image, with an external database and environment-based configuration.
  • How does a Jmix app expose data to other clients? The REST API add-on (secured, role-aware) or custom Spring MVC controllers.
  • What are Jmix add-ons? Ready-made modules (reports, BPM, email, charts, audit, multitenancy) installed via Studio.
  • Why sticky sessions? Vaadin keeps UI state in the server-side session.

Summary

  • A full business app = data model + generated views + roles + a few custom views and services.
  • Add-ons cover reports, workflows, email and APIs.
  • Deploy as a production-mode jar or Docker image with PostgreSQL, HTTPS and environment secrets.

You've completed the Jmix course! Continue with React or Angular to build public front ends that talk to your Java back ends.

items.title: React Introduction
items.excerpt: What React is, why companies like Meta, Netflix, Swiggy and Flipkart use it, how components and the virtual DOM work, and what you need to know before starting.
items.content:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. It's the most popular front-end technology in job listings, used by Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp Web), Netflix, Airbnb, Swiggy, Zomato, Flipkart and thousands of startups.

The problem React solves

With plain JavaScript, you update the page by hand:

// Plain JS: keep the screen in sync yourself
let count = 0;
const button = document.querySelector('#like');
const label = document.querySelector('#likes');
button.addEventListener('click', () => {
  count++;
  label.textContent = count + ' likes';          // remember to update EVERY place that shows count
  if (count === 10) document.querySelector('#badge').hidden = false;
});

In a big app (a feed, a cart, notifications, filters), keeping every part of the screen in sync with the data becomes a tangle of bugs.

React flips it around: you describe what the UI should look like for the current data, and React updates the page for you whenever the data changes.

function LikeButton() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>👍 {count} likes</button>
      {count >= 10 && <span className="badge">Popular!</span>}
    </div>
  );
}

No querySelector, no manual updates. Change count, and the button text and badge follow automatically.

Three big ideas

1. Components. A UI is built from small, reusable pieces, each a JavaScript function:

<App>
 ├── <Header>  (logo, <SearchBox>, <UserMenu>)
 ├── <CourseList>
 │     ├── <CourseCard>
 │     ├── <CourseCard>
 │     └── <CourseCard>
 └── <Footer>

Write CourseCard once, use it a hundred times with different data.

2. Declarative UI. Components return what the UI should be (JSX). React figures out how to change the real page.

3. One-way data flow. Data flows down from parents to children through props. Children notify parents through callback functions. This makes data changes easy to trace.

The virtual DOM and rendering

Changing the real browser DOM is slow. When state changes, React:

  1. Calls your component functions again to get the new UI description (a tree of plain objects, the "virtual DOM").
  2. Compares it with the previous one (reconciliation / "diffing").
  3. Applies only the minimal changes to the real DOM.

You'll see this animated in the rendering lesson.

React vs Angular vs Vue

All three are good. React has the biggest job market; Angular is common in large Indian IT service and enterprise projects (this site has courses for both).

What you should know first

  • HTML and CSS basics.
  • JavaScript: let/const, arrow functions, arrays (map, filter), objects, destructuring, spread (...), modules (import/export), promises and async/await. The JavaScript course on this site covers all of these.

React in 2026: the ecosystem

  • Vite: the standard tool to create and run React projects (next lesson).
  • React Router: pages and navigation.
  • TanStack Query: server data fetching and caching.
  • Next.js: a React framework for server rendering and full-stack apps.
  • React Native: mobile apps with the same ideas.

Learn React itself first: components, props, state, effects. Libraries change every couple of years; these fundamentals have stayed the same since hooks arrived in 2019.

Exercise

  1. Open a website you use daily (Swiggy, YouTube, LinkedIn) and sketch its component tree for one page.
  2. Mark which parts would need state (data that changes while you use the page).
  3. Revise JavaScript map, destructuring and arrow functions if they're not comfortable yet.
Hint for 2

Search text, selected filters, cart items, whether a menu is open, liked posts, notifications count: anything that changes on screen without reloading.

Interview corner

  • What is React? A JavaScript library for building component-based, declarative user interfaces.
  • What is the virtual DOM? An in-memory representation of the UI that React diffs to compute minimal real DOM updates.
  • Library or framework? A library focused on UI; routing, forms and data fetching come from the ecosystem.
  • What is one-way data flow? Data passes from parent to child via props; children communicate up via callbacks.

Summary

  • React builds UIs from components that describe the UI for the current data.
  • React re-renders and diffs to update the DOM efficiently.
  • Props flow down, events flow up.

Next: set up a project with Vite and learn JSX.

items.title: React Setup with Vite and JSX Basics
items.excerpt: Create a React project with Vite, understand the folder structure and how main.jsx mounts the app, then learn JSX - expressions in braces, className, self-closing tags, fragments and the rules that trip beginners.
items.content:
Let's create a React project and learn JSX, the HTML-like syntax React components return.

Create a project with Vite

You need Node.js 20+ (check with node -v). Then:

npm create vite@latest course-app -- --template react
cd course-app
npm install
npm run dev

Open the URL it prints (usually http://localhost:5173). Edit src/App.jsx, save, and the browser updates instantly (hot module replacement).

Use the react-ts template instead of react to get TypeScript. It's what most companies use. This course uses JavaScript so the React ideas stay in focus; everything transfers directly.

Project structure

course-app/
├── index.html          ← the single HTML page, with <div id="root"></div>
├── package.json        ← dependencies and scripts (dev, build, preview)
├── vite.config.js
└── src/
    ├── main.jsx        ← entry point: mounts <App /> into #root
    ├── App.jsx         ← your root component
    ├── App.css, index.css
    └── assets/
// src/main.jsx
import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import App from './App.jsx';
import './index.css';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>
);

StrictMode runs extra checks in development (it may call some functions twice on purpose to reveal bugs). It does nothing in production builds.

Your first component

// src/Welcome.jsx
export default function Welcome() {
  const name = 'Asha';
  const lessons = 12;
  const today = new Date(2026, 9, 17);

  return (
    <section className="welcome">
      <h1>Namaste, {name}!</h1>
      <p>You have {lessons} lessons left. That's about {lessons * 15} minutes.</p>
      <p>Today is {today.toLocaleDateString('en-IN', { weekday: 'long' })}.</p>
      <img src="/logo.svg" alt="VitalStack logo" width={48} />
    </section>
  );
}

A component is a function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns JSX.

JSX rules

JSX looks like HTML, but it's JavaScript underneath. Vite (with Babel/esbuild) turns <h1>Hi</h1> into React.createElement('h1', null, 'Hi').

// src/PriceTag.jsx
export default function PriceTag() {
  const price = 499;
  const onSale = true;
  return (
    <>
      {/* a fragment groups elements without adding a <div> */}
      <span className="price" style={{ fontWeight: 700 }}>₹{price}</span>
      {onSale && <span className="badge">Sale</span>}
    </>
  );
}

Inside { } you can put any expression (something that produces a value): variables, math, function calls, ternaries. You can't put statements like if or for directly; you'll use ternaries, && and map instead (lesson 6).

Components using components

// src/App.jsx
import Welcome from './Welcome.jsx';
import PriceTag from './PriceTag.jsx';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <main>
      <Welcome />
      <PriceTag />
    </main>
  );
}

Lowercase tags (<main>, <section>) are HTML elements; capitalised tags (<Welcome />) are your components.

Building for production

npm run build      # creates dist/ with optimised, minified files
npm run preview    # serve the build locally to test it

The dist folder is static files: deploy it to Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, or any web host (even shared hosting).

Common mistakes

  • Lowercase component names (<welcome /> is treated as an unknown HTML tag).
  • Returning two sibling elements without a wrapper or fragment.
  • Writing class= instead of className= (works with a warning, but avoid it).
  • Forgetting export default / the import, so the component is undefined.
  • Putting if statements inside JSX braces.

Exercise

  1. Create the project and replace App.jsx with your own Welcome component.
  2. Create a ProfileCard component that shows a name, city, photo and a "Follow" button, styled with a CSS class.
  3. Show "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening" depending on the current hour.
  4. Run npm run build and look inside dist.
Hint for 3

const hour = new Date().getHours(); const greeting = hour < 12 ? 'Good morning' : hour < 17 ? 'Good afternoon' : 'Good evening'; then <h2>{greeting}</h2>.

Interview corner

  • What is JSX? A syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup in JavaScript; it compiles to React.createElement calls (or the modern JSX runtime).
  • Why className? class is a reserved word in JavaScript.
  • What is a fragment? <>…</> groups children without adding a DOM node.
  • Why must components start with a capital letter? So JSX can tell components from HTML elements.

Summary

  • npm create vite@latest creates a React project; npm run dev runs it.
  • main.jsx renders <App /> into #root.
  • JSX: expressions in {}, className, closed tags, camelCase, one root (or a fragment).

Next: components and props.

items.title: React Components and Props
items.excerpt: Pass data into components with props, destructure them with defaults, use the children prop for layouts, pass functions as props to talk to parents, and split a page into reusable components.
items.content:
Components become powerful when you can customise them. Props (properties) are the inputs to a component, like arguments to a function.

Passing and reading props

// src/CourseCard.jsx
export default function CourseCard({ title, level, price, lessons = 0, isNew = false }) {
  return (
    <article className="course-card">
      <h3>{title} {isNew && <span className="badge">New</span>}</h3>
      <p>{level} · {lessons} lessons</p>
      <strong>{price === 0 ? 'Free' : `₹${price}`}</strong>
    </article>
  );
}
// src/App.jsx
import CourseCard from './CourseCard.jsx';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <div className="grid">
      <CourseCard title="Java Basics" level="Beginner" price={499} lessons={16} />
      <CourseCard title="React" level="Beginner" price={0} lessons={12} isNew />
      <CourseCard title="Spring Boot" level="Intermediate" price={799} />
    </div>
  );
}
  • Strings can be passed as title="Java"; anything else needs braces: price={499}, tags={['java', 'oop']}, user={{ name: 'Asha' }}.
  • A prop with no value (isNew) means true.
  • Destructuring in the parameter list ({ title, level }) is the common style; defaults (lessons = 0) handle missing props.

Props are read-only

A component must never change its props. They belong to the parent. If something needs to change over time, it's state (next lesson).

function Bad({ price }) {
  price = price * 0.9;   // ❌ don't modify props
}

Think of a component as a pure function: same props → same output. This makes React apps predictable.

The children prop

Whatever you put between a component's tags arrives as children. Perfect for layout and wrapper components:

// src/Card.jsx
export default function Card({ title, children }) {
  return (
    <div className="card">
      <h2 className="card-title">{title}</h2>
      <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
    </div>
  );
}
// src/Profile.jsx
import Card from './Card.jsx';

export default function Profile() {
  return (
    <Card title="Your progress">
      <p>Java: 60% complete</p>
      <button>Continue learning</button>
    </Card>
  );
}

Passing functions: talking to the parent

Data flows down; to send something up, the parent passes a function:

// src/EnrollButton.jsx
export default function EnrollButton({ course, onEnroll }) {
  return <button onClick={() => onEnroll(course)}>Enroll in {course}</button>;
}
// src/Catalog.jsx
import EnrollButton from './EnrollButton.jsx';

export default function Catalog({ onMessage }) {
  function handleEnroll(course) {
    onMessage(`Enrolled in ${course}!`);
  }
  return (
    <div>
      <EnrollButton course="Java" onEnroll={handleEnroll} />
      <EnrollButton course="React" onEnroll={handleEnroll} />
    </div>
  );
}

Name callback props onSomething (onEnroll, onClose, onChange), and handler functions handleSomething.

Splitting a page into components

When should you create a new component?

  • A piece is repeated (cards, list items, buttons).
  • A piece has its own job (search box, navbar, modal).
  • A file is getting too long (more than ~150 lines is a hint).

One component per file, named like the component (CourseCard.jsx).

Passing many props: spread

const course = { title: 'SQL', level: 'Beginner', price: 299, lessons: 15 };
<CourseCard {...course} />          // same as title={course.title} level={…} …

Handy, but explicit props are easier to read. Use spread sparingly.

If you pass a prop through three or four components that don't use it themselves, just to reach a deep child ("prop drilling"), consider composition with children, or React Context (lesson 9).

Exercise

  1. Create a UserBadge component with name, role and avatarUrl props, and a default avatar when none is given.
  2. Create a Modal component that shows title, children and a close button that calls onClose.
  3. Build a ProductCard that shows a strike-through original price when a discountPercent prop is given.
  4. Render three CourseCards from an array (preview of lesson 6): courses.map(c => <CourseCard key={c.title} {...c} />).
Hint for 3

const finalPrice = discountPercent ? Math.round(price * (100 - discountPercent) / 100) : price; and show <s>₹{price}</s> only when discountPercent is set.

Interview corner

  • What are props? Read-only inputs passed from a parent to a child component.
  • Props vs state? Props come from the parent and can't be changed by the child; state is owned and updated by the component itself.
  • What is the children prop? The content nested between a component's opening and closing tags.
  • How does a child send data to its parent? By calling a function the parent passed down as a prop.

Summary

  • Props customise components; destructure them with defaults.
  • Never mutate props; components should be pure.
  • children enables wrapper/layout components; callback props send data up.

Next: state, the memory of a component.

items.title: React State with useState
items.excerpt: Give components memory with useState, see why setCount(count + 1) twice adds only 1 in an animation, use updater functions, and update objects and arrays immutably.
items.content:
Props come from outside. State is a component's own memory: data that changes while the user interacts (a counter, an input's text, whether a menu is open, items in a cart). When state changes, React re-renders the component with the new value.

useState

// src/Counter.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);      // [current value, setter], initial value 0

  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>+1</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(0)}>Reset</button>
    </div>
  );
}
  • useState(0) returns the current value and a function to change it.
  • Calling setCount(...) schedules a re-render; on the next render, count has the new value.
  • Each <Counter /> on the page has its own independent count.

Why not a normal variable? let count = 0; count++ changes the variable, but React doesn't know it should re-render, and the next render starts again at 0.

The surprise: state is a snapshot

Inside one render, count is a constant. Setting it doesn't change it immediately. Watch what happens when you call the setter twice:

// src/AddTwo.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function AddTwo() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const [score, setScore] = useState(0);

  function addTwoBroken() {
    setCount(count + 1);       // count is 0 in this render → "set to 1"
    setCount(count + 1);       // still 0 → "set to 1" again
  }

  function addTwoCorrect() {
    setScore(s => s + 1);      // updater function: gets the latest value
    setScore(s => s + 1);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={addTwoBroken}>count: {count}</button>
      <button onClick={addTwoCorrect}>score: {score}</button>
    </div>
  );
}

After one click each: count: 1, score: 2.

Rule: when the new state depends on the old state, pass a function: setX(prev => prev + 1).

React also batches updates: several setX calls in one event handler cause just one re-render.

State with objects: copy, don't mutate

// src/ProfileForm.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function ProfileForm() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: 'Asha', city: 'Pune', xp: 120 });

  function moveTo(city) {
    // ❌ user.city = city;  setUser(user);   → same object, React may skip the re-render
    setUser({ ...user, city });              // ✅ a NEW object with the change
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <p>{user.name} lives in {user.city} ({user.xp} XP)</p>
      <button onClick={() => moveTo('Bengaluru')}>Move to Bengaluru</button>
      <button onClick={() => setUser(u => ({ ...u, xp: u.xp + 10 }))}>+10 XP</button>
    </div>
  );
}

React decides whether to re-render by checking if the state value is a different object (Object.is). Mutating the same object keeps the same reference, so the UI can go stale. Always create new objects and arrays.

State with arrays

// src/TodoList.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

export default function TodoList() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState([{ id: 1, text: 'Learn JSX', done: true }]);
  const [text, setText] = useState('');

  function add() {
    if (!text.trim()) return;
    setTodos(prev => [...prev, { id: Date.now(), text: text.trim(), done: false }]);   // add
    setText('');
  }
  const toggle = id => setTodos(prev => prev.map(t => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)));   // update
  const remove = id => setTodos(prev => prev.filter(t => t.id !== id));                              // remove

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} placeholder="New task" />
      <button onClick={add}>Add</button>
      <ul>
        {todos.map(t => (
          <li key={t.id}>
            <label>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => toggle(t.id)} />
              {t.done ? <s>{t.text}</s> : t.text}
            </label>
            <button onClick={() => remove(t.id)} aria-label={`Remove ${t.text}`}>×</button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <p>{todos.filter(t => !t.done).length} left</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Where should state live?

  • Keep state in the lowest common parent of the components that need it ("lifting state up").
  • Don't store what you can calculate: if you have todos, compute remaining during render instead of storing it in separate state.

Hooks rules: call useState (and every hook) at the top level of your component, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions. React identifies each piece of state by the order of hook calls.

Exercise

  1. Build a like button that toggles between 🤍 and ❤️ and counts likes.
  2. Make a "step counter" with +1, +5 and reset buttons, using updater functions.
  3. Build a shopping cart with add, increase/decrease quantity and remove, showing the total price.
  4. What does this show after one click? setN(n + 5); setN(m => m * 2); with n = 1.
Hint for 4

The first call queues "set to 6", the second queues a function that receives 6 and returns 12. Result: 12.

Interview corner

  • What is state? Data owned by a component that changes over time and triggers re-renders when updated.
  • Why use an updater function? State is a snapshot per render; updater functions receive the latest pending value, so consecutive updates don't get lost.
  • Why must state be immutable? React compares references to detect changes; mutation keeps the same reference.
  • What is batching? Grouping multiple state updates from one event into a single re-render.

Summary

  • const [x, setX] = useState(initial); setting state schedules a re-render.
  • State is a snapshot: use setX(prev => …) when the new value depends on the old.
  • Never mutate objects/arrays in state; create new ones with spread, map, filter.

Next: events and forms.

items.title: React Events and Forms
items.excerpt: Handle clicks, typing and submits in React, build controlled inputs (text, select, checkbox, radio), validate a sign-up form, prevent default submission and keep one state object for many fields.
items.content:
Users interact through events: clicking, typing, submitting. React handles events with props like onClick and onChange, and forms with controlled inputs, where React state is the single source of truth.

Handling events

function Demo() {
  function handleClick(event) {
    console.log('clicked', event.target);
  }
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>                    {/* pass the function */}
      <button onClick={() => alert('Hi!')}>Say hi</button>              {/* inline arrow */}
      <input onKeyDown={e => e.key === 'Enter' && console.log('search')} />
    </>
  );
}
  • Pass a function, don't call it: onClick={handleClick} ✅, onClick={handleClick()} ❌ (runs during render).
  • To pass arguments, wrap it: onClick={() => remove(id)}.
  • Events are camelCase: onClick, onChange, onSubmit, onMouseEnter, onFocus, onBlur, onKeyDown.
  • event.preventDefault() and event.stopPropagation() work as in the DOM.

Controlled inputs

A controlled input's value comes from state, and every keystroke updates the state:

const [name, setName] = useState('');
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />

Now name is always in sync with what's on screen, so you can validate, transform (e.target.value.toUpperCase()) or reset (setName('')) easily.

A complete sign-up form

// src/SignupForm.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';

const empty = { name: '', email: '', course: 'java', level: 'beginner', terms: false };

function validate(f) {
  const errors = {};
  if (f.name.trim().length < 2) errors.name = 'Enter your name';
  if (!/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(f.email)) errors.email = 'Enter a valid email';
  if (!f.terms) errors.terms = 'Please accept the terms';
  return errors;
}

export default function SignupForm({ onSignup }) {
  const [form, setForm] = useState(empty);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});
  const [submitted, setSubmitted] = useState(false);

  function handleChange(e) {
    const { name, value, type, checked } = e.target;
    setForm(f => ({ ...f, [name]: type === 'checkbox' ? checked : value }));   // one handler for all fields
  }

  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();                           // stop the browser reloading the page
    const found = validate(form);
    setErrors(found);
    if (Object.keys(found).length > 0) return;
    onSignup?.(form);
    setSubmitted(true);
    setForm(empty);
  }

  if (submitted) return <p role="status">Welcome aboard! Check your email.</p>;

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} noValidate>
      <label>
        Name
        <input name="name" value={form.name} onChange={handleChange} />
      </label>
      {errors.name && <p className="error">{errors.name}</p>}

      <label>
        Email
        <input name="email" type="email" value={form.email} onChange={handleChange} />
      </label>
      {errors.email && <p className="error">{errors.email}</p>}

      <label>
        Course
        <select name="course" value={form.course} onChange={handleChange}>
          <option value="java">Java</option>
          <option value="react">React</option>
          <option value="sql">SQL</option>
        </select>
      </label>

      <fieldset>
        <legend>Level</legend>
        {['beginner', 'intermediate'].map(l => (
          <label key={l}>
            <input type="radio" name="level" value={l} checked={form.level === l} onChange={handleChange} /> {l}
          </label>
        ))}
      </fieldset>

      <label>
        <input type="checkbox" name="terms" checked={form.terms} onChange={handleChange} /> I accept the terms
      </label>
      {errors.terms && <p className="error">{errors.terms}</p>}

      <button type="submit">Create free account</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Key techniques:

  • One state object for the whole form, and one handleChange using the input's name with a computed key [name].
  • Checkboxes use checked, not value.
  • e.preventDefault() in onSubmit stops the full-page reload.
  • Pressing Enter in a field submits the form automatically (because of <form onSubmit> + a submit button). That's better than onClick on the button.
  • Errors are shown next to the fields that caused them.

Uncontrolled inputs (and when to use them)

You can also read values directly from the DOM with FormData when you don't need live validation:

function QuickSearch({ onSearch }) {
  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(e.currentTarget);
    onSearch(data.get('q'));
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="q" defaultValue="java" />
      <button>Search</button>
    </form>
  );
}

defaultValue sets the initial value without making it controlled. For big forms, libraries like React Hook Form (with Zod for validation schemas) reduce boilerplate.

Client-side validation is for user experience. The server must validate again (as in the Spring Boot course): anyone can bypass your React form with a direct API call.

Common mistakes

  • onClick={handleClick()}: runs immediately on every render.
  • A controlled input with value but no onChange: it becomes read-only (React warns).
  • Switching an input between undefined and a string value ("uncontrolled to controlled" warning): initialise with ''.
  • Forgetting e.preventDefault() in submit handlers.

Exercise

  1. Build a login form (email + password) with a "show password" checkbox that toggles the input type.
  2. Add a character counter under a textarea: "42 / 200", turning red over 200.
  3. Validate that "password" and "confirm password" match before submitting.
  4. Add a "Reset" button that clears the form and the errors.
Hint for 1

<input type={show ? 'text' : 'password'} value={password} onChange={e => setPassword(e.target.value)} /> with a separate show state controlled by the checkbox.

Interview corner

  • Controlled vs uncontrolled components? Controlled inputs take their value from React state; uncontrolled inputs keep their own DOM state, read via refs or FormData.
  • Why call preventDefault on submit? To stop the browser's default full-page form submission.
  • How do you handle many inputs with one handler? Use each input's name and a computed property: setForm(f => ({ ...f, [name]: value })).
  • What is a synthetic event? React's cross-browser wrapper around native events.

Summary

  • Attach handlers with onClick, onChange, onSubmit; pass functions, don't call them.
  • Controlled inputs: value + onChange bound to state; checkboxes use checked.
  • Validate on submit, show errors per field, prevent the default submit.

Next: rendering lists and conditional content.

items.title: React Lists, Keys and Conditional Rendering
items.excerpt: Render arrays with map, understand why keys matter (and why the index is a bad key), filter and sort lists with derived values, and show content conditionally with &&, ternaries and early returns.
items.content:
Most screens are lists: courses, messages, products, search results. And most screens show different things depending on state: loading or loaded, logged in or not, empty or full.

Rendering a list with map

// src/CourseList.jsx
export default function CourseList({ courses }) {
  if (courses.length === 0) return <p>No courses match your filters.</p>;   // early return

  return (
    <ul>
      {courses.map(course => (
        <li key={course.id}>
          {course.title} {course.free ? <strong>(Free)</strong> : <span>₹{course.price}</span>}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

map turns each data item into a JSX element. React renders an array of elements in order.

Keys

Each item in a list needs a key that is unique among siblings and stable (the same item always gets the same key). React uses keys to match items between renders: which ones were added, removed or moved.

  • ✅ Use ids from your data: key={course.id}.
  • ⚠️ The array index (key={i}) only works for lists that never reorder, filter or insert. Otherwise React mixes up items: an input's typed text or a checkbox can "jump" to the wrong row.
  • ❌ Random keys (Math.random()) make React recreate every item on every render: slow, and inputs lose focus.

Filtering and sorting: derive, don't store

// src/Catalog.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import CourseList from './CourseList.jsx';

const COURSES = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Java Basics', level: 'beginner', price: 499, free: false },
  { id: 2, title: 'HTML', level: 'beginner', price: 0, free: true },
  { id: 3, title: 'Spring Boot', level: 'intermediate', price: 799, free: false },
  { id: 4, title: 'React', level: 'beginner', price: 599, free: false },
  { id: 5, title: 'Hibernate', level: 'advanced', price: 999, free: false },
];

export default function Catalog() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [level, setLevel] = useState('all');
  const [sort, setSort] = useState('title');

  // derived during render: no extra state, always consistent
  const visible = COURSES
    .filter(c => level === 'all' || c.level === level)
    .filter(c => c.title.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()))
    .toSorted((a, b) => (sort === 'price' ? a.price - b.price : a.title.localeCompare(b.title)));

  return (
    <div>
      <input placeholder="Search courses" value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <select aria-label="Level" value={level} onChange={e => setLevel(e.target.value)}>
        <option value="all">All levels</option>
        <option value="beginner">Beginner</option>
        <option value="intermediate">Intermediate</option>
        <option value="advanced">Advanced</option>
      </select>
      <select aria-label="Sort" value={sort} onChange={e => setSort(e.target.value)}>
        <option value="title">A to Z</option>
        <option value="price">Price: low to high</option>
      </select>
      <p>{visible.length} of {COURSES.length} courses</p>
      <CourseList courses={visible} />
    </div>
  );
}

The filtered list isn't state: it's computed from state (query, level, sort) on every render. Storing it separately would mean keeping two things in sync, which is how bugs start. (toSorted returns a sorted copy; sort would mutate the constant array.)

Conditional rendering patterns

// 1. if / early return: for whole-component alternatives
if (loading) return <Spinner />;

// 2. ternary: one thing OR another
{isLoggedIn ? <UserMenu /> : <LoginButton />}

// 3. &&: something OR nothing
{unread > 0 && <span className="badge">{unread}</span>}

// 4. a variable prepared before return, for complex cases
let banner = null;
if (plan === 'free') banner = <UpgradeBanner />;
else if (trialEndsSoon) banner = <TrialBanner />;

The && trap: {count && <Badge />} renders 0 when count is 0, because 0 is a value React displays. Use {count > 0 && <Badge />}.

Grouping lists

const byLevel = Object.groupBy(COURSES, c => c.level);    // { beginner: [...], intermediate: [...], ... }

{Object.entries(byLevel).map(([lvl, list]) => (
  <section key={lvl}>
    <h3>{lvl}</h3>
    <CourseList courses={list} />
  </section>
))}

Common mistakes

  • Missing keys (React warns in the console) or index keys on reorderable lists.
  • Putting the key on the wrong element: it belongs on the outermost element returned by map.
  • Sorting state arrays in place (.sort() mutates).
  • Storing filtered/derived data in its own state.

Exercise

  1. Show a "No results" message with a "Clear filters" button when the search finds nothing.
  2. Add a "Free only" checkbox filter.
  3. Group the catalog by level with a heading per group.
  4. Show a "Bestseller" badge only for courses with more than 1,000 students (add a students field).
Hint for 1

The button calls setQuery('') and setLevel('all'). Show it with {visible.length === 0 && …}.

Interview corner

  • Why does React need keys? To identify items across renders so it can preserve state and update the DOM efficiently.
  • Why not use the index as a key? When items are inserted, removed or reordered, indexes shift, so React associates state with the wrong items.
  • What is derived state? Values computed from existing props/state during render instead of being stored separately.
  • Ways to render conditionally? if/early return, ternary, &&, or JSX stored in variables.

Summary

  • Render arrays with map and give each item a stable, unique key (an id).
  • Compute filtered/sorted lists during render from state.
  • Use early returns, ternaries and && (with a boolean!) for conditional UI.

Next: useEffect and fetching data from an API.

items.title: React useEffect and Fetching Data
items.excerpt: Synchronise components with the outside world using useEffect, watch the dependency array and cleanup in an animation, fetch data with loading and error states, cancel stale requests, and know when you don't need an effect.
items.content:
Rendering should be pure: compute JSX from props and state, nothing else. But apps must talk to the outside world: fetch data, start timers, subscribe to events, update the page title. That's what effects are for.

useEffect basics

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function Clock() {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(new Date());

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setNow(new Date()), 1000);   // start something
    return () => clearInterval(id);                            // cleanup: stop it
  }, []);                                                      // [] = run after the first render only

  return <p>{now.toLocaleTimeString('en-IN')}</p>;
}
  • The effect runs after React has updated the screen.
  • The returned function is the cleanup: it runs before the effect runs again and when the component is removed (unmounted).
  • The dependency array says when to re-run the effect.

Dependencies, animated

Pick a dependency array and watch when the effect and its cleanup run as userId changes and the component unmounts:

Include every prop, state or function from the component that the effect uses. The ESLint rule react-hooks/exhaustive-deps (enabled in Vite's template) warns you when you forget one.

Fetching data properly

// src/CourseDetails.jsx
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export default function CourseDetails({ courseId }) {
  const [course, setCourse] = useState(null);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('loading');       // 'loading' | 'ok' | 'error'

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setStatus('loading');
    fetch(`/api/courses/${courseId}`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(res => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then(data => { setCourse(data); setStatus('ok'); })
      .catch(err => { if (err.name !== 'AbortError') setStatus('error'); });

    return () => controller.abort();                     // cancel if courseId changes or we unmount
  }, [courseId]);

  if (status === 'loading') return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (status === 'error') return <p role="alert">Could not load the course. Please try again.</p>;
  return (
    <article>
      <h2>{course.title}</h2>
      <p>{course.lessons} lessons · ₹{course.price}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

Every fetch needs three states: loading, error and success. Users on slow mobile networks will see all of them.

Why the AbortController? If the user quickly clicks course 1 then course 2, the response for course 1 might arrive after course 2's and overwrite it (a race condition). Aborting the old request on cleanup prevents stale data.

With async/await

The effect function itself can't be async, so define an async function inside:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  async function load() {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/courses?level=${level}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    if (!ignore) setCourses(data);
  }
  load();
  return () => { ignore = true; };                       // ignore late responses
}, [level]);

Calling your Spring Boot API

In development, configure Vite to proxy /api to Spring Boot so there are no CORS problems:

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  server: { proxy: { '/api': 'http://localhost:8080' } },
});

For authenticated requests, add the JWT from the Spring Boot security lesson:

fetch('/api/me', { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });

You might not need an effect

Effects are for synchronising with external systems. Common misuses:

In real projects, use a data-fetching library like TanStack Query (useQuery). It handles caching, loading/error states, retries, refetching on focus and race conditions for you. Learn the effect version first so you understand what it's doing.

StrictMode runs effects twice in development

In development, StrictMode mounts, unmounts and re-mounts components once to check that your cleanup works. If you see two requests in the Network tab, that's why. It doesn't happen in production. A correct cleanup (abort/ignore) makes it harmless.

Exercise

  1. Fetch posts from https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=5 and show their titles with loading and error states.
  2. Add a select to choose a user id (1-10) and fetch that user's posts; cancel stale requests.
  3. Update document.title to "(3) VitalStack" when there are 3 unread messages.
  4. Find an effect in your code that could be a calculation during render instead.
Hint for 3

useEffect(() => { document.title = unread > 0 ? \(${unread}) VitalStack\ : 'VitalStack'; }, [unread]);

Interview corner

  • What is useEffect for? Synchronising a component with external systems (network, timers, subscriptions, DOM APIs) after rendering.
  • What does the dependency array do? Controls when the effect re-runs: on changes to listed values; [] means only after mount.
  • What is the cleanup function? A function returned from the effect that undoes it before re-running and on unmount.
  • How do you avoid race conditions when fetching? Abort the previous request or ignore its result in cleanup.

Summary

  • Effects run after render; return a cleanup to undo them.
  • List every dependency; [] runs once.
  • Fetch with loading/error/success states and cancel stale requests.
  • Don't use effects for things you can compute during render or do in event handlers.

Next: how React renders and how to make it fast.

items.title: React Rendering and Performance - memo, useMemo, useCallback
items.excerpt: See exactly which components re-render when state changes, use React.memo to skip unchanged children, useMemo for expensive calculations, useCallback for stable functions, and measure with the Profiler.
items.content:
React is fast by default, but understanding when components re-render helps you avoid slow screens and fix them when they happen. This is a favourite interview topic.

What triggers a re-render?

A component re-renders when:

  1. Its state changes.
  2. Its parent re-renders (by default, all children re-render too, even if their props didn't change).
  3. A context it uses changes (next lesson).

Re-rendering means calling the component function again and diffing the result. It does not mean the DOM is rebuilt: React only touches what actually changed.

Watch it

Click Like and compare a plain CourseList with one wrapped in React.memo:

React.memo: skip a child when props are the same

// src/Dashboard.jsx
import { memo, useCallback, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

export const renders = { list: 0 };                   // for the demo: count renders

const CourseList = memo(function CourseList({ courses, onSelect }) {
  renders.list++;
  return (
    <ul>
      {courses.map(c => <li key={c.id} onClick={() => onSelect(c.id)}>{c.title}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
});

const ALL = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Java', price: 499 },
  { id: 2, title: 'React', price: 599 },
  { id: 3, title: 'SQL', price: 299 },
];

export default function Dashboard() {
  const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);
  const [maxPrice, setMaxPrice] = useState(1000);
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null);

  const affordable = useMemo(                         // same array object until maxPrice changes
    () => ALL.filter(c => c.price <= maxPrice),
    [maxPrice]
  );

  const handleSelect = useCallback(id => setSelected(id), []);   // same function every render

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setLikes(l => l + 1)}>👍 {likes}</button>
      <button onClick={() => setMaxPrice(500)}>Under ₹500</button>
      <p>Selected: {selected ?? 'none'}</p>
      <CourseList courses={affordable} onSelect={handleSelect} />
    </div>
  );
}

Clicking 👍 re-renders Dashboard, but CourseList is skipped: memo compares its props, and both are the same objects as last time. Clicking "Under ₹500" changes affordable, so the list re-renders.

Why useMemo and useCallback are needed here

Without them, memo wouldn't help:

const affordable = ALL.filter(c => c.price <= maxPrice);   // a NEW array every render
const handleSelect = id => setSelected(id);                // a NEW function every render

memo compares props with Object.is: a new array or function is "different" even with the same contents, so the child re-renders anyway.

Don't optimise everything

Memoisation has a cost: extra memory and comparisons on every render, and more complex code. Most components render in well under a millisecond. Optimise when:

  • You measured a slow interaction (React DevTools Profiler shows which components rendered and how long they took).
  • A component renders a big list or a heavy chart and its parent changes often.
  • A calculation is genuinely expensive (sorting/filtering thousands of items).

Often the best optimisation is structural: move state down into the component that needs it (so fewer components re-render), or pass expensive parts as children so they aren't re-created by the state owner. And for very long lists, use virtualisation (react-window, @tanstack/react-virtual) to render only visible rows.

Keys reset state

Changing a component's key makes React treat it as a brand-new component: state is reset.

<CommentBox key={postId} postId={postId} />    // typing a comment, then switching posts, clears the box

Other performance tools

  • Code splitting: const Admin = lazy(() => import('./Admin.jsx')) with <Suspense> loads heavy pages only when visited.
  • useTransition / useDeferredValue: keep typing responsive while a heavy list updates in the background.
  • Production builds: always measure with npm run build && npm run preview; development mode is much slower.
  • React Compiler (React 19 era): automatically memoises components and values at build time, reducing the need for manual memo/useMemo/useCallback.

Exercise

  1. Add console.log('render', name) to components in an app and click around. Which ones re-render?
  2. Wrap a list component in memo and confirm it stops re-rendering when an unrelated parent state changes.
  3. Break the memo by passing an inline arrow onSelect={id => setSelected(id)}. Then fix it with useCallback.
  4. Profile a page with React DevTools and find the slowest component.
Hint for 3

An inline arrow is a new function on each render, so memo's shallow comparison sees a changed prop. useCallback(id => setSelected(id), []) returns the same function every time.

Interview corner

  • When does a component re-render? When its state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it consumes changes.
  • What does React.memo do? Skips re-rendering if props are shallowly equal to the previous props.
  • useMemo vs useCallback? useMemo memoises a computed value; useCallback memoises a function (useCallback(fn, deps) ≈ useMemo(() => fn, deps)).
  • Is re-rendering the same as updating the DOM? No: React diffs and only commits actual changes to the DOM.

Summary

  • Re-renders come from state, parent renders and context.
  • memo skips unchanged children; useMemo/useCallback keep props stable so memo works.
  • Measure first with the Profiler; restructure state before adding memoisation.

Next: sharing state with Context and useReducer.

items.title: React Context and useReducer
items.excerpt: Share data like the logged-in user, theme or cart across many components without prop drilling using Context, and manage complex state transitions with useReducer - combined into a cart store.
items.content:
Some data is needed almost everywhere: the logged-in user, the theme, the language, the cart. Passing it through every component's props ("prop drilling") gets painful. Context lets any component read a value directly. And when state logic gets complex, useReducer keeps it organised.

Context in three steps

// src/ThemeContext.jsx
import { createContext, useContext, useState } from 'react';

const ThemeContext = createContext(null);                     // 1. create

export function ThemeProvider({ children }) {                  // 2. provide
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  const toggle = () => setTheme(t => (t === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'));
  return <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, toggle }}>{children}</ThemeContext.Provider>;
}

export function useTheme() {                                   // 3. consume (a custom hook)
  const ctx = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useTheme must be used inside <ThemeProvider>');
  return ctx;
}
// src/ThemeButton.jsx
import { useTheme } from './ThemeContext.jsx';

export default function ThemeButton() {
  const { theme, toggle } = useTheme();             // no props needed, however deep this is
  return <button onClick={toggle}>Theme: {theme}</button>;
}

Wrap the app once (in main.jsx or App.jsx):

<ThemeProvider>
  <App />
</ThemeProvider>

Every component that calls useTheme() re-renders when the value changes.

useReducer: state transitions in one place

When updates follow rules ("add to cart", "change quantity", "apply coupon", "clear"), scattering setState calls across handlers gets messy. A reducer is a pure function: (currentState, action) → newState.

// src/cartReducer.js
export const initialCart = { items: [], coupon: null };

export function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add': {
      const existing = state.items.find(i => i.id === action.item.id);
      const items = existing
        ? state.items.map(i => (i.id === action.item.id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } : i))
        : [...state.items, { ...action.item, qty: 1 }];
      return { ...state, items };
    }
    case 'setQty':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: state.items
          .map(i => (i.id === action.id ? { ...i, qty: action.qty } : i))
          .filter(i => i.qty > 0),
      };
    case 'coupon':
      return { ...state, coupon: action.code === 'LEARN20' ? { code: 'LEARN20', percent: 20 } : null };
    case 'clear':
      return initialCart;
    default:
      throw new Error('Unknown action: ' + action.type);
  }
}

export function cartTotal(state) {
  const subtotal = state.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);
  return state.coupon ? Math.round(subtotal * (100 - state.coupon.percent) / 100) : subtotal;
}

Reducers are plain functions: easy to read, and easy to unit test without rendering anything.

Context + reducer = a small store

// src/CartContext.jsx
import { createContext, useContext, useReducer } from 'react';
import { cartReducer, initialCart, cartTotal } from './cartReducer.js';

const CartContext = createContext(null);

export function CartProvider({ children }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, initialCart);
  const value = { items: state.items, coupon: state.coupon, total: cartTotal(state), dispatch };
  return <CartContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</CartContext.Provider>;
}

export function useCart() {
  const ctx = useContext(CartContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useCart must be used inside <CartProvider>');
  return ctx;
}
// src/Shop.jsx
import { CartProvider, useCart } from './CartContext.jsx';

const COURSES = [{ id: 1, title: 'Java', price: 500 }, { id: 2, title: 'React', price: 600 }];

function AddButtons() {
  const { dispatch } = useCart();
  return COURSES.map(c => (
    <button key={c.id} onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'add', item: c })}>Add {c.title}</button>
  ));
}

function CartSummary() {
  const { items, total, coupon, dispatch } = useCart();
  return (
    <aside>
      <p>{items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0)} items · Total ₹{total}{coupon && ` (${coupon.code} applied)`}</p>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'coupon', code: 'LEARN20' })}>Apply LEARN20</button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'clear' })}>Clear</button>
    </aside>
  );
}

export default function Shop() {
  return (
    <CartProvider>
      <AddButtons />
      <CartSummary />
    </CartProvider>
  );
}

Add Java twice and React once: 3 items · Total ₹1600. Apply LEARN20: Total ₹1280 (LEARN20 applied).

useState or useReducer?

When not to use Context

  • For data only one or two levels down: just pass props.
  • For frequently changing values used by many components (e.g. mouse position): every consumer re-renders on each change. Split contexts (separate state and dispatch), or use a state library.
  • For server data (courses from an API): use TanStack Query, which caches per query.

For large apps, teams often use Zustand or Redux Toolkit for global client state. Redux uses exactly the reducer + actions idea you just learned, so this lesson is your foundation for both.

Exercise

  1. Create an AuthContext with user, login(name) and logout(), and show "Hi, Asha" in a header far down the tree.
  2. Add remove and increment actions to the cart reducer.
  3. Write unit tests (plain function calls) for cartReducer.
  4. Persist the cart in localStorage (hint: next lesson's custom hook, or an effect in the provider).
Hint for 3

const s1 = cartReducer(initialCart, { type: 'add', item: { id: 1, price: 500 } }); expect(s1.items[0].qty).toBe(1); No React needed.

Interview corner

  • What problem does Context solve? Prop drilling: passing data through many layers that don't use it.
  • Downside of Context? All consumers re-render when the value changes; it's not a full state management solution for frequently-changing data.
  • What is a reducer? A pure function computing the next state from the current state and an action.
  • useReducer vs Redux? Same pattern; Redux adds a global store, middleware and devtools.

Summary

  • createContext + a Provider + useContext (wrapped in a custom hook) share values without prop drilling.
  • useReducer centralises state transitions in a pure, testable function.
  • Together they make a simple app-wide store.

Next: refs and custom hooks.

items.title: React useRef and Custom Hooks
items.excerpt: Use useRef to focus inputs and keep values between renders without re-rendering, then extract reusable logic into custom hooks like useLocalStorage, useDebounce and useFetch.
items.content:
Two tools that make React code cleaner: refs for things outside React's render cycle, and custom hooks for sharing logic between components.

useRef for DOM elements

// src/SearchBox.jsx
import { useRef } from 'react';

export default function SearchBox() {
  const inputRef = useRef(null);
  return (
    <div>
      <input ref={inputRef} placeholder="Search" />
      <button onClick={() => inputRef.current.focus()}>Focus search</button>
    </div>
  );
}

React sets inputRef.current to the DOM element. Use this for focusing, scrolling (el.scrollIntoView()), measuring sizes, playing videos, or integrating non-React libraries (charts, maps).

useRef for values that shouldn't trigger renders

A ref is a box { current: … } that survives re-renders and doesn't cause one when changed:

// src/Stopwatch.jsx
import { useRef, useState } from 'react';

export default function Stopwatch() {
  const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0);
  const intervalRef = useRef(null);                 // the timer id: not shown on screen

  function start() {
    if (intervalRef.current) return;                // already running
    intervalRef.current = setInterval(() => setSeconds(s => s + 1), 1000);
  }
  function stop() {
    clearInterval(intervalRef.current);
    intervalRef.current = null;
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <p>{seconds}s</p>
      <button onClick={start}>Start</button>
      <button onClick={stop}>Stop</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Don't read or write ref.current during rendering (except initialisation): refs are for event handlers and effects.

Custom hooks: reusable logic

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with **use and that calls other hooks. It lets components share stateful logic** (not state itself: each component gets its own copy).

useLocalStorage

// src/hooks/useLocalStorage.js
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useLocalStorage(key, initialValue) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState(() => {          // lazy initialiser: runs once
    try {
      const saved = localStorage.getItem(key);
      return saved !== null ? JSON.parse(saved) : initialValue;
    } catch {
      return initialValue;
    }
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    try { localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); } catch { /* storage full or blocked */ }
  }, [key, value]);

  return [value, setValue];
}

useDebounce

Wait until the user stops typing before searching:

// src/hooks/useDebounce.js
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useDebounce(value, delay = 400) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);                     // typing again cancels the previous timer
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}

useFetch

The fetch logic from lesson 7, reusable:

// src/hooks/useFetch.js
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useFetch(url) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ data: null, error: null, loading: true });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!url) return;
    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState(s => ({ ...s, loading: true, error: null }));
    fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); return r.json(); })
      .then(data => setState({ data, error: null, loading: false }))
      .catch(error => { if (error.name !== 'AbortError') setState({ data: null, error, loading: false }); });
    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [url]);

  return state;
}

Using them together

// src/CourseSearch.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { useDebounce } from './hooks/useDebounce.js';
import { useFetch } from './hooks/useFetch.js';
import { useLocalStorage } from './hooks/useLocalStorage.js';

export default function CourseSearch() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useLocalStorage('last-search', '');
  const debounced = useDebounce(query, 400);
  const { data, loading, error } = useFetch(debounced ? `/api/courses?q=${encodeURIComponent(debounced)}` : null);

  return (
    <div>
      <input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} placeholder="Search courses" />
      {loading && debounced && <p>Searching…</p>}
      {error && <p role="alert">Search failed</p>}
      <ul>{data?.map(c => <li key={c.id}>{c.title}</li>)}</ul>
    </div>
  );
}

The component reads like a description of what it does; the "how" lives in hooks you can reuse and test separately.

Popular ready-made hook collections: usehooks-ts, ahooks, react-use. Writing a few yourself first is the best way to understand hooks deeply, and a common interview task ("write useDebounce").

Rules of hooks (again)

  1. Only call hooks at the top level (not in loops, conditions or nested functions).
  2. Only call hooks from React components or other custom hooks.
  3. Custom hook names must start with use, so the linter can check the rules.

Exercise

  1. Write useToggle(initial) returning [on, toggle].
  2. Write useOnlineStatus() using the online/offline window events.
  3. Write useWindowWidth() and show "mobile" below 600px.
  4. Write usePrevious(value) with a ref, and show "price went up/down".
Hint for 2

const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine); useEffect(() => { const on = () => setOnline(true), off = () => setOnline(false); window.addEventListener('online', on); window.addEventListener('offline', off); return () => { window.removeEventListener('online', on); window.removeEventListener('offline', off); }; }, []);

Interview corner

  • What is useRef used for? Accessing DOM nodes and storing mutable values that persist across renders without causing re-renders.
  • useRef vs useState? Updating a ref doesn't re-render; updating state does.
  • What is a custom hook? A function starting with use that composes hooks to share stateful logic between components.
  • Do two components using the same custom hook share state? No: each call has its own state.

Summary

  • useRef holds DOM elements and render-independent values.
  • Custom hooks extract reusable logic: useLocalStorage, useDebounce, useFetch.
  • Follow the rules of hooks; name custom hooks useSomething.

Next: pages and navigation with React Router.

items.title: React Router - Pages and Navigation
items.excerpt: Add multiple pages to a React single-page app with React Router - routes, links, nested layouts, URL parameters, query strings, navigation in code, 404 pages and protected routes.
items.content:
A React app is a single page: one index.html. But users expect URLs (/courses, /courses/42, /profile), working back buttons and shareable links. React Router maps URLs to components without reloading the page.

npm install react-router-dom

Basic routes

// src/App.jsx
import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link, NavLink, Outlet } from 'react-router-dom';
import CoursesPage from './CoursesPage.jsx';
import CoursePage from './CoursePage.jsx';
import ProfilePage from './ProfilePage.jsx';
import RequireAuth from './RequireAuth.jsx';

function Layout() {
  return (
    <>
      <nav>
        <Link to="/">VitalStack</Link>
        <NavLink to="/courses">Courses</NavLink>              {/* gets class "active" on its page */}
        <NavLink to="/profile">Profile</NavLink>
      </nav>
      <main><Outlet /></main>                                {/* the child route renders here */}
    </>
  );
}

const Home = () => <h1>Learn to code for free</h1>;
const NotFound = () => <h1>404: Page not found</h1>;

export function AppRoutes() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route element={<Layout />}>                           {/* layout route: shared nav */}
        <Route index element={<Home />} />                   {/* "/" */}
        <Route path="courses" element={<CoursesPage />} />
        <Route path="courses/:slug" element={<CoursePage />} />
        <Route path="profile" element={<RequireAuth><ProfilePage /></RequireAuth>} />
        <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />            {/* anything else */}
      </Route>
    </Routes>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <AppRoutes />
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}
  • <Link to="/courses"> changes the URL without reloading (unlike <a href>).
  • <NavLink> adds an active class for styling the current page.
  • A layout route (no path, with <Outlet />) wraps pages with shared UI.

URL parameters and query strings

// src/CoursePage.jsx
import { useParams, useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';

const COURSES = { java: 'Java Basics', react: 'React' };

export default function CoursePage() {
  const { slug } = useParams();                     // from "courses/:slug"
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const title = COURSES[slug];

  if (!title) return <p>Course not found.</p>;
  return (
    <article>
      <h1>{title}</h1>
      <button onClick={() => navigate('/courses')}>Back to all courses</button>
    </article>
  );
}
// src/CoursesPage.jsx
import { Link, useSearchParams } from 'react-router-dom';

const LIST = [
  { slug: 'java', title: 'Java Basics', level: 'beginner' },
  { slug: 'react', title: 'React', level: 'beginner' },
  { slug: 'spring', title: 'Spring Boot', level: 'intermediate' },
];

export default function CoursesPage() {
  const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();    // ?level=beginner
  const level = params.get('level') ?? 'all';
  const shown = LIST.filter(c => level === 'all' || c.level === level);

  return (
    <div>
      <select aria-label="Level" value={level}
              onChange={e => setParams(e.target.value === 'all' ? {} : { level: e.target.value })}>
        <option value="all">All</option>
        <option value="beginner">Beginner</option>
        <option value="intermediate">Intermediate</option>
      </select>
      <ul>{shown.map(c => <li key={c.slug}><Link to={`/courses/${c.slug}`}>{c.title}</Link></li>)}</ul>
    </div>
  );
}

Storing filters in the URL (instead of only in state) means users can bookmark and share filtered views, and the back button works as expected.

Protected routes

// src/RequireAuth.jsx
import { Navigate, useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

export function isLoggedIn() {
  return Boolean(localStorage.getItem('token'));
}

export default function RequireAuth({ children }) {
  const location = useLocation();
  if (!isLoggedIn()) {
    return <Navigate to="/login" replace state={{ from: location.pathname }} />;   // come back after login
  }
  return children;
}
// src/ProfilePage.jsx
export default function ProfilePage() {
  return <h1>Your profile</h1>;
}

After a successful login, navigate(location.state?.from ?? '/', { replace: true }) sends the user back where they wanted to go.

Hiding a page in React is not security. A protected route only improves the user experience. The real protection is your API (Spring Security returning 401/403). Never trust the client.

Deploying a router app

With BrowserRouter, refreshing /courses/java asks the server for that path. Static hosts must send index.html for unknown paths:

  • Netlify: a _redirects file with /* /index.html 200.
  • Vercel / Cloudflare Pages: SPA fallback setting or rewrites config.
  • Apache / shared hosting: an .htaccess rewrite to index.html.

Data routers (going further)

React Router 6.4+ also offers createBrowserRouter with loaders (fetch data before a page renders), actions (handle form submissions) and error boundaries per route. Frameworks like Remix/React Router 7 build on this.

Exercise

  1. Add an About page and a link in the nav.
  2. Add /courses/:slug/lessons/:lessonId as a nested route with an <Outlet /> inside CoursePage.
  3. Build a login page that saves a fake token and redirects back to the page the user came from.
  4. Add a search box on the courses page that stores the query in ?q=.
Hint for 4

setParams(p => { const n = new URLSearchParams(p); value ? n.set('q', value) : n.delete('q'); return n; }) keeps other parameters like level.

Interview corner

  • What is client-side routing? Changing the URL and rendering matching components in JavaScript without full page reloads.
  • Link vs a tag? Link navigates through the router (no reload); a full <a href> reloads the whole app.
  • How do you read route parameters? useParams(); query strings with useSearchParams().
  • How do you protect routes? A wrapper component that redirects with <Navigate> when unauthenticated (backed by server-side checks).

Summary

  • BrowserRouter + Routes + Route map URLs to components; Link/NavLink navigate.
  • Layout routes with <Outlet /> share UI; :params and search params make URLs meaningful.
  • Redirect unauthenticated users with <Navigate>; configure SPA fallback when deploying.

Next: build a complete project.
