items.title: React Project: Course Hub Front End
items.excerpt: Build a complete React front end for the Spring Boot enrollment API - an API client, pages with React Router, enrollment with optimistic UI and error messages, progress bars, a leaderboard and deployment.
items.content:
Time to connect everything. You'll build Course Hub, a React front end for the Course Enrollment API from the Spring Boot course: browse courses, enroll, track progress and see the leaderboard.

Features

  • /: all courses with an Enroll button.
  • /my-courses: your enrollments with progress bars and a "+1 lesson" button.
  • /leaderboard: top learners.
  • Clear loading and error states; friendly messages for API errors (e.g. "max 3 active courses").

Project setup

npm create vite@latest course-hub -- --template react
cd course-hub
npm install react-router-dom

Point Vite's dev proxy at the Spring Boot app (lesson 7) so /api calls reach http://localhost:8080.

1. A small API client

Keep all HTTP details in one module. Components call functions, not URLs:

// src/api.js
async function request(path, options = {}) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api${path}`, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    ...options,
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    let message = `Request failed (${res.status})`;
    try {
      const problem = await res.json();              // Spring's ProblemDetail
      if (problem.detail) message = problem.detail;
    } catch { /* not JSON */ }
    throw new Error(message);
  }
  return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json();
}

export const api = {
  courses: () => request('/courses'),
  enrollments: studentId => request(`/students/${studentId}/enrollments`),
  enroll: (studentId, courseId) =>
    request('/enrollments', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ studentId, courseId }) }),
  progress: (enrollmentId, lessons) =>
    request(`/enrollments/${enrollmentId}/progress`, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ lessons }) }),
  leaderboard: () => request('/leaderboard?top=10'),
};

The server's ProblemDetail detail ("Finish a course first: max 3 active courses") becomes the error message the user sees.

2. A reusable data hook

// src/useApi.js
import { useCallback, useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useApi(loader, deps) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ data: null, error: null, loading: true });

  const reload = useCallback(() => {
    setState(s => ({ ...s, loading: true }));
    return loader()
      .then(data => setState({ data, error: null, loading: false }))
      .catch(error => setState({ data: null, error, loading: false }));
  }, deps);   // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

  useEffect(() => { reload(); }, [reload]);
  return { ...state, reload };
}

3. Pages

// src/CoursesPage.jsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { api } from './api.js';
import { useApi } from './useApi.js';

export default function CoursesPage({ studentId }) {
  const { data: courses, error, loading } = useApi(() => api.courses(), []);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState(null);
  const [busy, setBusy] = useState(null);

  async function enroll(course) {
    setBusy(course.id);
    setMessage(null);
    try {
      await api.enroll(studentId, course.id);
      setMessage({ type: 'ok', text: `Enrolled in ${course.title}. Happy learning!` });
    } catch (e) {
      setMessage({ type: 'error', text: e.message });
    } finally {
      setBusy(null);
    }
  }

  if (loading) return <p>Loading courses…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>;

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Courses</h1>
      {message && <p role={message.type === 'error' ? 'alert' : 'status'} className={message.type}>{message.text}</p>}
      <ul className="grid">
        {courses.map(c => (
          <li key={c.id} className="card">
            <h3>{c.title}</h3>
            <p>{c.totalLessons} lessons</p>
            <button disabled={busy === c.id} onClick={() => enroll(c)}>
              {busy === c.id ? 'Enrolling…' : 'Enroll'}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </section>
  );
}
// src/MyCoursesPage.jsx
import { api } from './api.js';
import { useApi } from './useApi.js';

function ProgressBar({ percent }) {
  return (
    <div className="bar" role="progressbar" aria-valuenow={percent} aria-valuemin={0} aria-valuemax={100}>
      <div style={{ width: `${percent}%` }} />
    </div>
  );
}

export default function MyCoursesPage({ studentId }) {
  const { data, error, loading, reload } = useApi(() => api.enrollments(studentId), [studentId]);

  async function completeLesson(id) {
    await api.progress(id, 1);
    reload();                                           // refresh from the server: it owns the rules
  }

  if (loading && !data) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>;
  if (data.length === 0) return <p>You haven't enrolled in any course yet.</p>;

  return (
    <section>
      <h1>My courses</h1>
      {data.map(e => (
        <article key={e.id} className="card">
          <h3>{e.course} {e.finished && '🎉'}</h3>
          <ProgressBar percent={e.percent} />
          <p>{e.completed} lessons · {e.percent}%</p>
          {!e.finished && <button onClick={() => completeLesson(e.id)}>+1 lesson</button>}
        </article>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
// src/LeaderboardPage.jsx
import { api } from './api.js';
import { useApi } from './useApi.js';

export default function LeaderboardPage() {
  const { data, error, loading } = useApi(() => api.leaderboard(), []);
  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>;
  return (
    <ol className="leaderboard">
      {data.map((row, i) => (
        <li key={row.student}>
          {['🥇', '🥈', '🥉'][i] ?? `#${i + 1}`} {row.student}: {row.lessonsCompleted} lessons
        </li>
      ))}
    </ol>
  );
}

4. The app shell

// src/App.jsx
import { BrowserRouter, NavLink, Route, Routes } from 'react-router-dom';
import CoursesPage from './CoursesPage.jsx';
import MyCoursesPage from './MyCoursesPage.jsx';
import LeaderboardPage from './LeaderboardPage.jsx';

export function Shell({ studentId }) {
  return (
    <>
      <nav>
        <NavLink to="/">Courses</NavLink>
        <NavLink to="/my-courses">My courses</NavLink>
        <NavLink to="/leaderboard">Leaderboard</NavLink>
      </nav>
      <main>
        <Routes>
          <Route path="/" element={<CoursesPage studentId={studentId} />} />
          <Route path="/my-courses" element={<MyCoursesPage studentId={studentId} />} />
          <Route path="/leaderboard" element={<LeaderboardPage />} />
        </Routes>
      </main>
    </>
  );
}

export default function App() {
  const studentId = 1;                // after adding login: read it from your auth context / JWT
  return (
    <BrowserRouter>
      <Shell studentId={studentId} />
    </BrowserRouter>
  );
}

5. Run it end to end

  1. Start the Spring Boot API (./mvnw spring-boot:run) and register a student with id 1 (POST /api/students).
  2. Start React (npm run dev), open http://localhost:5173.
  3. Enroll in four courses: the fourth shows "Finish a course first: max 3 active courses", straight from the server's business rule.
  4. Complete lessons on My courses and watch the progress bars and the leaderboard update.

6. Deploy

npm run build          # dist/ contains static files
  • Host dist/ on Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages (with SPA fallback), or serve it from Spring Boot by copying it into src/main/resources/static.
  • In production, call the API by its full URL (an env variable like VITE_API_URL read with import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL), and allow that origin in Spring's CORS configuration.

Ideas to extend it

  1. Login with JWT (Spring Boot security lesson): store the token in an AuthContext, attach Authorization: Bearer … in api.js, and protect pages with RequireAuth.
  2. TanStack Query instead of useApi, with automatic refetching after mutations.
  3. Optimistic updates: show the new progress immediately and roll back on error.
  4. Tests with Vitest + Testing Library, mocking fetch.
  5. TypeScript: type the API responses (type Enrollment = { id: number; course: string; … }).
Hint for 1

In request, read the token from localStorage (or your context) and add ...(token && { Authorization: \Bearer ${token}\ }) to the headers.

A deployed full-stack project (Spring Boot API + React UI, with a README and a live link) is one of the strongest things you can put on a fresher CV. Recruiters can click it and see it working.

Summary

  • Centralise HTTP in an API module that turns ProblemDetail errors into messages.
  • A small useApi hook handles loading, errors and reloads.
  • Pages + React Router + the server's rules = a real full-stack app.

Congratulations on finishing the React course! Next, try the Angular course to compare the two most popular front-end frameworks.

items.title: Angular Introduction
items.excerpt: What Angular is, why banks, enterprises and Indian IT companies choose it, how it compares with React, and the building blocks you'll learn - components, templates, signals, services, routing, forms and RxJS.
items.content:
Angular is a complete front-end framework from Google for building large web applications. Where React gives you a UI library and lets you choose the rest, Angular ships everything in one box: components, routing, forms, HTTP, testing and a powerful CLI. That consistency is why enterprises, banks, insurance companies and big IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Capgemini) use it heavily.

What you build with Angular

  • Internet banking and trading dashboards
  • Admin panels and ERP front ends
  • Insurance, HR and healthcare portals
  • Google products (Google Cloud Console, Firebase console) and many Microsoft, Deutsche Bank and Forbes apps

The building blocks

           ┌──────────────── Angular application ────────────────┐
 Browser ──│ Router  ──▶  Components (template + class + styles)  │
           │                 │ data binding, @if/@for, pipes       │
           │                 ▼                                    │
           │              Services (business logic, state)        │
           │                 │ dependency injection               │
           │                 ▼                                    │
           │              HttpClient + RxJS ──▶ REST API (Spring Boot)
           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A first look

// src/app/hello.component.ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-hello',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <h1>Namaste, {{ name() }}!</h1>
    <button (click)="likes.set(likes() + 1)">👍 {{ likes() }}</button>
    @if (likes() >= 10) {
      <span class="badge">Popular!</span>
    }
  `,
})
export class HelloComponent {
  name = signal('Asha');
  likes = signal(0);
}

The template describes the UI; when likes changes, Angular updates the button and shows the badge automatically.

Angular vs React

Both are excellent. Angular shines in large teams and long-lived enterprise projects, where every project looking the same is a big advantage. Learning both makes you very employable.

Modern Angular (v17+)

Angular changed a lot recently. If you see old tutorials, know the difference:

Prerequisites

  • HTML and CSS
  • JavaScript (ES6+): classes, arrow functions, modules, promises
  • TypeScript basics: types, interfaces, classes. You'll pick up the rest as you go, and TypeScript also helps in React and Node.

Angular releases a major version every six months, but upgrades are smooth thanks to ng update. Learn the concepts in this course and you can follow any recent version.

Exercise

  1. Install Node.js 20+ if you haven't already (node -v).
  2. List three apps you use that look like "dashboards with lots of forms and tables": good Angular candidates.
  3. Revise TypeScript interfaces and classes.
Hint for 3

interface Course { id: number; title: string; price?: number } declares a shape; price? means optional. Classes can implements Course.

Interview corner

  • What is Angular? A TypeScript-based front-end framework by Google with components, DI, routing, forms, HTTP and tooling built in.
  • Angular vs AngularJS? AngularJS (1.x) was a JavaScript MVC framework; Angular (2+) is a complete rewrite in TypeScript with components.
  • What are standalone components? Components that declare their own dependencies without NgModules, the default since Angular 17.
  • What are signals? Reactive primitives holding values; Angular tracks where they're read and updates only what depends on them.

Summary

  • Angular is a complete, opinionated framework written in TypeScript.
  • Components, templates, signals, services with DI, router, forms and HttpClient are its core.
  • Modern Angular uses standalone components, @if/@for and signals.

Next: create a project with the Angular CLI.

items.title: Angular CLI, Project Setup and Structure
items.excerpt: Install the Angular CLI, create and run a project, understand main.ts, app.config.ts and the root component, and generate components and services with ng generate.
items.content:
The Angular CLI creates projects, generates code, runs a dev server, builds for production and runs tests. You'll use it every day.

Install and create a project

npm install -g @angular/cli
ng new course-app
#   Which stylesheet format? CSS
#   Enable SSR? No (for now)
cd course-app
ng serve -o          # opens http://localhost:4200

Edit a file and the browser reloads automatically.

Project structure

course-app/
├── angular.json              ← CLI configuration (build, serve, test)
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json             ← TypeScript settings (strict mode on)
└── src/
    ├── index.html            ← contains <app-root></app-root>
    ├── main.ts               ← bootstraps the app
    ├── styles.css            ← global styles
    └── app/
        ├── app.component.ts      ← root component (class)
        ├── app.component.html    ← its template
        ├── app.component.css     ← its styles (scoped to this component)
        ├── app.config.ts         ← app-wide providers (router, HttpClient…)
        └── app.routes.ts         ← routes

How the app starts

// src/main.ts
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { appConfig } from './app/app.config';
import { AppComponent } from './app/app.component';

bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig).catch(err => console.error(err));
// src/app/app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig, provideZoneChangeDetection } from '@angular/core';
import { provideRouter } from '@angular/router';
import { provideHttpClient } from '@angular/common/http';
import { routes } from './app.routes';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideZoneChangeDetection({ eventCoalescing: true }),
    provideRouter(routes),
    provideHttpClient(),          // add this when you start calling APIs
  ],
};
  1. index.html contains <app-root>.
  2. main.ts bootstraps AppComponent, whose selector is app-root, with the providers from app.config.ts.
  3. Angular renders the component's template inside <app-root>.

The root component

// src/app/app.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { RouterOutlet } from '@angular/router';
import { WelcomeComponent } from './welcome/welcome.component';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [RouterOutlet, WelcomeComponent],     // components used in the template
  templateUrl: './app.component.html',
  styleUrl: './app.component.css',
})
export class AppComponent {
  title = 'course-app';
}
<!-- src/app/app.component.html -->
<app-welcome />
<router-outlet />

Generating code

ng generate component welcome        # or: ng g c welcome
ng g service services/course          # or: ng g s services/course
ng g interface models/course
ng g pipe pipes/duration
ng g guard auth

ng g c welcome creates welcome/welcome.component.ts, .html, .css and a .spec.ts test file. To use it, add WelcomeComponent to the parent's imports array and put <app-welcome /> in the template.

// src/app/welcome/welcome.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-welcome',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <section class="welcome">
      <h1>Welcome to {{ site }}</h1>
      <p>{{ lessons }} lessons · about {{ lessons * 15 }} minutes</p>
    </section>
  `,
  styles: `.welcome { padding: 16px; border-radius: 12px; background: #e8f5ee; }`,
})
export class WelcomeComponent {
  site = 'VitalStack';
  lessons = 12;
}

Small components can use inline template and styles; bigger ones use separate templateUrl/styleUrl files.

Other CLI commands

Keep "strict": true in tsconfig.json (the default). Strict TypeScript and Angular's strict template checking catch typos and null errors in templates at build time, before users see them.

Common mistakes

  • Using a component in a template but forgetting to add it to imports → "'app-welcome' is not a known element".
  • Editing files in dist/ (they're regenerated on every build).
  • Mixing old NgModule tutorials with standalone components.

Exercise

  1. Create a project and run it.
  2. Generate a header component that shows the site name and a nav, and use it in AppComponent.
  3. Generate a footer component with the current year (new Date().getFullYear()).
  4. Run ng build and look at the files in dist/.
Hint for 3

In the class, year = new Date().getFullYear(); and in the template © {{ year }} VitalStack.

Interview corner

  • What does the Angular CLI do? Scaffolds projects and code, serves, builds, tests and upgrades Angular apps.
  • How does an Angular app bootstrap? main.ts calls bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig), rendering the root component into its selector in index.html.
  • What is app.config.ts for? App-wide providers such as the router, HttpClient and interceptors.
  • What files make up a component? A TypeScript class with @Component, a template, styles and usually a spec test.

Summary

  • ng new, ng serve, ng generate, ng build cover daily work.
  • main.ts bootstraps the root component with providers from app.config.ts.
  • Standalone components list what they use in imports.

Next: components and templates in depth.

items.title: Angular Components, Inputs and Outputs
items.excerpt: Build reusable Angular components, pass data in with input(), send events out with output(), project content with ng-content, and use lifecycle hooks like ngOnInit and ngOnDestroy.
items.content:
Like React components, Angular components are reusable building blocks. A parent passes data in through inputs and listens to events coming out through outputs.

A component with inputs

// src/app/course-card/course-card.component.ts
import { Component, computed, input, output } from '@angular/core';

export interface Course {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  level: 'Beginner' | 'Intermediate' | 'Advanced';
  price: number;
  lessons: number;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-card',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <article class="card">
      <h3>{{ course().title }} @if (isNew()) { <span class="badge">New</span> }</h3>
      <p>{{ course().level }} · {{ course().lessons }} lessons</p>
      <strong>{{ priceLabel() }}</strong>
      <button (click)="enroll.emit(course())">Enroll</button>
    </article>
  `,
})
export class CourseCardComponent {
  course = input.required<Course>();          // must be provided
  isNew = input(false);                       // optional, default false
  enroll = output<Course>();                  // an event the parent can listen to

  priceLabel = computed(() => (this.course().price === 0 ? 'Free' : `₹${this.course().price}`));
}
  • input.required<T>() and input(default) create signal inputs: read them by calling them, course().
  • output<T>() creates an event; call .emit(value) to send it.
  • computed() derives a value that updates when its inputs change.

Older code uses decorators, which work the same way and you'll see them everywhere:

@Input({ required: true }) course!: Course;
@Input() isNew = false;
@Output() enroll = new EventEmitter<Course>();

Using it from a parent

// src/app/catalog/catalog.component.ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { Course, CourseCardComponent } from '../course-card/course-card.component';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-catalog',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CourseCardComponent],
  template: `
    @for (c of courses; track c.id) {
      <app-course-card [course]="c" [isNew]="c.id === 3" (enroll)="onEnroll($event)" />
    }
    @if (message()) {
      <p role="status">{{ message() }}</p>
    }
  `,
})
export class CatalogComponent {
  courses: Course[] = [
    { id: 1, title: 'Java Basics', level: 'Beginner', price: 499, lessons: 16 },
    { id: 2, title: 'HTML', level: 'Beginner', price: 0, lessons: 10 },
    { id: 3, title: 'Angular', level: 'Intermediate', price: 699, lessons: 12 },
  ];
  message = signal('');

  onEnroll(course: Course) {
    this.message.set(`Enrolled in ${course.title}!`);
  }
}
  • [course]="c" binds an input (square brackets: data into the child).
  • (enroll)="onEnroll($event)" listens to an output (round brackets: events out of the child); $event is the emitted value.

Content projection with ng-content

Like React's children, <ng-content> places whatever the parent puts between the tags:

// src/app/panel/panel.component.ts
import { Component, input } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-panel',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <section class="panel">
      <header><h2>{{ title() }}</h2><ng-content select="[panel-actions]" /></header>
      <div class="body"><ng-content /></div>
    </section>
  `,
})
export class PanelComponent {
  title = input('');
}
<app-panel title="Your progress">
  <button panel-actions>Reset</button>     <!-- goes to the select="[panel-actions]" slot -->
  <p>Java: 60% complete</p>                 <!-- goes to the default slot -->
</app-panel>

Lifecycle hooks

export class ClockComponent implements OnInit, OnDestroy {
  now = signal(new Date());
  private timer?: ReturnType<typeof setInterval>;

  ngOnInit() { this.timer = setInterval(() => this.now.set(new Date()), 1000); }
  ngOnDestroy() { clearInterval(this.timer); }
}

With signal inputs, most "react to input changes" logic becomes computed() or effect() instead of ngOnChanges.

Component styles are scoped

Styles in a component's styles/styleUrl apply only to that component's template (Angular adds unique attributes behind the scenes). .card in CourseCardComponent won't leak into other components. Global styles go in src/styles.css.

Split components into presentational ("dumb") components that only use inputs/outputs (like CourseCard) and container ("smart") components that talk to services (like Catalog). Presentational components are easy to reuse and test.

Exercise

  1. Create a UserBadgeComponent with name (required) and role (default "Student") inputs.
  2. Add a remove output to CourseCardComponent and remove the course from the parent's list when it fires.
  3. Build a ModalComponent with a title input, projected content and a closed output.
  4. Add a ClockComponent and check (with console.log) that ngOnDestroy runs when it's hidden with @if.
Hint for 2

Make courses a signal in the parent: courses = signal<Course[]>([...]) and onRemove(c: Course) { this.courses.update(list => list.filter(x => x.id !== c.id)); }.

Interview corner

  • @Input vs @Output? Inputs pass data from parent to child; outputs emit events from child to parent.
  • What is content projection? Inserting parent-provided content into a child's template with <ng-content>.
  • constructor vs ngOnInit? Constructor for DI and simple setup; ngOnInit after inputs are initialised, for data loading.
  • What are signal inputs? input()/input.required() that expose inputs as read-only signals.

Summary

  • Inputs (input(), @Input) bring data in; outputs (output(), @Output) send events out.
  • <ng-content> projects parent content; component styles are scoped.
  • Lifecycle hooks: init in ngOnInit, clean up in ngOnDestroy.

Next: the four kinds of data binding, animated.

items.title: Angular Data Binding - Interpolation, Property, Event, Two-Way
items.excerpt: Watch the four kinds of Angular data binding in an animation, then use interpolation, property binding, event binding, two-way binding with ngModel and model(), class and style bindings, and template reference variables.
items.content:
Data binding connects your component class (data) with the template (what users see). Angular has four kinds, and their brackets tell you which way data flows.

The four bindings, animated

Pick a binding type and watch where the data moves:

Memory trick: [ ] brings data in to the element, ( ) sends events out, and [( )] is "banana in a box": both.

All four in one component

// src/app/binding-demo/binding-demo.component.ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { FormsModule } from '@angular/forms';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-binding-demo',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [FormsModule],                               // needed for ngModel
  template: `
    <h2>{{ title }}</h2>                                 <!-- interpolation -->
    <img [src]="logoUrl" [alt]="title + ' logo'" width="48" />   <!-- property binding -->
    <button (click)="like()" [disabled]="likes() >= 5">👍 {{ likes() }}</button>   <!-- event + property -->
    <input [(ngModel)]="name" placeholder="Your name" />  <!-- two-way -->
    <p>Hello {{ name || 'stranger' }}</p>
  `,
})
export class BindingDemoComponent {
  title = 'Java Basics';
  logoUrl = '/assets/java.svg';
  likes = signal(0);
  name = '';

  like() { this.likes.update(n => n + 1); }
}

Property binding vs attribute binding

Property binding sets DOM properties ([value], [disabled], [src], [hidden]). Some HTML attributes have no matching property (ARIA, colspan), so use attr.:

<td [attr.colspan]="span">…</td>
<button [attr.aria-label]="'Remove ' + course.title">×</button>

Class and style bindings

<li [class.done]="task.done" [class.urgent]="task.priority === 'high'">{{ task.title }}</li>
<div [class]="{ card: true, selected: isSelected, disabled: !enabled }"></div>
<div [style.width.%]="progress">{{ progress }}%</div>
<p [style.color]="balance < 0 ? 'crimson' : 'green'">₹{{ balance }}</p>

Event binding details

<input (input)="query = $any($event.target).value" />     <!-- $event is the DOM event -->
<input (keyup.enter)="search()" />                        <!-- key filters -->
<form (ngSubmit)="save()">…</form>                        <!-- forms module submit -->
<div (mouseenter)="hover = true" (mouseleave)="hover = false"></div>

Template reference variables

#name gives a template element a name you can use elsewhere in the template:

<input #search placeholder="Search courses" />
<button (click)="find(search.value); search.value = ''">Search</button>

Two-way binding on your own components: model()

// src/app/rating/rating.component.ts
import { Component, model } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-rating',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    @for (star of [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; track star) {
      <button type="button" (click)="value.set(star)" [attr.aria-label]="star + ' stars'">
        {{ star <= value() ? '★' : '☆' }}
      </button>
    }
  `,
})
export class RatingComponent {
  value = model(0);          // a two-way bindable signal
}
<app-rating [(value)]="myRating" />
<p>You rated {{ myRating }} stars</p>

model() combines an input and an output (valueChange) so parents can use [( )] with your component.

Keep templates simple. If an expression gets longer than a few words ([class.x]="a && (b || c) && !d"), move it into a computed() signal or a method with a clear name. Templates are for displaying, classes are for logic.

Common mistakes

  • Using [(ngModel)] without importing FormsModule: "Can't bind to 'ngModel'".
  • [src]="'logo.png'" vs src="logo.png": inside [ ] the value is an expression, so plain strings need quotes.
  • Calling heavy methods in templates ({{ calculateTotal() }}): they run on every change detection. Prefer computed signals.

Exercise

  1. Build a temperature converter: an input bound with [(ngModel)] and a live Fahrenheit result.
  2. Add a "dark card" toggle button that adds a class with [class.dark].
  3. Make a progress bar whose width comes from a number input ([style.width.%]).
  4. Use the RatingComponent with [(value)] and show "Thanks!" after rating.
Hint for 1

celsius = 25; and in the template {{ celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 | number:'1.0-1' }} °F (the number pipe formats decimals, next lesson).

Interview corner

  • Types of data binding? Interpolation, property binding, event binding and two-way binding.
  • How does two-way binding work? [(x)] is shorthand for [x]="val" (xChange)="val = $event".
  • Property vs attribute binding? Property binding sets DOM properties; [attr.name] sets HTML attributes.
  • What is a template reference variable? A #ref name for an element or component usable elsewhere in the template.

Summary

  • {{ }} and [ ] move data into the view, ( ) brings events back, [( )] does both.
  • Class, style and attribute bindings handle styling and accessibility.
  • model() gives your components two-way binding.

Next: control flow (@if, @for) and pipes.
items.subject: angular

items.title: Angular Control Flow and Pipes
items.excerpt: Show and repeat content with @if, @else, @for with track and @empty, and @switch, format values with built-in pipes (date, currency, number, uppercase), and write your own custom pipe.
items.content:
Templates need logic: show a spinner while loading, repeat a card for each course, format prices and dates. Angular's built-in control flow and pipes handle this cleanly.

@if / @else

@if (loading()) {
  <p>Loading…</p>
} @else if (error()) {
  <p role="alert">{{ error() }}</p>
} @else {
  <app-course-list [courses]="courses()" />
}

Store the result of an expression with as:

@if (user(); as u) {
  <p>Welcome back, {{ u.name }}</p>
}

@for with track and @empty

@for (course of courses(); track course.id; let i = $index, last = $last) {
  <li>{{ i + 1 }}. {{ course.title }} @if (!last) { <hr /> }</li>
} @empty {
  <li>No courses match your search.</li>
}
  • track is required. It tells Angular how to identify items (like React's key), so it can move DOM nodes instead of recreating them. Track by a unique id.
  • Context variables: $index, $first, $last, $even, $odd, $count.
  • @empty renders when the list is empty.

@switch

@switch (course.level) {
  @case ('Beginner') { <span class="badge green">Beginner</span> }
  @case ('Advanced') { <span class="badge red">Advanced</span> }
  @default { <span class="badge">{{ course.level }}</span> }
}

Pipes: format values in templates

A pipe transforms a value for display: {{ value | pipeName:arg1:arg2 }}.

// src/app/pipes-demo/pipes-demo.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { CurrencyPipe, DatePipe, DecimalPipe, PercentPipe, UpperCasePipe, TitleCasePipe, SlicePipe, JsonPipe } from '@angular/common';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-pipes-demo',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CurrencyPipe, DatePipe, DecimalPipe, PercentPipe, UpperCasePipe, TitleCasePipe, SlicePipe, JsonPipe],
  template: `
    <p>{{ price | currency:'INR' }}</p>                      <!-- ₹1,499.50 -->
    <p>{{ price | currency:'INR':'symbol':'1.0-0' }}</p>     <!-- ₹1,500 -->
    <p>{{ joined | date:'d MMM y' }}</p>                     <!-- 17 Oct 2026 -->
    <p>{{ joined | date:'shortTime' }}</p>                   <!-- 9:30 AM -->
    <p>{{ rating | number:'1.1-1' }}</p>                     <!-- 4.7 -->
    <p>{{ progress | percent }}</p>                          <!-- 63% -->
    <p>{{ name | uppercase }} / {{ 'spring boot basics' | titlecase }}</p>
    <p>{{ description | slice:0:20 }}…</p>
    <pre>{{ settings | json }}</pre>                          <!-- debugging -->
  `,
})
export class PipesDemoComponent {
  price = 1499.5;
  joined = new Date(2026, 9, 17, 9, 30);
  rating = 4.666;
  progress = 0.63;
  name = 'asha';
  description = 'Learn Angular from scratch with projects';
  settings = { theme: 'dark', lang: 'en' };
}

Import each pipe you use in the component's imports (or CommonModule for all of them).

The async pipe subscribes to an Observable and shows its latest value (lesson 10): {{ courses$ | async }}.

A custom pipe

// src/app/duration.pipe.ts
import { Pipe, PipeTransform } from '@angular/core';

@Pipe({ name: 'duration', standalone: true })
export class DurationPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(minutes: number | null | undefined, style: 'short' | 'long' = 'short'): string {
    if (minutes == null || minutes < 0) return '';
    const h = Math.floor(minutes / 60);
    const m = minutes % 60;
    if (style === 'long') {
      return [h && `${h} hour${h > 1 ? 's' : ''}`, m && `${m} minute${m > 1 ? 's' : ''}`].filter(Boolean).join(' ') || '0 minutes';
    }
    return h ? `${h}h ${m}m` : `${m}m`;
  }
}
<p>{{ 135 | duration }}</p>          <!-- 2h 15m -->
<p>{{ 135 | duration:'long' }}</p>   <!-- 2 hours 15 minutes -->
<p>{{ 45 | duration }}</p>           <!-- 45m -->

Pipes are pure by default: Angular re-runs them only when the input value changes, which makes them faster than calling methods in templates.

Old Angular code uses structural directives *ngIf, *ngFor and [ngSwitch]. They still work, but @if/@for/@switch are faster, need no imports, and @for's required track prevents a classic performance mistake. Migrate with ng generate @angular/core:control-flow.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting track in @for (compile error) or tracking by $index in lists that reorder.
  • Using pipes without importing them: "No pipe found with name 'currency'".
  • Doing filtering/sorting in custom pipes that run on every change: use computed signals instead.

Exercise

  1. Show a list of courses with numbered items, "No courses" when empty, and a different badge per level with @switch.
  2. Show each course's price with the currency pipe and its release date with date:'mediumDate'.
  3. Write a truncate pipe: {{ text | truncate:30 }} adds "…" when longer.
  4. Write a timeAgo pipe that turns a Date into "5 minutes ago" / "2 days ago".
Hint for 3

transform(value: string, max = 50) { return value.length > max ? value.slice(0, max).trimEnd() + '…' : value; }

Interview corner

  • What does track do in @for? Identifies items so Angular can reuse DOM nodes when the list changes.
  • What is a pipe? A template function that transforms values for display.
  • Pure vs impure pipes? Pure pipes run only when inputs change (by reference); impure pipes run on every change detection.
  • @if vs *ngIf? Same purpose; @if is the built-in control flow syntax (Angular 17+), faster and needs no import.

Summary

  • @if/@else, @for (with track and @empty) and @switch control templates.
  • Pipes format values: currency, date, number, percent, uppercase, async.
  • Custom pipes implement PipeTransform.

Next: signals, Angular's reactive state.
items.subject: angular

items.title: Angular Signals - signal, computed and effect
items.excerpt: Manage state the modern Angular way with signals - create and update them with set and update, derive values with computed, run side effects with effect, keep arrays immutable, and build a signal-based cart.
items.content:
Signals are Angular's modern way to hold state. A signal is a value that notifies anything reading it when it changes, so Angular knows exactly which parts of the page to update.

Creating and reading signals

import { signal } from '@angular/core';

const count = signal(0);        // create with an initial value
console.log(count());           // read by CALLING it: 0
count.set(5);                   // replace the value
count.update(n => n + 1);       // compute from the current value: 6

In a template, call it too: {{ count() }}. When the signal changes, that spot in the template updates.

computed: derived values

import { computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

const price = signal(500);
const quantity = signal(2);
const total = computed(() => price() * quantity());    // 1000

quantity.set(3);
console.log(total());                                  // 1500: recalculated automatically
  • A computed signal tracks the signals it reads and recalculates only when one of them changes.
  • It's lazy and cached: reading total() ten times computes once.
  • It's read-only: you can't set a computed.

effect: side effects

An effect runs when signals it reads change. Use it to sync with things outside Angular (localStorage, logging, a chart library):

import { effect } from '@angular/core';

effect(() => {
  localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(items()));   // re-runs whenever items changes
});

Effects must be created in an injection context (a constructor or field initialiser of a component/service). Don't use effects to set other signals: that's what computed is for.

A signal-based cart

// src/app/cart.store.ts
import { Injectable, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

export interface CartItem { id: number; title: string; price: number; qty: number; }

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CartStore {
  private readonly _items = signal<CartItem[]>([]);
  readonly items = this._items.asReadonly();                       // components can read, not write
  readonly count = computed(() => this._items().reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0));
  readonly total = computed(() => this._items().reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0));
  readonly coupon = signal<string | null>(null);
  readonly payable = computed(() => (this.coupon() === 'LEARN20' ? Math.round(this.total() * 0.8) : this.total()));

  add(course: { id: number; title: string; price: number }) {
    this._items.update(items => {
      const found = items.find(i => i.id === course.id);
      return found
        ? items.map(i => (i.id === course.id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } : i))   // new array, new object
        : [...items, { ...course, qty: 1 }];
    });
  }

  remove(id: number) {
    this._items.update(items => items.filter(i => i.id !== id));
  }

  clear() {
    this._items.set([]);
    this.coupon.set(null);
  }
}
// src/app/cart-view/cart-view.component.ts
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { CartStore } from '../cart.store';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-cart-view',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <button (click)="cart.add({ id: 1, title: 'Java', price: 500 })">Add Java</button>
    <button (click)="cart.add({ id: 2, title: 'Angular', price: 600 })">Add Angular</button>
    <button (click)="cart.coupon.set('LEARN20')">Apply LEARN20</button>
    <p class="summary">{{ cart.count() }} items · ₹{{ cart.payable() }}</p>
    <ul>
      @for (item of cart.items(); track item.id) {
        <li>{{ item.title }} × {{ item.qty }} <button (click)="cart.remove(item.id)">Remove</button></li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CartViewComponent {
  cart = inject(CartStore);
}

Add Java twice and Angular once: 3 items · ₹1600. Apply LEARN20: 3 items · ₹1280. The service is the single source of truth; any component that injects CartStore sees the same cart.

Immutability still matters

Signals compare values with Object.is by default. If you mutate an array in place (items().push(x)) and set the same array, readers aren't notified. Always produce new arrays/objects in update, just like React state.

Signals and RxJS

Angular apps also use RxJS Observables (for HTTP, events over time). Convert between them with @angular/core/rxjs-interop:

import { toSignal, toObservable } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';

courses = toSignal(this.http.get<Course[]>('/api/courses'), { initialValue: [] });

You'll use this in lesson 10.

Rule of thumb in modern Angular: signals for state (what the UI shows), RxJS for events and async streams (HTTP, debounced search, websockets), and toSignal to bring stream results into templates.

Exercise

  1. Create a counter component with count, double = computed(...) and +1 / reset buttons.
  2. Add a remaining computed signal to a to-do list that counts unfinished tasks.
  3. Persist the cart to localStorage with an effect, and load it in the signal's initial value.
  4. Add a discountPercent signal and make payable use it.
Hint for 3

private readonly _items = signal<CartItem[]>(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('cart') ?? '[]')); and in the constructor effect(() => localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(this._items())));

Interview corner

  • What is a signal? A reactive value container; reading it registers a dependency, and changes notify dependents.
  • signal vs computed vs effect? Writable state; derived read-only state; side effects reacting to signal changes.
  • Why are signals good for performance? Angular knows exactly which views depend on which signals, enabling fine-grained updates (and zoneless change detection).
  • set vs update? set replaces the value; update computes the new value from the current one.

Summary

  • signal(initial), read with x(), change with set/update.
  • computed derives cached values; effect syncs with the outside world.
  • Keep updates immutable; put shared signal state in services.

Next: services and dependency injection.
items.subject: angular

items.title: Angular Services and Dependency Injection
items.excerpt: Move logic and shared data into services, see how Angular's injector hierarchy decides which instance you get in an animation, use providedIn root vs component providers, inject(), and injection tokens for configuration.
items.content:
Components should focus on the UI. Business logic, data access and shared state belong in services. Angular's dependency injection (DI) creates services and hands them to whoever needs them, the same idea as Spring's IoC container.

A service

// src/app/course.service.ts
import { Injectable, computed, signal } from '@angular/core';

export interface Course { id: number; title: string; level: string; price: number; }

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })          // one shared instance for the whole app
export class CourseService {
  private readonly courses = signal<Course[]>([
    { id: 1, title: 'Java Basics', level: 'Beginner', price: 499 },
    { id: 2, title: 'Angular', level: 'Intermediate', price: 699 },
    { id: 3, title: 'SQL', level: 'Beginner', price: 299 },
  ]);

  readonly all = this.courses.asReadonly();
  readonly beginnerCount = computed(() => this.courses().filter(c => c.level === 'Beginner').length);

  byId(id: number) { return this.courses().find(c => c.id === id); }

  add(title: string, level: string, price: number) {
    const id = Math.max(0, ...this.courses().map(c => c.id)) + 1;
    this.courses.update(list => [...list, { id, title, level, price }]);
    return id;
  }
}

Injecting it

// src/app/course-list/course-list.component.ts
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { CourseService } from '../course.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-list',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <p>{{ courses.all().length }} courses ({{ courses.beginnerCount() }} for beginners)</p>
    <ul>
      @for (c of courses.all(); track c.id) { <li>{{ c.title }}</li> }
    </ul>
    <button (click)="courses.add('Spring Boot', 'Intermediate', 799)">Add Spring Boot</button>
  `,
})
export class CourseListComponent {
  courses = inject(CourseService);           // modern style
  // or: constructor(private courses: CourseService) {}   ← constructor injection (classic style)
}

You never write new CourseService(). Angular creates it the first time someone asks for it, and gives everyone the same instance. Two components showing courses stay in sync automatically.

The injector hierarchy, animated

Angular has a tree of injectors mirroring your component tree. inject(X) starts at the asking component and walks up until some injector can provide X. Switch between a root service and a component-level service:

Where a service is provided

// src/app/editor/editor.component.ts
import { Component, Injectable, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Injectable()                                  // no providedIn: must be provided somewhere
export class DraftService {
  text = signal('');
}

@Component({
  selector: 'app-editor',
  standalone: true,
  providers: [DraftService],                   // each <app-editor> gets its OWN DraftService
  template: `<textarea [value]="draft.text()" (input)="draft.text.set($any($event.target).value)"></textarea>
             <small>{{ draft.text().length }} chars</small>`,
})
export class EditorComponent {
  draft = inject(DraftService);
}

Two <app-editor> components on a page now have independent drafts.

Injection tokens for configuration

Inject values that aren't classes (API URLs, feature flags) with an InjectionToken:

// src/app/tokens.ts
import { InjectionToken } from '@angular/core';

export const API_URL = new InjectionToken<string>('API_URL', {
  providedIn: 'root',
  factory: () => '/api',                        // default value
});
const apiUrl = inject(API_URL);                // '/api', or whatever app.config.ts provides:
// providers: [{ provide: API_URL, useValue: 'https://api.vitalstack.co.in' }]

Provider recipes: useClass (swap implementations, e.g. a mock), useValue, useFactory, useExisting.

Why DI matters for testing

In tests, replace real services with fakes:

TestBed.configureTestingModule({
  providers: [{ provide: CourseService, useValue: { all: () => [], beginnerCount: () => 0 } }],
});

Your component code doesn't change at all. Same benefit as constructor injection in Spring.

inject() only works in an injection context: field initialisers, constructors, and functions called from them (like route guards and interceptors). Calling it inside a click handler or setTimeout throws "inject() must be called from an injection context".

Exercise

  1. Create an AuthService with a user signal and login(name) / logout(), and show the user's name in a header component.
  2. Add a ToastService that holds a list of messages, with a ToastsComponent that displays and auto-removes them.
  3. Make a CounterService without providedIn, provide it in a component, and show that two instances of that component count independently.
  4. Create a FEATURE_FLAGS token and hide a "Beta" menu item when the flag is off.
Hint for 2

messages = signal<string[]>([]); show(msg: string) { this.messages.update(m => [...m, msg]); setTimeout(() => this.messages.update(m => m.slice(1)), 3000); }

Interview corner

  • What is dependency injection in Angular? A system where injectors create and supply dependencies, declared via providers and requested with inject() or constructors.
  • What does providedIn: 'root' mean? A single app-wide instance from the root injector, tree-shakable if unused.
  • How do you get a separate service instance per component? List it in the component's providers.
  • What is an InjectionToken? A key for injecting non-class values like configuration.

Summary

  • Services hold logic and shared state; @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) makes app-wide singletons.
  • inject() walks up the injector tree; component providers create per-component instances.
  • Injection tokens provide configuration; DI makes testing easy.

Next: routing between pages.

items.title: Angular Routing - Pages, Parameters, Guards and Lazy Loading
items.excerpt: Map URLs to components with the Angular Router - routerLink, route parameters with input binding, query params, child routes, functional guards for login, lazy loading pages and a 404 route.
items.content:
The Angular Router turns your single-page app into something that feels like many pages: each URL shows a component, the back button works, and links can be shared.

Defining routes

// src/app/app.routes.ts
import { Routes } from '@angular/router';
import { HomeComponent } from './pages/home.component';
import { CoursesComponent } from './pages/courses.component';
import { CourseDetailComponent } from './pages/course-detail.component';
import { NotFoundComponent } from './pages/not-found.component';
import { authGuard } from './auth.guard';

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: HomeComponent, title: 'VitalStack' },
  { path: 'courses', component: CoursesComponent, title: 'Courses' },
  { path: 'courses/:id', component: CourseDetailComponent },
  {
    path: 'dashboard',
    canActivate: [authGuard],                                       // only for logged-in users
    loadComponent: () => import('./pages/dashboard.component').then(m => m.DashboardComponent),   // lazy loaded
  },
  { path: 'home', redirectTo: '', pathMatch: 'full' },
  { path: '**', component: NotFoundComponent, title: 'Page not found' },   // must be last
];

Enable the router and component input binding (route params arrive as inputs):

// src/app/app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core';
import { provideRouter, withComponentInputBinding } from '@angular/router';
import { routes } from './app.routes';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding())],
};

Navigation links and the outlet

// src/app/app.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { RouterLink, RouterLinkActive, RouterOutlet } from '@angular/router';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [RouterOutlet, RouterLink, RouterLinkActive],
  template: `
    <nav>
      <a routerLink="/" routerLinkActive="active" [routerLinkActiveOptions]="{ exact: true }">Home</a>
      <a routerLink="/courses" routerLinkActive="active">Courses</a>
      <a routerLink="/dashboard" routerLinkActive="active">Dashboard</a>
    </nav>
    <router-outlet />
  `,
})
export class AppComponent {}

routerLink navigates without reloading; routerLinkActive adds a CSS class on the current page; <router-outlet> is where the matched component appears.

Pages

// src/app/pages/home.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({ selector: 'app-home', standalone: true, template: `<h1>Learn to code for free</h1>` })
export class HomeComponent {}
// src/app/pages/not-found.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({ selector: 'app-not-found', standalone: true, template: `<h1>404: Page not found</h1>` })
export class NotFoundComponent {}
// src/app/pages/courses.component.ts
import { Component, computed, input } from '@angular/core';
import { RouterLink } from '@angular/router';

export const COURSES = [
  { id: 1, title: 'Java Basics', level: 'beginner' },
  { id: 2, title: 'Angular', level: 'intermediate' },
  { id: 3, title: 'SQL', level: 'beginner' },
];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-courses',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [RouterLink],
  template: `
    <a routerLink="/courses" [queryParams]="{ level: 'beginner' }">Beginner only</a>
    <ul>
      @for (c of shown(); track c.id) {
        <li><a [routerLink]="['/courses', c.id]">{{ c.title }}</a></li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CoursesComponent {
  level = input<string>();                          // from ?level=beginner (input binding)
  shown = computed(() => COURSES.filter(c => !this.level() || c.level === this.level()));
}
// src/app/pages/course-detail.component.ts
import { Component, computed, inject, input } from '@angular/core';
import { Router } from '@angular/router';
import { COURSES } from './courses.component';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-detail',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    @if (course(); as c) {
      <h1>{{ c.title }}</h1>
      <button (click)="back()">All courses</button>
    } @else {
      <p>Course not found.</p>
    }
  `,
})
export class CourseDetailComponent {
  id = input.required<string>();                    // from /courses/:id
  private router = inject(Router);
  course = computed(() => COURSES.find(c => c.id === Number(this.id())));

  back() { this.router.navigate(['/courses']); }    // navigate in code
}

Without input binding, read parameters with inject(ActivatedRoute).paramMap / queryParamMap (Observables).

Guards: protecting routes

A functional guard decides whether navigation may continue:

// src/app/auth.guard.ts
import { inject } from '@angular/core';
import { CanActivateFn, Router } from '@angular/router';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';

export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = (route, state) => {
  const auth = inject(AuthService);
  if (auth.isLoggedIn()) return true;
  return inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login'], { queryParams: { returnUrl: state.url } });   // redirect
};
// src/app/auth.service.ts
import { Injectable, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AuthService {
  private readonly token = signal<string | null>(localStorage.getItem('token'));
  isLoggedIn() { return this.token() !== null; }
  login(token: string) { localStorage.setItem('token', token); this.token.set(token); }
  logout() { localStorage.removeItem('token'); this.token.set(null); }
}
// src/app/pages/dashboard.component.ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({ selector: 'app-dashboard', standalone: true, template: `<h1>Your dashboard</h1>` })
export class DashboardComponent {}

Other guard types: canMatch (pick routes / prevent lazy loading), canDeactivate ("You have unsaved changes"), and resolve (load data before showing a page).

Guards improve UX; they are not security. The API (Spring Security) must check permissions too, because anyone can call your API directly.

Lazy loading

loadComponent (or loadChildren for a group of routes) splits that page into a separate JavaScript file, downloaded only when the user first visits it. The initial download stays small, which matters on mobile networks.

Child routes

{
  path: 'account',
  component: AccountLayoutComponent,          // has its own <router-outlet>
  children: [
    { path: '', redirectTo: 'profile', pathMatch: 'full' },
    { path: 'profile', component: ProfileComponent },
    { path: 'certificates', component: CertificatesComponent },
  ],
}

Deploying

Like React, the server must send index.html for deep links like /courses/2 (SPA fallback rewrite on Netlify, Vercel, Firebase Hosting, Nginx or Apache).

Exercise

  1. Add an About page and a nav link.
  2. Add a level select on the courses page that navigates with query params.
  3. Build a login page that calls auth.login('demo') and redirects to returnUrl.
  4. Lazy load the courses page with loadComponent and check the extra JS file in DevTools' Network tab.
Hint for 3

const returnUrl = inject(ActivatedRoute).snapshot.queryParamMap.get('returnUrl') ?? '/'; this.router.navigateByUrl(returnUrl);

Interview corner

  • What is lazy loading? Loading a route's code only when it's first navigated to (loadComponent/loadChildren).
  • What are route guards? Functions like canActivate, canMatch, canDeactivate that allow, block or redirect navigation.
  • How do you read route parameters? Component input binding (withComponentInputBinding), or ActivatedRoute's paramMap/snapshot.
  • routerLink vs href? routerLink navigates inside the SPA without a full page reload.

Summary

  • Routes map paths to components; <router-outlet> displays them; routerLink navigates.
  • Route and query params arrive as inputs with withComponentInputBinding.
  • Functional guards protect pages; loadComponent lazy-loads them; ** catches 404s.

Next: forms with validation.

items.title: Angular Reactive Forms and Validation
items.excerpt: Build robust forms with typed reactive forms - FormBuilder, built-in validators, showing errors at the right time, a custom cross-field validator, dynamic FormArray fields and template-driven forms for simple cases.
items.content:
Angular has two ways to build forms. Reactive forms define the form model in TypeScript and are the standard choice for real applications. Template-driven forms (with ngModel) are fine for very small forms.

A reactive sign-up form

// src/app/signup/signup.component.ts
import { Component, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { AbstractControl, FormBuilder, ReactiveFormsModule, ValidationErrors, Validators } from '@angular/forms';

function passwordsMatch(group: AbstractControl): ValidationErrors | null {
  const pass = group.get('password')?.value;
  const confirm = group.get('confirm')?.value;
  return pass && confirm && pass !== confirm ? { mismatch: true } : null;
}

@Component({
  selector: 'app-signup',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [ReactiveFormsModule],
  template: `
    @if (done()) {
      <p role="status">Welcome, {{ done() }}! Check your email.</p>
    } @else {
      <form [formGroup]="form" (ngSubmit)="submit()" novalidate>
        <label>Name <input formControlName="name" /></label>
        @if (showError('name')) { <small class="error">Name needs at least 2 letters</small> }

        <label>Email <input formControlName="email" type="email" /></label>
        @if (showError('email')) { <small class="error">Enter a valid email</small> }

        <label>Course
          <select formControlName="course">
            <option value="java">Java</option>
            <option value="angular">Angular</option>
          </select>
        </label>

        <div formGroupName="passwords">
          <label>Password <input formControlName="password" type="password" /></label>
          <label>Confirm <input formControlName="confirm" type="password" /></label>
        </div>
        @if (form.controls.passwords.hasError('mismatch') && form.controls.passwords.touched) {
          <small class="error">Passwords don't match</small>
        }

        <label><input type="checkbox" formControlName="terms" /> I accept the terms</label>
        <button type="submit">Create free account</button>
      </form>
    }
  `,
})
export class SignupComponent {
  private fb = inject(FormBuilder).nonNullable;
  done = signal<string | null>(null);

  form = this.fb.group({
    name: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(2)]],
    email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]],
    course: ['java'],
    passwords: this.fb.group(
      { password: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(8)]], confirm: [''] },
      { validators: passwordsMatch }
    ),
    terms: [false, Validators.requiredTrue],
  });

  showError(name: 'name' | 'email') {
    const c = this.form.controls[name];
    return c.invalid && (c.touched || c.dirty);        // don't shout before the user has typed
  }

  submit() {
    if (this.form.invalid) {
      this.form.markAllAsTouched();                    // reveal every error on submit
      return;
    }
    const value = this.form.getRawValue();             // fully typed: { name: string, email: string, … }
    this.done.set(value.name);
  }
}

How it works

  • FormBuilder creates a tree of FormGroups and FormControls. nonNullable means reset() goes back to the initial values instead of null.
  • [formGroup] connects the <form>; formControlName and formGroupName connect inputs to controls.
  • Each control tracks its value, validity (valid/invalid, errors), and interaction state (touched, dirty, pristine).
  • The form model is typed: form.getRawValue().email is a string, and typos are compile errors.

Built-in validators

Errors live in control.errors, e.g. { minlength: { requiredLength: 2, actualLength: 1 } }, so you can show precise messages.

Custom validators

passwordsMatch above is a cross-field validator on a group. A single-field custom validator:

export function noSpaces(control: AbstractControl): ValidationErrors | null {
  return /\s/.test(control.value ?? '') ? { noSpaces: true } : null;
}
// username: ['', [Validators.required, noSpaces]]

Async validators (e.g. "is this username taken?" via HTTP) return an Observable or Promise.

Reacting to changes

this.form.controls.course.valueChanges.subscribe(course => {
  console.log('Course changed to', course);
});

valueChanges is an Observable: combine it with RxJS operators like debounceTime for live search (next lesson).

Dynamic fields with FormArray

skills = this.fb.array([this.fb.control('Java')]);
addSkill() { this.skills.push(this.fb.control('')); }
removeSkill(i: number) { this.skills.removeAt(i); }
<div formArrayName="skills">
  @for (s of skills.controls; track $index; let i = $index) {
    <input [formControlName]="i" /> <button type="button" (click)="removeSkill(i)">×</button>
  }
</div>
<button type="button" (click)="addSkill()">Add skill</button>

Template-driven forms (quick forms)

<form #f="ngForm" (ngSubmit)="search(f.value.q)">
  <input name="q" ngModel required minlength="2" />
  <button [disabled]="f.invalid">Search</button>
</form>

Simpler for tiny forms, but logic lives in the template and it's harder to test. For anything with real validation, use reactive forms.

Show errors after the user leaves a field (touched) or on submit (markAllAsTouched), not while they're still typing their first character. And always validate again on the server: the Spring Boot course's ProblemDetail errors can be mapped back to these fields.

Exercise

  1. Add a phone field with an Indian mobile number pattern and a clear error message.
  2. Disable the submit button while the form is invalid, and show a summary of all errors on submit.
  3. Add a FormArray of up to 5 "learning goals".
  4. Write an async validator that rejects the email taken@example.com after 500 ms (use of(...).pipe(delay(500))).
Hint for 1

phone: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.pattern(/^[6-9]\d{9}$/)]] and show the error when form.controls.phone.hasError('pattern').

Interview corner

  • Reactive vs template-driven forms? Reactive: model defined in TS, explicit, typed, testable; template-driven: model inferred from ngModel directives in the template.
  • FormControl vs FormGroup vs FormArray? A single value; a named group of controls; a dynamic list of controls.
  • touched vs dirty? Touched: the field lost focus at least once; dirty: the value was changed by the user.
  • How do you write a cross-field validator? A validator function on the FormGroup that reads multiple controls.

Summary

  • Reactive forms: FormBuilder + Validators + formControlName.
  • Show errors on touched/dirty or after submit with markAllAsTouched.
  • Custom, cross-field and async validators cover complex rules; FormArray handles dynamic lists.

items.title: Angular HttpClient and RxJS
items.excerpt: Call REST APIs with HttpClient, understand Observables, watch an RxJS pipe filter, map and take values in an animation, build a debounced live search with switchMap, handle errors and add a JWT interceptor.
items.content:
Angular talks to back ends (like the Spring Boot API you built) through HttpClient, which returns Observables from the RxJS library. Observables are streams of values over time, and RxJS operators let you transform them like a pipeline.

Setup

// in app.config.ts providers:
provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]))

A data service

// src/app/course-api.service.ts
import { HttpClient, HttpParams } from '@angular/common/http';
import { Injectable, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { Observable, catchError, map, of, throwError } from 'rxjs';

export interface Course { id: number; title: string; totalLessons: number; }

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CourseApi {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);
  private base = '/api/courses';

  list(): Observable<Course[]> {
    return this.http.get<Course[]>(this.base);
  }

  search(q: string): Observable<Course[]> {
    const params = new HttpParams().set('q', q);
    return this.http.get<Course[]>(`${this.base}/search`, { params }).pipe(
      catchError(() => of([]))                              // on error, show no results instead of breaking
    );
  }

  get(id: number): Observable<Course> {
    return this.http.get<Course>(`${this.base}/${id}`).pipe(
      catchError(err => throwError(() => new Error(err.error?.detail ?? 'Could not load the course')))
    );
  }

  create(title: string, totalLessons: number): Observable<Course> {
    return this.http.post<Course>(this.base, { title, totalLessons });
  }

  titles(): Observable<string[]> {
    return this.list().pipe(map(list => list.map(c => c.title)));
  }
}

The detail field comes from Spring's ProblemDetail errors, so users see the server's real message.

Observables in 60 seconds

  • An Observable is lazy: nothing happens until someone subscribes. http.get() doesn't send a request until then.
  • It can emit many values over time (keystrokes, websocket messages); HTTP emits one value then completes.
  • Operators go inside .pipe(...) and each returns a new Observable.

Watch values flow through filter, map and take:

Showing data: toSignal or the async pipe

// src/app/course-page/course-page.component.ts
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { CourseApi } from '../course-api.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-page',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <ul>
      @for (c of courses(); track c.id) { <li>{{ c.title }} ({{ c.totalLessons }} lessons)</li> }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class CoursePageComponent {
  courses = toSignal(inject(CourseApi).list(), { initialValue: [] });    // subscribes and unsubscribes for you
}

The alternative is the async pipe: @for (c of courses$ | async; track c.id). Both manage the subscription automatically, so there are no memory leaks.

Live search with debounce and switchMap

// src/app/live-search/live-search.component.ts
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { FormControl, ReactiveFormsModule } from '@angular/forms';
import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, filter, map, switchMap } from 'rxjs';
import { CourseApi } from '../course-api.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-live-search',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [ReactiveFormsModule],
  template: `
    <input [formControl]="query" placeholder="Search courses" />
    <ul>
      @for (c of results(); track c.id) { <li>{{ c.title }}</li> }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class LiveSearchComponent {
  private api = inject(CourseApi);
  query = new FormControl('', { nonNullable: true });

  results = toSignal(
    this.query.valueChanges.pipe(
      map(q => q.trim()),
      debounceTime(300),                 // wait until typing pauses
      distinctUntilChanged(),            // ignore if unchanged
      filter(q => q.length >= 2),        // at least 2 characters
      switchMap(q => this.api.search(q)) // cancel the previous request when a new query arrives
    ),
    { initialValue: [] }
  );
}

Typing "java" fast sends one request, not four, and a slow response for "ja" can never overwrite the results for "java", because switchMap cancels it. This is the classic RxJS interview example.

Interceptors: add the JWT to every request

// src/app/auth.interceptor.ts
import { HttpInterceptorFn } from '@angular/common/http';

export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('token');
  if (!token || !req.url.startsWith('/api')) return next(req);
  return next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }));
};

Requests are immutable, so you clone them with changes. Interceptors are also the place for global error handling (e.g. redirect to login on 401) and loading indicators.

Proxy to Spring Boot in development

{
  "/api": { "target": "http://localhost:8080", "secure": false }
}

Save it as proxy.conf.json and run ng serve --proxy-config proxy.conf.json (or set proxyConfig in angular.json).

Manual subscribe() calls in components are where memory leaks come from. Prefer toSignal or the async pipe. If you must subscribe, use takeUntilDestroyed() from @angular/core/rxjs-interop to unsubscribe automatically.

Exercise

  1. Show courses from the Spring Boot API with a loading message and an error message.
  2. Add a "create course" form that POSTs and then refreshes the list.
  3. Use forkJoin to load courses and the leaderboard in parallel.
  4. Add an interceptor that redirects to /login when any response is 401.
Hint for 4

return next(req).pipe(catchError(err => { if (err.status === 401) inject(Router).navigate(['/login']); return throwError(() => err); })); (call inject(Router) at the top of the interceptor function).

Interview corner

  • Observable vs Promise? Observables are lazy, can emit many values, are cancellable and composable with operators; promises are eager and resolve once.
  • switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap? switchMap cancels the previous inner stream; mergeMap runs all concurrently; concatMap queues them in order.
  • How do you avoid memory leaks? async pipe, toSignal, takeUntilDestroyed, or unsubscribing in ngOnDestroy.
  • What is an HTTP interceptor? A function that can inspect/modify every request and response (auth headers, errors, logging).

Summary

  • HttpClient returns Observables; wrap API calls in services.
  • RxJS operators (map, debounceTime, switchMap, catchError) build data pipelines.
  • toSignal/async handle subscriptions; interceptors add tokens and handle errors globally.

items.title: Angular Change Detection and Performance
items.excerpt: Understand how Angular checks components for changes, compare Default and OnPush in an animation, use signals and immutable inputs, @for track, @defer blocks, lazy routes and the production build to keep apps fast.
items.content:
Angular keeps the page in sync with your data through change detection. Knowing how it works lets you build apps that stay fast with hundreds of components, a common senior-level interview topic.

How change detection works

  1. Something happens: a click, a timer, an HTTP response.
  2. Angular (traditionally via zone.js, which patches browser APIs) notices and runs change detection.
  3. It walks the component tree from the root, re-evaluating each component's template bindings and updating the DOM where values changed.

With the Default strategy, every component is checked on every event. For a small app that's fine. For a dashboard with 500 components and a ticking clock, it's wasted work.

Default vs OnPush, animated

Run both strategies through a timer tick and a new course being added:

With ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush, Angular checks a component only when:

  • one of its inputs receives a new reference,
  • an event happens inside it (or its children),
  • a signal it reads in its template changes,
  • the async pipe receives a new value, or it's explicitly marked (markForCheck).
// src/app/course-table/course-table.component.ts
import { ChangeDetectionStrategy, Component, input } from '@angular/core';

export interface Row { id: number; title: string; students: number; }

@Component({
  selector: 'app-course-table',
  standalone: true,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <table>
      @for (r of rows(); track r.id) {
        <tr><td>{{ r.title }}</td><td>{{ r.students }}</td></tr>
      }
    </table>
  `,
})
export class CourseTableComponent {
  rows = input.required<Row[]>();
}

The immutability rule

With OnPush, mutating an input array does nothing visible, because the reference is the same:

// ❌ the OnPush table won't update
this.rows.push(newRow);

// ✅ a new array reference: the table updates
this.rows = [...this.rows, newRow];
// or with a signal:
this.rows.update(r => [...r, newRow]);
// src/app/dashboard/dashboard.component.ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { CourseTableComponent, Row } from '../course-table/course-table.component';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-dashboard',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CourseTableComponent],
  template: `
    <button (click)="addWrong()">Add (mutate)</button>
    <button (click)="addRight()">Add (new array)</button>
    <app-course-table [rows]="rows" />
  `,
})
export class DashboardComponent {
  rows: Row[] = [{ id: 1, title: 'Java', students: 1200 }];

  addWrong() { this.rows.push({ id: this.rows.length + 1, title: 'Mutated', students: 0 }); }
  addRight() { this.rows = [...this.rows, { id: this.rows.length + 1, title: 'Angular', students: 800 }]; }
}

Click "Add (mutate)": the table doesn't change. Click "Add (new array)": the table shows both new rows (the mutated one was in the array all along, just not rendered).

Signals and the zoneless future

Signals tell Angular exactly which components need updating. With signals + OnPush, Angular can skip whole subtrees. Angular 18+ also offers zoneless change detection (provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection(), stable as provideZonelessChangeDetection() in newer versions), dropping zone.js entirely for smaller bundles and faster apps. Code written with signals and OnPush today is ready for it.

Other performance tools

**@for track by id**: when a list refreshes from the server, tracking by id lets Angular keep existing DOM rows instead of rebuilding them all.

**@defer blocks** load parts of a page lazily:

@defer (on viewport) {
  <app-reviews [courseId]="id()" />          <!-- its code loads when scrolled into view -->
} @placeholder {
  <p>Reviews</p>
} @loading (minimum 300ms) {
  <p>Loading reviews…</p>
}

Triggers: on idle (default), on viewport, on interaction, on hover, on timer(2s), when condition.

Lazy routes (loadComponent/loadChildren) keep the first download small.

Avoid heavy template calls: {{ total() }} with a computed signal is cached; {{ calculateTotal() }} as a plain method runs on every check.

Pure pipes cache by input.

Production builds: ng build enables ahead-of-time compilation, tree shaking, minification and budgets (warnings when bundles grow too big, configured in angular.json).

Images: NgOptimizedImage (<img ngSrc="..." width height priority>) adds lazy loading and size hints.

Make OnPush your default (ng g c name --change-detection OnPush, or set it in angular.json schematics) and use signals for state. You'll rarely think about change detection again, and when something doesn't update, the first question is "did I mutate instead of creating a new reference?".

Measuring

  • Angular DevTools (browser extension): component tree, change detection profiler showing how long each component's check took.
  • Chrome Lighthouse and the Performance tab for load time and long tasks.

Exercise

  1. Build the dashboard example and observe the mutate vs new-array behaviour.
  2. Convert the rows field in DashboardComponent to a signal and use update.
  3. Wrap a heavy chart component in @defer (on viewport) and check the Network tab when scrolling.
  4. Run Angular DevTools' profiler on your app and find the component that takes longest to check.
Hint for 2

rows = signal<Row[]>([...]), pass [rows]="rows()", and addRight() { this.rows.update(r => [...r, newRow]); }.

Interview corner

  • What is change detection? The process of syncing the DOM with component state by re-evaluating template bindings.
  • Default vs OnPush? Default checks every component on each event; OnPush checks only on new input references, internal events, signal changes, async pipe emissions or manual marking.
  • Why must inputs be immutable with OnPush? OnPush compares input references; mutation keeps the same reference, so the change is missed.
  • What is @defer? A template block that lazy-loads its components based on triggers like viewport or idle.

Summary

  • Angular checks components after events; OnPush limits checks to real changes.
  • Use immutable updates and signals; track lists by id.
  • @defer, lazy routes and production builds keep apps fast.

Next: build a complete Angular project.
