items.title: 3Sum
items.excerpt: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero. Sort, fix one number, then run two pointers on the rest, skipping duplicates.
items.content:
3Sum = fix one number + Two Sum on a sorted list. The tricky part is avoiding duplicate triplets.

The problem

Return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from nums with a + b + c == 0.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Sort first. Then for each number nums[i], you need two numbers after it that sum to -nums[i].

Hint 2

On a sorted list, that's two pointers: too small → move left up; too big → move right down.

Hint 3

Skip a number equal to the previous one (for i, and after finding a triplet) to avoid duplicates.

Brute force, O(n³)

Check every triplet and put sorted triplets in a set. It works for tiny inputs only.

The easy idea

After sorting [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]:

  • Fix -4: need two numbers summing to 4 from [-1, -1, 0, 1, 2]: none.
  • Fix -1: need 1 from [-1, 0, 1, 2]: (-1, 2) and (0, 1) → two triplets.
  • The next -1 is the same as before: skip it, or we'd repeat triplets.

Here is the two-pointer step after fixing the first -1: search the rest, [-1, 0, 1, 2], for a pair summing to 1:

Solution

def three_sum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                            # same first number: skip
        if nums[i] > 0:
            break                               # all remaining are positive
        lo, hi = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while lo < hi:
            total = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]
            if total < 0:
                lo += 1
            elif total > 0:
                hi -= 1
            else:
                out.append([nums[i], nums[lo], nums[hi]])
                lo += 1
                hi -= 1
                while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo - 1]:
                    lo += 1                     # skip duplicate seconds
    return out

print(three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]))  # [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
print(three_sum([0, 1, 1]))              # []
print(three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0]))           # [[0, 0, 0]]

Complexity

  • Time O(n²): sorting is O(n log n), then n two-pointer passes of O(n).
  • Space O(1) extra (ignoring the output and the sort).

Similar problems

Two Sum II, 3Sum Closest, 4Sum, 3Sum Smaller, Valid Triangle Number.

items.title: Trapping Rain Water
items.excerpt: How much rain collects between bars of different heights? The water above each bar depends on the tallest walls on its left and right.
items.content:
A famous "hard" problem that becomes easy once you think about one bar at a time.

The problem

height[i] is a bar of width 1. After rain, how many units of water are trapped between the bars?

Example

[0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1] → 6 (# is a bar, ~ is trapped water)

              #
      # ~ ~ ~ # # ~ #
  # ~ # # ~ # # # # # #
0 1 0 2 1 0 1 3 2 1 2 1

Hints

Hint 1

Look at one bar. Water above it rises to the LOWER of (tallest bar on its left, tallest bar on its right), minus its own height.

Hint 2

Precompute "tallest to the left" and "tallest to the right" for every position with two passes.

Hint 3

For O(1) space: two pointers. The side with the smaller max is the one whose water you already know.

The key formula

For each position i:

water[i] = min(max_left[i], max_right[i]) - height[i]

Think of a bathtub: water rises only as high as the shorter of its two walls.

Solution 1: precompute both sides, O(n) space

def trap_arrays(height):
    n = len(height)
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    left = [0] * n
    right = [0] * n
    left[0] = height[0]
    for i in range(1, n):
        left[i] = max(left[i - 1], height[i])
    right[-1] = height[-1]
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        right[i] = max(right[i + 1], height[i])
    return sum(min(left[i], right[i]) - height[i] for i in range(n))

print(trap_arrays([0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]))  # 6

Solution 2: two pointers, O(1) space

Keep the tallest wall seen from each end. Whichever side has the smaller tallest wall is the limiting side, so its water is already decided: compute it and move that pointer inwards.

def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            water += left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            water += right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1
    return water

print(trap([0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]))  # 6
print(trap([4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]))                    # 9
print(trap([]))                                    # 0

Complexity

A monotonic stack solution also exists (it fills water layer by layer); mention it if asked for alternatives.

Similar problems

Container With Most Water, Product of Array Except Self, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Trapping Rain Water II (3D, uses a heap).

items.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
items.excerpt: Buy once, sell once, maximise profit. Track the cheapest price so far in a single pass.
items.content:
One pass, two variables. The classic "keep the best so far" trick.

The problem

prices[i] is a stock's price on day i. Buy on one day and sell on a later day. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

If you sell on day i, the best day to have bought is the cheapest day BEFORE i.

Hint 2

Walk through the days keeping the cheapest price seen so far.

Brute force, O(n²)

def max_profit_slow(prices):
    best = 0
    for buy in range(len(prices)):
        for sell in range(buy + 1, len(prices)):
            best = max(best, prices[sell] - prices[buy])
    return best

print(max_profit_slow([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))  # 5

The easy idea: "if only I'd bought at the lowest point"

Walk through the days with a notebook holding one number: the cheapest price so far. Each day, ask: "If I sold today, what's my profit?" Keep the best answer.

Solution

def max_profit(prices):
    cheapest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        cheapest = min(cheapest, p)
        best = max(best, p - cheapest)
    return best

print(max_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))  # 5
print(max_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]))     # 0

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(1).

The family of stock problems

  • Unlimited transactions (II): add every upward step: sum(max(0, b - a) for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])).
  • At most 2 or k transactions (III, IV): dynamic programming with states.
  • With cooldown or fee: DP with "holding" and "not holding" states.
def max_profit_many(prices):
    return sum(max(0, b - a) for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:]))

print(max_profit_many([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]))  # 7

Similar problems

Maximum Subarray (Kadane is the same idea in disguise), Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II, III and with Cooldown.

items.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
items.excerpt: The textbook sliding window problem. Grow the window to the right; when a letter repeats, shrink from the left.
items.content:
If you master this problem, you understand sliding windows.

The problem

Return the length of the longest substring (continuous part) of s with no repeated characters.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Checking every substring is O(n³) or O(n²). Instead, keep one window that is always valid.

Hint 2

Move the right edge forward one letter at a time. If that letter is already in the window, move the left edge past its previous position.

Hint 3

A dictionary storing each letter's last index lets the left edge jump in one step.

Brute force, O(n²)

def longest_unique_slow(s):
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s)):
        seen = set()
        for j in range(i, len(s)):
            if s[j] in seen:
                break
            seen.add(s[j])
            best = max(best, j - i + 1)
    return best

print(longest_unique_slow("abcabcbb"))  # 3

The easy idea: a caterpillar

The window is a caterpillar crawling along the string. Its head eats the next letter. If that letter is already inside the caterpillar, its tail moves forward until the old copy is gone. Record the longest the caterpillar ever gets. Press play:

Solution

def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    last = {}                        # letter -> last index seen
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1      # jump past the old copy
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

print(length_of_longest_substring("abcabcbb"))  # 3
print(length_of_longest_substring("bbbbb"))     # 1
print(length_of_longest_substring("pwwkew"))    # 3
print(length_of_longest_substring(""))          # 0
print(length_of_longest_substring("abba"))      # 2

The last[ch] >= left check matters: in "abba", when the second a arrives, the old a is already outside the window, so the left edge must not move backwards.

Complexity

  • Time O(n): each index is visited once by right; left only moves forward.
  • Space O(k) for k different characters.

Similar problems

Longest Repeating Character Replacement, Minimum Window Substring, Permutation in String, Fruit Into Baskets.

Learn the pattern: Sliding Window.

items.title: Minimum Window Substring
items.excerpt: Find the smallest part of a string that contains every letter of another string. Expand until valid, then shrink while valid.
items.content:
The "hard" sliding window: expand until the window works, then shrink it as much as possible.

The problem

Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). Return "" if there is none.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Count what you NEED from t with a dictionary.

Hint 2

Move the right edge until the window has everything. Then move the left edge to shrink while it still has everything, recording the best.

Hint 3

Keep a counter missing = how many required characters are still missing, so checking "valid?" is O(1).

The easy idea: shopping list

You have a shopping list (t). Walk along a street of shops (s), adding items to your basket (expand right). The moment the basket has everything, try returning items from the start of your trip that you don't need (shrink left), as long as the basket stays complete. Each complete basket is a candidate; keep the shortest.

Solution

from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    missing = len(t)                 # characters still needed
    left = 0
    best_start, best_len = 0, float("inf")
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if need[ch] > 0:
            missing -= 1             # this character was useful
        need[ch] -= 1
        while missing == 0:          # window is valid: try to shrink
            if right - left + 1 < best_len:
                best_start, best_len = left, right - left + 1
            need[s[left]] += 1
            if need[s[left]] > 0:
                missing += 1         # we just dropped something required
            left += 1
    return "" if best_len == float("inf") else s[best_start:best_start + best_len]

print(min_window("ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC"))  # BANC
print(min_window("a", "a"))                # a
print(min_window("a", "aa") == "")         # True

need[ch] can go negative: that means the window has extra copies we could give away.

Complexity

  • Time O(len(s) + len(t)): both edges only move forward.
  • Space O(k) for the character counts.

Template to remember

for right in range(n):
    add s[right]
    while window is valid:
        record answer
        remove s[left]; left += 1

Swap "while valid" for "while invalid" and you get the template for "longest window" problems.

Similar problems

Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Permutation in String, Find All Anagrams in a String, Substring with Concatenation of All Words.

Learn the pattern: Sliding Window.

items.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
items.excerpt: Count continuous subarrays that add up to k, even with negative numbers. Prefix sums plus a hash map of counts.
items.content:
Sliding windows fail when numbers can be negative. Prefix sums + a dictionary don't.

The problem

Return how many continuous subarrays of nums sum to exactly k.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

sum(i..j) = prefix[j + 1] − prefix[i]. So a subarray sums to k when two prefix sums differ by exactly k.

Hint 2

While walking, ask: "How many earlier prefix sums equal current − k?" A dictionary of counts answers instantly.

Hint 3

Start the dictionary with {0: 1}: the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.

Brute force, O(n²)

def subarray_sum_slow(nums, k):
    count = 0
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, len(nums)):
            total += nums[j]
            if total == k:
                count += 1
    return count

print(subarray_sum_slow([1, 1, 1], 2))  # 2

The easy idea: kilometre markers

A running total is like the kilometre marker on a highway. The distance between two markers is the sum of the road between them. To find stretches of exactly k km, at each marker ask: "How many earlier markers read current − k?"

Here is how prefix sums turn any range sum into one subtraction:

Solution

def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen = {0: 1}                 # prefix sum -> how many times seen
    total = count = 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen.get(total - k, 0)
        seen[total] = seen.get(total, 0) + 1
    return count

print(subarray_sum([1, 1, 1], 2))           # 2
print(subarray_sum([1, 2, 3], 3))           # 2
print(subarray_sum([3, -1, 2, -2, 4], 2))   # 4

Why not a sliding window?

A window assumes adding numbers makes the sum bigger. With negatives, shrinking can make the sum grow, so the window can't decide which way to move. Prefix sums don't care about signs.

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(n) for the dictionary.

Similar problems

Two Sum (same "look up the partner" trick), Continuous Subarray Sum, Subarray Sums Divisible by K, Contiguous Array, Path Sum III.

Learn the pattern: Prefix Sums.

items.title: Maximum Subarray
items.excerpt: Find the continuous part of a list with the biggest sum. Kadane's algorithm: keep going while the running sum helps, restart when it hurts.
items.content:
Kadane's algorithm is five lines long and one of the most-asked interview algorithms ever.

The problem

Return the largest sum of any non-empty continuous subarray of nums.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

At each position, the best subarray ENDING here either extends the previous one or starts fresh here.

Hint 2

Extend only if the previous running sum is positive. A negative running sum only drags you down.

Brute force, O(n²)

def max_subarray_slow(nums):
    best = nums[0]
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        total = 0
        for j in range(i, len(nums)):
            total += nums[j]
            best = max(best, total)
    return best

print(max_subarray_slow([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))  # 6

The easy idea: carrying a backpack

You walk along the list carrying a backpack of points. Each number adds or removes points. If your backpack ever goes negative, drop it and start fresh: carrying debt can only make future totals smaller. Remember the heaviest the backpack ever got. Watch:

Solution

def max_subarray(nums):
    current = best = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        current = max(x, current + x)   # start fresh or extend
        best = max(best, current)
    return best

print(max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))  # 6
print(max_subarray([1]))                              # 1
print(max_subarray([-3, -1, -2]))                     # -1

Starting with nums[0] (not 0) handles the all-negative case correctly.

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(1).

Follow-up: return the subarray itself

Remember where the current run started, and save the start and end whenever best improves:

def max_subarray_range(nums):
    current, best = nums[0], nums[0]
    start = best_l = best_r = 0
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        if current + nums[i] < nums[i]:
            current, start = nums[i], i
        else:
            current += nums[i]
        if current > best:
            best, best_l, best_r = current, start, i
    return nums[best_l:best_r + 1]

print(max_subarray_range([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))  # [4, -1, 2, 1]

Similar problems

Maximum Product Subarray, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, Maximum Sum Circular Subarray, Largest Sum of Averages.

Learn the pattern: Kadane's Algorithm.

items.title: Binary Search
items.excerpt: Find a target in a sorted list in O(log n). The bug-free template, first and last position, and search insert position.
items.content:
Simple to describe, famously easy to get wrong. Learn one template and use it everywhere.

The problem

Given a sorted list nums and a target, return the target's index, or -1 if it's not there. Your solution must be O(log n).

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Look at the middle. If it's too small, the target can only be in the right half.

Hint 2

Keep lo and hi as the range still possible. Stop when lo > hi.

The easy idea: the number guessing game

"I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100." Guess 50. "Higher!" Now it's 51–100: guess 75. Each guess halves the range, so 7 guesses are always enough for 100 numbers. Play it:

Solution

def search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1           # target is to the right
        else:
            hi = mid - 1           # target is to the left
    return -1

print(search([-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], 9))  # 4
print(search([-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], 2))  # -1
print(search([5], 5))                   # 0

Complexity

  • Time O(log n): a million items need about 20 steps.
  • Space O(1).

Variation: first and last position

With duplicates, find the first index where nums[i] >= target (a "lower bound"). Don't stop when you find the target; keep searching left.

def lower_bound(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

def search_range(nums, target):
    first = lower_bound(nums, target)
    if first == len(nums) or nums[first] != target:
        return [-1, -1]
    return [first, lower_bound(nums, target + 1) - 1]

print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 8))  # [3, 4]
print(search_range([5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], 6))  # [-1, -1]
print(lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 6], 2))          # 1

lower_bound is also the answer to Search Insert Position: where would the target go to keep the list sorted?

Common bugs

  • while lo < hi vs while lo <= hi mixed up with hi = mid vs hi = mid - 1: pick one template and stick to it.
  • Infinite loops when lo = mid (the range never shrinks).

Similar problems

Search Insert Position, Find First and Last Position, Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Koko Eating Bananas, Sqrt(x).

Learn the pattern: Binary Search.

items.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
items.excerpt: A sorted list was rotated at an unknown point. Binary search still works, because one half is always sorted.
items.content:
The key insight: when you cut a rotated sorted list in half, at least one half is still perfectly sorted.

The problem

A sorted list of distinct numbers was rotated, e.g. [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] became [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find target's index in O(log n), or return -1.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid]. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted.

Hint 2

In a sorted half, you can check in O(1) whether the target lies inside it. If yes, search there; otherwise search the other half.

The easy idea: a clock face

Imagine the numbers written around a clock that was turned. Cut it in the middle: one side runs smoothly upward (sorted), the other side contains the "jump". For the smooth side you can tell instantly whether the target is between its ends. That decides which half to keep.

[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]
 lo       mid      hi
 4 <= 7  → left half [4..7] is sorted
 target 0 is not in 4..7 → search the right half

Solution

def search_rotated(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:                    # left half sorted
            if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:                                        # right half sorted
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1

print(search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 0))  # 4
print(search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 3))  # -1
print(search_rotated([1], 0))                    # -1
print(search_rotated([3, 1], 1))                 # 1

Related: find the minimum

The minimum is where the "jump" is. Compare the middle with the right end:

def find_min(nums):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1          # the drop is to the right
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

print(find_min([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]))  # 0
print(find_min([11, 13, 15, 17]))       # 11

Complexity

  • Time O(log n), space O(1).

Similar problems

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (with duplicates), Find Peak Element, Binary Search.

Learn the pattern: Binary Search.

items.title: Koko Eating Bananas
items.excerpt: Binary search on the answer. Find the slowest eating speed that still finishes all bananas in time.
items.content:
This problem teaches a superpower: binary search on the answer, even when there's no sorted list in sight.

The problem

There are piles of bananas, piles[i] in each. Koko eats at speed k bananas per hour; each hour she picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, she finishes it and waits). She has h hours. Return the minimum k that lets her eat everything in time.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

For a fixed speed k, you can compute the hours needed: sum of ceil(pile / k).

Hint 2

If speed k works, every faster speed also works. "Works / doesn't work" flips exactly once as k grows.

Hint 3

Binary search k between 1 and max(piles) for the first speed that works.

The easy idea: "too slow / fast enough"

Line up every possible speed: 1, 2, 3, … max pile. They look like this:

speed: 1  2  3  4  5  6 ... 11
works: ✗  ✗  ✗  ✓  ✓  ✓ ... ✓

A row of ✗ followed by a row of ✓ is sorted. Binary search finds the first ✓ in O(log max) checks instead of trying every speed.

Solution

def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    def hours(k):
        return sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)   # ceil(p / k)

    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if hours(mid) <= h:
            hi = mid             # fast enough: try slower
        else:
            lo = mid + 1         # too slow
    return lo

print(min_eating_speed([3, 6, 7, 11], 8))         # 4
print(min_eating_speed([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 5))   # 30
print(min_eating_speed([30, 11, 23, 4, 20], 6))   # 23

(p + k - 1) // k is integer ceiling division without floats.

Complexity

  • Time O(n log m) for n piles and largest pile m: log m guesses, each costs O(n).
  • Space O(1).

The template: binary search on the answer

Whenever a problem asks for the minimum (or maximum) value that satisfies a condition, and the condition is monotonic (once true, stays true), use:

lo, hi = smallest possible answer, largest possible answer
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if works(mid): hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1

Similar problems

Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days, Split Array Largest Sum, Minimum Number of Days to Make Bouquets, Sqrt(x).

items.title: Valid Parentheses
items.excerpt: Are the brackets balanced and correctly nested? Push opening brackets on a stack; each closing bracket must match the top.
items.content:
The classic stack problem. Your code editor does this every time it highlights a matching bracket.

The problem

Given a string of ()[]{} characters, return True if every bracket is closed by the same type, in the correct order.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed. "Last in, first out" means a stack.

Hint 2

On an opening bracket, push it. On a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its partner.

Hint 3

At the end, the stack must be empty (nothing left open).

The easy idea: stacking plates

Every opening bracket is a plate put on a pile. A closing bracket must match the top plate, and then removes it. If it doesn't match, or there's no plate, the string is invalid. Play it, then try your own brackets:

Solution

def is_valid(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in pairs:                       # closing bracket
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
        else:
            stack.append(ch)                  # opening bracket
    return not stack

print(is_valid("()[]{}"))    # True
print(is_valid("{[()()]}"))  # True
print(is_valid("(]"))        # False
print(is_valid("([)]"))      # False
print(is_valid("(("))        # False
print(is_valid(")"))         # False

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(n) for the stack in the worst case.

Follow-ups

  • Only one bracket type? A counter is enough: +1 for (, −1 for ), never below 0, ending at 0.
  • Minimum additions to make it valid? Count unmatched opens and unmatched closes.
def min_add_to_make_valid(s):
    open_count = additions = 0
    for ch in s:
        if ch == "(":
            open_count += 1
        elif open_count:
            open_count -= 1
        else:
            additions += 1          # a ")" with nothing to match
    return additions + open_count

print(min_add_to_make_valid("())"))   # 1
print(min_add_to_make_valid("((("))   # 3

Want to practise under time pressure? Play Bracket Blitz in the Brain Games.

Similar problems

Generate Parentheses, Longest Valid Parentheses, Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses, Decode String.

Learn the pattern: Stacks.

items.title: Min Stack
items.excerpt: Design a stack that returns its minimum in O(1). Store the minimum-so-far alongside every item.
items.content:
A design question that tests whether you can trade a little memory for speed.

The problem

Design a stack with push(x), pop(), top() and get_min(), all in O(1).

Example

push(-2), push(0), push(-3)
get_min() → -3
pop()
top()     → 0
get_min() → -2

Hints

Hint 1

Scanning for the minimum is O(n). You need the answer ready at all times.

Hint 2

When you push x, the new minimum is min(x, current minimum). Store that together with x.

Hint 3

When you pop, the previous minimum is automatically back on top.

The easy idea: sticky notes

Each plate you add to the pile gets a sticky note saying "smallest plate at or below me". The top plate's note always has the answer. When you remove a plate, the note on the next plate is still correct, because it was written when that plate was on top.

push -2 → (-2, min -2)
push  0 → ( 0, min -2)
push -3 → (-3, min -3)   ← get_min() reads -3
pop     → back to ( 0, min -2)

Solution

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []                   # (value, min at or below)

    def push(self, x):
        current_min = min(x, self.items[-1][1]) if self.items else x
        self.items.append((x, current_min))

    def pop(self):
        self.items.pop()

    def top(self):
        return self.items[-1][0]

    def get_min(self):
        return self.items[-1][1]

s = MinStack()
s.push(-2)
s.push(0)
s.push(-3)
print(s.get_min())  # -3
s.pop()
print(s.top())      # 0
print(s.get_min())  # -2

Complexity

  • Every operation O(1) time.
  • O(n) space (each item stores one extra number).

Follow-up: save memory

Keep a second stack of minimums, pushing only when a new value is less than or equal to the current minimum. Pop from it only when the popped value equals its top. Same O(1) time; less memory when the minimum rarely changes.

Similar problems

Max Stack, Implement Queue using Stacks, Online Stock Span, Sliding Window Maximum.

Learn the pattern: Stacks.

items.title: Daily Temperatures
items.excerpt: How many days until a warmer day? A monotonic stack of waiting days answers it in one pass.
items.content:
The friendliest introduction to the monotonic stack: a stack that keeps its items in decreasing order.

The problem

Given daily temperatures, return a list where answer[i] is the number of days you must wait after day i for a warmer temperature, or 0 if none comes.

Example

[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73] → [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]

Hints

Hint 1

Brute force looks ahead from every day: O(n²).

Hint 2

Keep a stack of days still WAITING for a warmer day. Their temperatures are decreasing from bottom to top.

Hint 3

When a warm day arrives, it answers every waiting day on top of the stack that is colder.

Brute force, O(n²)

def daily_temps_slow(temps):
    out = [0] * len(temps)
    for i in range(len(temps)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(temps)):
            if temps[j] > temps[i]:
                out[i] = j - i
                break
    return out

print(daily_temps_slow([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]))  # [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]

The easy idea: a queue of short people

Picture people standing in a line, each waiting to see someone taller arrive. When a tall person shows up, everyone shorter at the back of the line gets their answer and leaves. The line always goes from tallest (front) to shortest (back). That's a monotonic stack. Watch it with "next greater element":

Solution

def daily_temperatures(temps):
    out = [0] * len(temps)
    waiting = []                         # indexes, temps decreasing
    for i, t in enumerate(temps):
        while waiting and temps[waiting[-1]] < t:
            j = waiting.pop()
            out[j] = i - j               # day j finally got a warmer day
        waiting.append(i)
    return out

print(daily_temperatures([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]))  # [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]
print(daily_temperatures([30, 40, 50, 60]))                  # [1, 1, 1, 0]
print(daily_temperatures([30, 20, 10]))                      # [0, 0, 0]

Store indexes on the stack, not temperatures: you need the index to compute the distance.

Complexity

  • Time O(n): each day is pushed once and popped at most once, even though there's a while inside a for.
  • Space O(n) for the stack.

Similar problems

Next Greater Element I and II, Online Stock Span, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Car Fleet.

Learn the pattern: Monotonic Stack.

items.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
items.excerpt: The biggest rectangle that fits under a bar chart. For each bar, find how far it can stretch left and right with a monotonic stack.
items.content:
A "hard" problem whose solution is a short loop once you see the trick.

The problem

heights[i] is a bar of width 1. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the histogram.

Examples

      #
    # #
    # #
    # #   #
#   # # # #
# # # # # #
2 1 5 6 2 3

Hints

Hint 1

Every rectangle's height equals its SHORTEST bar. So try each bar as "the shortest one".

Hint 2

For bar i as the shortest, the rectangle stretches left and right until a SHORTER bar blocks it.

Hint 3

Keep a stack of bars with increasing heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop: the popped bar's right blocker is the new bar, and its left blocker is the bar below it on the stack.

Brute force, O(n²)

def largest_rect_slow(heights):
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(heights)):
        low = heights[i]
        for j in range(i, len(heights)):
            low = min(low, heights[j])
            best = max(best, low * (j - i + 1))
    return best

print(largest_rect_slow([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))  # 10

The easy idea: how far can each bar stretch?

Take the bar of height 5 (index 2). Stretch it sideways: to the right it can cover index 3 (height 6 ≥ 5), but index 4 (height 2) blocks it. To the left, index 1 (height 1) blocks it immediately. Width 2, area 10.

The stack keeps bars in increasing height order. When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on top has just found its right blocker, so compute its area and pop it.

Solution

def largest_rectangle(heights):
    stack = []                                  # indexes, heights increasing
    best = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):       # 0 at the end flushes the stack
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1   # left blocker
            width = i - left - 1                # i is the right blocker
            best = max(best, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return best

print(largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))  # 10
print(largest_rectangle([2, 4]))              # 4
print(largest_rectangle([1, 1, 1, 1]))        # 4

The extra 0 at the end makes sure every bar is popped and measured.

Complexity

  • Time O(n): each bar is pushed and popped once.
  • Space O(n) for the stack.

Similar problems

Maximal Rectangle (apply this to each row of a 0/1 matrix), Trapping Rain Water, Daily Temperatures, Sum of Subarray Minimums.

Learn the pattern: Monotonic Stack.

items.title: Reverse Linked List
items.excerpt: Flip the direction of every arrow in a linked list with three pointers. Iterative and recursive versions.
items.content:
The most common linked list question. Practise it until you can write it with your eyes closed.

The problem

Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it and return the new head.

1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 becomes 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1.

Hints

Hint 1

Walk through the list and turn each node's next arrow around to point backwards.

Hint 2

Before turning an arrow, save where it pointed, or you'll lose the rest of the list.

Hint 3

Three variables: prev, cur and nxt.

The easy idea: turning around a conga line

People in a conga line each hold the shoulders of the person in front. To reverse it, go person by person: remember who was in front (nxt), turn around to hold the person behind (prev), then step forward. Watch the arrows flip:

Solution: iterative, O(1) space

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def reverse_list(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next       # 1. remember the rest
        cur.next = prev      # 2. flip the arrow
        prev = cur           # 3. move prev forward
        cur = nxt            # 4. move cur forward
    return prev              # prev is the new head

print(to_list(reverse_list(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))))  # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
print(to_list(reverse_list(build([1]))))              # [1]
print(to_list(reverse_list(None)))                    # []

Solution: recursive

Reverse the rest of the list, then hook the current node onto its end:

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def reverse_recursive(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head      # the next node now points back at me
    head.next = None
    return new_head

head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3)))
r = reverse_recursive(head)
print(r.val, r.next.val, r.next.next.val)  # 3 2 1

Complexity

Interviewers usually prefer the iterative version; be ready to write both.

Similar problems

Reverse Linked List II (only a section), Palindrome Linked List, Reverse Nodes in k-Group, Reorder List.

Learn the pattern: Linked Lists.

items.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
items.excerpt: Zip two sorted linked lists into one sorted list. The dummy node trick removes every special case.
items.content:
This problem introduces the dummy node, a trick that simplifies almost every linked list problem.

The problem

Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list, reusing the existing nodes, and return its head.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Compare the two front nodes; the smaller one goes next in the result.

Hint 2

Start with a fake "dummy" node so you never have to special-case the first node.

Hint 3

When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other list in one step.

The easy idea: merging two sorted queues

Two queues of people sorted by height merge into one door. Each time, the shorter of the two people at the front goes through. When one queue is empty, the rest of the other walks straight through. It's the merge step of merge sort.

The dummy node is like a doorman standing at the front of the new queue: you always have something to attach to, and at the end you return dummy.next.

Solution

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def merge_two(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b              # attach whatever is left
    return dummy.next

print(to_list(merge_two(build([1, 2, 4]), build([1, 3, 4]))))  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]
print(to_list(merge_two(build([]), build([]))))                # []
print(to_list(merge_two(build([]), build([0]))))               # [0]

Complexity

  • Time O(n + m), space O(1) (nodes are reused, only pointers change).

Recursive version

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def merge_rec(a, b):
    if not a or not b:
        return a or b
    if a.val <= b.val:
        a.next = merge_rec(a.next, b)
        return a
    b.next = merge_rec(a, b.next)
    return b

m = merge_rec(ListNode(1, ListNode(5)), ListNode(2))
print(m.val, m.next.val, m.next.next.val)  # 1 2 5

Elegant, but uses O(n + m) stack space.

Similar problems

Merge k Sorted Lists, Merge Sorted Array, Sort List (merge sort on a linked list), Add Two Numbers.

Learn the pattern: Linked Lists.

items.title: Linked List Cycle
items.excerpt: Does a linked list loop back on itself? A tortoise and a hare running at different speeds will meet if there's a loop.
items.content:
Floyd's "tortoise and hare" is one of the most elegant tricks in computer science.

The problem

Return True if the linked list contains a cycle (some node's next points back to an earlier node).

Examples

3 → 2 → 0 → -4
    ↑        |
    └────────┘      → True

1 → 2 → None        → False

Hints

Hint 1

Simple version: store every visited node in a set. Seeing one twice means a cycle. That's O(n) space.

Hint 2

For O(1) space: two pointers, one moving 1 step, one moving 2 steps.

Hint 3

If there's a cycle, the fast one laps the slow one and they meet. If not, fast reaches the end.

Solution 1: a set, O(n) space

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.next = val, None

def has_cycle_set(head):
    seen = set()
    while head:
        if head in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(head)
        head = head.next
    return False

a, b = ListNode(1), ListNode(2)
a.next, b.next = b, a
print(has_cycle_set(a))  # True

The easy idea: runners on a circular track

Two runners start together; one runs twice as fast. On a straight road, the fast one simply reaches the finish. On a circular track, the fast runner eventually catches up with the slow one from behind. Meeting = loop. Watch the pointers:

Solution 2: fast and slow pointers, O(1) space

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.next = val, None

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False

nodes = [ListNode(v) for v in [3, 2, 0, -4]]
for x, y in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
    x.next = y
print(has_cycle(nodes[0]))   # False
nodes[-1].next = nodes[1]    # -4 points back to 2
print(has_cycle(nodes[0]))   # True
print(has_cycle(None))       # False

Complexity

  • Time O(n): once both are inside the loop, the gap shrinks by 1 each step.
  • Space O(1).

Follow-up: where does the cycle start?

After they meet, move one pointer back to the head. Move both one step at a time; they meet exactly at the cycle's start.

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.next = val, None

def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            slow = head
            while slow is not fast:
                slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next
            return slow
    return None

nodes = [ListNode(v) for v in [3, 2, 0, -4]]
for x, y in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
    x.next = y
nodes[-1].next = nodes[1]
print(cycle_start(nodes[0]).val)  # 2

Similar problems

Linked List Cycle II, Middle of the Linked List, Happy Number, Find the Duplicate Number.

Learn the pattern: Fast and Slow Pointers.

items.title: LRU Cache
items.excerpt: Design a cache that throws out the least recently used item when full, with O(1) get and put. A hash map plus an ordered list.
items.content:
One of the most-asked design questions. It combines a hash map (fast lookup) with an ordering structure (who was used last).

The problem

Build LRUCache(capacity) with:

  • get(key): return the value, or -1 if missing. Using a key makes it "recently used".
  • put(key, value): insert or update. If the cache is over capacity, remove the least recently used key.

Both must be O(1).

Example

cache = LRUCache(2)
put(1, 1); put(2, 2)
get(1)    → 1     (1 is now the most recent)
put(3, 3)         (full: evict 2, the least recent)
get(2)    → -1
put(4, 4)         (evict 1)
get(1)    → -1
get(3)    → 3
get(4)    → 4

Hints

Hint 1

A dictionary gives O(1) lookup, but doesn't know which key is oldest.

Hint 2

You need an order you can update in O(1): move an item to the "recent" end, remove from the "old" end.

Hint 3

A doubly linked list (or Python's OrderedDict, which is built on one) does exactly that.

The easy idea: a pile of books on your desk

Every time you use a book, you put it on top of the pile. When the desk is full, the book at the bottom (unused for longest) goes back to the shelf. The dictionary tells you instantly where each book is in the pile.

Solution 1: OrderedDict (great to mention first)

from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.data = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return -1
        self.data.move_to_end(key)          # now most recent
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)   # remove least recent

cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 1)
cache.put(2, 2)
print(cache.get(1))  # 1
cache.put(3, 3)
print(cache.get(2))  # -1
cache.put(4, 4)
print(cache.get(1), cache.get(3), cache.get(4))  # -1 3 4

Solution 2: build it yourself (what interviewers often want)

A dictionary maps keys to nodes of a doubly linked list. Two dummy nodes, head (oldest side) and tail (newest side), remove all special cases.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key, self.val = key, val
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _remove(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def _add_newest(self, node):
        node.prev, node.next = self.tail.prev, self.tail
        self.tail.prev.next = node
        self.tail.prev = node

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.map:
            return -1
        node = self.map[key]
        self._remove(node)
        self._add_newest(node)
        return node.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            self._remove(self.map[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = node
        self._add_newest(node)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            oldest = self.head.next
            self._remove(oldest)
            del self.map[oldest.key]

c = LRU(2)
c.put(1, 1)
c.put(2, 2)
print(c.get(1))  # 1
c.put(3, 3)
print(c.get(2))  # -1
print(c.get(3))  # 3

The node stores its key so that when it's evicted from the list, you can also delete it from the dictionary.

Complexity

  • get and put: O(1).
  • Space: O(capacity).

Similar problems

LFU Cache, Design Twitter, Time Based Key-Value Store, Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).

Learn the patterns: Hashing and Linked Lists.

items.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
items.excerpt: How many levels does a tree have? A three-line recursive answer, plus the level-by-level BFS version.
items.content:
The "hello world" of tree recursion: trust that the recursive call solves the smaller problem.

The problem

Return the maximum depth of a binary tree: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Example

    3
   / \
  9  20
     / \
    15   7

Depth = 3 (3 → 20 → 15).

Hints

Hint 1

The depth of a tree = 1 + the deeper of its two subtrees.

Hint 2

An empty tree has depth 0. That's the base case.

The easy idea: ask your children

Every node asks its two children: "How deep are you?" Each child asks its own children, and so on. Leaves answer 1. Each node replies "1 + the bigger answer I got". The root's reply is the answer. Watch a recursive traversal visit the nodes:

Solution: recursion (DFS)

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def max_depth(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    return 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right))

root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(max_depth(root))          # 3
print(max_depth(None))          # 0
print(max_depth(TreeNode(1)))   # 1

Solution: level by level (BFS)

Count how many levels a breadth-first search processes:

from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def max_depth_bfs(root):
    if not root:
        return 0
    q, depth = deque([root]), 0
    while q:
        depth += 1
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
    return depth

root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(max_depth_bfs(root))  # 3

Complexity

  • Time O(n): every node is visited once.
  • Space O(h) for recursion, where h is the height (O(n) for a skewed tree, O(log n) for a balanced one).

The template you just learned

def solve(node):
    if node is None: return BASE
    left = solve(node.left)
    right = solve(node.right)
    return COMBINE(node, left, right)

Minimum depth, tree size, path sums, balanced check and diameter all use it.

items.title: Invert Binary Tree
items.excerpt: Mirror a binary tree by swapping every node's left and right children. Short, famous and a perfect recursion warm-up.
items.content:
Made famous by a tweet from a well-known developer who was asked it in an interview. It's short, but it checks that you really understand recursion.

The problem

Mirror a binary tree: every node's left and right children swap places. Return the root.

     4                4
   /   \            /   \
  2     7    →     7     2
 / \   / \        / \   / \
1   3 6   9      9   6 3   1

Hints

Hint 1

At each node, swap its two children.

Hint 2

Then do the same for both subtrees. The order (swap first or recurse first) doesn't matter.

The easy idea: a mirror

Hold the tree up to a mirror. Every left becomes right and every right becomes left, at every level. So: swap my two children, then ask each child to mirror itself.

Solution: recursion

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def invert(root):
    if root:
        root.left, root.right = invert(root.right), invert(root.left)
    return root

def level_values(root):
    out, level = [], [root] if root else []
    while level:
        out += [n.val for n in level]
        level = [c for n in level for c in (n.left, n.right) if c]
    return out

root = TreeNode(4, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3)), TreeNode(7, TreeNode(6), TreeNode(9)))
print(level_values(invert(root)))  # [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]
print(invert(None))                # None

Solution: iterative with a queue

from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def invert_iterative(root):
    q = deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        node.left, node.right = node.right, node.left
        for child in (node.left, node.right):
            if child:
                q.append(child)
    return root

r = invert_iterative(TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2), TreeNode(3)))
print(r.left.val, r.right.val)  # 3 2

Complexity

  • Time O(n): each node is swapped once.
  • Space O(h) for recursion, or O(w) for the queue (w = widest level).

Similar problems

Symmetric Tree (is a tree its own mirror?), Same Tree, Flip Equivalent Binary Trees, Merge Two Binary Trees.

items.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
items.excerpt: Return the tree's values level by level. BFS with a queue, processing one whole level per loop.
items.content:
Breadth-first search on a tree, with one twist: group the values by level.

The problem

Return the node values level by level, left to right, as a list of lists.

    3
   / \
  9  20
     / \
    15   7

Answer: [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]

Hints

Hint 1

A queue visits nodes in order of their distance from the root.

Hint 2

At the start of each loop, the queue holds exactly one full level. Its length tells you how many nodes to take.

The easy idea: floors of a building

Visit the building floor by floor. On each floor, greet everyone from left to right, and write down who lives on the floor below them. When the floor is done, move to the list you just wrote. Watch the queue:

Solution

from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def level_order(root):
    if not root:
        return []
    out, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):          # exactly this level's nodes
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

root = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
print(level_order(root))  # [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]
print(level_order(None))  # []

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(w) where w is the widest level (up to n/2 for a full tree).

Easy variations (change one line)

from collections import deque

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def levels(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        out.append([n.val for n in q])
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            n = q.popleft()
            q.extend(c for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)
    return out

root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(4)), TreeNode(3, None, TreeNode(5)))
lv = levels(root)
print(lv)                                                  # [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5]]
print([lvl[-1] for lvl in lv])                             # [1, 3, 5]
print([l if i % 2 == 0 else l[::-1] for i, l in enumerate(lv)])  # [[1], [3, 2], [4, 5]]
print([sum(l) / len(l) for l in lv])                       # [1.0, 2.5, 4.5]
  • Right side view: the last value of each level.
  • Zigzag order: reverse every other level.
  • Average of levels: sum ÷ count per level.

items.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
items.excerpt: Is a tree a valid BST? Checking only parent and child is a trap; pass an allowed range down the tree instead.
items.content:
A problem with a famous trap. Checking that each node is bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child is not enough.

The problem

Return True if the tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are bigger.

Examples

    2              5
   / \            / \
  1   3          1   6
                    / \
 → True            3   7     → False

The second tree fails: 3 sits in the right subtree of 5, so it must be bigger than 5.

Hints

Hint 1

Each node must lie in a RANGE determined by all its ancestors, not just its parent.

Hint 2

Going left, the upper limit becomes the parent's value. Going right, the lower limit becomes the parent's value.

Hint 3

Alternative: an inorder traversal of a BST is strictly increasing.

The trap

In the second tree, every parent-child pair looks fine: 1 < 5 < 6, and 3 < 6 < 7. Yet 3 is in the right subtree of 5, so it must be bigger than 5. Comparing only with the parent misses this; you need to check each node against all its ancestors.

The easy idea: a narrowing window

The root may be anything: range (−∞, +∞). Step left from a node with value v: everything there must be below v. Step right: everything must be above v. Each step narrows the window. Watch a BST search narrow the range the same way:

Solution: pass the range down

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def is_valid_bst(root, low=float("-inf"), high=float("inf")):
    if root is None:
        return True
    if not (low < root.val < high):
        return False
    return (is_valid_bst(root.left, low, root.val) and
            is_valid_bst(root.right, root.val, high))

print(is_valid_bst(TreeNode(2, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(3))))       # True
bad = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(6, TreeNode(3), TreeNode(7)))
print(is_valid_bst(bad))                                         # False
print(is_valid_bst(TreeNode(2, TreeNode(2))))                    # False

Solution: inorder must increase

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def is_valid_inorder(root):
    prev = float("-inf")
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        if node.val <= prev:
            return False
        prev = node.val
        node = node.right
    return True

print(is_valid_inorder(TreeNode(8, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(6)), TreeNode(10))))  # True

Complexity

  • Time O(n), space O(h).

Similar problems

Kth Smallest Element in a BST, Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST, Recover Binary Search Tree, Convert Sorted Array to BST.

items.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
items.excerpt: Find the deepest node that has both p and q below it. One elegant recursion that reports what it found upwards.
items.content:
The "family tree" question: what's the closest shared ancestor of two people?

The problem

Given a binary tree and two nodes p and q in it, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants. A node counts as a descendant of itself.

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4

Hints

Hint 1

Ask each subtree: "Did you find p or q?"

Hint 2

If the left subtree found one and the right subtree found the other, the current node is the answer.

Hint 3

If only one side found something, pass that result upwards.

The easy idea: reporting up the chain

Every node asks both children: "Did you see p or q down there?" Each child reports back the node it found (or nothing).

  • If a node is p or q, it reports itself.
  • If both children report something, p and q are on different sides: I'm the lowest common ancestor.
  • If only one child reports, pass that report up.

Solution

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def lca(root, p, q):
    if root is None or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    left = lca(root.left, p, q)
    right = lca(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return root              # p and q are on different sides
    return left or right         # pass up whatever was found

n7, n4 = TreeNode(7), TreeNode(4)
n2 = TreeNode(2, n7, n4)
n5 = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(6), n2)
n1 = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(0), TreeNode(8))
root = TreeNode(3, n5, n1)
print(lca(root, n5, n1).val)  # 3
print(lca(root, n5, n4).val)  # 5
print(lca(root, n7, n4).val)  # 2

Complexity

  • Time O(n): each node is visited once.
  • Space O(h) for the recursion.

The BST shortcut

In a binary search tree, values guide you: if both p and q are smaller than the node, go left; if both are bigger, go right; otherwise the current node is where they split.

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def lca_bst(root, p, q):
    while root:
        if p < root.val and q < root.val:
            root = root.left
        elif p > root.val and q > root.val:
            root = root.right
        else:
            return root

bst = TreeNode(6, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(0), TreeNode(4)), TreeNode(8, TreeNode(7), TreeNode(9)))
print(lca_bst(bst, 2, 8).val)  # 6
print(lca_bst(bst, 2, 4).val)  # 2

O(h) time, O(1) space.

Similar problems

items.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
items.excerpt: Find the k-th largest number without sorting everything. A min-heap of size k, plus quickselect for an average O(n).
items.content:
A favourite because it has three good answers, each with a different trade-off.

The problem

Return the k-th largest element in nums (in sorted order, not the k-th distinct).

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Sorting works in O(n log n). Can you avoid sorting everything?

Hint 2

Keep only the k largest numbers seen so far in a MIN-heap. The smallest of them (the top) is the k-th largest.

Hint 3

Quickselect partitions like quicksort but only recurses into one side: O(n) on average.

Solution 1: sort, O(n log n)

def kth_largest_sort(nums, k):
    return sorted(nums, reverse=True)[k - 1]

print(kth_largest_sort([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2))  # 5

The easy idea: a VIP list with k seats

A club has only k VIP seats. Each new number arrives; if the seats are full and the newcomer beats the weakest VIP, the weakest leaves. At the end, the weakest VIP is the k-th largest overall. A min-heap keeps "the weakest VIP" at the top. Watch a heap organise itself:

Solution 2: min-heap of size k, O(n log k)

import heapq

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    heap = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(heap, x)
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)          # the weakest VIP leaves
    return heap[0]

print(kth_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2))           # 5
print(kth_largest([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4))  # 4

Works on an endless stream of numbers too, using only O(k) memory.

Solution 3: quickselect, O(n) average

Pick a pivot, split into bigger, equal and smaller groups, and continue only in the group that contains the answer.

import random

def quickselect(nums, k):
    pivot = random.choice(nums)
    bigger = [x for x in nums if x > pivot]
    equal = [x for x in nums if x == pivot]
    smaller = [x for x in nums if x < pivot]
    if k <= len(bigger):
        return quickselect(bigger, k)
    if k <= len(bigger) + len(equal):
        return pivot
    return quickselect(smaller, k - len(bigger) - len(equal))

print(quickselect([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2))           # 5
print(quickselect([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4))  # 4

Complexity

Similar problems

items.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
items.excerpt: Merge many sorted linked lists into one. A min-heap always tells you which list has the next smallest value.
items.content:
Merging 2 sorted lists is easy. With k lists, a heap decides which list goes next.

The problem

Given k sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list.

Example

1 → 4 → 5
1 → 3 → 4
2 → 6
merged: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4 → 5 → 6

Hints

Hint 1

At each step, the next node is the smallest among the k current heads.

Hint 2

Finding the minimum of k heads by scanning costs O(k). A min-heap does it in O(log k).

Hint 3

Put (value, list index, node) in the heap; the index breaks ties so nodes are never compared.

The easy idea: k checkout lines

Several sorted queues of people (shortest first) merge into one door. A supervisor watches only the front person of every queue and always lets the shortest of them through; then that queue's next person steps up. A min-heap is the supervisor.

Solution

import heapq

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val, self.next = val, next

def build(values):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(values):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    while head:
        out.append(head.val)
        head = head.next
    return out

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    dummy = tail = ListNode(0)
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        tail.next = node
        tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

lists = [build([1, 4, 5]), build([1, 3, 4]), build([2, 6])]
print(to_list(merge_k_lists(lists)))  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]
print(to_list(merge_k_lists([])))     # []

Alternative: divide and conquer

Merge the lists in pairs (like merge sort): k lists → k/2 → k/4 → … → 1. Same O(N log k) time, no heap needed.

def merge_two(a, b):
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            out.append(a[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(b[j]); j += 1
    return out + a[i:] + b[j:]

def merge_k_pairs(lists):
    if not lists:
        return []
    while len(lists) > 1:
        lists = [merge_two(lists[i], lists[i + 1]) if i + 1 < len(lists) else lists[i]
                 for i in range(0, len(lists), 2)]
    return lists[0]

print(merge_k_pairs([[1, 4, 5], [1, 3, 4], [2, 6]]))  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]

Complexity

  • Time O(N log k) for N total nodes: each node is pushed and popped once, each heap operation is O(log k).
  • Space O(k) for the heap.

Merging lists one by one into a growing result is O(N · k): mention why the heap is better.

Similar problems

items.title: Number of Islands
items.excerpt: Count groups of connected land in a grid. Each time you step on new land, count it and flood fill the whole island.
items.content:
Possibly the most-asked graph question of all time, and it doesn't even look like a graph.

The problem

A grid has "1" (land) and "0" (water). An island is land connected up, down, left or right. Count the islands.

Example

1 1 0 0 0
1 1 0 1 0
0 0 1 0 0
0 0 0 1 1

Answer: 4

Hints

Hint 1

Treat each land cell as a node connected to its land neighbours.

Hint 2

Scan the grid. When you find land you haven't visited, that's a new island.

Hint 3

Immediately "sink" the whole island with DFS or BFS so its other cells aren't counted again.

The easy idea: the paint bucket

Scan the map like reading a book. Whenever you find unpainted land, add 1 to the counter and use the paint bucket tool: it spreads to every connected land cell and paints them. Painted land is never counted again. Watch it:

Solution: DFS

def num_islands(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

    def sink(r, c):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols or grid[r][c] != "1":
            return
        grid[r][c] = "0"
        sink(r + 1, c); sink(r - 1, c); sink(r, c + 1); sink(r, c - 1)

    count = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1
                sink(r, c)
    return count

grid = [list("11000"), list("11010"), list("00100"), list("00011")]
print(num_islands(grid))  # 4
print(num_islands([list("11110"), list("11010"), list("11000"), list("00000")]))  # 1

Solution: BFS (no recursion limit)

from collections import deque

def num_islands_bfs(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    seen, count = set(), 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1" and (r, c) not in seen:
                count += 1
                seen.add((r, c))
                q = deque([(r, c)])
                while q:
                    cr, cc = q.popleft()
                    for nr, nc in ((cr + 1, cc), (cr - 1, cc), (cr, cc + 1), (cr, cc - 1)):
                        if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] == "1" and (nr, nc) not in seen:
                            seen.add((nr, nc))
                            q.append((nr, nc))
    return count

print(num_islands_bfs(["11000", "11010", "00100", "00011"]))  # 4

This version doesn't modify the grid (uses a seen set), a common follow-up request.

Complexity

  • Time O(rows × cols), space O(rows × cols) in the worst case (all land).

Follow-ups

  • Diagonals count too? Add the 4 diagonal directions.
  • Largest island area? Make the fill return its size.
  • Islands added one at a time? Union-find (Number of Islands II).

Similar problems

Max Area of Island, Rotting Oranges, Surrounded Regions, Number of Closed Islands, Pacific Atlantic Water Flow.

items.title: Rotting Oranges
items.excerpt: How many minutes until every orange rots? Multi-source BFS where each level of the queue is one minute.
items.content:
This problem teaches multi-source BFS: start the search from many places at once.

The problem

In a grid, 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange and 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, each rotten orange rots its fresh neighbours (up, down, left, right). Return the minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that's impossible.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

The rot spreads in waves, like ripples. Waves = BFS levels.

Hint 2

Put ALL rotten oranges in the queue at the start, not just one.

Hint 3

Count fresh oranges first. At the end, if any are left, return -1.

The easy idea: ripples from many stones

Throw several stones into a pond at once. Ripples spread from all of them simultaneously, one ring per second. The time until the whole pond is rippled is the number of rings. Each rotten orange is a stone; each BFS level is one minute.

minute 0    minute 1    minute 2    minute 3    minute 4
2 1 1       2 2 1       2 2 2       2 2 2       2 2 2
1 1 0       2 1 0       2 2 0       2 2 0       2 2 0
0 1 1       0 1 1       0 1 1       0 2 1       0 2 2

Solution

from collections import deque

def oranges_rotting(grid):
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    q, fresh = deque(), 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == 2:
                q.append((r, c))
            elif grid[r][c] == 1:
                fresh += 1
    minutes = 0
    while q and fresh:
        for _ in range(len(q)):                 # one minute
            r, c = q.popleft()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                    grid[nr][nc] = 2
                    fresh -= 1
                    q.append((nr, nc))
        minutes += 1
    return minutes if fresh == 0 else -1

print(oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [0, 1, 1]]))  # 4
print(oranges_rotting([[2, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1]]))  # -1
print(oranges_rotting([[0, 2]]))                           # 0

The while q and fresh condition stops as soon as nothing fresh is left, so we don't count an extra empty minute.

Complexity

  • Time O(rows × cols), space O(rows × cols) for the queue.

Similar problems

Walls and Gates, 01 Matrix (distance to nearest 0), As Far from Land as Possible, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix.

items.title: Course Schedule
items.excerpt: Can you finish every course given the prerequisites? Only if there's no cycle. Kahn's algorithm takes courses as soon as they're unlocked.
items.content:
A dependency problem in disguise: it's really asking "does this directed graph have a cycle?"

The problem

There are n courses labelled 0 to n−1. prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take b before a. Return True if you can finish all courses.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Draw an arrow b → a for each pair. You can finish everything only if the arrows never form a loop.

Hint 2

Count how many prerequisites each course still needs (its in-degree). Courses needing 0 can be taken right now.

Hint 3

Taking a course unlocks others: decrease their counts. If you manage to take all n courses, the answer is True.

The easy idea: unlocking levels in a game

In a game, some levels unlock only after others are beaten. Start with every level that's already unlocked. Each time you beat one, cross it off the requirements of the levels it unlocks. If you eventually beat every level, there was no impossible loop. Watch it:

Solution: Kahn's algorithm

from collections import deque

def can_finish(n, prerequisites):
    unlocks = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    needs = [0] * n
    for course, req in prerequisites:
        unlocks[req].append(course)
        needs[course] += 1
    q = deque(c for c in range(n) if needs[c] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in unlocks[c]:
            needs[nxt] -= 1
            if needs[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return taken == n

print(can_finish(2, [[1, 0]]))                          # True
print(can_finish(2, [[1, 0], [0, 1]]))                  # False
print(can_finish(4, [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]))  # True

Course Schedule II: return the order

Same code; collect the courses as you take them:

from collections import deque

def find_order(n, prerequisites):
    unlocks = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    needs = [0] * n
    for course, req in prerequisites:
        unlocks[req].append(course)
        needs[course] += 1
    q = deque(c for c in range(n) if needs[c] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        c = q.popleft()
        order.append(c)
        for nxt in unlocks[c]:
            needs[nxt] -= 1
            if needs[nxt] == 0:
                q.append(nxt)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

print(find_order(4, [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]))  # [0, 1, 2, 3]
print(find_order(2, [[1, 0], [0, 1]]))                  # []

Complexity

  • Time O(V + E) for V courses and E prerequisites.
  • Space O(V + E) for the graph.

Watch out

The pair [a, b] means b first. Getting the arrow direction backwards is the most common bug.

Similar problems

Course Schedule II, Alien Dictionary, Minimum Height Trees, Parallel Courses, Find All Possible Recipes.

items.title: Network Delay Time
items.excerpt: How long until a signal reaches every computer? Dijkstra's shortest paths, then take the slowest arrival.
items.content:
The friendliest Dijkstra problem: compute all shortest paths from one source, then read off the biggest.

The problem

times[i] = [u, v, w] means a signal from node u reaches node v after w time units (one-way). Nodes are labelled 1 to n. A signal is sent from node k. Return how long until all nodes receive it, or -1 if some never do.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Every node receives the signal at its SHORTEST distance from k.

Hint 2

Weighted edges with non-negative weights → Dijkstra with a min-heap.

Hint 3

The answer is the largest of those shortest distances (if every node was reached).

The easy idea: rumour spreading

A rumour starts in one town. It always reaches the nearest town that hasn't heard it yet next. Once a town hears it, that time is final. The rumour is "complete" when the last town hears it. A heap keeps the next-closest town ready. Watch Dijkstra:

Solution

import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

def network_delay_time(times, n, k):
    graph = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v, w in times:
        graph[u].append((v, w))
    arrived = {}                          # node -> final time
    heap = [(0, k)]
    while heap:
        t, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if node in arrived:
            continue                      # already reached faster
        arrived[node] = t
        for nb, w in graph[node]:
            if nb not in arrived:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (t + w, nb))
    return max(arrived.values()) if len(arrived) == n else -1

print(network_delay_time([[2, 1, 1], [2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1]], 4, 2))  # 2
print(network_delay_time([[1, 2, 1]], 2, 1))                        # 1
print(network_delay_time([[1, 2, 1]], 2, 2))                        # -1
print(network_delay_time([[1, 2, 4], [1, 3, 1], [3, 2, 1]], 3, 1))  # 2

The last example shows why plain BFS fails: the direct edge 1 → 2 costs 4, but 1 → 3 → 2 costs only 2.

Complexity

  • Time O(E log V) with a heap.
  • Space O(V + E).

Similar problems

Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, Path With Minimum Effort, Path with Maximum Probability, Swim in Rising Water.

items.title: Word Ladder
items.excerpt: Change one letter at a time to turn one word into another. Words are nodes, one-letter changes are edges, and BFS finds the shortest ladder.
items.content:
There's no graph in the input, but the moment you see "fewest steps", think BFS and build the graph yourself.

The problem

Transform begin into end by changing one letter at a time; every intermediate word must be in word_list. Return the number of words in the shortest such sequence (including both ends), or 0 if impossible.

Example

begin = "hit", end = "cog", word_list = ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot", "log", "cog"]

hit → hot → dot → dog → cog → 5

Hints

Hint 1

Each word is a node. Two words are connected if they differ by exactly one letter.

Hint 2

"Shortest sequence" in an unweighted graph → BFS.

Hint 3

To find neighbours fast, try changing each position to every letter a–z and check the set of words.

The easy idea: a game of stepping stones

Each valid word is a stepping stone. From a stone you can jump to any stone that differs by one letter. BFS explores all stones 1 jump away, then 2 jumps, and so on; the first time it lands on the end word, that's the fewest jumps. Watch BFS spread in waves on a small graph:

Solution

from collections import deque
from string import ascii_lowercase

def ladder_length(begin, end, word_list):
    words = set(word_list)
    if end not in words:
        return 0
    q = deque([(begin, 1)])
    seen = {begin}
    while q:
        word, steps = q.popleft()
        if word == end:
            return steps
        for i in range(len(word)):
            for ch in ascii_lowercase:
                nxt = word[:i] + ch + word[i + 1:]
                if nxt in words and nxt not in seen:
                    seen.add(nxt)
                    q.append((nxt, steps + 1))
    return 0

words = ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot", "log", "cog"]
print(ladder_length("hit", "cog", words))                         # 5
print(ladder_length("hit", "cog", ["hot", "dot", "dog", "lot", "log"]))  # 0

Complexity

  • Time O(N · L · 26) for N words of length L (each word tries L × 26 changes; building each new string costs O(L) more).
  • Space O(N) for the queue and the seen set.

Speed-up: bidirectional BFS

Search from both ends at once and stop when the two searches meet. Each side only has to go half as deep, which is dramatically faster on big dictionaries, a great follow-up to mention.

Similar problems

Word Ladder II (return all shortest ladders), Minimum Genetic Mutation, Open the Lock, Shortest Path in Binary Matrix.
